verdict.summary: gen_hash splits large hash literals to keep both the codegen value-stack pointer and the OP_HASH/OP_HASHADD element-count operands bounded. The attacker-controlled input (element count of a hash literal compiled from untrusted source) is checked on every loop iteration by 'if (val && cursp() >= slimit)' with slimit in {GEN_VAL_STACK_MAX, INT16_MAX}, which flushes accumulated pairs and resets len before len can approach a 16-bit operand boundary; per-element pushes (two per pair) keep len <= ~(slimit+1)/2 <= ~16384. Stack accounting was simulated at boundary cases (empty hash, exactly-at-limit, one-past-limit, kwrest-first, consecutive kwrest, mixed with intermediate flushes) and pop_n(len*2), pop_n(len*2+1), and the update-branch pop() exactly balance every path. No memory-corruption, operand-truncation, underflow, or amplification trigger could be instantiated; the only dereference precondition (parser cons-structure at nint(tree->car->car->car)) is not violable by any statement in this code. Not vulnerable.

assumptions: genop_2 is assumed to take 16-bit operands (uint16_t) as in the mruby compiler; this helper is not shown, but even if operands were wider, the in-loop flush at 'if (val && cursp() >= slimit)' bounds len by the code's own logic, so no sink depends on the assumption for safety.
The parser is assumed to guarantee the cons-cell shape dereferenced at nint(tree->car->car->car) (line 9) and non-NULL car chains; this guarantee cannot be quoted from the given code.

The constants GEN_VAL_STACK_MAX and GEN_LIT_ARY_MAX are assumed to be within ranges such that slimit (at most INT16_MAX) keeps the value stack and any downstream 16-bit stack-size field safe; their definitions are not shown.

codegen(s, expr, val) is assumed to leave exactly one stack value when val is true, as per the compiler's internal contract; this code's pop_n counts (len*2, len*2+1) are built on it and were verified self-consistent.
The 'limit' parameter is unused anywhere in the body; it has no data flow and no security effect.
limitations: A NULL dereference at tree->car->car->car (line 9) would require the in-process parser to emit a malformed hash item; no statement in this code can produce that, so the trigger is speculative (contract violation by a callee not shown).

A crash of the compiler process while compiling attacker-supplied source of the party's own choosing is an equal-privilege robustness issue per the impact model, not a vulnerability; no disclosure, corruption, or amplification was instantiated.
Resource use is linear in input size (one loop iteration and O(1) bytecode per element); no superlinear or unbounded amplification exists in this function.

verdict.summary: vidioc_querycap passes the device's externally set card label, dev->card_label, directly as the snprintf format string: `snprintf(cap->card, labellen, dev->card_label);`. No statement in this code sanitizes or wraps the label in a literal format ("%s"), so any conversion specifier planted in the label (e.g. %s, %p) makes the kernel's vsnprintf consume nonexistent varargs, dereferencing garbage pointers and copying arbitrary kernel memory into cap->card, which the V4L2 ioctl core then copies back to the unprivileged caller (kernel info disclosure) or faults the kernel (DoS). The labellen bound protects only the destination size, not the format semantics.

evidence.reason: Format string injection (CWE-134): dev->card_label, an externally configurable device label whose content this code never validates, is used as the snprintf format argument instead of a literal. Trigger instantiated: label = "%s%s%s" → labellen = min(32,32) = 32 → snprintf processes %s conversions against an empty vararg list, dereferencing garbage pointers into cap->card, which is then copied back to the unprivileged ioctl caller (kernel memory disclosure) or oopses the kernel (DoS).

Origin of the tainted value: dev->card_label arrives inside the device structure retrieved from the file; its label content crosses a trust boundary (set by a different party than the process issuing QUERYCAP) and no statement between this line and the sink at line 14 constrains it.

assumptions: cap is a kernel-allocated v4l2_capability that the V4L2 ioctl core copies back to the calling userspace process after this handler returns 0; this copy-back is what turns a poisoned cap->card into a disclosure.

dev->card_label content originates from driver configuration not shown in this snippet (module parameter / device-creation config); the code given contains no validation of that content, so per guard anchoring it is treated as attacker-influenced data reaching the format sink.
Modern kernel printf no longer supports %n, so the concrete impact vectors are %s/%p-style conversions (garbage-pointer dereference, disclosure, kernel oops) rather than %n writes.
sizeof(cap->card) and sizeof(dev->card_label) are both 32 per the kernel UAPI and driver struct; labellen therefore equals 32 in practice, but the min() computation is safe for any relative sizes.
limitations: labellen (lines 5-7) computes min(sizeof(cap->card), sizeof(dev->card_label)), which correctly bounds the destination; no CWE-131 off-by-one exists at the boundary sizes (equal, smaller label buffer, smaller card buffer all tested safe).

A NULL return from video_get_drvdata(dev->vdev) would cause a NULL dereference at lines 9-10, but drvadata is set at device registration by driver-internal statements not shown, and no attacker path in this code can unset it; classified as a contract question, not a vulnerability.
strlcpy (line 13) is deprecated in current kernels (CWE-676 family) but is used with a literal source and correct size here; no defect instantiated.

If the only party able to set the label were the identical privileged operator running the process (single-user, equal privilege for both label planting and QUERYCAP), the crash-only outcome would reduce to a robustness bug; the vulnerability finding rests on the label originator and the ioctl caller being distinct parties.

verdict.summary: GetEXIFProperty parses attacker-controlled EXIF profile bytes, but every sink is guarded on every path by quoted, boundary-correct checks: entry reads by 'if (q > (exif+length-12)) break;', value offsets by the three dir_offset checks, stack pushes by 'level < (MaxDirectoryStack-2)' (max index 14 of 16), the next-IFD read by an explicit end-check, and the EXIFMultipleValues format loop by the 'length=MaxTextExtent-1' clamp. No trigger simulation reaches an out-of-bounds access, overflow, unbounded push, or amplification with concrete values, so the code is not vulnerable as written.

assumptions: AcquireString(property) allocates strlen(property)+MagickPathExtent (>= MaxTextExtent) per the MagickCore API; 'FormatLocaleString(key,MaxTextExtent,...)' after 'key=AcquireString(property);' is safe only under this contract, which is not shown in the given code.

FormatLocaleString behaves like vsnprintf (returns chars that would be written, never negative for the fixed numeric formats used); ReadPropertyByte/Short/Long read 1/2/4 bytes with the documented endianness and sign extension; MaxTextExtent is at least 2.

GetImageProfile/GetStringInfoDatum/GetStringInfoLength return a buffer whose length matches the profile; the header-scan loop 'while (length != 0)' assumes ReadPropertyByte advances exif and decrements length atomically.
limitations: On a 32-bit-only build, '(size_t) components*tag_bytes[format]' could wrap, but the wrapped value is still either caught by 'number_bytes < components' or rejected by '((size_t) dir_offset+number_bytes) > length' before any out-of-bounds access; the code declares ssize_t/size_t and the wrap is not exercised as written.

If FormatLocaleString could return a negative value, 'length' in EXIFMultipleValues could underflow and write at buffer-1; the fixed formats ('%.20g','%hd','%hu','%f') cannot produce a negative return, so the trigger is speculative.

The duplicate-tag check compares 'directory_stack[i].directory == (exif+tag_offset1)' instead of the newly pushed 'exif+offset', so genuine duplicate directories are not always detected; however the entry-level dedup 'if (GetValueFromSplayTree(exif_resources,q) == q) break;' bounds all re-processing, leaving no memory-safety or amplification consequence.
Repeated processing of the same directory across do-while iterations is bounded by the splay-tree dedup and the level cap; no infinite loop was instantiated.

verdict.summary: mrb_ary_shift_m fully validates the script-controlled shift count before any sink: negative n raises (verbatim guard: if (n < 0) mrb_raise(mrb, E_ARGUMENT_ERROR, "negative array shift");), oversized n is clamped (if (n > len) n = len;), and zero-length cases return early (if (len == 0 || n == 0) return mrb_ary_new(mrb);). After these guards n is in [1, len] on every path, so mrb_ary_new_from_values, the shared pointer/len adjustment, the in-place copy loop, and ARY_SET_LEN all operate within the array's own bounds. ary_modify_check runs before all mutation, blocking frozen receivers. The only deviation found ([].shift(-1) returning [] instead of ArgumentError) reaches no memory, injection, or authz sink and is a robustness issue only.

assumptions: mrb_get_args with the "i" specifier raises (RangeError/TypeError) for integers outside mrb_int range or non-integer classes, so n always fits the signed mrb_int type.

ARY_LEN, ARY_PTR, ARY_SET_LEN, and ARY_SHARED_P are assumed to read/write the same header union fields this code mutates, and heap.len is the shared array's view length; these macros are not shown in the given code.
ary_modify_check (not shown) is assumed to raise FrozenError on frozen receivers, consistent with the mruby codebase.

ary_make_shared (not shown) preserves the array length; it is unreachable for embedded arrays because embedded capacity is a small compile-time constant below ARY_SHIFT_SHARED_MIN, and Ruby-level code cannot construct an embedded array exceeding that capacity.
The mruby VM is single-threaded per mrb_state, so no concurrent-mutation window exists inside this function.
Allocation failure inside mrb_ary_new_from_values is assumed to raise/abort per mruby allocator semantics rather than returning NULL.
limitations: Spec deviation with no security sink: because if (len == 0 || n == 0) return mrb_ary_new(mrb); precedes the negative check, [].shift(-1) returns [] instead of raising ArgumentError; the negative value is never used, so this is a behavioral/robustness bug only.

All worst cases examined are confined to the interpreter process of the party supplying the script input (equal privilege), so even hypothetical degenerate behavior would not constitute a cross-boundary security impact.

verdict.summary: No primary vulnerability is instantiated in this code. The comparison buffer 'tmp' is allocated at exactly the same 'len' (line 7) that bounds the memcmp (line 13), is freed exactly once on every path, and the comparison result is reduced to a boolean. The only defect-shaped candidates (out-of-bounds read of 'md' if the caller passes an undersized buffer, fail-open when digest_length returns 0, uninitialized 'tmp' if digest_final under-fills, non-constant-time memcmp) all require a caller/callee contract violation or degenerate framework state that no statement in this function can produce, since the interface carries no length for 'md' and 'len' derives solely from the registered algorithm.

assumptions: xmalloc is assumed to never return NULL (it aborts the process on allocation failure); this is xmalloc's documented semantics but is not quotable from the given code.

digest_final is assumed, per its interface, to write exactly digest_length(d) bytes into tmp and to return nonzero on failure; if it could return success with the buffer partially unfilled, line 13 would read uninitialized heap (CWE-457), but this code contains no statement that can produce that state.
digest_length is assumed to return the registered algorithm's fixed non-negative output length; this code never assigns or constrains it.
The intended use context (embedded bootloader digest verification) is assumed for impact modeling; the function itself parses nothing.
limitations: Speculative (contract): if a caller passes an 'md' buffer smaller than digest_length(d), line 13 'ret = memcmp(md, tmp, len);' reads out of bounds. The interface provides no length for 'md', so no guard can exist inside this function; the trigger requires the caller to violate the implicit domain, and the observable effect is at most a crash or a boolean oracle, not content disclosure.

Speculative (contract): if digest_length(d) returned 0, xmalloc(0) followed by memcmp of 0 bytes would make verification trivially succeed (fail-open). A 'if (!len) return -EINVAL;' guard after line 4 is genuinely absent, but no statement in this code can instantiate len == 0; it requires a degenerate registered digest algorithm.
Speculative (contract): a negative digest_length(d) would be widened to a huge size_t at xmalloc/memcmp; only producible by a corrupted 'd' outside this code's data flow.

Hardening note: memcmp is not constant-time, so this verify callback is unsuitable as-is for keyed MAC verification where a timing side channel could aid forgery; for plain digests the attacker can already compute the compared value, so no secret is leaked in the plain-digest use this generic helper targets.

verdict.summary: flatpak_dir_ensure_bundle_remote consumes attacker-controlled content from a bundle file (commit checksum, origin remote URL, embedded GPG keyring, collection ID) via flatpak_bundle_load and persists it into the installation's trusted remote configuration through flatpak_dir_modify_remote and flatpak_dir_create_origin_remote without verifying the bundle commit's GPG signature against the embedded keys or validating the origin. A malicious bundle file can therefore install arbitrary commit content and register an attacker-controlled update remote whose keys the installation subsequently trusts (crypto verification bypass; cf. CVE-2024-32462).

evidence.reason: Origin of attacker-controlled data: the bundle file's content is parsed here, yielding to_checksum, ref, origin, included_gpg_data (embedded GPG keyring bytes) and collection_id. No statement on any subsequent path verifies the commit's GPG signature against included_gpg_data or validates origin/collection_id; the only guard (line 34 'if (metadata == NULL)') merely rejects a failed parse.

evidence.snippet:
remote = flatpak_dir_create_origin_remote (self,
                                                 origin,
                                                 id,
                                                 basename,
                                                 flatpak_decomposed_get_ref (ref),
                                                 gpg_data,
                                                 collection_id,
evidence.reason: Sink: unverified attacker-supplied origin (update URL), gpg_data (bundle-embedded keyring, selected at line 37 when no extra_gpg_data is given), and collection_id are persisted as a new remote in the user's installation. Trigger fully instantiated: a user installing an untrusted .flatpak bundle (extra_gpg_data NULL) reaches this call with all attacker values concrete, permanently trusting the attacker's key and update source without any signature check in this code.

evidence.snippet:
if (!flatpak_dir_modify_remote (self, remote, new_config,
                                          gpg_data, cancellable, error))
evidence.reason: Sink on the already-deployed path: the bundle-embedded attacker keyring (gpg_data) is imported into the existing origin remote's GPG trust store; the only preceding check is 'if (gpg_data != NULL)' (line 45), a presence check, not a validation that the keys sign the bundle's commit.

assumptions: The internals of flatpak_bundle_load, flatpak_dir_create_origin_remote and flatpak_dir_modify_remote are not shown; per guard anchoring, no signature verification or origin sanitization performed inside them is assumed to exist, since none can be quoted from the given code.
extra_gpg_data is treated as a contract input supplied by the local operator (e.g. CLI --gpg-file); the attacker-influenced path is the bundle file's embedded data selected at line 37.

The subsequent deploy of the bundle commit by the caller (using the returned ref/checksum/metadata) is assumed to follow the same unverified path, as no verification statement appears in this function.
limitations: Memory safety was reviewed (GLib autoptr throughout, no raw buffers or arithmetic on attacker sizes) and no memory-corruption candidate was found in this snippet.

The deployed-branch key import (lines 51-52) yields full impact only when combined with attacker control of the update content; the primary, directly instantiated exploit path is the create_origin_remote branch for a not-yet-installed ref.
Remote-name construction from basename (line 60) and any sanitization occur inside the not-shown callee and were not evaluated.

verdict.summary: digest_generic_verify reads exactly digest_length(d) bytes from the caller-supplied md using constant-time crypto_memneq, allocates tmp with the matching size via xmalloc(len), always assigns ret before use, and frees tmp exactly once on every path. The only unguarded preconditions — md spanning len bytes and xmalloc not returning NULL — are caller/environment preconditions that no attacker-controlled input value can violate within this code: the read length is driver-fixed and independent of md content, and the allocation size is a small driver constant. No trigger with attacker-instantiated preconditions reaches a memory, comparison, or control-flow defect.

assumptions: xmalloc is assumed to be the allocator that never returns NULL (panics/exits on failure), consistent with its 'x' naming convention; its implementation is not shown, so this is an assumption, not a quoted guard. This does not affect the verdict because triggering it requires allocation failure that no attacker input can induce (len is a small driver-fixed constant).

digest_final is assumed to write exactly digest_length(d) bytes into tmp per the digest API contract; the driver's write length is not shown, so a driver writing more than its declared length would be a callee contract violation outside this code.

digest_length is assumed to return a small non-negative driver constant per algorithm; a driver declaring a negative or huge length would be a callee contract violation not producible by this code's own flow.

crypto_memneq is assumed to perform a length-bounded constant-time comparison over exactly its third argument bytes; its implementation is not shown. The choice of crypto_memneq over memcmp indicates the timing-oracle mitigation is intended and present at the call site.
limitations: Speculative OOB read (would be CWE-125): if a caller passed a buffer shorter than digest_length(d) as md, crypto_memneq(md, tmp, len) at line 13 would read out of bounds. The precondition (undersized caller buffer) is a size-contract violation; attacker-influenced digest content cannot shrink the caller's buffer, and this code neither parses nor sizes md, so the trigger could not be instantiated.

Robustness only: tmp = xmalloc(len) is not NULL-checked before digest_final(d, tmp) at line 9. Only realizable under allocator failure (or if xmalloc's no-NULL contract were violated), which no attacker input can induce; worst case is termination of the same process with nothing disclosed, written, or amplified.

If len were 0 (a driver declaring zero-length digests), xmalloc(0) behavior is library-defined; the comparison reads zero bytes and verification would compare nothing, but no driver in this code's flow declares such a length, so this is a contract edge, not an instantiated defect.

verdict.summary: In this Count-op kernel, every attacker-reachable sink is guarded by quotable checks. The splits-tensor invariants (num_batches > 0; splits_values(0) == 0; splits_values(num_batches) == num_values) provably pin the while-loop index batch_idx to [1, num_batches], so the reads splits_values(batch_idx) stay within the num_batches+1-element tensor and the writes per_batch_counts[batch_idx - 1] stay within the num_batches-element vector for every idx in [0, num_values), including boundary cases (idx=0, idx=num_values-1, non-monotonic splits). weight_values(idx) is bounded by the weights.shape() == values.shape() check, and value is filtered by value >= 0 && (maxlength_ <= 0 || value < maxlength_) before use as a keyed accumulator entry. Remaining concerns (int truncation of NumElements at >=2^31 elements, arithmetic inside the unshown GetOutputSize/OutputSparse helpers, missing non-decreasing validation of splits causing only misattributed batch counts) could not be instantiated as security impacts within this code and are recorded as limitations/assumptions.

assumptions: BatchedMap<W> is assumed to be a keyed (map/unordered_map-backed) container per its usage pattern per_batch_counts[batch_idx - 1][value] with default-construction, +=, and ++ ; its definition is not shown, so if it were instead a dense array indexed by value, the value filter at line 44 would be the relevant guard to re-audit.

GetOutputSize(max_value, maxlength_, minlength_) and OutputSparse<W>(...) are called but their bodies are not shown; per guard anchoring no safety is assumed for them, but no defective statement inside them is visible to instantiate a trigger (e.g., a possible max_value + 1 overflow when maxlength_ <= 0 and value == T::max cannot be verified).
OP_REQUIRES / OP_REQUIRES_OK are assumed to abort the op computation with an error status when the condition fails (standard TensorFlow framework semantics).
Dtype agreement (splits is int64, values of type T, weights of type W) is enforced by kernel registration, treated as an interface contract.
limitations: OOB read of splits_values / OOB write of per_batch_counts via crafted splits: dismissed as guarded. The checks splits_values(0) == 0 (lines 27-29) and splits_values(num_batches) == num_values (lines 30-33) make batch_idx >= 1 and batch_idx <= num_batches provable for all idx in [0, num_values); the trigger precondition (while-condition true at batch_idx == num_batches, i.e., idx >= num_values) is un-instantiable. Non-monotonic splits were explicitly simulated and only cause values to be attributed to different batches, with no out-of-range index.

Integer truncation of int num_batches = splits.NumElements() - 1 and int num_values = values.NumElements(): requires tensors with >= 2^31 elements (17+ GB); even at that scale the end-check compares against the same wrapped num_values so no out-of-bounds index results, and wrapped-negative num_batches is rejected by num_batches > 0. Not exercised by the code as written (STEP 4 branch c).
Resource consumption from BatchedMap<W>(num_batches): allocation proportional to attacker input size, no unbounded amplification from a small input; robustness, not a DoS vulnerability.

Potential defects inside the unshown helpers GetOutputSize (e.g., max_value + 1 overflow for signed T when maxlength_ <= 0) and OutputSparse cannot be analyzed from the given code; if those helpers are defective this analysis would not detect it.
Missing non-decreasing validation of splits permits semantically wrong batch attribution (a correctness issue), but no security impact was instantiated in this code.

verdict.summary: ValidateInputs correctly guards every memory-access sink on the only path to it: matrix/vector shape checks, a_values length == nnz, a_shape length == ndims, a_shape->NumElements() == b->dims() (which, since a_shape is a verified vector, bounds the shape-equality loop), and a complete index range check 'idx < 0 || idx >= a_shape_flat(didx)' that rejects both boundary cases (-1 and exactly-at-limit). Non-negativity of a_shape values is implied by forced equality with b->dim_size(i) over every element. The only unverified properties (int64 dtype of a_indices/a_shape, a_values dtype matching b) are op-registration contracts outside this code and are recorded as assumptions. No injection, crypto, or amplification sinks exist.

assumptions: a_indices and a_shape are assumed to have dtype int64 (Index): the code calls flat_inner_dims<Index>() and flat<Index>() without any dtype check, and dtype selection happens at op registration, which is not shown. If a kernel were registered with int32 indices, flat<Index> would reinterpret the buffer; this is an interface-contract assumption, not something enforceable or violable by the tensor contents themselves.
a_values dtype matching b's dtype and the semantic use of a_values downstream are assumed to be enforced by the op kernel; this function only validates shapes and indices.

Tensor shape dims (dim_size) are assumed non-negative and consistent with the allocated buffer, per the Tensor class contract; the code has no statement enforcing this but it is a framework invariant, not attacker-controlled content.
limitations: The index-validation double loop is O(nnz * ndims), proportional to the attacker-supplied tensors the caller already had to allocate and transfer; no amplification beyond input size, so no CWE-400 finding.

Type-confusion via a non-int64 a_indices is speculative: its precondition (a kernel instantiation with mismatched dtype) lives in op-registration code not shown and cannot be instantiated by any statement in this code.
This analysis covers only the ValidateInputs function; downstream consumers of the validated tensors (not shown) are out of scope.

verdict.summary: diST_box_read sizes a heap buffer from the unvalidated, file-supplied box size s->size. The allocation expression sizeof(char) * (s->size+1) wraps to zero when s->size is the maximum of its unsigned width (a value directly expressible in the attacker-crafted box size/largesize field), so gf_malloc(0) returns a non-NULL zero-capacity chunk on mainstream allocators; gf_bs_read_data then copies attacker-controlled stream bytes into that chunk (heap out-of-bounds write with attacker-controlled content and length) and the terminator write p->content_script_types[s->size] lands one byte before the chunk. No bound on s->size exists anywhere in the function. Independently, the return value of gf_bs_read_data is discarded, so a truncated file leaves the tail of the buffer as uninitialized heap while it is published as a NUL-terminated C string, enabling heap disclosure when the box is dumped or re-serialized.

evidence.reason: Buffer size miscalculation leading to out-of-bounds write: with s->size at the max of its unsigned width (attacker-settable box size field, e.g. 0xFFFFFFFF or largesize 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF), s->size+1 wraps to 0, gf_malloc(0) yields a non-NULL zero-capacity chunk that passes the line-6 NULL check, gf_bs_read_data then copies attacker file bytes into it (heap overflow write), and the line-8 index s->size wraps to ptr-1 for a second OOB write. No statement in the function bounds s->size.

Unchecked partial read: gf_bs_read_data returns the number of bytes actually copied, which is discarded. On a truncated file where fewer than s->size bytes remain in the stream, the unread tail of the gf_malloc buffer stays uninitialized heap, and line 8 publishes it as a NUL-terminated C string (content_script_types), disclosing heap contents when the parsed box is later printed or re-serialized. No comparison of bytes read against s->size exists on any path.

Origin of the tainted values: this box-reader callback is the intake point for data crossing a trust boundary; s->size (parsed from the attacker-supplied ISO box header) and the byte stream bs enter here with no validation of the declared size against the stream's remaining bytes anywhere in this function.

assumptions: GF_Box::size is an unsigned integer field (64-bit in the GPAC codebase this function originates from, 32-bit in older variants); the wrap trigger at line 5 is expressible under either width, differing only in which file field carries it (32-bit size field vs 64-bit largesize field).
gf_bs_read_data copies min(size, bytes available in bs) and returns the count; its size parameter is u32 in GPAC, so a 64-bit s->size is truncated at the line-7 call.

gf_malloc(0) returns a non-NULL zero-capacity allocation on mainstream allocators such as glibc; on platforms where malloc(0) returns NULL the line-6 check would catch that case, making the line-7 overflow platform-dependent.

The disclosure impact of the unchecked read assumes the parsed content_script_types string is consumed downstream (box dump, info tools, or re-serialization), which is the normal use of this box in the library this code belongs to; the defect of discarding the read count is in this function.
limitations: A lower-ranked availability issue exists: with no check of s->size against the bytes remaining in the stream, a ~12-byte box header can force an allocation of up to ~4 GiB (larger with a 64-bit size) that is retained per box, an attacker-scalable memory-exhaustion vector (CWE-400); it is real but ranked below the confirmed out-of-bounds write and does not drive the CWE list.
On allocators where malloc(0) returns NULL, the oversized-size wrap at line 5 is caught by the line-6 check; the OOB write then depends on the platform's zero-size allocation semantics.

Worst case for the size-wrap trigger on a hypothetical allocator returning NULL for size 0 is a clean GF_OUT_OF_MEM return, which alone would be a robustness outcome, not a security impact; the vulnerability verdict rests on mainstream allocator behavior and the unchecked-partial-read finding, both instantiated above.

verdict.summary: This mruby codegen routine consumes an in-process AST built by the parser. Pointer-chain dereferences (tree->cdr->car, tree->cdr->cdr->car) are unguarded in this code but their NULL-ness cannot be instantiated: only the parser's node constructors (not shown) create NODE_CALL/NODE_SCALL nodes, and they always populate the method-symbol and args slots by grammar. The argument-count n is clamped (gen_values limit 13/14, negative sentinel mapped to 15, n capped at 15) and every n adjustment is paired with a matching push/pop, so no stack underflow, operand mismatch, or integer overflow is reachable. Worst residual outcomes are controlled codegen_error aborts and malformed-AST NULL derefs that require the parser to violate its contract.

assumptions: gen_values honors its limit parameter and returns at most the limit (13 or 14) or a negative sentinel for variable-length argument lists; its body is not shown.

The parser (not shown) always constructs NODE_CALL/NODE_SCALL with non-NULL cdr->car (method symbol) and cdr->cdr (args node), and NODE_GVAR/LVAR/etc. with non-NULL cdr holding the symbol; these are interface contracts relied on by the dereferences at lines 80 and 103.
If this compiler is fed untrusted source text in a hosting service, malformed-AST robustness of the whole pipeline would need re-evaluation at the parser intake point, which is outside this snippet.
limitations: Speculative candidate dismissed: NULL-pointer dereference of tree->cdr->cdr->car (or tree->cdr->car) would require a NODE_CALL node lacking its args node or method symbol — only producible by the parser violating its construction contract, not by any flow in this code. Recorded as CWE-476-shaped robustness risk, not a vulnerability here.
gen_values, gen_hash, genop_*, attrsym, and new_sym are not shown; defects inside them were not assessed.

A compiler stack imbalance from an operand-count mismatch would produce incorrect bytecode, not memory corruption in this code; boundary walk at n=13/14/15 found each increment paired with matching push/pop, so no imbalance was instantiated.

verdict.summary: yank_copy_line as given is the post-patch form: 'if (exclude_trailing_space) bd->endspaces = 0;' is executed before both the allocation and the strip loop on every path, so s = bd->textlen and all reads stay within textstart[0..textlen-1]; the write *pnew = NUL cannot precede the buffer because the strip loop decrements pnew at most textlen times (each iteration also decreases s by at least 1, bounded by 'while (s > 0 && ...)'), and the memsets/memmove all fit inside the quoted allocation 'alloc(bd->startspaces + bd->endspaces + bd->textlen + 1)'. No guard-less sink reachable with attacker-influenced buffer text was found.

assumptions: The consistency between bd->textstart and bd->textlen (textstart points to textlen valid bytes) is an interface contract with the core blockwise-yank machinery in the same process; this function performs no parsing of raw external data itself.
bd->startspaces and bd->endspaces are non-negative as computed by the caller (contract); negative values would corrupt the memsets but are not producible by any statement in this function.
y_idx is bounded by the caller's yank loop matching the allocated size of y_current->y_array (contract).
alloc() semantics (returns NULL on failure, allocates the requested byte count) follow Vim's documented core contract.
limitations: Historical context: the pre-patch version of this function lacked 'bd->endspaces = 0;' and computed 'int s = bd->textlen + bd->endspaces;' with endspaces > 0, reading textstart[textlen+endspaces-1] out of bounds; in the code as given that trigger is not instantiable because the same exclude_trailing_space flag zeroes endspaces before every use.

Theoretical int overflow of 'bd->startspaces + bd->endspaces + bd->textlen + 1' requires roughly 2^31 bytes of in-buffer text or virtual columns in the operator's own editor session; not producible by a realistic attacker input, and a wrapped negative would typically become a huge size_t causing alloc to fail (return FAIL).

When a whitespace byte (0x20/0x09) is a continuation byte of a multibyte character, the strip loop's s can skip backward by more than one byte per pnew--, which can leave stale bytes before the NUL in the yank register; this is cosmetic (in-bounds) with no memory-safety or disclosure effect.
A crash confined to the operator's own editor process from self-supplied buffer content would be a robustness issue, not a security impact; no such reachable crash was found in the given code anyway.

verdict.summary: iloc_box_read allows attacker-controlled allocation amplification: the inner extent loop is bounded only by the attacker-supplied extent_count (u16, line 51) while its per-iteration consumption of the remaining box size is itself attacker-controlled and can be exactly zero (offset_size = length_size = 0 makes line 66's ISOM_DECREASE_SIZE argument 0; version 0 or index_size 0 consumes nothing at lines 59-65). One GF_ItemExtentEntry is allocated per iteration (line 55), so a ~384 KB crafted iloc box (item_count = 65535, extent_count = 65535) drives roughly 4.3 billion allocations (~170 GB) before any size check fires, causing memory/CPU exhaustion of any process parsing the untrusted media file.

evidence.reason: Sink: the inner loop bound is the attacker-supplied extent_count with no cap tying it to the remaining box size, and each iteration allocates one GF_ItemExtentEntry. With item_count = extent_count = 0xFFFF (both maxima of their u16 domains), this executes ~4.3e9 allocations from a ~384 KB box, exhausting memory/CPU of the process parsing the attacker's file (CWE-400).

Missing-check site: the only per-iteration size guard takes the attacker-controlled offset_size + length_size, whose boundary value 0+0 makes the check a no-op, so the loop is never tethered to ptr->size; no other statement bounds extent_count against remaining size.
Origin of the tainted loop bound: extent_count is read directly from the untrusted file as an unvalidated u16 (up to 65535) and used at line 53 with zero minimum per-iteration size consumption.

Origin of the zero-consumption enabler: 4-bit attacker-controlled sizes with minimum 0; setting both to 0 makes the per-iteration size accounting at line 66 consume nothing, decoupling the extent loop from the declared box size.

assumptions: ISOM_DECREASE_SIZE is defined outside the shown code; assumed to validate remaining box size against its argument and subtract it. The finding does not depend on the exact definition because the argument at line 66 is attacker-set to exactly 0, which passes under any semantics of the macro.

gf_bs_read_int / gf_bs_read_u16 / gf_bs_read_u32 and the box framework (which sets ptr->version and initializes ptr->size from the declared box size) are external; ptr->version is treated as attacker-influenced file content since it originates from the same untrusted file.
GF_SAFEALLOC is assumed to allocate-and-zero one heap object per call; the amplification factor uses a conservative ~40-48 bytes per extent entry including allocator overhead.
limitations: gf_bs_read_int is called with nBits up to 8*15 = 120 (lines 45, 61, 68, 69), exceeding the typical 32-bit domain of a u32-returning bit reader; any shift UB would occur inside the unshown callee, so it is not confirmed as a vulnerability in this code. The u32 return also truncates values wider than 32 bits, which is a value-correctness issue, not memory safety here.

The outer item loop always consumes at least 6 bytes of declared box size per iteration (lines 30/33, 43, 50), so item_count alone cannot exceed box_size/6; the defect is specifically the zero-consumption inner extent loop multiplied by the outer count.
Impact is availability only (memory/CPU exhaustion while parsing one untrusted media file); no memory corruption, disclosure, or code execution was instantiated in this code.

If reads occur past the physical end of a truncated file, the behavior is decided by the unshown bitstream overflow handling; it does not change the finding, since the trigger file can simply contain the full ~384 KB payload.

verdict.summary: flatpak_dir_ensure_bundle_remote imports GPG key material embedded in an attacker-supplied bundle file into the trust configuration of an already-trusted remote without verifying that the bundle is signed by a key already trusted for that remote. When the ref is already deployed, gpg_data (selected at line 44 from the bundle's included_gpg_data when no operator keys are given) is passed to flatpak_dir_modify_remote for the existing origin remote (lines 58-59), and in the fresh-install path the bundle's origin URL and keys are installed together as the update remote (lines 68-77). An attacker who gets a victim to install a malicious bundle can therefore control the verification keys (and update URL) used for future updates of installed software.

evidence.snippet:
if (!flatpak_dir_modify_remote (self, remote, new_config,
                                          gpg_data, cancellable, error))
evidence.reason: Sink: attacker-controlled GPG key material (gpg_data, sourced from the bundle file's included_gpg_data) is imported into the trust configuration of an existing remote (`remote`, the origin of the already-deployed ref). The only guard on this path is the presence check `if (gpg_data != NULL)` at line 52; no check verifies the bundle is signed by a key already trusted for `remote`, so the trigger is fully instantiated by an attacker-crafted bundle for an installed ref with extra_gpg_data == NULL.

Origin of the tainted value: when the operator supplies no extra keys, the GPG keys used for the remote trust update are taken from included_gpg_data, which is parsed directly out of the attacker-controlled bundle file by flatpak_bundle_load (lines 27-33) and reaches the modify_remote/create_origin_remote sinks unvalidated.

assumptions: flatpak_bundle_load (lines 27-33) is not shown; whether it performs any GPG verification of the bundle against its included keys is unknown and, per guard anchoring, was not used to dismiss the finding.

The semantics of flatpak_dir_modify_remote (whether imported keys replace or augment the remote's keyring) and flatpak_dir_create_origin_remote are not shown; the finding rests on the key material and origin URL being written into persistent remote trust configuration.
flatpak_bundle_load is assumed to fail (return NULL metadata) when the bundle lacks a ref, so `ref` is non-NULL at lines 46/65/72; this could not be verified from the given code.

flatpak_deploy_data_get_origin is assumed to return a non-NULL origin for deployed refs; if it could return NULL, g_strdup(NULL) would pass a NULL remote name to flatpak_dir_modify_remote (contract question, not instantiated).
limitations: The result of ostree_repo_copy_config (line 56) is not checked for NULL before being passed to flatpak_dir_modify_remote; robustness only, no attacker-instantiated security effect in this code.

In the already-deployed branch with gpg_data == NULL (no operator keys and no keys in the bundle), no keys are imported and a later update pull may fail; robustness/availability of a later operation, not a vulnerability in this code.
The metadata-presence check at line 38 is correctly guarded only when out_metadata is requested, which matches the function's contract; no defect found there.
Memory management (g_autoptr/g_steal_pointer at lines 82-95) and the out-parameter handling were reviewed and found correct.

verdict.summary: MapStageOp::Compute forwards the attacker-controlled 'indices' tensor to map->put without validating that its element count matches the number of 'values' tensors (which size the tuple at lines 21-23). The only guard in the function, key_tensor->NumElements() > 0, constrains a different input. A graph/session caller can supply indices with more elements than values, driving count-paired index access against the undersized tuple inside the staging-map insertion, causing a heap out-of-bounds read (crash and potential disclosure of adjacent heap memory retained in the staging area).

evidence.reason: Sink and missing-check site: indices_tensor (arbitrary attacker-controlled element count, admitted at line 12 with no validation) is passed together with a tuple whose size is fixed to values_tensor.size() by the loop at lines 21-23. No statement between input and this call checks indices_tensor->NumElements() == values_tensor.size(), so a mismatched count reaches the count-paired index use in put, producing an out-of-bounds read of the tuple.

Origin of the taint: the attacker-supplied 'indices' tensor (whose element count is unbounded and unvalidated) and the attacker-supplied 'values' list (whose independently chosen count sizes the tuple) both enter here across the graph/session trust boundary; their counts are never reconciled before the sink at line 26.

assumptions: The implementation of StagingMap::put is not shown; per guard anchoring, any validation it might perform cannot be quoted and is not relied upon. The impact mechanism (indices count paired positionally against tuple elements, causing OOB access when counts mismatch) is inferred from the documented role of 'indices' as per-element index data for the ordered staging map, not from quotable code.

Attacker model: op-kernel tensor inputs are treated as attacker-data originating from a graph/session caller at a different trust boundary (e.g., an untrusted model executed by a serving or sandboxed TensorFlow process).
dtype checks on key/indices are presumed to exist only outside the shown code and are not used to dismiss any candidate.
limitations: If the unshown StagingMap::put independently validates the indices/values count equality, the mismatch would be rejected downstream; that enforcement cannot be verified from the given code, and this function remains the intake point whose missing validation is the defect.
A mismatch where indices has FEWER elements than values does not clearly produce out-of-bounds access; only the indices-count-greater-than-values-count direction is claimed to have OOB-read impact.

Crash-only consequences for an operator feeding their own local process with no disclosure or retention would be a robustness issue, but that equal-privilege scenario does not apply to the cross-boundary graph/session attacker modeled here.

verdict.summary: Array.prototype.splice implementation clamps every attacker-derived value before use: start is clamped to [0, length] by 'start = (start < 0) ? njs_max(length + start, 0) : njs_min(start, length);' (no signed wrap is reachable, since a non-negative length is added only to a negative start), delete is clamped to [0, length - start] by 'delete = njs_min(njs_max(delete, 0), length - start);' or set to 'length - start', items = nargs - 3 is guarded by 'else if (nargs > 2)', and the new length is capped by 'if (njs_slow_path((length + delta) > NJS_MAX_LENGTH))'. From these invariants the fast-path memcpy destination satisfies start + items <= length + delta, with capacity guaranteed by 'njs_array_expand(vm, array, 0, delta)' when delta > 0 and by capacity >= length otherwise; the deleted-array copy is bounded by the checked allocation 'njs_array_alloc(vm, 0, delete, 0)' plus the NULL test; and the slow path uses generic property operations with indices in [0, length + delta]. Edge values (INT64_MIN/INT64_MAX start and delete, delete = length - start exactly, delta = 0, count = 0, start + delete = length) were simulated and all fall inside the bounds. Remaining issues (huge allocations or O(length) loops for script-chosen huge lengths, potential value misordering from the constant direction flag passed to njs_array_copy_within) are equal-privilege robustness/correctness concerns, not cross-boundary security impact.

assumptions: njs_object_length always assigns *length and returns only NJS_OK or NJS_ERROR, matching the checked 'if (njs_slow_path(ret == NJS_ERROR))'; a third return code leaving length uninitialized would be a helper defect, not instantiated here.
njs_value_to_integer clamps NaN/±Infinity to values whose subsequent clamping in this code (quoted in STEP 2) is safe regardless of whether the hardware indefinite value INT64_MIN is produced.

njs_array_alloc(vm, 0, delete, 0) either allocates at least delete initialized slots or returns NULL (checked), computing sizes in 64-bit; a 32-bit size truncation inside that helper cannot be verified from this code.
njs_array_expand(vm, array, 0, delta) guarantees capacity >= length + delta for the fast array; this is the capacity fact the fast-path memcpy bound proof relies on.

The args frame holds at least nargs njs_value_t slots (interface contract of the VM call machinery that also underlies njs_arg), so the memcpy source read of items = nargs - 3 values from &args[3] is in-frame.

For a fast array, njs_object_length returns array->length and no user JS can execute between that read and the fast-path writes, so 'array->length - (start + delete)' and the memcpy bound use the same length value.

NJS_MAX_LENGTH is at least as large as any array length the VM can produce; length values above it from non-array-like objects are neutralized by the quoted (length + delta) > NJS_MAX_LENGTH check combined with the failed huge njs_array_alloc.
limitations: Script-initiated resource consumption: setting a sparse array length to NJS_MAX_LENGTH and splicing it triggers either a ~64 GB njs_array_alloc attempt (fails -> NJS_ERROR, graceful) or O(2^32) property operations in njs_array_copy_within / the delete loop; the caller here is script code running at equal privilege with the process (it could loop forever on its own), so per the impact model this is robustness/DoS at equal privilege, not a cross-boundary vulnerability.

Potential data misordering: the fast path passes a constant direction flag 0 to njs_array_copy_within while the slow path passes 'delta < 0'; if that helper performs element-wise overlapping copies on fast arrays honoring the flag, one shift direction could duplicate elements. This is value corruption within the same array (no memory unsafety, no cross-boundary disclosure) and depends on unshown helper internals.

After 'njs_array_alloc' returns NULL the code returns NJS_ERROR without posting an exception itself; it relies on the allocation helper having set a memory-error exception, otherwise the VM would continue with no pending error - a helper-contract robustness point, not instantiated as a defect here.

verdict.summary: This is the patched form of TensorFlow's Tensor::FromProto: it validates the proto shape (TensorShape::IsValid) and dtype (DT_INVALID and CASES default rejection) before decoding, and rejects failed or null decode results. Attacker-controlled tensor_content and N are passed to Helper<T>::Decode / FromProtoField<T>, but the copy/allocation sinks live in those helpers, not in this code, so no memory-safety defect is instantiable here. The only in-function behavior of note is the documented acceptance of partial shapes (N == -1), whose potential misuse would occur in consumers outside this snippet.

assumptions: CASES_WITH_DEFAULT dispatches template T consistently with proto.dtype() and sets dtype_error for every unlisted dtype value in both the decode branch and the else branch; the macro body is not shown.

TensorShape::IsValid (called at line 4) is assumed to reject shapes with negative dimensions other than the unknown -1 and shapes whose element product overflows int64, matching the code comment that all num_elements values besides 0 and -1 'should be invalid by construction'; its semantics are not shown.

Helper<T>::Decode and FromProtoField<T> are assumed to validate tensor_content length against N * sizeof(T) and to return nullptr on allocation failure; neither their checks nor their copy code is shown, so per guard anchoring these enforcements are unverifiable assumptions.
DT_INVALID is assumed to be the only dtype value excluded by line 5; any other unknown dtype is nevertheless rejected by the CASES default (dtype_error = true) in both branches.
limitations: Partial-shape tensors (N == -1 from a dim of -1) are accepted and returned as valid Tensors with a set dtype and null buffer; the object is left with num_elements() == -1. Any memory-unsafe use (negative element count feeding size or offset math) would occur in downstream consumers not shown, so the trigger is speculative for this code.

The call p = Helper<T>::Decode(a, content, N) (and FromProtoField<T>) passes attacker-controlled content bytes and attacker-influenced element count N to a sink outside the given snippet; if those helpers fail to check content.size() against N * sizeof(T), a heap out-of-bounds write would occur there, not here. This cannot be confirmed or refuted from the given code.

Very large but non-overflowing shapes can force a huge allocation attempt; failure surfaces as p == nullptr and a clean return false (allocation failure is not attacker-scalable amplification), assuming helpers return nullptr rather than crash on allocation failure.

verdict.summary: The op never validates that the attacker-controlled sparse rank (truth_st_shape.dims(), derived from the truth_shape tensor) is at least 2. With a rank-1 truth_shape, group_dims is empty, output_shape ends up scalar (dims()==0), the 'output_elements > 0' check still passes (scalar has 1 element), and 'output_strides[output_shape.dims() - 1] = 1' performs an out-of-bounds write at index -1 into an empty vector (data()==nullptr), crashing/corrupting the serving process from untrusted input. A rank-0 truth_shape similarly turns 'std::vector<int64_t> group_dims(truth_st_shape.dims() - 1)' into a size of (size_t)-1, aborting the process.

evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds write sink. When the attacker supplies a rank-1 truth_shape, output_shape receives zero dims (the AddDim loop never runs) yet 'output_elements > 0' passes because a scalar has num_elements()==1; output_strides is then an empty vector with data()==nullptr and 'output_strides[output_shape.dims() - 1] = 1' writes 8 bytes at index (size_t)-1, i.e. nullptr-8 — an out-of-bounds write reachable from fully attacker-controlled tensor content with no dims() lower-bound check on any path.

Origin of the tainted value: truth_st_shape.dims() comes from the attacker-supplied truth_shape tensor via MakeShape (lines 26-28). With dims()==1 this line produces an empty group_dims, which cascades to output_shape.dims()==0 and the index -1 write at line 66; with dims()==0 it constructs a vector of size (size_t)-1, aborting the process. No check of the shown code bounds dims() away from 0 or 1.

assumptions: ValidateShapes(...) is called with OP_REQUIRES_OK (lines 15-18) but its body is not shown; per guard anchoring, any rank/emptiness checks it might perform cannot be relied on, and this code is treated as the last line of defense for the attacker-supplied shape tensors.

sparse::SparseTensor::Create(...) and TensorShapeUtils::MakeShape(...) internals are not shown; only their return statuses are verified (lines 21, 26, 35, 40). No assumption is made that Create validates indices against the declared shape.
normalize_ is a kernel attribute configured by the graph author and treated as internal-trusted.
limitations: The rank-0 variant (empty truth_shape) crashes earlier at line 46 via std::vector<int64_t>((size_t)-1) throwing length_error/aborting — a crash-only consequence of the same missing lower-bound validation and the same one-line fix; not counted as a separate primary.

The five output_t(loc) writes are guarded by the quotable check 'OP_REQUIRES(ctx, 0 <= loc && loc < output_elements, ...)' on every path; even with int64 wrap in the inner_product the write stays within the output tensor, so those sites are not vulnerabilities.
gtl::LevenshteinDistance performs O(n*m) work on attacker-sized sequences — inherent quadratic amplification of the op's documented function, noted but not graded as a vulnerability.

A hypothesis/truth rank mismatch would reach dim_size(d) out of range only if the not-shown SparseTensor::Create accepted a rank/order mismatch; its OP_REQUIRES_OK-checked status makes this speculative.
Practical impact of the confirmed OOB write is a deterministic near-null write (nullptr-8), i.e. process crash / cross-boundary denial of service, not a controllable corruption primitive.

verdict.summary: The afra box parser validates entry_count against the remaining declared box size with an exact per-entry byte divisor (16 for 8-byte time + 8-byte offset, 12 for 8-byte time + 4-byte offset, selected after the long_offsets flag is read), and every bitstream read in both loops is individually preceded by an ISOM_DECREASE_SIZE call whose byte count exactly matches the subsequent read. All allocations are null-checked and list insertion indices stay in lockstep with list growth. The only asymmetry is that global_entry_count lacks an upfront density check, but its loop is bounded per-iteration by ISOM_DECREASE_SIZE against the declared remaining size, and triggering unbounded amplification would require the outer (unshown) box parser to accept a declared box size far exceeding the actual file bytes plus silent EOF reads — preconditions not instantiable within this code. A small per-entry leak exists on error return paths but is a robustness issue only.

assumptions: ISOM_DECREASE_SIZE is the standard GPAC macro that returns GF_ISOM_INVALID_FILE when the remaining box size is smaller than the requested byte count and decrements ptr->size otherwise; its body is not included in the given code.
gf_bs_read_int/gf_bs_read_u16/gf_bs_read_u32/gf_bs_read_u64 return 0 (or partial data) when the bitstream is exhausted rather than performing out-of-bounds accesses; implementation not shown.
ptr->size is initialized by the outer box parser from the file's box size field and is consistent with the bytes actually available in the bitstream for this box; that clamp, if any, is not shown.
ptr->local_access_entries and ptr->global_access_entries are non-NULL lists created by the box constructor (not shown).
limitations: Speculative CWE-400: global_entry_count (line 32) has no upfront density check like the entry_count guard at lines 13-14; its loop is bounded only per-iteration by ISOM_DECREASE_SIZE. Unbounded amplification from a tiny file would additionally require the unshown outer parser to accept a declared box size far exceeding actual file bytes and bitstream reads to return silently at EOF — neither precondition could be instantiated from statements in this code, so it is not counted as a vulnerability here.

Robustness: an entry allocated with gf_malloc leaks if a subsequent ISOM_DECREASE_SIZE in the same loop iteration fails and the function returns early, and the return value of gf_list_insert is ignored; bounded, error-path-only leak with no cross-boundary impact.
Contract: passing a NULL box pointer or a list pointer not created by the box constructor would crash; treated as interface contract, not attack data.

verdict.summary: Analysis of DefaultCertValidator::updateDigestForSessionId found no security vulnerabilities. All parameters are interface-contract arguments (hash_buffer declared as EVP_MAX_MD_SIZE, hash_length overwritten before use, md expected to be initialized). All return values from X509_digest and EVP_DigestUpdate are checked with RELEASE_ASSERT. Buffer writes are bounded by SHA256 digest size (32 bytes) within the declared EVP_MAX_MD_SIZE (64 bytes). Hash list iterations use container-internal size() and data() which are inherently consistent. No attacker-controlled data reaches any sink without proper validation.

assumptions: verify_certificate_hash_list_ and verify_certificate_spiki_list_ are assumed to be std::vector<std::vector<uint8_t>> or similar standard container types where size() and data() are internally consistent
BoringSSL's SHA256_Update handles (nullptr, 0) gracefully by returning early when len == 0
RELEASE_ASSERT in Envoy is always active in both debug and release builds
The caller of updateDigestForSessionId provides a properly initialized bssl::ScopedEVP_MD_CTX and a hash_buffer of at least EVP_MAX_MD_SIZE bytes as documented by the parameter declaration
ca_cert_, verify_certificate_hash_list_, and verify_certificate_spki_list_ are set from trusted configuration sources and are not directly attacker-controlled at this function's entry point
limitations: If a caller violates the documented contract by passing a hash_buffer smaller than EVP_MAX_MD_SIZE (64 bytes), X509_digest writing 32 bytes could overflow the buffer. This is speculative as it requires a contract violation by the caller, not attacker-controlled data.

If verify_certificate_hash_list_ or verify_certificate_spki_list_ were somehow populated with extremely large entries (approaching SIZE_MAX elements), the multiplication hash.size() * sizeof(value_type) could theoretically overflow. This is not practically achievable given memory constraints and configuration-based population of these lists.

verdict.summary: The SVDF Prepare function indexes tensor shape arrays (TfLiteIntArray::data[]) without ever validating the dimensionality of the model-provided tensors. weights_time->dims->data[1], input->dims->data[1], weights_feature->dims->data[1], and the data[0] reads all execute with no NumDimensions/rank check on those tensors (only 'state' is checked, at the NumDimensions(state)==2 line). A malicious .tflite model declaring a 1-D weights_time (or 1-D input/weights_feature, or 0-D tensors) causes heap out-of-bounds reads one past the dims allocation, with the leaked value (memory_size) used in subsequent shape comparisons.

evidence.reason: Primary sink: reads index 1 of weights_time's shape array with no preceding check that the tensor has at least 2 dimensions; a schema-legal 1-D weights_time tensor in a crafted model makes this a heap OOB read, and the value flows into the state-shape comparison at lines 49-50.

Same missing-dimensionality defect: data[1] of input and weights_feature is read as part of a comparison without verifying either tensor's dims->size >= 2; a 1-D input or weights_feature triggers an OOB heap read.

evidence.snippet:
const int batch_size = input->dims->data[0];
  const int num_filters = weights_feature->dims->data[0];
evidence.reason: Same root cause: data[0] is read without verifying dims->size >= 1, so a legal 0-D (scalar) tensor in the model produces an out-of-bounds read one past the empty shape allocation.

assumptions: Model file content (tensor shapes, SVDF rank, quantization params) is attacker-controlled: this operator prepares a downloaded/third-party .tflite model, and the model originator is the attacker per the trust-boundary model.
TfLiteIntArray instances backing tensor dims are heap allocations sized exactly to their declared element count, so indexing at or beyond data[size-1] reads past the allocation.

GetInputSafe guarantees the fetched tensor pointers are non-null when the listed tensor indices exist (interpreter helper contract, not shown); the confirmed OOB reads do not depend on this, since a legally-shaped 1-D tensor satisfies every contract.
limitations: Negative rank is not rejected: 'TF_LITE_ENSURE(context, rank != 0)' permits rank < 0, and rank = -1 yields a negative num_units (num_filters / -1) that is passed to ResizeTensor as a negative dimension; the harmful use occurs inside ResizeTensor, which is not part of this code, so this trigger is speculative here.
'memory_size * num_filters' can overflow int at line 49-50, weakening the state-shape invariant; any resulting memory-safety violation would materialize in Eval, which is not shown.

TfLiteIntArrayCreate results (output_size_array, scratch_size_array, temporaries, per-hybrid arrays) are dereferenced without NULL checks; only reachable under malloc failure, which an attacker cannot induce.

If weights_time->dims were null (tensor with no shape metadata), the read would be a null dereference crashing the operator at equal privilege with no disclosure — robustness, not a distinct vulnerability.

verdict.summary: In iloc_box_read, the extent_entry loop is bounded only by the attacker-controlled u16 extent_count while its per-iteration size decrement ISOM_DECREASE_SIZE(ptr, (ptr->offset_size+ptr->length_size)) can be exactly 0 when the 4-bit offset_size and length_size nibbles are both 0 (and version 0 skips the index read). Each iteration then performs an unchecked-count heap allocation (gf_malloc of GF_ItemExtentEntry) that is retained via gf_list_add, so a ~22-byte box yields 65,535 allocations and a ~400KB box yields ~4.3 billion allocations (hundreds of GB retained, hours of CPU): attacker-scalable resource amplification when parsing untrusted media files.

evidence.reason: Origin of the zero-cost condition: both 4-bit nibbles are read straight from the untrusted box with no check that their sum is nonzero; an attacker sets both to 0, making every extent iteration consume 0 bytes of the remaining box size.

The allocation sink: the loop's only bound is the attacker-supplied extent_count (u16, up to 65535 per item) and each iteration heap-allocates a GF_ItemExtentEntry, with no requirement that any box-size bytes be consumed; instantiated trigger: version=0, offset_size=length_size=0, extent_count=0xFFFF gives 65,535 retained allocations from a ~22-byte box, scaling to billions of allocations from a ~400KB box.

The only per-iteration size guard, and it decrements exactly 0 bytes when offset_size and length_size are both 0, so it can never terminate the extent loop regardless of remaining size; the minimal fix (reject offset_size+length_size==0, or force nonzero per-iteration consumption) is absent from the code.

assumptions: ISOM_DECREASE_SIZE(ptr, N) returns an error when ptr->size < N and otherwise subtracts N (macro body not shown); the STEP 4 trigger survives any variant of this comparison, since the attacker-controlled decrement is 0.
gf_bs_read_int(bs, 0) consumes 0 bits and returns 0 (callee not shown).
The box framework sets ptr->version and ptr->size from the attacker-supplied box header/payload before calling this reader; both are therefore attacker-influenced inputs.
gf_list_add retains each allocated extent entry in a list owned by the box until the box is destroyed, so the allocations persist during parsing.
limitations: gf_bs_read_int is called with up to 120 bits (offset_size/length_size/base_offset_size each up to 15) while returning u32; any assertion or out-of-range behavior inside the callee (not shown) is speculative, and the truncation itself is only a functional issue.
The result of gf_list_new() (line 51) is not checked; a NULL there would be passed to gf_list_add, but this is reachable only through allocation failure, not attacker input.

All gf_bs_read_* calls in this function are preceded by matching ISOM_DECREASE_SIZE counts, so no box-relative over-read was confirmed beyond the zero-consumption amplification path (macro semantics assumed).

verdict.summary: GroupedConvFunctor::operator() computes num_groups = in_depth / patch_depth and later tensor.dim_size(3) / num_groups without any zero check on the divisors. An attacker supplying a graph/model with filter depth dim_size(2)==0, or with input depth smaller than filter patch depth (yielding num_groups==0), triggers an integer division by zero (SIGFPE) that terminates the whole inference process — a denial-of-service across the service boundary for any party that can submit or supply a model/graph to a TensorFlow runtime.

evidence.reason: Integer division by zero: patch_depth comes directly from the attacker-controlled filter shape (filter.dim_size(2)) and is used as divisor with no zero check anywhere in the function. Trigger: filter shape [1,1,0,8] makes in_depth/patch_depth = 16/0, raising SIGFPE and killing the process.

Second division-by-zero sink: when in_depth < patch_depth (e.g. input depth 1, filter depth 2), line 12 produces num_groups == 0 and tensor.dim_size(3) / num_groups divides by zero (first invoked via post_shuffle at the Tensor input_shuffled construction), crashing the process. Same defect also at line 26 in post_shuffle.

assumptions: explicit_paddings is assumed to always contain at least 6 elements; this is enforced by the Conv2D op schema outside the given code, so the unchecked explicit_paddings[2]..[5] indexing at lines 27-30 is treated as a contract issue, not a vulnerability.
data_format is assumed validated by the op registration framework; the DCHECK at line 6 is a debug-only assertion, but the attribute is an op-contract value.

Tensor shapes (input.dim_size, filter.dim_size) are attacker-controlled per the TensorFlow threat model where graphs/models originate from untrusted parties; no shape validation for this kernel exists inside the given code.
limitations: Truncation when in_depth % patch_depth != 0 (e.g. depth 7, patch 3 → num_groups=2) yields mis-shaped Eigen views whose element counts are always ≤ the underlying buffer sizes, so no out-of-bounds read/write is provable from this code; the observable effect is silently incorrect convolution results. If the not-shown functor::SpatialConvolution writes channels derived from the filter rather than the output slice, an OOB could exist, but that cannot be verified here.

Crash-only impact: if the only parties invoking this code run unprivileged local processes on their own graphs with no service boundary, the SIGFPE would be a robustness bug rather than a DoS vulnerability; under the standard TF serving/untrusted-model model it is a denial of service.

verdict.summary: The Quantize kernel never validates that num_slices (input.dim_size(axis_), line 8) equals minmax_shape.num_elements() (the element count of input_min_range/input_max_range and of the freshly allocated output_min/output_max tensors). The slice loop (line 49) runs to num_slices while reading min_ranges(i)/max_ranges(i) and passing &output_min_tensor->flat<float>()(i) / &output_max_tensor->flat<float>()(i) into QuantizeSlice, which writes through those pointers. An attacker supplying a model with, e.g., axis=1, input shape [2,1000,2] and min/max range tensors of shape [1] causes roughly a thousand heap out-of-bounds reads and out-of-bounds writes of attacker-data-derived floats past 4-byte heap allocations, corrupting the heap of the process executing the untrusted model.

evidence.reason: Unguarded sink: the loop is bounded by num_slices (attacker-controlled via axis_ and input shape) but min_ranges/max_ranges and output_min_tensor/output_max_tensor contain only minmax_shape.num_elements() elements. For i >= minmax_shape.num_elements(), min_ranges(i)/max_ranges(i) read out of bounds and &output_min_tensor->flat<float>()(i) / &output_max_tensor->flat<float>()(i) are out-of-bounds element addresses that QuantizeSlice writes through, producing heap out-of-bounds reads and writes. No statement in this code equates num_slices with minmax_shape.num_elements().

Origin of the tainted loop bound: num_slices is taken from the attacker-controlled input tensor's axis_ dimension, fully decoupled from the independent attacker-controlled shape of input_min_range/input_max_range (minmax_shape).

The output min/max tensors are allocated with minmax_shape (e.g., 1 element) while the loop at line 49 indexes them up to num_slices-1 (e.g., 999); this is the size the missing num_slices == minmax_shape.num_elements() check should protect, and no such check exists on any path.

assumptions: Eigen single-index operator() and TF vec<float>() perform no release-build bounds enforcement; this is assumed (and no bounds check exists in the given code), since the Eigen/Tensor internals are not shown.

Op-level shape inference / attribute validation code is not shown; per guard anchoring it cannot be used to reject the primary candidate, whose trigger is instantiated entirely by statements in this code.
limitations: Candidate dismissed as speculative: axis_ >= input.dims() would make input.dim_size(axis_) (line 8) and output->dim_size(i) (line 40) access dimensions past the tensor rank, but the concrete release-build behavior of TensorShape::dim_size past rank is outside the given code and could not be instantiated beyond the num_slices defect.

Candidate dismissed as speculative: if input_min_range/input_max_range are empty tensors on the num_slices == 1 path, input_min_range.template flat<float>()(0) (lines 21-22) reads from an empty/possibly null base; reachability of an empty tensor past op shape checks is not shown, and the primary finding does not depend on it.
The exact contents written out of bounds are computed quantization min/max floats derived from attacker input data, so the attacker influences but does not fully control the written values.

verdict.summary: Matrix dimensions are read as int64 via dim_size() but stored into 32-bit int variables (m, k, n, k2). The only guards (k == k2 and m/n/k >= 0) operate on the already-truncated values, so a dimension of 2^32+3 truncates to 3 and passes all checks. The output is then allocated from the truncated dims (TensorShape({m, n})) while the Eigen contract / DoMatMul compute from the tensors' real int64 shapes, producing a massive heap out-of-bounds write (e.g., a 4294967299x1 result written into a 3x1 buffer).

evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted values: dim_size() returns int64 but the receivers m, k, n, k2 are int, truncating attacker-controlled dimensions across the 32-bit boundary (4294967299 becomes 3).

The output buffer is sized from the truncated m and n; with a.dim_size(0)=4294967299 the guard at line 18 (m >= 0 && n >= 0 && k >= 0, checked only on the truncated int) passes and only a 3 x n buffer is allocated.

Unguarded write sink: the contract computes from the tensors' real shapes (4294967299 x 1 result) and writes into the undersized 3 x n output TensorMap, a heap out-of-bounds write; no dimension-consistency check between out and the contract operands exists anywhere in this code.

assumptions: The op consumes tensors and attributes (transpose_a_, transpose_b_, a_is_sparse_, b_is_sparse_) supplied across a service boundary (session client / graph author), per the attacker-impact model.
Eigen release builds elide dimension-mismatch assertions; no such check is quotable in the given code, so the contract sink is treated as unguarded here.

Triggering requires materializing a tensor with a dimension >= 2^32 (~17 GB for the minimal [2^32+3, 1] float matrix), which is feasible on large-memory hosts running TF servers; the allocation itself can be induced by a small request (e.g., a Fill op node).
limitations: Potential bfloat16 type confusion in the sparse transpose_b path (right_tr allocated with right->dtype() but shuffled via matrix<TR>()/matrix<TL>()) would surface as a dtype CHECK abort, not memory corruption, and requires a kernel-registration contract violation not producible by statements in this code — speculative.
Negative truncation (e.g., dim 2^31+5) is correctly rejected by the quotable guard 'OP_REQUIRES(ctx, m >= 0 && n >= 0 && k >= 0, ...)' and is not a defect.
The k==k2 truncation-bypass variant causes an out-of-bounds read of b during contraction in addition to the write overflow; it shares the same root cause (lines 9-12).

verdict.summary: adts_decode_extradata sizes a bitstream reader over attacker-supplied extradata (`init_get_bits(&gb, buf, size * 8)`) and, when the parsed channel configuration is 0, calls ff_copy_pce_data(&pb, &gb) without ever checking how many bits remain in gb. The PCE's element and comment counts are read from the same attacker bits, so a short extradata declaring a full PCE drives get_bits reads hundreds of bits past the end of buf. The out-of-bounds bytes are stored in adts->pce_data with the recorded pce_size and later emitted into the muxer's ADTS output, giving an out-of-bounds heap read with disclosure potential.

evidence.reason: The sink: ff_copy_pce_data(&pb, &gb) reads the PCE from gb, whose loop counts come from the attacker's bits, but the function never validates the reader's remaining bits (no get_bits_left check exists anywhere in the code). With an 8-byte extradata whose parsed chan_config is 0 and whose PCE declares maximal element/comment counts, the copy consumes ~600 bits against 48 remaining, reading past the end of buf; the read bytes are captured in pce_data/pce_size and later written to the output ADTS stream. Trigger fully instantiated from attacker-controlled extradata content alone.

Origin of the tainted reader: gb is bounded to exactly size*8 bits of the attacker-supplied extradata, yet after skip_bits_long(&gb, off) (line 12) and three flag bits (lines 25, 29, 33) no statement in the function accounts for the remaining bits before the PCE copy at line 41, so the reader index can exceed the buffer the attacker truncated.

assumptions: ff_copy_pce_data consumes PCE fields (element counts, LFE/aux/comment counts) from gb via get_bits with loop bounds taken from those attacker-read values and performs no remaining-bits check of its own; the function body is not shown, but the copy sink is reached with a reader this code sized and never re-validated.
avpriv_mpeg4audio_get_config2 returns a non-negative bit offset within the parsed configuration for well-formed prefixes and fills m4ac; the parse is of attacker bytes but its body is not shown.

skip_bits_long and the default bitstream reader clamp the index to size_in_bits+8, so the three single-bit flag reads at lines 25/29/33 stay within the reader's padding allowance; this behavior is in code not shown.
The struct definition (not shown) allocates pce_data[MAX_PCE_SIZE] large enough for the structural maximum of a PCE, so the put_bits write side is bounded; the defect is on the read side.
limitations: size * 8 at line 8 overflows signed int when size >= 268435456 (2^28): the overflow occurs in this code, but instantiating it requires the upstream demuxer to supply a >=256 MiB extradata buffer, a trigger state no statement in this code can produce; additionally init_get_bits' internal validation of the negative bit count is not shown and the return value at line 8 is ignored. Recorded as speculative, not counted toward the verdict.

If avpriv_mpeg4audio_get_config2 can return off > size*8 (parser over-read), the reader index after line 12 would already be past the buffer; this depends on parser behavior not shown and could not be instantiated here.

Worst case for the primary finding is a bounded over-read (hundreds of bytes past buf) that is either disclosed via pce_data in the output stream or crashes the process while processing untrusted file content; since the input crosses a trust boundary and disclosure is possible, it is treated as a vulnerability, not mere robustness.

verdict.summary: setup_seccomp consumes only contract inputs and one attacker-influenced string (arch), whose content is used exclusively in strcmp comparisons against compile-time literals to select constant libseccomp architecture IDs; no attacker-controlled value reaches any memory, size, index, allocation, command, path, or injection sink. All loop bounds are compile-time constants or static NULL-terminated arrays, allocation and export results are checked, and the tmpfile is created anonymously with a constant path. The error paths that ignore non-EFAULT seccomp_rule_add failures and the ignored seccomp_rule_add_exact returns are fail-open in shape, but every argument to those calls is a compile-time constant or pre-validated within the function, so no attacker-reachable input can instantiate a trigger; these and the devel-mode relaxations are design/robustness limitations, not vulnerabilities in this code.
