verdict.summary: In njs_module_path, when dir != NULL the bounds check 'if (njs_slow_path(length > NJS_MAX_PATH))' only accounts for dir->length + 1 (trailing slash) because line 'length = dir->length;' overwrites the earlier 'length = info->name.length;'. The subsequent njs_cpymem(p, info->name.start, info->name.length) then copies an attacker-controlled module-name string of unbounded length into the fixed stack buffer char src[NJS_MAX_PATH + 1], producing a stack buffer overflow with attacker-chosen bytes. Trigger: any import/require name longer than NJS_MAX_PATH - dir->length - 1 resolved against a non-NULL search directory.

evidence.reason: This assignment discards the module-name length previously stored at 'length = info->name.length;' (line 9), so the guard 'if (njs_slow_path(length > NJS_MAX_PATH))' at line 25 validates only dir->length + trail and never bounds info->name.length, although that many attacker-controlled bytes are copied into src[NJS_MAX_PATH + 1] at line 39.

Unguarded sink: njs_cpymem copies info->name.length attacker-supplied bytes (the import module name from executed JS source, e.g. 4096 bytes) into the stack buffer src[NJS_MAX_PATH + 1] at offset dir->length + trail, writing far past the end of the buffer; the trailing NUL write is likewise out of bounds. Simulated trigger: dir = {"/opt/lib", 8}, name length 4096 → check at line 25 sees length 9, passes, copy writes src[9..4104] past the 2049-byte buffer.

assumptions: NJS_MAX_PATH is the njs header constant (2048 in upstream njs); the finding holds for any value since info->name.length is never bounded in the dir != NULL branch.
info->path is assumed declared as char path[NJS_MAX_PATH + 1] by the njs_module_info_t definition (not shown); the realpath sink was not treated as overflowing on that basis.

dir points at the configured module search directories supplied by the caller (njs module lookup); at least one non-NULL dir is used in the normal import-resolution flow, which is the branch containing the defect.

The module name info->name is parsed from the executed JavaScript source; the attacker model assumes script content crossing a trust boundary (untrusted script executed by the engine), which is the standard intake for this function.
limitations: The dir == NULL branch is safely bounded: length = info->name.length is checked against NJS_MAX_PATH before the copy, and the NUL write at index NJS_MAX_PATH fits exactly in src[NJS_MAX_PATH + 1].
dir->start[dir->length - 1] at line 18 is guarded by the preceding 'if (length == 0) { return NJS_DECLINED; }' check, so no underflow index is reachable.
Integer wrap of length++ would require dir->length == SIZE_MAX, not producible from operator-configured search paths, and the subsequent check would reject it anyway.

verdict.summary: DecodeChunk validates attacker-controlled 64-bit chunk offsets with wrap-prone arithmetic: `offsets[i] + k > size` wraps modulo 2^64 for offset values near UINT64_MAX, so the check passes and `head + offsets[i]` points before the buffer. The subsequent memcpy calls then read out of bounds (up to 8 bytes in the scanline path, 16 bytes in the tiled path, stored into decoded-image tile metadata), giving an out-of-bounds read with heap disclosure and crash potential from a crafted EXR offset table.

evidence.reason: Defective guard: offsets[y_idx] is an attacker-controlled uint64 from the EXR offset table; adding sizeof(int)*2 in 64-bit unsigned arithmetic wraps for offsets near 2^64 (e.g., 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF8 + 8 = 0), so the check passes and no other bound on offsets exists in this code.

Instantiated OOB read sink: with offsets[0] = 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF8 and size = 100, the line-184 guard computes 0 and passes, data_ptr becomes head - 8, and memcpy reads bytes head[-8..-5] outside the size-byte buffer (line 197 reads head[-4..-1] likewise); triggered purely by file-supplied offset values.

Defective guard in the tiled branch: same integer wrap; with offsets[tile_idx] = 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF0 the sum is 4 (mod 2^64), the check passes for any size >= 4, and no other validation of offsets exists in this code.

Instantiated OOB read sink: data_ptr = head + 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF0 wraps to head - 16 and memcpy reads 16 bytes entirely before the buffer; those bytes become tile_coordinates[0..3], and lines 149-150 store them as exr_image->tiles[].offset_x/offset_y, disclosing adjacent heap memory through the decoded image.

assumptions: offsets, head and size are supplied by the EXR parsing caller from the file's chunk offset table and byte stream; per the trust model these are attacker-data and this function is the intake point responsible for validating them against size — no external validation was assumed.

Helper functions ComputeChannelLayout, AllocateImage, DecodePixelData and DecodeTiledPixelData are not shown; none of their internal behavior is relied on for the confirmed findings, whose sinks (the memcpy calls) are in this code.
limitations: 32-bit-only: size_t(data_width) * size_t(data_height) * size_t(num_channels) (lines 160-161) can wrap on 32-bit size_t, and the guard at line 162 is explicitly fail-open there (`sizeof(void*) == 8 ? ... : false`); the harmful allocation-sizing sink is inside AllocateImage (not shown), so this is speculative for the given code.

data_window[3] + 1 (line 214-215) signed-overflows when data_window[3] == INT_MAX (reachable since only data_height is bounded), but the wrapped end_line_no forces num_lines <= 0 -> invalid_data; no memory-unsafe use in this code.

calloc (lines 82-83) and AllocateImage (lines 87, 174) results are not NULL-checked; triggering requires an allocation failure inducible only with an enormous attacker-supplied offset table, and the failure mode is a NULL-deref crash of the decoding process.
static_cast<int>(num_blocks) (line 181) and static_cast<int>(num_tiles) (line 154) truncate only when offsets.size() > INT_MAX, which requires a multi-gigabyte offset table.
Early returns inside the tile loop (lines 98, 114, 117, 129) leak the already-allocated tiles/images (robustness, not security).
invalid_data is written from OpenMP parallel threads (acknowledged at line 58) — a data race on an error flag with no security impact.
Non-wrapped offset values are handled correctly by the existing guards (verified at boundaries: offset = size-8 and offset = size-7); only values within 8/20 of 2^64 wrap.

verdict.summary: In the GPU MatrixSolve kernel, the dimension reads 'const int64 n = input.dim_size(ndims - 1);' and 'const int64 nrhs = rhs.dim_size(ndims - 1);' are executed before any rank validation. The checks 'ndims >= 2' and 'rhs.dims() == ndims' appear only afterwards, so an attacker (session/Serving client) passing a scalar input (ndims = 0 -> dim_size(-1)) or a rank-mismatched rhs (e.g., input rank 2, rhs rank 1 -> rhs.dim_size(1) beyond rhs's rank) causes an out-of-domain/negative index into the TensorShape storage, an out-of-bounds read that can abort the process (denial of service across the service boundary).

evidence.reason: Unvalidated index use before validation: ndims comes from the attacker-controlled input tensor rank and is immediately used as index ndims-1 on input (line 5) and, using input's rank instead of rhs's own rank, on rhs (line 6). With a scalar input ndims = 0 gives dim_size(-1); with input rank 2 and rhs rank 1, rhs.dim_size(1) reads beyond rhs's rank. No check on ndims or rhs.dims() precedes these lines, so the negative/out-of-range index reaches the shape accessor, an out-of-bounds read triggered by a single attacker-supplied op call.

evidence.snippet:
OP_REQUIRES_ASYNC(
        context, ndims >= 2,
        errors::InvalidArgument("Input must have rank >= 2, got ", ndims),
        done);
evidence.reason: The guard that would reject ndims = 0 (and, together with the later 'rhs.dims() == ndims' check, the rank mismatch) is placed only after the dim_size(ndims - 1) reads, so it never protects lines 5-6: it is a check positioned after the use, the root cause of the improper index validation.

assumptions: TensorShape/Tensor::dim_size is a helper not shown; per guard anchoring, any bounds enforcement inside it cannot be relied on, and this code supplies it an out-of-domain index (ndims-1 with ndims = 0, or an index beyond rhs's rank) with no preceding check.
adjoint_ and CudaSolver helpers (GetrfBatched, GetrsBatched, scratch allocation) are assumed to honor their documented contracts; the analysis only relies on the values this code passes to them.
The op's input tensors are attacker-data: the kernel is the public entry point consuming session-supplied tensor shapes, and no shape constraint code is present in this function.
limitations: Signed overflow in the batching loops 'for (int batch = 0; batch < batch_size; ++batch)' (int counter vs int64 bound) would produce negative wild-pointer writes once batch_size >= 2^31, but triggering requires successfully allocating tens of GB of tensors (input, rhs, pivots, copies) in a single op call; this precondition could not be instantiated from the code itself and is recorded as speculative.
'128 * batch_size' can overflow only at batch_size >= 2^57, unreachable given the allocations that must succeed first.

The garbage values returned by the out-of-bounds dim_size reads are discarded by the subsequent validation checks, so there is no direct information-disclosure path; the demonstrated impact is the out-of-bounds read/undefined behavior and potential process abort (remote denial of service).

verdict.summary: pjmedia_rtcp_xr_rx_rtcp_xr parses attacker-controlled RTCP XR report blocks without validating that each block's length (rb_len) or extent fits within the received packet buffer. The loop condition only checks each block header's start position, and the sole check on rb_len is `if (rb_len)`, which merely skips zero-length blocks. A remote RTCP peer can send a block with bt=BT_STATS/BT_VOIP_METRICS/BT_RR_TIME/BT_DLRR and a minimal rb_len; the code then reads the full fixed-size block struct (12 to ~80 bytes) from the buffer, causing a heap out-of-bounds read of up to tens of bytes past the packet buffer, with the leaked values stored into session statistics and log output.

evidence.reason: Missing-check site (root cause): the loop bound only validates that each report block's header START lies inside the declared packet; the attacker-controlled block length rb_len is never compared against pkt_len, size, or the minimum struct size required by the block type. The only guard, `if (rb_len)`, just skips zero-length blocks, so a block declaring rb_len=1 (8 bytes) is accepted for struct types of 12-80 bytes.

Tainted-pointer origin: rb_stats aliases rb_hdr, whose block extent was never validated; with a 16-byte packet (pkt_len=3, size=16), the check `if ((pkt_len + 1) > (size / 4))` passes at exactly the limit, and a BT_STATS block with rb_len=1 at word 2 sets rb_stats = pkt+8 from which ~40 bytes are subsequently read.

Out-of-bounds read sink: with the instantiated trigger (size=16, pkt_len=3, BT_STATS block at word 2 with specific=0xFF and rb_len=1), rb_stats->lost reads bytes 16-19 of a 16-byte buffer, and subsequent dup/jitter/toh reads extend ~28 bytes past the heap buffer; the values are stored into sess->stat.tx.stat_sum, which is queryable and logged.

Largest overread sink of the same root cause: a BT_VOIP_METRICS block (struct ~80 bytes) placed near the buffer end with an unvalidated rb_len causes reads up to ~72 bytes past the packet buffer, reaching line 183 onward with all preconditions instantiated by the same 16-byte trigger packet.

assumptions: pkt and size carry a received RTCP XR packet from a remote media peer; this function is the decoder/intake for that data, so packet content (including bt, specific, and block length fields) is attacker-influenced.

Struct sizes (pjmedia_rtcp_xr_rb_rr_time and rb_dlrr = 12 bytes, rb_stats ≈ 40 bytes, rb_voip_mtc ≈ 80 bytes, report-block header = 4 bytes, rtcp_xr->buf at byte offset 8) are taken from the PJSIP headers these types belong to; the given snippet does not include the struct definitions.
pj_ntohs/pj_ntohl perform byte-order conversion without validation, as their contracts state.
limitations: Lines 14 and 17 read rtcp_xr->common.pt and rtcp_xr->common.length before any check that size >= 4; a size < 4 would cause a 1-3 byte overread. The trigger could not be instantiated from statements in this code (RTCP sub-packet sizes are conventionally derived from length fields as (len+1)*4 >= 4 at the caller, which is not shown), so this is recorded as a speculative secondary issue, not a finding.
The pointer advance at lines 46-47 can move rb_hdr past one-past-the-end of the buffer, but the loop condition at line 23 then terminates the loop before any dereference; no security impact.
No out-of-bounds write exists in this function: all writes target the sess structure; the defect class is limited to out-of-bounds reads.

verdict.summary: updateDigestForSessionId hashes only operator-controlled configuration (CA cert, pin lists, SAN matchers, CRL, policy flags) into a session-ID digest; no network-attacker data reaches any sink. All memory operations are bounded: X509_digest output is fixed by EVP_sha256() (32 bytes into an EVP_MAX_MD_SIZE buffer), container updates pass lengths matched to their own data pointers with byte-sized value_type (no scaling or overflow at realistic sizes), scalar updates use fixed sizeof, and null guards 'if (ca_cert_ != nullptr)' and 'if (config_ != nullptr)' are present on all dereference paths. No trigger with attacker-instantiated preconditions and boundary-crossing impact could be simulated.

assumptions: Member fields (ca_cert_, verify_certificate_hash_list_, verify_certificate_spki_list_, verify_trusted_ca_, config_) are initialized by the class constructor, which is not shown; no statement in this code leaves them unwritten.
bssl::ScopedEVP_MD_CTX md is initialized by the caller before this function is invoked (interface contract; the parameter is a reference).
EVP_DigestUpdate in BoringSSL accepts a zero-length update without dereferencing a null data pointer.
MessageUtil::hash(matcher) returns a size_t (std::hash-style, non-cryptographic); this is a design weakening of the config binding but is not attacker-instantiable since matchers are operator config.
limitations: Speculative: size_t overflow in 'hash.size() * sizeof(value_type)' requires a near-SIZE_MAX container size that no code path or realistic config can produce.

Speculative: two distinct SAN-matcher sets colliding under MessageUtil::hash could weaken the session-resumption config binding, but both configurations originate from the operator, not from a network attacker; no trust boundary is crossed.

Speculative: the comment claims all acceptance-relevant settings are hashed; a validator setting omitted from this digest would allow resumption across mismatched configs, but no specific omitted field is identifiable from the given code.

Robustness only: an empty pin-list container passes data()==nullptr with length 0 to EVP_DigestUpdate; zero-length updates are handled by BoringSSL and the input is operator config, so no security effect.

verdict.summary: RestoreTensor validates restore_index only against input 1's element count (line 17-18: "OP_REQUIRES(context, size > restore_index, ...)" where size = tensor_name_t.NumElements()), then indexes input 2 with the same unvalidated index at line 59-60 ("context->input(2).flat<tstring>()(restore_index)") without any check of input 2's NumElements. An attacker across the op-input trust boundary (e.g., a session client issuing a restore op with restore_slice=true, tensor_names of N>=1 elements, and shape_and_slices of 0 or fewer than N elements) causes a heap out-of-bounds read of a 32-byte tstring object; the OOB tstring's metadata is then read by .empty() and its view/pointer fields are dereferenced by ParseShapeAndSlice, enabling further out-of-bounds/arbitrary reads with memory-disclosure potential or a crash. The trigger needs no caller-contract violation: even a fully valid restore_index=0 with an empty input 2 triggers the OOB read.

evidence.reason: Heap out-of-bounds read (CWE-125, root cause CWE-129): input 2 is indexed with restore_index without any validation of its element count. The only bounds check on restore_index in the function applies to a different variable ("const int64_t size = tensor_name_t.NumElements(); OP_REQUIRES(context, size > restore_index, ...)" at lines 17-18) and constrains input 1, not input 2. Trigger instantiated with restore_index=0, input(1) of 1 element (passes line 18), input(2) of 0 elements: flat<tstring>()(0) reads a tstring past an empty heap buffer; .empty() (line 61) and ParseShapeAndSlice (lines 63-65) then read and dereference the OOB object's metadata/pointer fields.

assumptions: restore_index is supplied by the caller (an op loop index); the analysis does not rely on its provenance because the OOB trigger holds for in-contract values (restore_index=0) whenever input 2 is smaller than input 1.

checkpoint::ParseShapeAndSlice and reader->CopySliceData internals are not shown; whether slice_to_load is validated to fit inside parsed_shape/output_shape inside those helpers cannot be verified from the given code.

restore_slice=true is assumed to imply the op registered a third input (op-registration contract), so context->input(2) itself exists; the defect is the missing size check, not the access to the input slot.
Eigen's flat()(i) accessor is assumed to perform no release-mode bounds checking, consistent with the known behavior of Eigen TensorMap in TensorFlow release builds.
limitations: Line 51 uses context->expected_output_dtype(0) instead of restore_index in the error message text; cosmetic diagnostic defect with no security effect.

Attacker-supplied saved_shape drives allocate_output(restore_index, output_shape, &t); the allocation is bounded by the attacker's own checkpoint size and allocator limits, so no amplification beyond input scale was provable.
CopySliceData write-sizing could not be analyzed because its implementation is not shown; any defect there would be in code outside the given snippet.

If this code were run entirely in-process by the same user who supplies all inputs and files (no service boundary), the crash-only portion of the outcome would be a robustness issue; the finding stands on the op-input trust boundary that this function's own input handling implements.

verdict.summary: In yank_copy_line, the trailing-whitespace loop tests the byte at bd->textstart + s - 1 before testing s > 0 (C evaluates the left operand of && first). When the yanked region is entirely whitespace (or textlen is 0), s reaches exactly 0 and the loop condition dereferences bd->textstart[-1], a one-byte out-of-bounds heap read before the start of the line text. The s > 0 bound exists but is a check-after-use; no earlier guard on s exists anywhere in the function.

evidence.reason: Check-after-use / boundary defect at the memory-read sink: the dereference *(bd->textstart + s - 1) is evaluated before the s > 0 guard on the right of &&. With attacker-supplied all-whitespace yanked text (or textlen == 0), s decrements to exactly 0 (mb_head_off returns 0 for ASCII whitespace in the s update on line 23), so the condition reads bd->textstart[-1], one byte before the region, a heap out-of-bounds read; the trigger is fully instantiated by the simulation and the bound check is absent from every earlier line.

Origin of the tainted index: s is initialized from attacker-influenced bd->textlen (line content length) plus bd->endspaces (zeroed at line 6 on the exclude_trailing_space path) with no lower-bound or positivity check, allowing s to be 0 when the line-21 dereference computes the index s - 1 = -1.

assumptions: bd->textstart is assumed to point at a valid region of at least bd->textlen bytes and bd->textlen >= 0; the pointer itself is a contract argument, but the CONTENT it points to is attacker-supplied edited text, which is what drives s to 0.
bd->textlen, bd->startspaces, bd->endspaces are assumed non-negative per the block-parsing callers; no negative-value check exists in this code.
mb_head_off is assumed (per its semantics) to return 0 for ASCII whitespace bytes, which is why s decrements by exactly 1 per iteration and the loop terminates at s == 0 rather than going negative.
alloc() is assumed to return NULL on failure only; the NULL case is handled at lines 7-9.
limitations: The write *pnew = NUL (line 27) was analyzed and is in-bounds: the line-7 allocation of startspaces+endspaces+textlen+1 bytes bounds pnew, and loop iterations (each decrementing s by at least 1 via line 23) keep pnew >= base + startspaces.

y_current->y_array[y_idx] (line 10) has no bounds check in this function; y_idx is a contract index supplied by the caller's yank loop over the array that caller allocated, so it is not treated as attacker-data here.
Integer overflow in the line-7 allocation size would require bd->textlen near INT_MAX, which this code's own statements cannot produce; speculative.

The out-of-bounds byte read at bd->textstart[-1] does not flow into any output (the loop exits at s == 0 regardless of the byte's value), so impact is the OOB read itself and crash potential under hardened allocators, not direct information disclosure.

verdict.summary: The grouped convolution launcher computes num_groups = in_depth / patch_depth directly from attacker-controlled tensor shapes (line 12) with no check that patch_depth is nonzero or that in_depth is divisible by patch_depth. A crafted Conv2D op in a model with filter dim_size(2)==0 causes a SIGFPE at line 12; a filter whose patch_depth exceeds the input depth makes num_groups==0, and the lambdas at lines 18-21/24-27 then divide by num_groups (first invoked via allocate_temp at line 37), also causing a SIGFPE; non-divisible depths cause CHECK-fail aborts in Tensor::shaped. Any of these deterministically kills the process (e.g., a serving process) that ingests the untrusted model, a denial-of-service impact across the trust boundary.

evidence.reason: Root cause and primary sink: patch_depth comes from the attacker-controlled filter shape (line 11) and is used as a divisor at line 12 with no validation for zero or divisibility. Instantiated trigger: a model with a Conv2D filter of shape [3,3,0,8] gives patch_depth=0 and in_depth/patch_depth raises SIGFPE at line 12, terminating the process consuming the untrusted model.

Second divide-by-zero sink: when patch_depth > in_depth (e.g., input depth 2, filter patch_depth 8), line 12 truncates num_groups to 0, and this lambda, first invoked at line 37 (TensorShape(post_shuffle(input)) inside allocate_temp), executes tensor.dim_size(3) / 0, producing a SIGFPE. The zero divisor is produced by this code's own statement at line 12, and no guard on num_groups exists on any path.

assumptions: The size of explicit_paddings (must be 2*rank, i.e., 8 entries for Conv2D, when padding==EXPLICIT) is validated by the op-level caller code not shown; this code indexes explicit_paddings[2..5] (lines 76-79) with no local size check.
row_stride, col_stride, row_dilation, col_dilation are consumed by the op's shape function to size the output tensor and are passed through to SpatialConvolution unvalidated here (contract).
data_format routing (only NHWC reaches this functor) is enforced by the caller; the sole local check, DCHECK(data_format == FORMAT_NHWC) at line 6, compiles out in release builds.
Tensor shapes are treated as attacker-data per the untrusted-model threat model: the originator of the SavedModel/graph controls filter and input shapes.
limitations: OOB read candidate on explicit_paddings[2..5] with a short vector under padding==EXPLICIT is speculative: triggering requires the unseen op-level validation to be bypassed; the precondition could not be instantiated within this code.

The non-divisible case where per-group element counts coincidentally match (e.g., in_depth=6, patch_depth=4 giving num_groups=1 and per-group input depth 6 > filter depth 4) yields semantically incorrect convolution output (Eigen under-read) rather than memory corruption; integrity issue only.

Impact of the confirmed defects is process termination (SIGFPE / CHECK-fail abort), i.e., denial of service on the process ingesting the attacker's model; no memory corruption, disclosure, or injection was demonstrated.

verdict.summary: This function is a thin delegation wrapper: it copies params.axis and params.batch_dims into op_params and forwards input/positions/output tensors to optimized_ops::Gather. No memory access, allocation, arithmetic, loop, or injection sink exists in the given code, so no trigger can be instantiated within this snippet. Potential out-of-bounds indexing of input by unchecked positions values would occur inside optimized_ops::Gather, whose body was not provided and cannot be analyzed here.

verdict.summary: NULL pointer dereference in the MOOV handling of gf_isom_parse_movie_boxes_internal: after parsing an attacker-supplied moov, every track in mov->moov->trackList is dereferenced as trak->Media->information->sampleTable->sampleGroups without any check that the attacker's moov actually contained the mandatory mdia/minf/stbl child boxes. verdict.summary: BD_DecMFFieldVec reads the vector length nbFields directly from the untrusted BIFS bitstream (up to 2^31-1 from 36 header bits) and uses it without any bound check to size the MF allocation (gf_sg_vrml_mf_alloc) and to drive the decode loop (for (i=0; i<nbFields; i++)). verdict.summary: In gf_avc_parse_nalu the return value of svc_parse_slice is deliberately discarded ('/*ret = */svc_parse_slice(bs, avc, &n_state);'), so when the attacker-controlled SVC slice payload fails to parse, n_state keeps an unset (NULL) sps pointer copied at line 13 from fresh state. That unvalidated state is passed unconditionally to avc_compute_poc at line 34 and committed to avc->s_info at lines 37/40, poisoning persistent parser state with nal_unit_type 20 and sps NULL. On a following regular slice NALU the code reaches 'if (avc->s_info.sps->poc_type == n_state.sps->poc_type)' guarded only by 'assert(avc->s_info.sps);', which is compiled out in release builds and never covers n_state.sps. A crafted H.264 stream containing a malformed SVC slice NALU therefore crashes the process parsing the untrusted media (NULL pointer dereference), a denial of service crossing the trust boundary between the file originator and the parser operator. The code demonstrates the correct error-check pattern for the sibling helper at line 54-55, confirming the omission at line 29 is the defect.

evidence.reason: Missing-check site: the error return of svc_parse_slice is discarded, so a failed parse of an attacker-crafted SVC slice leaves n_state.sps NULL (copied from fresh avc->s_info at line 13) and slice fields unpopulated; this state is then passed unconditionally to avc_compute_poc at line 34 and later committed to avc->s_info at lines 37/40. Trigger: first NALU of type 20 with malformed slice payload.

Unguarded dereference: avc->s_info.sps is checked only by an assert (a no-op under NDEBUG in release builds) and n_state.sps is never checked anywhere in the function. After the SVC path commits {nal_unit_type = 20, sps = NULL} into avc->s_info, a following regular slice NALU with matching frame_num, field_pic_flag and non-zero nal_ref_idc passes the comparisons at lines 58-76 and dereferences the NULL avc->s_info.sps here.

assumptions: AVCState and avc->s_info are zero-initialized before the first NALU (standard for a freshly reset parser), so avc->s_info.sps is NULL and nal_unit_type is 0 until a slice is committed by this function.

svc_parse_slice signals parse failure with a negative return value, consistent with the sibling helper avc_parse_slice whose return is checked at line 55 ('if (ret < 0) return ret;') and with the commented-out 'ret =' at line 29 showing the author knew it returns a status.
avc_compute_poc consumes si->sps (the POC computation needs the SPS poc_type), so passing a slice info with NULL sps is invalid input for it.
assert is compiled out under NDEBUG, i.e. release builds of the parser have no runtime guard at line 77.
limitations: The exact crash statement depends on helpers not shown: if avc_compute_poc dereferences si->sps unconditionally, the crash occurs inside the call at line 34; if it tolerates NULL, the poisoned commit at lines 37/40 leads to the crash directly at line 79 in this function. Either way the root cause, the discarded error return at line 29 plus the assert-only guard, is in this code.

Line 127 '(s32) gf_bs_read_ue(bs)' truncates a u32 to s32, but all values that become negative (0x80000000..0xFFFFFFFF) are rejected by line 128, and last_ps_idx is not used as an index within this function; no defect instantiated here.
All memcpy calls in this function are fixed-size same-structure copies (sizeof(AVCSliceInfo)); no variable-length copy or allocation-sizing defect exists in this code.
The impact is denial of service (process crash on parsing untrusted media); no memory corruption, disclosure, or injection sink was found in this function.

verdict.summary: The function builds the U2F signature payload into a fixed 200-byte stack buffer `data_signed` using a sequence of memcpy calls whose lengths (rpid_hash_len, credential_id_len, cert_x_len, cert_y_len) are attacker-controlled values from the WebAuthn registration response and are never bounds-checked against the buffer size. A network peer registering a credential can supply a credentialId (or COSE coordinate) longer than the remaining space, causing a stack buffer overflow with memory corruption; even a credentialId of 71 bytes with canonical component sizes writes past the end.

evidence.reason: Root cause: unchecked memcpy of attacker-controlled credential_id_len bytes into the fixed stack buffer data_signed[200] (declared line 9). No statement in the function compares data_signed_offset against the buffer size, so with a peer-supplied registration response containing a credentialId of, e.g., 300 bytes, execution reaches line 108 with data_signed_offset=65 and copies 300 bytes into a 200-byte stack buffer, writing 165 bytes out of bounds (memory corruption). The same unchecked pattern applies to lines 102, 111, 114, and 117.

Line 60's condition json_object_get(j_params, "root-ca-list") != json_null() is true when the key is missing (Jansson returns NULL) and false only when explicitly set to JSON null; whether this creates an authz gap depends on validate_certificate_from_root, which is not shown.
The MIN(o_strlen("x5c"), cbor_string_length(key)) prefix comparisons at lines 31 and 33 let short or empty map keys match; this is a robustness issue with no demonstrated security impact.

Even well-formed authenticator responses can overflow the buffer: standard component sizes leave only 70 bytes of headroom for the credentialId, which is commonly larger in practice, so the defect is reachable without malice as well as with it.

verdict.summary: mrb_ary_shift_m validates the shift count before every memory access: zero lengths return early (line 12), negative counts raise (line 13), and n > len is clamped to len (line 14). The element copy loop runs only with 1 <= n < len and touches indices strictly below len, and the shared pointer bump moves at most len elements. All guards were quoted and edge-tested (n = 0, n = len, n = len+1, n = -1, MRB_INT_MIN) and found correct, and the counterfactual search confirmed each needed check is present on the only path to each sink.

assumptions: mrb_get_args with format |i writes n only when it returns nonzero, and the shown code assumes it never executes guest Ruby code (no to_int callback); this is hidden callee behavior that could not be quoted.
ary_make_shared(mrb, a) sets the shared flag and preserves ARY_LEN and the buffer contents, so the goto at line 24 re-enters L_SHIFT only in a valid shared state.
ARY_LEN(a) equals a->as.heap.len for shared and heap arrays, and embedded arrays cannot exceed ARY_SHIFT_SHARED_MIN, so the ary_make_shared path is never taken for an embedded array.
The garbage collector does not move objects and keeps a reachable through the receiver on the VM stack and val through the GC arena across the allocating calls at lines 15 and 23.
ARY_SHIFT_SHARED_MIN is a positive constant and the core GC runs no Ruby level callbacks, so no re-entrancy window exists between the len capture at line 4 and its uses.
limitations: TOCTOU on len: len is captured at line 4 before the argument is parsed at line 8. If a build of mrb_get_args executed an attacker defined to_int that mutates the receiver, the clamp at line 14 would use a stale len and line 15 could read out of bounds (potential CWE-125). The trigger could not be instantiated because no statement in the given code provably runs guest code before line 15.

Uninitialized n (CWE-908): if mrb_get_args could return nonzero without writing n, lines 12 and 14 would read an uninitialized value. This requires the hidden callee to violate its format contract and was not instantiated.

If ary_make_shared returned without setting the shared flag, the goto at line 24 would bump the pointer of a non-shared array and later produce an interior pointer at free time; this depends entirely on hidden callee behavior.

When n equals len on the shared path, a->as.heap.ptr is left one element past the buffer end with len 0; within this function it is never dereferenced, and safety depends on length guards and the shared base pointer handling in the rest of array.c, which is not shown.

verdict.summary: This PixMap header parser reads only attacker-supplied file fields through bounds-checked reader helpers and contains no memory writes, allocation sizing, or injection sinks. The single arithmetic hazard, division by bi->pixelsize, is guarded on its only path by 'if(bi->pixelsize>0)', and the u16-derived divisor range 1..65535 excludes both zero and signed-overflow cases (edge-tested at 0, 1, 65535). The conditional read of bi->pdwidth when pixelsize==0 relies on the caller's zero-initialized struct (deark convention) and, even then, the value reaches only a clamp comparison with no security sink in this function.

assumptions: dbuf_getu16be, dbuf_getu32be, and pict_read_fixed are deark's bounds-checked readers that safely handle positions past the end of the data (returning 0), so the reads at pos+0 through pos+35 cannot access memory out of bounds; this enforcement lives in the dbuf layer and is not quotable from this code.

The struct fmtutil_macbitmap_info pointed to by bi is allocated zero-initialized by deark's callers (de_malloc zeroes memory), so bi->pdwidth is 0 rather than indeterminate when the pixelsize>0 branch is skipped.
bi->rowbytes and bi->npwidth are populated by the caller from 16-bit file fields, bounding bi->rowbytes*8 far below any i64 overflow; no in-function bound is quotable.
limitations: Potential use-of-uninitialized-value pattern (CWE-457): a crafted file setting pixelsize (u16 at pos+18) to 0 causes 'if(bi->pdwidth < bi->npwidth)' to read a field this function never wrote on that path. The trigger is speculative: indeterminacy requires a caller to violate the zero-initialization contract, and within this function the value only affects a clamp comparison (no memory, disclosure, or injection sink).
bi->rowbytes*8 could overflow only if rowbytes approached 2^61, which the u16-derived caller source cannot produce; an incorrect pdwidth also has no sink inside this function.
Truncating casts (int)pos, (int)pack_size, (int)plane_bytes affect debug output text only and have no security effect.

If the dbuf reader layer did not bounds-check, reads at pos+0..pos+35 with an out-of-range pos could misbehave, but no statement in this code can produce such a pos, and the worst case would be a crash of the process the operator ran on the attacker's own file.

verdict.summary: MakeDataset validates only tensor ranks, never dtypes or element contents: attacker-supplied tensors of a non-int64 dtype, or a dense_shape with negative/overflowing elements, reach matrix<int64>() (line 32), vec<int64>() and TensorShape(...) (line 44), whose internal CHECK failures abort the whole process. As a public op kernel that is the intake point for graph/session-supplied tensors, this is an attacker-triggerable denial of service on a shared TensorFlow process.

evidence.snippet:
for (int64_t i = 0; i < indices->dim_size(0); ++i) {

dense_shape is only rank-checked (lines 19-22): a non-int64 dense_shape CHECK-aborts inside vec<int64>(), and an int64 dense_shape with negative or overflowing elements CHECK-aborts inside the TensorShape constructor, again aborting the process from attacker-controlled input.

The abort behavior of Tensor::matrix<int64>()/vec<int64>() (CHECK on dtype) and of the TensorShape constructor (CHECK on negative/overflowing dims) is TensorFlow framework behavior, not visible in the given code.
