GetStagingMap (line 3) is assumed to return a valid map or an error status such that OP_REQUIRES_OK prevents any NULL dereference at line 31; its implementation is not shown.
Node attributes from def() (capacity, memory_limit, dtypes, shapes, shared_name) are consumed by GetStagingMap/put, not by this code; their default values and enforcement are unknown.
The attacker model assumes graph/program authors are untrusted relative to the process running the model (TensorFlow threat model); input reachability is not in question, only in-code consequence.
limitations: SPECULATIVE (C1): indices_tensor is fetched at line 12 and forwarded to map->put at line 31 with no validation of dtype, shape, or element count, in contrast to the two checks applied to key_tensor. If StagingMap<Ordered>::put reads indices as flat int64 scalar data without its own checks, an empty or mistyped indices tensor could cause a CHECK-failure abort or an out-of-bounds read there. That defective statement is outside the given code, so this candidate could not be triggered within this analysis and must not flip the verdict.

SPECULATIVE (C2): the error message claims 'key must be an int64 scalar' but the code only enforces NumElements() == 1; a scalar key of any dtype passes. Harm requires an unshown consumer (put/get/peek) to reinterpret the key as int64; unverifiable here.

SPECULATIVE (C3): values_tensor dtypes/shapes are not checked against the map's declared attributes before insertion; if put trusts them, a dtype-confusion-on-read could occur when the tuple is later retrieved. Sink external.

SPECULATIVE (C4): no capacity or memory-limit check appears in this code before insertion; unbounded retention (CWE-400-style) is possible only if both the map attributes and put permit it, which cannot be established from the given code, and unlimited staging buffers are the op's documented design.

verdict.summary: pj_scan_get_char validates the current pointer against scanner->end and rejects NUL before every buffer read; the sole pointer advance (a single ++ of a guarded in-bounds pointer) cannot exceed end, and the post-increment dereference is short-circuited by the PJ_SCAN_CHECK_EOF EOF check on the same condition chain. No attacker-instantiable memory-safety, validation, or injection defect exists in the given code; the only candidate depending on an unshown macro (PJ_SCAN_CHECK_EOF) is speculative.

assumptions: PJ_SCAN_CHECK_EOF(c) and PJ_SCAN_IS_PROBABLY_SPACE(c) are pjlib scanner.h macros whose definitions are not included in the given code; PJ_SCAN_CHECK_EOF is assumed to perform the end-pointer EOF check (c != scanner->end) that its name and its uniform pre-deref usage in pjlib indicate. The analysis of the post-increment *s depends on this.

scanner->curptr and scanner->end are assumed to satisfy the pj_scan_init contract (curptr <= end, end within/at one past the buffer); a scanner initialized otherwise is a contract violation, not attacker data, and the entry guard s >= scanner->end additionally contains curptr > end corruption.

pj_scan_syntax_err invoked on attacker-supplied content could terminate the process if the scanner were initialized without a recovery handler; that behavior resides in code not shown and is a contract/robustness concern, not an instantiated vulnerability here, since this function itself returns 0 (fail-closed) on that path.
The signed-char widening in 'chr = *s' returns a negative int for bytes >= 0x80; no sink in this function consumes it for memory access or sizing, so it has no security effect in the given code.

verdict.summary: ValidateInputs is the trust-boundary validation gate for the SparseDenseCwise* ops but is incomplete. It verifies only that a_indices is a matrix (line 3) and never checks a_indices->dim_size(1) against the rank it itself fixes and enforces for a_shape (line 16 and the per-dimension loop at lines 22-23), and it never checks that a_values has as many elements as a_indices has rows. An attacker supplying op inputs with a_indices of shape [N, K] where K != b->dims() (or a short a_values) receives Status::OK, and the consuming functor then indexes a_indices(i, j) for j in [0, b->dims()) (and a_values(i) for i < N), reading past the end of the attacker-sized heap buffers — an out-of-bounds read in the shared model-serving process, plus downstream use of the out-of-bounds index values.

evidence.reason: a_indices is an attacker-controlled op input, and this IsMatrix check is the ONLY validation it receives; it establishes merely that the shape has 2 dimensions. The function goes on to fix the sparse rank equal to b->dims() and to verify a_shape per-dimension, but no statement anywhere checks a_indices->dim_size(1) == b->dims(). Simulated trigger: a_indices of shape [3,1] with a_shape [2]{2,2} and b <2,2> passes every check and reaches `return Status::OK();` at line 30 with dim_size(1)=1 != rank=2, so the consumer indexes a_indices(i, j) for j in [0,2) and reads past the [3,1] heap buffer — heap out-of-bounds read enabled by the missing check.

This is the rank-invariant origin on the candidate's data-flow path: the function enforces sparse rank == dense rank and per-dimension equality for a_shape, yet applies no analogous dimension check to a_indices->dim_size(1), which must equal that same rank under the SparseTensor contract. This asymmetry is the enabling condition for the out-of-bounds read.

Same root cause, second instance: a_values is validated only to be a vector; a_values->NumElements() is never compared to a_indices->dim_size(0). Trigger: a_indices [5,2] with a_values [1] passes all checks and returns Status::OK at line 30, so the consumer reads a_values(i) for i < 5 past the 1-element heap buffer — out-of-bounds read from incomplete validation.

assumptions: Dtype dispatch for a_indices/a_values/a_shape/b is declared in the op registration (not shown); the type-safety of a_shape->flat<Index>() at line 21 depends on that registration enforcing DT_INT64 for a_shape, which cannot be verified from the given code.

The consumer that reads a_indices(i, j) for j < b->dims() and a_values(i) for i < a_indices->dim_size(0) is not shown; the out-of-bounds consequence follows from the SparseTensor contract that a_indices has shape [nnz, rank] with rank == a_shape->NumElements(), which this validation function exists to enforce.
b->dims() returning a non-negative int, and TensorShape internal dimension limits, are framework contracts not visible in this code.
limitations: The coordinate VALUES inside a_indices are also unvalidated here; whether the consumer bounds-checks them before indexing the output cannot be determined from the given code, so no separate index-value finding was raised.
The int loop counter at line 22 could only misbehave if b->dims() exceeded INT_MAX, which the int-typed dims() cannot express; non-triggerable.

The in-function reads a_shape_flat(i) and b->dim_size(i) (lines 22-23) are correctly guarded by the line 16 equality check, including the empty/zero-rank edge case; no in-function memory defect was found.

verdict.summary: This function is the SELinux ptrace_traceme LSM hook: it authorizes a PTRACE_TRACEME request by requiring the parent (the prospective tracer) to hold PROCESS__PTRACE permission over the current task, via avc_has_perm with subject task_sid_obj(parent) and target task_sid_obj(current). No attacker-controlled data (buffers, lengths, indices, paths, parsed content) enters this code; its only parameter is a kernel-internal task pointer supplied under the LSM hook contract, and the permission direction and error propagation are correct. All generated candidates (NULL-parent dereference, use-after-free on parent, TOCTOU, NULL audit data) are contract-dependent, not attacker-instantiable, or non-security quality issues; no vulnerability exists in this code.

assumptions: avc_has_perm performs the actual policy lookup and returns 0 on allow and a negative errno otherwise; its contract is enforced outside the given code.
The ptrace syscall layer invoking this hook supplies a valid, live parent task (current->real_parent) under tasklist_lock/RCU; this code performs no non-NULL validation of parent itself.
task_sid_obj returns valid u32 SIDs for valid task_struct pointers; the SELinux state machine guarantees SID validity.
limitations: If a caller ever passed NULL as parent, task_sid_obj(parent) would dereference NULL; the trigger is unreachable under the LSM hook contract (speculative, no attacker-instantiable path in this code).
Passing NULL as the common_audit_data argument means AVC denials raised here carry no supplementary audit context; audit detail is reduced with no boundary-crossing security effect.

verdict.summary: xml_parse_node recurses once per nested element (and once per PI/comment prefix) with no depth limit anywhere in the function. An attacker-supplied XML document with deep nesting (e.g., '<a>' repeated tens of thousands of times, ~3 input bytes per stack frame) drives unbounded recursion and exhausts the process stack, crashing the process that parses the untrusted document. This is a cross-boundary denial of service: the attacker only needs to deliver the document, and no statement in this code bounds the depth.

evidence.reason: Uncontrolled recursion (CWE-674): each nested element in the attacker-controlled document causes a self-call with no depth bound. The trigger is fully instantiated: with input '<a><a><a>...' the code reaches this call on every level (name parsed at line 50, attributes loop exited at line 53, '>' consumed at line 76, loop condition satisfied at lines 80-81), and a document of a few hundred KB produces a stack frame count exceeding any real stack, crashing the process parsing untrusted XML.

Second recursion site of the same defect: the PI branch (and identically the comment branch at line 40) recurses instead of looping, so a document composed of repeated PI/comment prefixes (4 bytes per frame) also scales stack depth linearly with attacker input, with no depth check anywhere in the function.

assumptions: pj_scan_* helpers throw a syntax-error exception on end-of-buffer per their library contract (implementations not shown); direct *scanner->curptr derefs in this function rely on that contract.

pj_scan_get_quotes (line 59) is assumed to return attr->value including both quote characters (slen >= 2), making 'attr->value.slen -= 2' (line 62) safe; this is a helper contract, not a guard present in this code.
The scanner buffer layout (sentinel/NUL termination) is established at scan-init outside this code; derefs of scanner->curptr+1 assume a readable byte follows a confirmed '<' when data remains.
alloc_node/alloc_attr return non-NULL from the pool allocator; this code does not check their results, which is the library's documented pool contract.
limitations: Speculative: attr->value.slen -= 2 could underflow only if pj_scan_get_quotes returned a value shorter than the two quote characters, which would violate the helper's contract and cannot be produced by statements in this code; not counted as a vulnerability.

Speculative: a 1-byte out-of-bounds read at *scanner->curptr or *(scanner->curptr+1) would require the scanner to sit exactly at the end of a non-sentinel buffer; this depends on scanner internals and the caller's buffer, neither shown, so the trigger precondition could not be instantiated here.

Correctness-only: the '<!' comment loop (lines 30-39) terminates a comment at the first embedded '>' (e.g. '<!-- a>b -->'), mis-parsing the remainder; no memory-safety, disclosure, or amplification effect was demonstrated, so it is recorded as a spec/robustness issue, not a vulnerability.
Severity limited to denial of service: the demonstrated impact is stack exhaustion (process crash); no control-flow hijack or disclosure was provable from this code alone.

verdict.summary: In SparseTensorSliceDatasetOp::MakeDataset, the check that indices and values correspond in count is only evaluated inside the branch taken when one of them is empty (if (num_indices == 0 || num_values == 0)). When both are non-zero and unequal (e.g., a 2-row indices matrix with a 1-element values vector), no statement in this code validates the mismatch; the inconsistent tensors are passed to sparse::SparseTensor::Create and stored in the returned Dataset. Iterating that dataset accesses values at offsets and sizes derived from the index rows, reading past the end of the values buffer (heap out-of-bounds read potential / process abort), reachable by any client that supplies the op's runtime tensor inputs.

evidence.reason: The indices/values correspondence check is gated on one side being zero. Edge case num_indices=4, num_values=1 (both non-zero, unequal) makes the line-18 condition false, so the equality at line 19 is never evaluated and no other statement in this code validates the mismatch before the tensors are combined. Root cause: improperly scoped input validation (CWE-20).

Sink where the unvalidated, mismatched indices/values pair (attacker-supplied runtime tensors, trigger fully instantiated at line 18's bypass) is consumed and baked into the returned Dataset; iteration then reads values at index-derived offsets and sizes, past the end of the values buffer (out-of-bounds read, CWE-125).

assumptions: Any validation performed inside sparse::SparseTensor::Create (body not shown) is an assumption and was not used to dismiss the primary candidate; per guard anchoring, only checks quotable from the given code count.
The op registration's dtype constraints (indices/dense_shape as int64) are treated as an interface contract enforced by kernel selection, not attack data.

The precise downstream mechanism (Tensor::Slice CHECK vs direct Eigen access in the dataset iterator) is outside the given code; impact is characterized from the invariant violation this code passes on.

Contract: dtype-mismatched inputs (e.g., int32 indices) hit dtype CHECKs inside Tensor::matrix<int64>()/vec<int64>() — crash-only robustness, framework contract.
Negative dense_shape entries reaching TensorShape construction cause a framework CHECK/error — crash-only robustness.
Cosmetic: the values-shape error message at line 29 prints indices->shape() instead of values->shape().

verdict.summary: The function's only memory-safety-relevant sink, qftf_list->lv_refcount++, lacks a NULL check on rettv.vval.v_list, and a callback returning a NULL list value (e.g., Vim9 null_list) would crash the process. However, the callback is authored and loaded by the same operator who runs this process, so the trigger input originates at equal privilege and the sole consequence is termination of that same process with no disclosure, corruption, or amplification. All other inputs (qf_winid, start_idx, end_idx) flow only into dict_add_number with the dict allocation NULL-checked on the single path. No cross-trust-boundary vulnerability is present in this code.

assumptions: call_callback(cb, 0, &rettv, 1, args) is assumed to fully initialize rettv when it returns non-FAIL; this contract cannot be verified from the given code.
dict_add_number on a freshly dict_alloc_lock(VAR_FIXED)-allocated dict is assumed not to fail in a way affecting security; its return values are ignored in this code.
The 'quickfixtextfunc' callback and qfl->qf_qftf_cb are assumed to be set by the operator's own configuration/scripts at the same privilege as this process.
limitations: NULL pointer dereference (robustness): if the user-supplied callback returns a value with v_type == VAR_LIST and vval.v_list == NULL (e.g., Vim9 null_list), then qftf_list = rettv.vval.v_list yields NULL and qftf_list->lv_refcount++ crashes. The missing guard (rettv.vval.v_list != NULL) was confirmed absent by line-by-line search. Not classified as a vulnerability because the trigger value is produced by same-privilege Vim script and the impact is confined to crashing that same process.

rettv is declared uninitialized (typval_T rettv;) and is only guarded by the call_callback return-value check; a hypothetical contract violation by call_callback could expose an uninitialized read, but no statement in this code produces that state.
If call_callback returns FAIL after partially populating rettv, that value is never cleared, a bounded per-invocation leak with no attacker-scalable amplification.

verdict.summary: njs_function_frame_save performs unguarded writes (value copies via *p/*new++, local-pointer writes via *local++) into a caller-allocated frame whose size is never checked in this code, and reads function->u.lambda->temp without verifying the function is a lambda. However, every sizing quantity (value_count, args_count, args_offset, temp) is read from the same active frame/function object that the not-shown allocation also uses, and no statement in this code can produce the undersized-buffer, native-function, or NULL-frame state the triggers require, so no attack path is instantiable from the given code alone.

njs_function_frame_value_count, njs_function_frame_values, and njs_function_frame_args_count are consistent helpers such that end - start == value_count; their definitions are not shown.
vm, frame, vm->active_frame, active->function, and function->u.lambda are non-NULL per caller contract; this code contains no NULL checks.

limitations: Speculative: if the caller's frame-size computation ever diverges from the loops in this function (e.g., args_count exceeding the reserved local-pointer slots), the '*local++ = p++;' loop writes out of bounds; the undersized-buffer precondition cannot be instantiated from the given code.

Speculative: if active->function could be a native function, 'function->u.lambda->temp' reads the wrong union member and the computed value pointer would be garbage; reachability of that state is not shown.

Contract: 'native->arguments_offset = value + (function->args_offset - 1);' computes value - 1 if args_offset is 0; no statement in this code dereferences it, and whether args_offset can be 0 is not shown.

verdict.summary: Out-of-bounds read: the loop is bounded by bin->ne_header->SegCount, an attacker-controlled value taken from the parsed NE file header, and the body indexes bin->segment_entries[i] with no check that the array is non-NULL or holds SegCount entries. A crafted NE file whose segment table is shorter than the declared count (or whose entries failed to load) causes a heap over-read at se->length and the other entry fields; the out-of-bounds values propagate into returned section metadata (size, vsize, perm, paddr, name), giving disclosure potential and a crash of the process analyzing the untrusted file. The only guards in the code, 'if (!bin)' and 'if (!bs)', do not bound the index against the array capacity.

evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted bound: the loop limit is the file-controlled header field SegCount, used raw with no relation established to the capacity of bin->segment_entries; the header pointer itself is also dereferenced here without a NULL check.

Sink: i is bounded only by the attacker-controlled SegCount, and bin->segment_entries[i] is indexed without any capacity or NULL check in this code; the first dereference at se->length is a heap out-of-bounds read whose values flow into the returned RBinSection metadata.

assumptions: The loader/init code that allocates bin->segment_entries and fills bin->ne_header is not shown; per guard anchoring, any capacity guarantee (e.g., allocating exactly SegCount entries) cannot be quoted here and is not relied on — the loop is therefore treated as unguarded.

bin->alignment originates outside this snippet; its width is assumed such that (ut64)se->offset * bin->alignment cannot overflow ut64 for fixed-width 16-bit offset fields, so no integer-overflow candidate was retained.
__translate_perms is not shown; its output is treated only as a permissions mask derived from attacker-controlled flags.
limitations: NULL dereference of bin->ne_header (line 7) or bin->segment_entries (line 12) requires the unshown init code to hand back a partially initialized object; that trigger could not be instantiated from statements in this code alone and is recorded as a contract/robustness concern.
No attacker-scalable amplification: SegCount is a fixed-width header field, so the loop is bounded by that type's maximum, not by an attacker-unbounded count.
The early return at line 10 returns a partial segment list and leaves bin->segments unset; robustness only, no security effect.
r_str_newf at line 19 uses a constant format string with a literal %s argument; no format-string or injection issue.

verdict.summary: pj_scan_get_char dereferences scanner->curptr before and after increment with no explicit end-pointer bounds check; its memory safety rests entirely on the documented pj_scanner invariant that the scanned buffer is NUL-terminated and curptr is within it. The only guard, 'if (!chr)', tests the current byte for the NUL sentinel and, for every boundary case of attacker-controlled content inside a properly terminated buffer (empty buffer, single byte plus terminator, position at the terminator, high-bit bytes), keeps both dereferences in bounds. The one-past-the-buffer read after '++scanner->curptr' is reachable only when the scanner was initialized over a buffer lacking a NUL terminator or with curptr already out of range, which is a contract violation at the initialization site that no statement in this code can produce, so no trigger is instantiated here.

assumptions: pj_scan_skip_whitespace (line 13) is not shown; whether it re-checks for the NUL sentinel inside its loop cannot be verified from the given code.
pj_scan_syntax_err (line 6) is not shown; its callback/longjmp behavior and whether it can return are unknown.
The macro PJ_SCAN_IS_PROBABLY_SPACE is not shown; its exact classification of NUL and high-bit bytes is assumed from the pj_scanner framework.
The scanner's documented contract (NUL-terminated buffer, curptr in range at entry) is enforced at pj_scan_init / the buffer preparation site, which is outside the given code.
limitations: Speculative out-of-bounds read (CWE-125-family): if a caller initializes the scanner over a non-NUL-terminated buffer, '++scanner->curptr' followed by the read in 'if (PJ_SCAN_IS_PROBABLY_SPACE(*scanner->curptr) && scanner->skip_ws)' can read one byte past the allocation. This requires a caller violating the documented scanner contract; the violating state is not producible by any statement in this function, so it is a defect of the initialization site, not of this code.
Speculative out-of-bounds read at 'int chr = *scanner->curptr;' if the function is entered with curptr already past the buffer end, again a contract violation originating outside this code.

Error path returns 0 after pj_scan_syntax_err; a caller that ignores the sentinel could mis-handle end-of-input, a caller-contract robustness question with no instantiated security consequence in this code.

verdict.summary: No security vulnerability with instantiated cross-boundary impact was found. The argument-copy loop contains a genuine off-by-one (it iterates 'i < argc - first_arg' while copying 'argv[first_arg + i + 1]', so the last iteration passes argv[argc], which is NULL by the C standard, to xstrdup), and 'process->args_len = argc' overstates the stored count, but the args allocation of (argc + 1) slots keeps every read and write of this code and any args_len-bounded consumer loop in bounds, and the worst outcomes are a crash of, or a dropped argument in, the very process whose operator supplied the command line (equal privilege). LISTEN_FDS is parsed with unvalidated strtoll, but it is same-privilege environment input whose sink is outside this code.

assumptions: xstrdup, xmalloc0, xmalloc, dup_array, make_oci_process_user, crun_assert_n_args and init_libcrun_context are not shown; their NULL handling, allocation-failure behavior and validation semantics cannot be quoted from the given code.

The types and downstream use of crun_context.listen_fds / preserve_fds and of process->args / args_len inside libcrun_container_exec_with_options are not shown; analysis of those sinks is limited to what this code's own (argc + 1)-slot allocation bounds.
argc/argv originate from the CLI caller, taken to be the operator of the crun process at equal privilege; no code path in this listing exhibits argv crossing a privilege or service boundary.
limitations: Off-by-one (robustness, not security per the impact model): the loop 'for (i = 0; i < argc - first_arg; i++) process->args[i] = xstrdup (argv[first_arg + i + 1]);' reads argv[argc] (NULL by the C standard) on every exec-with-command invocation; the counterfactual fix 'i < argc - first_arg - 1' is absent from the code. Consequence is at most a NULL-deref crash of the operator's own crun process or silent dropping of the last command argument; the read of argv[argc] itself is in bounds.

Data-integrity bug: 'process->args_len = argc;' while only argc - first_arg strings are stored; consumers iterating i < args_len stay within the (argc + 1)-slot allocation and encounter zeroed NULL entries, so no out-of-bounds access is reachable from this code; consumer behavior is not shown.

Unvalidated environment input: 'crun_context.listen_fds = strtoll (getenv ("LISTEN_FDS"), NULL, 10);' has no range check, no LISTEN_PID check, and its result is added to preserve_fds; trigger requires the operator's own environment and the fd-handling sink is outside this code.

Speculative: integer overflow of '(argc + 1) * sizeof (*process->args)' would require argc near INT_MAX, which exec ARG_MAX limits preclude; a hostile privileged caller forwarding untrusted arguments to this CLI handler is not exhibited by the given code.

verdict.summary: In this TensorFlow op kernel, the parse-failure path calls result->Unref() on an object whose only reference is still owned by the local std::unique_ptr. Unref destroys the refcount-1 object, then OP_REQUIRES(context, false, ...) returns from Compute and the unique_ptr destructor deletes the freed pointer a second time. An attacker supplying an unparseable serialized ensemble proto (e.g., an untrusted SavedModel executed by a serving process) deterministically triggers a double free / heap corruption.

verdict.summary: In the uECC_VLI_NATIVE_LITTLE_ENDIAN path of uECC_sign_with_k, bcopy is called with source and destination swapped: bcopy((uint8_t *)tmp, private_key, BITS_TO_BYTES(curve->num_n_bits)) copies the blinding random value out of tmp INTO the const private_key buffer, instead of loading the private key into tmp. This writes to memory the interface declares read-only (faulting if the key resides in flash/rodata, otherwise silently destroying the caller's private key), and leaves tmp holding the blinding random rather than d, so the s component is computed as (e + r*blinding)/k instead of (e + r*d)/k; the function then returns 1 with an invalid signature.

evidence.reason: bcopy(src, dst, len) takes the source first, so this copies FROM tmp INTO private_key — the reversed direction. The const private_key parameter is overwritten with the blinding random value (line 46 produced tmp = uECC_generate_random_int(tmp, curve->n, num_n_words)), destroying the caller's key via an out-of-contract write through a const pointer, and tmp never receives the private key d as the parallel branch at line 63 does.

evidence.snippet: uECC_vli_modMult(s, tmp, s, curve->n, num_n_words); /* s = r*d */
evidence.reason: This use site proves tmp must hold the private key d at this point (comment s = r*d); because of the reversed copy at line 61, tmp holds the blinding random instead, so the signature s component is computed with the wrong scalar and the function returns 1 (line 81) with an invalid signature while the caller's key buffer has been corrupted.

assumptions: bits2int() (not shown) is assumed to clamp hash_size to the curve order width; upstream micro-ecc does this, but the clamping statement cannot be quoted from the given code.
curve structs (num_words, num_n_bits, num_bytes, n, p, G) and g_rng_function are library-internal trusted configuration.
The signature output buffer is contractually 2 * curve->num_bytes per the library's public API; this function does not check it.
uECC_VLI_NATIVE_LITTLE_ENDIAN is a supported build configuration of this library, so the defective branch is live code.
limitations: hash_size flows unvalidated into bits2int at line 70; if the unseen helper lacked its clamping, an oversized hash_size could over-read message_hash or overflow tmp[uECC_MAX_WORDS] — the sink is outside the given code, so this remains speculative.

The boundary value k == curve->n passes the line 23 guard because it uses 'uECC_vli_cmp(curve->n, k, num_n_words) != 1' (equal returns 0), but the resulting point-at-infinity yields p == 0 which is rejected by line 37 ('if (uECC_vli_isZero(p, num_words)) { return 0; }'), so it fails closed.

The numBits check at line 73 can spuriously reject valid signatures for curves where num_n_bits exceeds num_bytes * 8 (e.g., secp160r1, 161 bits in 20 bytes), but this is a fail-closed availability quirk with no security impact.

An out-of-bounds access requires args_count/args_offset to exceed the reservation made by the caller using the same function object; no statement in this function produces such an excess.

verdict.summary: finderrfunc walks VM-internal Lua stack frames and C-frame links only; every pointer dereference inside this code is guarded on all paths (frame > bot bounds the stack walk and the one-below-frame read, cf is NULL-checked after every cframe_prev and re-checked by the loop condition), and no statement in this code writes the frame or cframe fields, so no harmful value can be produced by its own data flow. No external content is consumed, so there is no trust-boundary intake to validate. Speculative scenarios (corrupted frame metadata, INT32_MIN nres, cyclic chains) require memory corruption or contract violation outside this code and are confined to the equal-privilege process.

assumptions: lua_State *L is a valid, live interpreter state as documented by the interface; L->base, tvref(L->stack), and L->cframe are maintained by the LuaJIT VM (contract argument, not attack data).

Frame-chain metadata (frame_typep, frame_ftsz) and cframe fields (nres, errfunc, prev, canyield) are written exclusively by VM machinery outside this function; this code reads them but never writes them. Chain consistency, valid frame sizes, and acyclicity are assumed, since no statement inside this code enforces them.

restorestack/savestack offsets are interpreted consistently by the caller (lj_err_run treats 0 as 'no handler' and applies restorestack to positive results); the errfunc stored in a cframe is assumed to be a valid savestack offset.
LJ_HASFFI is a compile-time build flag, not a runtime value.
limitations: Speculative (cannot be instantiated by this code's own flow): if cframe_nres(cf) were INT32_MIN, the negation in restorestack(L, -cframe_nres(cf)) would overflow signed int32 (line 6); no statement here writes nres, so triggering requires corruption outside this code.

Speculative: a zero-sized or out-of-stack frame (frame_prevd/frame_prevl not decreasing, or chain leaving the stack allocation) would defeat termination/bounds, but frame sizes are VM-written; a guest script can shape which frames exist, not their metadata, and corrupting metadata requires memory corruption at equal privilege (e.g., the script's own FFI misuse) - out of the attacker model for a defect in this code.

Speculative/contract: if cframe_errfunc(cf) returned 0 for a real handler at stack offset 0, a caller checking ef > 0 would drop it; whether slot 0 can hold an errorfunc is decided by VM code not shown, and this code deliberately uses >= 0 so the sentinel 0 is shared with 'not found'.
default: lua_assert(0) is a no-op in release builds but the code still returns 0 (fail-safe); all frame-type encodings are covered by the case labels, so the branch appears unreachable.

verdict.summary: The top-level ISO-BMFF box dispatcher dereferences mandatory-child pointers that a malformed attacker-supplied file can omit, with no guard anywhere in the function: mov->moof->mfhd->sequence_number in the GF_ISOM_OPEN_KEEP_FRAGMENTS path (moof without mfhd) and trak->Media->information->sampleTable in the default moov path (trak without mdia/minf/stbl). The code itself validates the analogous mandatory child for moov (if (!mov->moov->mvhd)), proving the omission. A crafted fragmented MP4 crashes the parsing process: a trust-boundary denial of service for any application processing untrusted media files or streams.

evidence.reason: NULL pointer dereference: mov->moof is assigned from the parsed box (line 309) but mfhd is a child box that the attacker's moof payload can omit; the string 'mfhd' appears only at this deref with no NULL check on any path (contrast the mvhd check at line 77). Trigger: a moof without mfhd in GF_ISOM_OPEN_KEEP_FRAGMENTS mode reaches this line with mfhd == NULL and crashes the process.

Unguarded NULL dereference chain on attacker-controlled box structure: a moov whose trak lacks mdia (or whose mdia/minf lacks stbl) yields trak->Media == NULL; no validation of Media/information/sampleTable exists anywhere in the loop, so the default (non-READ_DEBUG) path crashes while parsing a malformed moov.

evidence.snippet: e = gf_isom_parse_root_box(&a, mov->movieFileMap->bs, boxType, bytesMissing, progressive_mode);
evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted data: every box structure consumed by the switch (a->type, moof->mfhd, trak->Media chain) is parsed here from the file/stream bytes, which are attacker-controlled across the trust boundary; nothing between this intake and the sinks at lines 101 and 366 validates the mandatory child pointers.

assumptions: Child-box parsing inside gf_isom_parse_root_box and the box readers is not shown; per guard anchoring, no enforcement of mandatory children (mfhd in moof, mdia/minf/stbl in trak) can be assumed, so the derefs at lines 101 and 366 are treated as the last line of defense.

gf_isom_box_del, gf_list_add, gf_list_del_item NULL-handling is a callee contract not shown; gf_isom_box_del(mov->brand) with brand == NULL (OTYP before any FTYP) is classified as contract, not attack data.

openMode == GF_ISOM_OPEN_KEEP_FRAGMENTS and FragmentsFlags/signal_frag_bounds are application configuration, treated as fixed environment for the trigger, not attacker-controlled and not contract violations.

Box sizes (a->size) are treated as bounded by actually available data: the GF_ISOM_INCOMPLETE_FILE path (lines 35-45) prevents a box larger than the file from being returned, so u64 arithmetic on a->size cannot wrap at 2^64 scale.
limitations: Lines 381-383 check mov->root_ssix but call gf_isom_box_del(mov->seg_ssix) and never null seg_ssix: a latent double-free/UAF if root_ssix were ever set, but no statement in this code assigns root_ssix, so the block's precondition cannot be instantiated here; speculative.

In the merge path, gf_isom_box_del(a) at line 372 frees the moof while mov->moof (set at line 309) still points to it and is not reset, unlike the KEEP_FRAGMENTS path (line 367); within this function mov->moof is afterwards used only for truthiness (line 297, post-loop check), so any dereference of the dangling pointer would occur in code not shown.

assert(totSize >= mov->bytes_removed) at line 15 is compiled out in release builds; a totSize underflow at line 16 is possible in principle but bytes_removed is internal editing state, not attacker data.
Unchecked gf_list_new() at line 424 could yield gf_list_add(NULL, a), but this requires allocation failure no attacker can induce.

Impact is crash-only (availability); if the operator parsed only their own local files at equal privilege this would degrade to a robustness bug, but for the typical deployment of this parser (players, servers, transcoders, progressive/streamed input as indicated by progressive_mode) the file originator is across a trust boundary, making it a denial-of-service vulnerability.

verdict.summary: CopySliceData re-validates every attacker-influenced value reaching its sinks: the shard index is guarded by CHECK_GE(idx, 0) (idx defaults to -1 from FindWithDefault), the record must parse (ParseProtoUnlimited), the stored slice must be valid within the tensor shape (slice_s.SliceTensorShape status), and the stored data size must exactly equal the slice's element count before CopyDataFromTensorSliceToTensorSlice is called. The historical out-of-bounds read in this function is fixed by the quoted size check, which lies on the only path to the copy and whose equality is precisely the sink's precondition. Remaining candidates (destination over-write depending on unshown callee arithmetic and caller contract, a potential race on tss used outside mu_, int64 num_elements overflow requiring unshown TensorShape behavior, and fail-fast CHECK aborts on malformed checkpoints) could not be instantiated as concrete triggers within this code and are recorded as speculative limitations.

assumptions: checkpoint::TensorProtoDataSize<T> and checkpoint::TensorProtoData<T> account for the same underlying buffer in the same T-sized units, so the equality check at lines 48-49 is exactly the precondition of the source read at line 56; their implementations are not shown.
CopyDataFromTensorSliceToTensorSlice (not shown) computes the intersection of slice_s and slice clipped to tss->shape() so that destination offsets stay within a buffer sized to the requested slice.

LoadAllShards (line 11, not shown) inserts/reuses TensorSliceSet entries rather than freeing existing ones, and fname_to_index_/sss_ are built consistently by the constructor, so idx values returned by FindWithDefault are valid indices when found.

TensorShape construction inside SliceTensorShape rejects (returns a non-ok Status) shapes whose element count overflows int64; if it instead accepted them, the size check at line 48 could compare against a wrapped count.
limitations: Speculative C2/DoS: a checkpoint whose slice metadata references a filename not present in fname_to_index_ yields idx = -1 and aborts at CHECK_GE(idx, 0) (line 25) before any memory access; the guard preserves memory safety, and the worst case is fail-fast process termination on a malformed checkpoint.

Speculative C3: the size check at lines 48-55 constrains only the source buffer; an out-of-bounds write into the caller-provided data buffer would require the requested slice or the callee's offset arithmetic (both not fully validated in this code; callee not shown) to exceed the buffer sized by the caller's contract for slice. No concrete value sequence in this code instantiates it.

Speculative C4: tss is used at lines 42 and 56 after the mu_ scope ends at line 18; a concurrent call could execute LoadAllShards (line 11) in that window. This is only a use-after-free if LoadAllShards frees existing TensorSliceSet objects, which no statement in the given code exhibits.

Speculative C5: int64 overflow of shp_s.num_elements() (and of TensorShape element counts built from attacker-controlled checkpoint metadata) would require TensorShape/SliceTensorShape construction, not shown, to accept a wrapping dimension product; the guard if (!s.ok()) at line 43 is assumed to reject such shapes.

Attacker-controlled dtype confusion between the template parameter T and the dtype recorded in the stored TensorProto can yield semantically wrong data being copied, but the size check uses the same T-based accounting, so no out-of-bounds access follows; if the helper CHECKs dtype, a mismatched checkpoint merely aborts.

verdict.summary: elo_probe takes a reference on the parent USB device with usb_get_dev (line 16), but both error paths (hid_parse failure at lines 21-23 and hid_hw_start failure at lines 27-29) jump to err_free, which frees priv with kfree(priv) (line 39) without ever calling usb_put_dev. A malicious USB device whose malformed HID report descriptor makes hid_parse fail leaks one usb_device reference (and its associated kernel memory) on every probe, and repeated connect/replug cycles scale this retention without bound, enabling kernel memory exhaustion.

evidence.reason: Missing release site: both failure paths (goto err_free after hid_parse or hid_hw_start failure, lines 23 and 29) reach this label and free priv without dropping the usb_device reference taken at line 16; usb_put_dev appears nowhere in the function. Instantiated trigger: attacker's malformed report descriptor makes hid_parse return nonzero at line 20, control flows to err_free, kfree(priv) executes, and the usb_device reference is permanently leaked (attacker-scalable kernel memory retention).

Origin of the leaked reference: usb_get_dev increments the usb_device kref and stores the owning reference in priv->usbdev; on every error exit this reference is never released, so the usb_device structure is retained forever after the device disconnects.

assumptions: The global workqueue wq is initialized at module load time (module init not shown).

hid_is_usb(hdev) returning true implies hdev->dev.parent is a usb_interface, per HID core construction; the quoted guard at lines 7-8 is the only in-code enforcement of the type contract used at line 15.
hid_hw_start cleans up its own partially started state when it returns an error, per its documented contract.
elo_work and elo_remove (not shown) correctly handle the delayed work queued on the success path; no free of priv occurs after queueing within this function.
limitations: Stale driver data: hid_set_drvdata(hdev, priv) at line 18 persists after kfree(priv) at line 39 on failed probes, leaving hdev->dev.driver_data dangling. No statement in this code dereferences it after the free, and the driver is not bound on a failed probe, so no trigger could be instantiated; recorded as latent, speculative.

queue_delayed_work's return value at line 34 is ignored; if queueing fails, the broken-firmware periodic-read workaround silently does not run. Functional robustness only, no cross-boundary security effect.

The leak rate is bounded by the speed of USB connect/replug cycles; a purely physical attacker with USB port access could cause other harm directly, but the originator-of-untrusted-data model (malicious or fuzzed device, including emulated USB) still makes the retention attacker-scalable.

verdict.summary: get_visual_text computes the selected text from editor selection state. All memory accesses (ml_get_pos pointer, **pp read, mb_ptr2len index at pp+lenp-1) stay at or before the line's NUL terminator under the state invariants the code operates on: the lnum equality check 'if (VIsual.lnum != curwin->w_cursor.lnum)' forces a single-line selection, LT_POS with equal lnums reduces to a col order making lenp >= 1, 'if (**pp == NUL) *lenp = 0;' handles empty/at-EOL starts, and 'if (has_mbyte && *lenp > 0)' prevents a -1 index. The code contains no validation of selection columns against the current line length, so an out-of-range col would produce an out-of-bounds read; however, no attacker per the impact model can instantiate col > line length from this code's own statements or from file content alone: it requires the non-default 'virtualedit' option plus operator-side selection geometry (equal-privilege, self-inflicted) or externally-corrupted stale VIsual state, neither of which is producible here. The trigger is therefore speculative, and the code is judged not vulnerable.

assumptions: ml_get_curline() and ml_get_pos() return the current line's NUL-terminated buffer and ml_get_pos performs no clamping of pos->col; both helpers are outside the given code.

*mb_ptr2len() is NUL-safe within a line buffer (utf_ptr2len/utfc_ptr2len check continuation bytes for NUL and return 1 for NUL or incomplete sequences); this is enforced in unshown mbyte.c code, not quotable here.

The function is only invoked while a visual selection is active and consistent with the buffer; this code never checks VIsual_active, so that precondition is a caller contract, not an enforceable fact in this code.

Selection columns (VIsual.col, cursor.col) are valid in-line positions maintained by the editor core's movement code except under the 'virtualedit' option; whether 'virtualedit' is modeline-settable (i.e., attacker-plantable from file content) cannot be determined from the given code.
unadjust_for_sel() (line 7) is not shown; its effect on columns could not be analyzed.
The caller's use of the returned *pp/*lenp (copy length) is not shown and was not relied on.
limitations: Missing bounds check: neither cursor.col nor VIsual.col is validated against the current line length before '*pp = ml_get_pos(&curwin->w_cursor);' / '*pp = ml_get_pos(&VIsual);' and the index '(*mb_ptr2len)(*pp + (*lenp - 1))'. If invoked with a column past end-of-line, this yields a heap out-of-bounds read with disclosure potential (the 'selected' text would include adjacent heap bytes). Trigger is speculative: it requires the 'virtualedit' option with the operator extending a selection past EOL (equal-privilege, operator-self-inflicted) or stale VIsual state after an external buffer mutation; neither is instantiable from this code's statements or from file content alone under the attacker model.

The function never checks VIsual_active; if a caller invokes it with only stale selection state, the lnum check may pass while VIsual.col is stale. Reachability depends entirely on the unshown caller.
The else branch handles blockwise (Ctrl-V) selections with charwise column math (lenp = col difference + 1); on a single line this is memory-safe but semantically approximate.

When the selection end column equals the line length, *lenp counts the terminating NUL byte (lenp = col_diff + 1 reaches the NUL position, and mb_ptr2len there returns 1), so the returned text can include a trailing NUL; the byte is inside the allocation, so this is a cosmetic defect.
Linewise ('V') selections spanning multiple lines return FAIL at the lnum check; functional limitation, not a security issue.

verdict.summary: ReshapeSparseTensor (the tf.raw_ops.SparseTensorReshape kernel) never validates that the rank implied by input_shape_in matches the column count of input_indices_in. It forwards both to ReshapeSparseTensorFunctor (lines 101-104), which indexes the nnz x cols indices matrix with column j for every j in [0, input_shape.dims()). An attacker supplying an input_shape vector longer than the indices width triggers a heap out-of-bounds read (e.g., 1x2 indices with input_shape [2,2,2] and target [8] passes every check in the function); the over-read int64 is folded into the linear index and returned in the output indices tensor, giving a scalable heap memory disclosure across the op's trust boundary.

evidence.snippet:
OP_REQUIRES_OK(context, functor::ReshapeSparseTensorFunctor<Device>()(
                                context, input_shape, output_shape,
                                input_indices_in.matrix<int64>(),
                                result_indices->matrix<int64>()));
evidence.reason: Sink / missing-check site: the functor is invoked with input_shape (rank taken from the attacker-controlled vector input_shape_in) and the independently shaped input_indices_in matrix. No check anywhere in the function equates input_shape.dims() with input_indices_in.shape().dim_size(1); the only guards on these tensors are the IsMatrix/IsVector checks at lines 6-17, and lines 95-96 only test dense_size > 0 && product > 0. Trigger instantiated in STEP 4: input_indices_in shape [1,2] = [[5,7]], input_shape_in [2,2,2], target [8] passes all checks and reaches this call with rank 3 vs width 2, so the functor reads input_indices(0,2) past the 2-element heap buffer; the leaked value is written into the returned output indices.

Origin of the tainted bound: input_shape_in is attacker-controlled op input; its element count becomes input_shape.dims(), the rank later used by the functor as the column loop/index bound at lines 101-104, while the matrix width it is applied to comes from the separately attacker-chosen shape of input_indices_in (dim_size(1) never compared).

assumptions: The internal behavior of functor::ReshapeSparseTensorFunctor<Device> is not shown; the OOB read itself occurs there. This analysis relies on the upstream TensorFlow implementation, which iterates j in [0, input_shape.dims()) reading input_indices(i, j) using row-major Eigen mappings and performs no width-vs-rank validation; any claim that the helper bounds-checks would be an unverifiable assumption, and no such check is quotable from the given code.
Release builds of Eigen (EIGEN_NO_DEBUG) do not perform runtime bounds assertions on operator(), so the out-of-range access reads heap memory rather than aborting.
TensorShape internals (AddDim/set_dim/num_elements overflow handling, MaxDimensions enforcement) are not shown and are treated as unknown rather than as guards.
limitations: Candidate C2: signed int64 overflow at line 44 (product *= size) requires dims around 2^32 scale and, even when instantiated, only yields semantically wrong but in-bounds output values within this op; speculative, recorded not confirmed.

Candidate C3: passing a target_shape with more than MaxDimensions elements (or dims whose product overflows TensorShape's internal accounting) leads to unshown AddDim behavior, at worst an abort of the op's own process from the invoking party's input; robustness, not a vulnerability under the equal-privilege impact model.
The early-return path (lines 74-78) copies the inputs when shapes match; any inconsistency there is semantic, not memory-unsafe.
Allocation failures for extreme nnz/output_rank are handled by OP_REQUIRES_OK; no resource-amplification finding beyond the disclosed OOB read.

verdict.summary: rsi_init_usb_interface allocates rsi_dev with kzalloc (line 7) but never frees it on any error exit: when rsi_find_bulk_in_and_out_endpoints fails on a crafted USB device lacking bulk endpoints (goto fail_eps), when tx_buffer allocation fails, or when rsi_usb_init_rx fails (goto fail_rx), the function returns without kfree(rsi_dev). The code frees rsi_dev->tx_buffer on the fail_rx path, showing error-path cleanup was intended, but the rsi_dev object itself is leaked, allowing kernel memory retention that scales with repeated insertion of an attacker-controlled USB device.

evidence.reason: Error exit returns without freeing rsi_dev. Every non-success path (endpoint parsing failure at line 17, tx_buffer allocation failure at line 26, rsi_usb_init_rx failure falling through fail_rx at lines 52-53) reaches this label and returns while rsi_dev, allocated at line 7, is never passed to kfree anywhere in the function; only rsi_dev->tx_buffer is freed on the fail_rx path. Trigger: attacker-controlled USB device whose interface lacks bulk in/out endpoints makes rsi_find_bulk_in_and_out_endpoints (line 15) fail, leaking the kzalloc'd object per probe.
Origin of the leaked allocation: rsi_dev is allocated here and stored into adapter->rsi_dev at line 11 before validation, but no kfree(rsi_dev) exists on any error path in this function.

assumptions: The caller of rsi_init_usb_interface (probe path) is not shown; whether it frees adapter->rsi_dev on failure cannot be verified from the given code, and per guard anchoring no unseen caller-side cleanup is assumed to exist. The leak verdict rests on the absence of any free inside this function and the function's demonstrated self-cleanup pattern for tx_buffer.
rsi_find_bulk_in_and_out_endpoints and rsi_usb_init_rx internals are not shown; only their boolean return values are analyzed.
The USB device attached at pfunction is modeled as the attacker (crafted descriptors controlling which error branch is taken).
limitations: Allocations possibly performed inside rsi_usb_init_rx (e.g., rx control buffers) are not freed on the fail_rx path, but their producing statements are outside the given code and cannot be confirmed.

Potential dereference of the half-initialized adapter->rsi_dev (set at line 11 before endpoint validation) by caller error handling is speculative: the caller is not shown and no dereference occurs within this function.
The leak is low severity: each failed probe leaks one fixed-size object; exhaustion requires repeated physical insertion of the crafted device.

verdict.summary: pjmedia_rtcp_fb_parse_rpsi validates the RTCP length field with a raw, non-byte-swapped comparison (hdr->rtcp_common.length < 3). On little-endian hosts a wire length of 1 (bytes 00 01) reads as 256 and bypasses the guard, so rpsi_len = (pj_ntohs(length)-2)*4 underflows to SIZE_MAX-3; the buffer bound check 'length < rpsi_len + 12' then wraps to 'length < 8' and passes for any packet of at least 12 bytes. The function publishes rpsi->rpsi via pj_strset with slen = (truncated rpsi_bit_len + 7)/8 = 8186 bytes pointing at buf+14 of an attacker-sized buffer, producing a remote heap out-of-bounds read of roughly 8KB when the RPSI string is consumed (and direct OOB reads of buf[12]/buf[13] when length is 12-13).

evidence.reason: Defective guard: the 16-bit RTCP length field is stored in network byte order (line 24 decodes it with pj_ntohs), but this check compares the raw field without pj_ntohs. On little-endian hosts the attacker's wire value 0x0001 reads as 256, so the check passes and the minimum-length precondition for the subsequent (ntohs(length)-2) arithmetic is never enforced.

Unsigned integer underflow and defeated bound check: with wire length 1, (1-2)*4 yields rpsi_len = 0xFFFF...FC; the guard's own arithmetic 'rpsi_len + 12' wraps to 8, so 'length < 8' is false for every length >= 12 and the unbounded rpsi_len flows onward.

Sink: the underflowed rpsi_len produces rpsi_bit_len = 0xFFD0 (65488) after 16-bit truncation, and pj_strset publishes an 8186-byte string at buf+14 regardless of the actual buffer size (attacker may supply a 20-byte packet), plus direct OOB reads of buf[12]/buf[13] when length <= 13; consumers copying rpsi->rpsi perform a heap out-of-bounds read with disclosure/crash impact.

assumptions: sizeof(pjmedia_rtcp_fb_common) == 12 (2 bytes v/p/count/pt + 2-byte length + two 4-byte SSRCs), consistent with the code's own use of 'p = (pj_uint8_t*)hdr + sizeof(*hdr)' and the '+ 12' constant.

pjmedia_rtcp_fb_rpsi.rpsi_bit_len is declared pj_uint16_t in pjmedia/rtcp.h (not shown), so the huge size_t result truncates to 0xFFD0 = 65488 bits, giving slen = 8186; if the field were wider, slen would be even larger and the overread worse.
pj_size_t is 32- or 64-bit unsigned; the trigger works identically on both widths.
hdr->rtcp_common.length holds the wire value in network byte order, as proven by line 24 applying pj_ntohs to the same field.
The function is a public PJ_DEF API invoked on network-received RTCP PSFB packets, so buf/length constitute the trust-boundary intake point and are attacker-controlled.
limitations: The trigger requires a little-endian host (x86, ARM LE), which is the dominant deployment; on big-endian hosts the raw comparison coincides with host order and the code is safe.

The downstream memcpy/consumer of rpsi->rpsi is not shown; the OOB read materializes there (or directly at buf[12]/buf[13] within this function when the packet is 12-13 bytes), but the unbounded descriptor is created by this function.

A secondary boundary case (wire length 2, packet exactly 12 bytes) yields only a 1-2 byte overread at lines 29/43 before rejection; it shares the same root cause (endian-defective guard at line 18) and does not change the verdict.
16-bit truncation of rpsi_bit_len for large valid length fields (C4) was dismissed quantitatively: the truncated slen is always <= the bytes guaranteed by 'length < rpsi_len + 12'.

verdict.summary: This is the PCRE2 JIT compiler's extended-character-class code generator. All JIT-emitted memory reads are guarded: bitmap reads are preceded by 'CMP(SLJIT_GREATER, TMP1, 0, SLJIT_IMM, 255)' on every configuration where the character value can exceed 255 (16/32-bit always; 8-bit UTF conditionally, matching the '#if PCRE2_CODE_UNIT_WIDTH == 8 / if (common->utf)' guard), and the 32-bit non-UTF UCD lookup is clamped by 'CMP(SLJIT_LESS, TMP1, 0, SLJIT_IMM, MAX_UTF_CODE_POINT + 1)' with an UNASSIGNED_UTF_CHAR sentinel. The compares/invertcmp accounting balances exactly across the scan loop, four property pre-pass loops, and the generating loop, and all loops parse the bytecode identically (no desynchronization). Remaining candidates (unbounded property-value cc[1] indexing static UCD tables, max-min underflow from out-of-order ranges, missing XCL_END) require malformed compiled bytecode that only pcre2_compile produces, and it validates property names, range ordering, and class termination; this function is not the intake point for the regex source. Those triggers are not instantiable within this code's input surface and are recorded as speculative.

assumptions: The bytecode buffer pointed to by cc was produced by pcre2_compile in the same library, which validates property names against a fixed enumeration, rejects out-of-order ranges, and always terminates XCLASS data with XCL_END; PCRE2 does not treat tampered compiled-pattern buffers as part of its threat model.

Definitions of GETCHARINCTEST, SET_CHAR_OFFSET, SET_TYPE_OFFSET, XCLASS_* masks, UCD_BLOCK_SHIFT/MASK, and the static UCD tables follow the upstream PCRE2 headers, consistent with how this function uses them (pointer arithmetic on uint16_t/uint32_t tables, byte-scaled offsets).
8-bit non-UTF mode cannot produce character values above 255 because read_char decodes a single code unit in that configuration.
limitations: Speculative: a PT_BOOL/PT_CLIST/PT_GC/PT_SCX item with an out-of-range cc[1] would index ucd_boolprop_sets, ucd_caseless_sets, ucp_typerange, or ucd_script_sets out of bounds at JIT-generated runtime; no bound on cc[1] exists inside this function (only SLJIT_ASSERTs, which vanish in release builds). Trigger requires malformed compiled bytecode that pcre2_compile never emits, so it is a producer-contract violation, not a reachable defect.
Speculative: an XCL_RANGE with lo > hi would make max < min and produce a wrapped immediate in 'CMP(SLJIT_GREATER, TMP2, 0, SLJIT_IMM, max - min)'; the parser rejects such ranges at compile time.
Speculative: a bytecode stream without XCL_END would make the six 'while (*cc != XCL_END)' loops walk past the pattern buffer; termination relies on the producer always emitting the terminator.
Robustness only: the SLJIT_ASSERTs and SLJIT_UNREACHABLE markers are debug-only; in release builds malformed opcodes would be parsed silently, but no statement in this code can introduce them.

Wrong jump-list routing from the compares counter would only affect match results (logic), not memory safety; the accounting was verified to balance to zero for every item kind, including the PT_SCX PROP/NOTPROP asymmetry.

verdict.summary: All memory-writing sinks on in-code paths are guarded by quotable checks (tailen <= skb_tailroom(skb) before pskb_put; nr_frags < MAX_SKB_FRAGS before __skb_fill_page_desc; nfrags < 0 checked after skb_cow_data with goto out). The historical stale esp->esph defect is already fixed by the esph_offset save/restore present in this code. Speculative triggers requiring caller-contract violations (negative or INT_MAX-scale esp->tailen, esp->esph before the transport header, freed skb->sk) cannot be instantiated by any statement in this code and are recorded as limitations.

assumptions: esp_info fields (tailen, tfclen, plen, proto, esph) are produced by the XFRM/ESP caller (esp_output_tail and helpers, not shown); their bounds cannot be quoted from the given code and were traced as unbounded rather than dismissed.

skb_cow_data(skb, tailen, &trailer) success is taken to guarantee tailroom >= tailen on the returned trailer, per its documented kernel contract; this is a callee contract, not a guard quotable in this code.
skb_page_frag_refill(allocsize, pfrag, GFP_ATOMIC) success is taken to guarantee at least allocsize bytes available at pfrag->offset, per its documented contract.
esp_output_encap(x, skb, esp) is assumed to validate its own inputs and may modify esp fields; its code is not shown.
skb->sk lifetime is assumed to be held by the skb destructor while the skb exists, per kernel skb contract.
limitations: Negative esp->tailen would pass 'tailen <= skb_tailroom(skb)' and reach pskb_put/fill_trailer with a negative length; trigger requires the caller to produce a negative tailen, which no statement in this code can do (tailen is copied verbatim from esp->tailen). Speculative.

ALIGN(tailen, L1_CACHE_BYTES) on int tailen could wrap for tailen near INT_MAX; producer of such a value is not in this code and would also fail skb_page_frag_refill/skb_cow_data downstream. Speculative.
A negative esph_offset (esp->esph before skb_transport_header) would make the post-cow recompute point out of bounds; requires caller-contract violation at entry. Speculative.
refcount_add(tailen, &sk->sk_wmem_alloc) with sk = skb->sk would be a UAF if sk were freed mid-output; no statement in this code frees it. Speculative.
This function is a mid-pipeline kernel helper, not the intake point for packet data; the XFRM/ESP layer above it owns parsing and bounds computation for esp_info values.

verdict.summary: In the OrCAD tool-change-stop-switch branch, `tmps = get_line(fd++);` post-increments the local `gerb_file_t *fd` one whole struct past the single allocated gerb_file_t object. The very next statement then evaluates `fd->filename` through the incremented pointer, an out-of-bounds heap read whose indeterminate pointer value is passed as a %s argument to gerbv_stats_printf and dereferenced, causing a crash or disclosure of adjacent heap memory into the stored/displayed error stats. An attacker-supplied drill file containing a "TCST" sequence at a tool position fully instantiates the trigger.

evidence.reason: Origin of the defect: the post-increment advances the local fd (gerb_file_t *) by sizeof(gerb_file_t) past the single allocated gerb_file_t, and no subsequent statement restores it before fd is used again.

evidence.snippet:
gerbv_stats_printf(stats->error_list, GERBV_MESSAGE_NOTE, -1,
			_("Tool change stop switch found \"%s\" "
			    "at line %ld in file \"%s\""),
			tmps, file_line, fd->filename);
evidence.reason: Sink: `fd->filename` is evaluated through the incremented fd (fd_original+1), an out-of-bounds read of the filename member past the end of the allocated object; the indeterminate gchar* is then used as a %s argument and dereferenced. Trigger: attacker drill file with bytes 'T','C','S','T' passes `if((temp == 'C') && ((fd->ptr + 2) < fd->datalen))` and the nested 'S'/'T' checks, reaching this path with fd already incremented.

assumptions: TOOL_MIN/TOOL_MAX and the dimension of image->aperture[] are not shown; the quoted guard `if (tool_num < TOOL_MIN || tool_num >= TOOL_MAX)` was assumed consistent with the array bound, so the aperture indexing path was not treated as a finding.

fd is assumed to point to a single heap-allocated gerb_file_t (as produced by the file-open path not shown); if fd pointed into a larger array of at least two elements the read at fd+1 would be in-bounds, but no such allocation exists in the given code.

Implementations of gerb_fgetc, gerb_ungetc, get_line, gerb_fgetint, read_double, and gerbv_stats_printf are not shown; gerbv_stats_printf is assumed to format its arguments with printf semantics (so %s dereferences the garbage filename pointer).

The caller is assumed to have consumed the leading 'T' before calling this function, as implied by the comment "Sneak a peek at what's hiding after the 'T'"; this makes fd->ptr >= 4 at the `fd->ptr -= 4` statement.
limitations: `fd->ptr -= 4` underflow (negative ptr) could only occur if the caller had NOT consumed the leading 'T' before the call; that precondition contradicts the code's own comment and could not be instantiated — speculative.
`gerb_fgetint` overflow on very long tool-number strings depends on an implementation not shown, and its result is re-bounded by the quoted TOOL_MIN/TOOL_MAX check before any use — no reachable sink.

The `if ('\n' == temp || '\r' == temp) gerb_ungetc(fd);` inside the `if (EOF == temp)` block is dead code (temp is EOF there) and the double gerb_ungetc in the 'C','S',not-'T' path drops the 'C' from the stream; both are parsing-correctness issues with no demonstrated security effect.
A crash-only outcome on the tool-definition paths (e.g., g_new0 failure handled by GERB_FATAL_ERROR) is confined to allocation failure no attacker can induce.

verdict.summary: The element walk in QPaintEngineEx::stroke consumes the attacker-influenced QVectorPath element stream (types, points, elementCount) without validating it against the buffer extent. The CurveToElement arm reads six coordinates (points[0..5]) while the only bound on every path, `while (points < lastPoint)`, guarantees just one point, so a path whose type stream claims a curve with fewer than 3 elements remaining reads up to 32 bytes past the points buffer (same defect on the cosmetic branch). The default arm advances neither pointer, so any type value outside {MoveTo, LineTo, CurveTo} traps the loop in an infinite hang. Consequences: out-of-bounds heap read with disclosure potential and attacker-scalable unbounded work.

evidence.snippet:
case QPainterPath::CurveToElement:
                    d->activeStroker->cubicTo(points[0], points[1],
                                              points[2], points[3],
                                              points[4], points[5]);
evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds read (CWE-125): the sink consumes six coordinates but the only guard on the path is `while (points < lastPoint)`, which guarantees a single point. Trigger instantiated with a path of elementCount=2, points={x0,y0,x1,y1}, types={MoveToElement, CurveToElement}: after the MoveTo consumes 2 coordinates, the curve arm reads points[2..5] at offsets +4..+7, past the 4-qreal buffer.

Taint origin: the raw element-type stream, coordinate array, and element count enter unvalidated; lastPoint is computed as points + (pointCount<<1), covering only a one-point-per-iteration bound, and no statement in this code cross-checks the type stream against the array extents.

Infinite loop (CWE-835): for an element-type value outside the three handled cases (e.g., CurveToDataElement = 3), neither points nor types advances, so `while (points < lastPoint)` at line 111 never changes and the painting thread hangs forever; one tiny input yields unbounded work. Mirror site at lines 193-194.

Same out-of-bounds read on the cosmetic-pen branch: the guard `while (points < lastPoint)` at line 167 guarantees one point, but this arm dereferences three QPointF entries (six coordinates), reading past the buffer when fewer than 3 elements remain at a CurveToElement.

assumptions: `if (path.isEmpty()) return;` (lines 9-10) is assumed to imply elementCount > 0 and a non-null points array; QVectorPath::isEmpty() is implemented outside this code and could not be quoted.
QTransform::inverted() on a singular matrix and the qreal/QPointF layout compatibility of the `(const QPointF *) points` casts are guarantees external to this code.

The pen and transform values were taken at typical values (solid non-cosmetic and cosmetic pens) when simulating both branches; neither branch performs additional validation that would change the analysis.
limitations: In stock Qt, QVectorPath instances normally originate from QPainterPath conversion, which maintains type-stream/point consistency; reaching the defects here requires a caller that hands this engine a hand-built or desynchronized QVectorPath (private API or a bug in the producing code). Per the analysis rules this unquoted upstream enforcement cannot dismiss the candidates, but it bounds practical exploitability.
`pointCount << 1` (line 88) can overflow signed int only at roughly 2^30 elements (a multi-gigabyte input array), so that candidate was not instantiated.
A desync in which `types += 3` walks past the end of the types array (line 128/189) shares the same root cause as the primary out-of-bounds read and is not listed separately.
The maximum overread per curve element is 4 coordinates (32 bytes) and disclosure is indirect (values become rendered geometry), which is why severity is rated medium rather than high.

verdict.summary: The Ragel-generated Puma HTTP parser guards every buffer dereference with an explicit boundary check on every path: 'if ( p == pe ) goto _test_eof;' before the initial dispatch, and 'if ( ++p == pe ) goto _test_eofN;' before each state's case block, so network-controlled request bytes cannot drive an out-of-bounds read or write. Pointer-difference lengths passed to callbacks are computed between in-buffer positions, and body_start/header_done arithmetic stays within [0, len] at the boundary values (p == pe-1). The remaining defects are contract- or hardening-level: off > len is only guarded by a (NDEBUG-removable) assert on a caller-supplied resume offset, and stale mark offsets across differently-buffered resumed parses would require caller misuse. No trigger reachable by a network peer with memory-safety, injection, or amplification impact could be instantiated.

assumptions: MARK/PTR_TO/LEN and puma_parser_has_error are not in the given code; MARK was assumed to store a buffer-relative offset and PTR_TO/LEN to reconstruct in-buffer pointers, consistent with every MARK(mark, p) site executing at a guarded in-buffer p.
Callbacks (request_method, http_field, header_done, etc.) are assumed not to write through the pointers/lengths they receive; their bodies are outside the given code.
The caller is assumed to pass the same accumulated buffer and a consistent off when resuming a partial parse, per the incremental-parsing contract.
Whether the build defines NDEBUG (disabling all assert calls) is unknown from the given code.
limitations: Speculative (contract): off > len yields p > pe and an out-of-bounds read at the first '(*p)' dispatch; only enforcement is 'assert(off <= len && "offset past end of buffer");' which aborts and vanishes under NDEBUG, but off is a caller-owned resume offset the network attacker does not control — trigger not instantiated (STEP 4a).

Speculative (contract): mark/field_start offsets persisted in the parser are only valid against the buffer they were recorded in; a caller resuming with a different buffer would get out-of-bounds reads in the PTR_TO/LEN callback arguments. No statement in this code can produce that condition.
Hardening: all postconditions ('assert(parser->mark < len)', 'assert(parser->field_len <= len)', etc.) are assert-only and compiled out under NDEBUG; they diagnose but never recover.

Protocol leniency, not a memory defect in this code: signed-char comparisons in case 15/17 reject bytes >= 128 in header names, while case 20/21 accept them in request URIs and fragments; high-bit/NUL tolerance in request targets can enable cross-server request smuggling at layers above this parser.
snake_upcase_char((char *)p) casts away const and mutates the caller's buffer in place; safe for Puma's mutable request buffer, but a read-only buffer would be a caller contract violation.

Uninitialized or reused puma_parser state (including cs after an error, since 'if (!puma_parser_has_error(parser)) parser->cs = cs;' skips the store on error) is a caller responsibility; any cs value merely falls through the switch without memory access.

verdict.summary: The function passes the attacker-controlled parameter hash_size (unsigned, line 3) directly to bits2int (line 61) which writes into the fixed-size local stack buffer tmp[uECC_MAX_WORDS] (line 8), without any bound check on hash_size anywhere in this function. An attacker originating the data being signed can supply an oversized hash_size, producing an out-of-bounds write past tmp and memory corruption in the signing process.

evidence.reason: Sink: the attacker-controlled size parameter hash_size is passed unvalidated to bits2int, which writes into the fixed-size local buffer tmp[uECC_MAX_WORDS]. No check on hash_size exists anywhere in this function; if hash_size exceeds the buffer capacity, an out-of-bounds stack write occurs (CWE-787).
Origin: hash_size enters as an unsigned parameter with no bound enforcement at any point between this declaration and its sole use at line 61.
Destination buffer: fixed-capacity stack buffer that bits2int writes into using the unvalidated hash_size; overflow of this buffer is the out-of-bounds write consequence.

assumptions: The implementation of bits2int is not shown in the given code; per guard anchoring rules, any clamping it might perform internally cannot be verified and is treated as an assumption that cannot dismiss the unvalidated sink at line 61.
The uECC_MAX_WORDS macro value and sizeof(uECC_word_t) are not shown; overflow requires hash_size to exceed uECC_MAX_WORDS * sizeof(uECC_word_t), which an unsigned parameter can trivially do.
The signature output buffer size (2 * curve->num_bytes) is an interface contract with the caller; writes to signature at lines 48/68/70 assume the caller provides a conforming buffer.
limitations: When g_rng_function is NULL, tmp[0] is set to 1 (line 36), making the blinding factor constant and disabling side-channel protection of the modular inverse; this is a deliberate fallback for integrators who do not register an RNG and requires a physical side-channel attacker with a distinct attack model, so it is noted as a hardening concern rather than a confirmed vulnerability in this code.

The private_key buffer must have at least BITS_TO_BYTES(curve->num_n_bits) readable bytes; a shorter buffer causes an out-of-bounds read, but this is a caller contract violation, not a defect instantiated by this code's own data flow.

verdict.summary: All pointer dereferences are guarded by short-circuit bounds checks that hold at every edge value (from == end, one-past, overshoot by step-1): 'while (from < end)' (line 10), 'if (from >= end || data != *from)' (line 14), and 'while ((from < end) && (*from == data))' (line 20). The PCX run-count byte is provably bounded to 0xC1..0xCF by the max_run loop 'while (from - start >= max_run)' (line 23) together with 'start += max_run;' (line 26), because from-start is always an exact multiple of step, so '(from - start) / step + 0xc1' never exceeds 0xCF and decoded run lengths exactly match the input in all simulated boundary cases (run of 16 at the loop boundary, run of 20, and a run whose scan overshoots end by step-1). The only failure modes found require the caller to pass a stride outside the function's documented forward-scan domain (step <= 0 gives a hang or backwards out-of-bounds read; step > INT_MAX/15 overflows 'int max_run = step * MAX_RUN_COUNT'), which is an interface-contract violation this code's own flow cannot produce, so those triggers are speculative, not vulnerabilities in this code.

assumptions: 'byte' is assumed to be an unsigned char typedef (as in Ghostscript); if it were a plain signed char, 'data >= 0xc0' at lines 15 and 28 would never fire for high bytes, which would corrupt the output stream format but not cause memory unsafety in this process.

ptrdiff_t is assumed to be at least 32 bits and wider than int, so the comparisons 'from - start >= max_run' and the count arithmetic '(from - start) / step + 0xc1' do not themselves wrap for any realistic buffer; the code declares no narrower types.
gp_fputc is assumed to be the standard Ghostscript byte-output helper; its failure returns being ignored affects only output integrity on I/O errors.
limitations: Speculative (contract): step < 0 makes 'from += step' walk backwards; 'while (from < end)' (line 10) then never terminates, line 14 dereferences one byte before the buffer, line 20 walks backwards out of bounds, and with max_run negative the loop at line 23 emits 0xCF/data pairs forever, leaking adjacent process memory into the output file. Trigger precondition not instantiable: requires a caller passing a negative stride, which violates the forward-scan domain documented by the function's own control flow ('while (from < end)' with 'from += step'); this code's own statements never produce it.
Speculative (contract): step == 0 makes max_run 0 and the inner loop at line 20 never advances, hanging the process; same uninstantiable contract precondition.

Speculative (contract): step > INT_MAX/15 causes signed overflow in 'int max_run = step * MAX_RUN_COUNT;' (line 8); a negative max_run makes 'while (from - start >= max_run)' (line 23) loop forever emitting pairs (unbounded output growth). Requires an absurd stride far outside any real caller; not instantiable from this code.

Robustness only: 'from += step' (line 13) can form a pointer up to step-1 bytes beyond one-past-end (C UB in pointer formation), but no dereference occurs there because 'from >= end' short-circuits first at line 14; no memory is improperly read or written.
Robustness only: gp_fputc return values are ignored throughout, so a mid-stream write failure silently truncates output; no attacker-controllable security consequence in this process.

verdict.summary: In gf_avc_parse_nalu, after avc_parse_slice rebinds n_state.sps from the attacker-controlled current slice header, the comparison at line 80 dereferences n_state.sps without any NULL check, while the sibling pointer avc->s_info.sps is checked one statement earlier (lines 77-78). A crafted H.264 stream in which a slice references a parameter set whose SPS is absent drives n_state.sps to NULL and crashes the parsing process (denial of service) once the earlier matching checks (frame_num, field_pic_flag, nal_ref_idc, nal_unit_type) are satisfied, all of which are attacker-controlled bitstream fields.

evidence.reason: The only NULL guard on any sps pointer in the function checks avc->s_info.sps (the previous slice's SPS), but the very next statement dereferences n_state.sps (the current slice's SPS, rebound by avc_parse_slice from the attacker's slice header) with no check anywhere in the function; n_state.sps is NULL when the attacker's slice references a PPS whose SPS was never parsed, causing a NULL-pointer dereference and process crash on crafted media.

Origin of the tainted pointer: avc_parse_slice parses the attacker-controlled slice header (pps_id/sps_id read from the bitstream) and rebinds n_state.sps accordingly; a non-negative return passes the 'if (ret < 0) return ret;' check on the next line even when the resolved SPS is absent, letting the NULL reach the dereference at line 80.

assumptions: avc_parse_slice, svc_parse_slice, gf_avc_read_sps_bs_internal, gf_avc_read_pps_bs_internal and gf_bs_read_ue are not shown; their internal contracts cannot be quoted. In particular, the exact statement inside avc_parse_slice that can leave n_state.sps NULL (PPS referencing an unparsed SPS id) is inferred, not quoted; per the guard-anchoring rule this unshown helper cannot be used to validate the pointer this function dereferences.
AVCState avc is assumed non-NULL and zero-initialized by the caller; first-call behavior of n_state fields copied at line 13 depends on that initialization.
GF_AVC_NALU_* constants and struct layouts (AVCSliceInfo, AVC_SPS offset of poc_type) are taken from the surrounding codebase, not shown.
