limitations: Line 128 'avc->last_ps_idx = (s32) gf_bs_read_ue(bs);' accepts attacker-derived indices up to INT32_MAX (the '< 0' check only catches sign-wrapped values); last_ps_idx is not used as an index anywhere in this function, so any out-of-bounds access would occur at unshown call sites and is speculative here.

Line 29 discards svc_parse_slice's return value (fail-open parsing); no memory-safety, disclosure, or authz consequence is provable within this code, so it is recorded as robustness, not a vulnerability.

The primary defect's worst-case consequence is a crash (DoS) of the process parsing attacker-supplied media; if this function were only ever invoked by an equal-privilege user on their own local file with no service boundary, the same trigger would be a robustness bug rather than a security impact.

verdict.summary: In _inplace_src_spans, span extents derived from rendered (attacker-influenced) geometry are never validated against the capacity of the fixed-size mask buffer r->_buf. In the else branch, len = spans[1].x - spans[0].x (an unbounded difference of two attacker-derived integers) is used directly as the memset length into r->_buf ('memset (m, spans[0].coverage, --len)'), and m also advances cumulatively across iterations with no reset or total bound. A single partial-coverage span wider than the row buffer, or an accumulation of such spans, causes a heap out-of-bounds write with attacker-influenced length and byte value in any process using cairo to render untrusted content.

evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds write sink: the write pointer m and the memset length len are never compared to the end of r->_buf anywhere in the function; the only nearby check, 'if (len > 1)', merely excludes zero-length memsets and bounds nothing. Trigger fully instantiated: with num_spans=2, spans[0]={x:0, coverage:0x80}, spans[1]={x:65536}, the first two branch conditions (coverage==0xff, coverage==0x0) are false, and memset writes 65535 coverage bytes into the fixed-size row buffer, a heap overflow with attacker-influenced length and value.
Origin of the tainted length: a raw difference of two attacker-derived span x coordinates with no bound, range check, or clip validation on any path to the memset sink at line 85.

assumptions: r->_buf is a fixed-size mask row buffer allocated in _composite_spans (not shown); its capacity and any _buf_end field cannot be quoted from the given code, so no in-buffer bound for m can be assumed inside this function.

The scan converter that emits spans/num_spans is expected by design to produce non-decreasing spans within the clip extents, but that enforcement lives in code not shown and is not relied on; per historical reports in this exact function (OSS-Fuzz/CVE-2020-35492 family) that upstream invariant has failed in practice.
PIXMAN_HAS_OP_LERP only selects between composite paths; the overflow in the else branch is identical under either build configuration.
limitations: Out-of-bounds read of spans[1] when num_spans==1: the only guard, 'if (num_spans == 0)', does not reject the boundary value 1, but a single-element span array can only occur if the unseen span emitter violates its contract of terminating each row with a final span; speculative, not counted.
Signed overflow in spans[1].x - spans[0].x requires INT_MAX-scale coordinates and is not needed for the primary trigger, which uses ordinary positive values.
pixman_image_composite32 calls receiving out-of-range extents/widths (e.g., 'spans[1].x - spans[0].x, h') share the same unvalidated-span root cause and were not counted as separate findings.
Negative len from out-of-order spans merely desynchronizes the mask accumulation (robustness, no memory-safety effect at the memset since 'len > 1' is false).

verdict.summary: The Ragel-generated Puma HTTP/1.1 parser consumes attacker-controlled request bytes, but every pointer dereference is bounded: the entry read is guarded by `if ( p == pe ) goto _test_eof;` and every state advance by `if ( ++p == pe ) goto _test_eofN;`, verified on all 45 states and at boundary values (off == len, last-byte termination, empty-body header_done). The only unguarded path, off > len (p starts past pe so no ++p == pe check can ever match, yielding an unbounded out-of-bounds walk), is prevented solely by `assert(off <= len ...)`, which is a no-op under NDEBUG; however, off is an interface-contract argument whose documented domain is asserted in the code, and this code's own flow cannot produce off > len, so the trigger is speculative and does not establish a vulnerability in this code.

assumptions: MARK, PTR_TO, LEN macros and puma_parser_has_error are not shown; assumed standard Ragel semantics (LEN(mark, p) = p - (buffer + mark)) operating within the buffer, so all callback length arguments stay in-bounds.
The input buffer is assumed non-NULL and to have at least len readable bytes, per the documented interface contract.
Production builds of the extension are assumed to define NDEBUG, making all assert checks no-ops; this affects only the speculative off > len path and debug-only aborts.
snake_upcase_char is assumed to uppercase a single in-bounds character in place; the const cast-away write lands on the current p, which is bounds-checked.
parser->mark, field_start, field_len, query_start are assumed zero-initialized in the struct before first use (not shown).
limitations: Speculative (contract): the only enforcement of off <= len is `assert(off <= len && "offset past end of buffer");` — compiled out under NDEBUG. If a caller ever passes off > len, `p = buffer+off` starts past `pe = buffer+len`, no `++p == pe` check can ever match, and the parser walks unbounded past the buffer end (out-of-bounds read). The precondition (caller violating the documented domain) could not be instantiated from this code's own flow, so this is a defense-in-depth gap, not a confirmed vulnerability here.

Debug-only robustness: with a zero-length buffer (len == 0, off == 0) on a fresh parser, `assert(parser->mark < len)` and `assert(parser->field_start < len)` evaluate 0 < 0 and abort the process in debug builds; no effect in release builds and no disclosure or amplification.

Permissive parsing: in URI/fragment/query states (e.g. case 20/21/23/24/25/26), bytes 0x80-0xFF are negative as signed char and bypass the control-character rejections (`if ( 0 <= (*p) && (*p) <= 31 ) goto st0;` and `else if ( (*p) >= 0 ) goto st0;`), so high-bit bytes are accepted into request URIs. No memory-safety sink is violated inside this code; potential request-smuggling interoperability concern with other servers, not actionable here.

On parse error, `if (!puma_parser_has_error(parser)) parser->cs = cs;` leaves the previous parser->cs in place; a state-consistency quirk with no demonstrated memory or authorization effect in this code.

verdict.summary: This is the patched form of TensorFlow's BoostedTreesCreateEnsembleOp. The historical double-free on the parse-failure path (unique_ptr destructor firing on an object already destroyed by result->Unref()) is explicitly prevented by the guard 'result.release();  // Needed due to the `->Unref` above, to prevent UAF', which is placed on the only path of that branch before the OP_REQUIRES return; unique_ptr::release() does not dereference the dangling pointer, so no use-after-free or double-free occurs on any exit (parse-failure return, CreateResource error return, ALREADY_EXISTS fall-through, or normal return). Attacker-controlled values (stamp_token, serialized ensemble bytes, resource handle container/name) flow only into unshown callees (InitFromSerialized, CreateResource, HandleFromInput) and reach no memory, index, size, or injection sink inside this code. The only in-code misuse candidates are framework-level CHECK aborts on malformed tensor shape/dtype, which are dtype/shape contract issues enforced at graph construction and at worst cleanly abort the process executing the attacker-supplied graph.

assumptions: BoostedTreesEnsembleResource is a freshly allocated refcounted object with initial refcount 1 (constructor not shown), so a single Unref at line 15 destroys it exactly once.
InitFromSerialized (not shown) returns false on parse failure and true on success; its internal parsing of attacker-controlled serialized bytes cannot be analyzed here.

CreateResource and HandleFromInput (not shown) take the released raw pointer's ownership and handle ALREADY_EXISTS per their contracts; ownership semantics on their error paths cannot be verified from this code.
Op registration for this kernel enforces input dtypes and (per the op's shape function) scalar shapes at graph construction; this is a framework contract outside the given code.
OP_REQUIRES/OP_REQUIRES_OK semantics (set status and return) are the standard TensorFlow macros.
limitations: Supplying a non-scalar tensor to scalar<int64>() or scalar<tstring>() would hit a framework CHECK failure and abort the process; under the attacker/impact model this is at most a denial-of-service of the process already executing the attacker-supplied graph, with no disclosure, corruption, or amplification, and dtype/shape are contract-enforced at graph construction.
A potential leak of the newly created resource on CreateResource error paths depends on ownership semantics of unshown callee code and could not be instantiated from this code.
Defects in parsing attacker-controlled serialized ensemble data would reside inside InitFromSerialized, which is not part of the given code; no judgment on it is possible here.
The historical double-free of this op is fixed by the release() call at line 16; this candidate was rejected because the exact counterfactual guard is present and verified on every exit path.

verdict.summary: In the FTPWHO branch of dostor, an uploaded filename whose length is >= sizeof shm_data_cur->filename takes the else path where memcpy reads from &name[sl - sizeof shm_data_cur->filename - 1U]; at the boundary value sl == sizeof shm_data_cur->filename this size_t expression underflows to (size_t)-1, making the source pointer one byte before the filename buffer, so one byte out of bounds is read and persisted into shared memory (visible to ftpwho readers). Additionally the else branch copies exactly sizeof bytes and never writes a NUL, leaving shm_data_cur->filename unterminated for every long name. A remote FTP client controls the STOR argument and thus triggers this directly.

evidence.reason: Sink of the confirmed defect: for sl >= sizeof shm_data_cur->filename (attacker controls STOR name length via line 142), the source index sl - sizeof shm_data_cur->filename - 1U underflows at sl == sizeof shm_data_cur->filename to (size_t)-1, producing a source pointer one byte before the name buffer (1-byte out-of-bounds read persisted into shared memory), and the copy of exactly sizeof bytes never NUL-terminates the destination. The only nearby guard, 'if (sl < sizeof shm_data_cur->filename)' at line 150, admits this exact boundary value into the else branch; no clamping or terminator write exists on this path.

Origin of the tainted length: sl is the length of the attacker-supplied STOR filename; no statement in this code bounds it below sizeof shm_data_cur->filename, and the guard at line 150 passes the boundary value sl == sizeof shm_data_cur->filename into the defective else branch.

assumptions: checknamesanity(name, dot_write_ok) may reject some names, but no length bound is quotable from the given code; the presence of the truncation else branch indicates names of length >= sizeof shm_data_cur->filename are anticipated inputs.
Whether ul_init initializes ulhandler on failure is not shown; its failure path feeds ulhandler.total_uploaded into 'uploaded += ...' at line 193.
Consumers of shm_data_cur->filename (e.g., pure-ftpwho reading the shared segment) are outside this code; the unterminated array written here can cause string over-reads there.
Compile-time flags (FTPWHO, QUOTAS, SHOW_REAL_DISK_SPACE) determine which branches are built; the FTPWHO block containing the primary defect is included verbatim in the given code.
get_atomic_file, tryautorename, get_file_size, ul_check_free_space, and quota_update contracts are not shown; their return values are only relied on where this code checks them explicitly.
limitations: Uninitialized read candidate: if ul_init fails without initializing the handler, 'uploaded += (unsigned long long) ulhandler.total_uploaded;' (line 193) and displayrate (line 251) read uninitialized stack; speculative because ul_init's failure behavior is a callee contract not shown. The QUOTAS quota-exceeded path (goto afterquota at line 122) was simulated and does NOT hit these reads (overflow=1 selects the addreply branch and the goto jumps over line 193).

unlink(atomic_file) at end (lines 256-258) can destroy the pre-existing file that was renamed onto atomic_file at lines 45-46 when a later error path fires; data loss is confined to the uploading user's own file in a directory the user can already write/unlink in, so it is robustness, not a cross-boundary security impact.

FSTATFS(f, &statfsbuf) at line 180 runs after '(void) close(f);' at line 174; with no fd-reallocating call shown between them it fails with EBADF, making the SHOW_REAL_DISK_SPACE block dead/robustness-only.

TOCTOU on name between checknamesanity (line 33) and rename/open (lines 45-46, 57-61) would require a local racing party with write access to the same directory at equal privilege, and O_NOFOLLOW is used on the opens; speculative, no interleavable ordered pair exhibited.
The ASCII-mode gate 'restartat > (off_t) 1' at line 19 permits ASCII resume at offset exactly 1; correctness nit with no memory-safety effect demonstrated.

verdict.summary: QPaintEngineEx::stroke decodes the attacker-supplied element-type stream against the points buffer with only a 2-qreal loop bound (`while (points < lastPoint)`). A CurveToElement type decoded when fewer than 6 qreals remain makes cubicTo read up to 4 qreals (32 bytes) past the end of the points buffer on both the non-cosmetic and cosmetic paths; the types pointer itself is never length-bounded. The out-of-bounds heap values become stroke geometry that is rasterized, giving disclosure potential and a possible crash at a page boundary.

evidence.snippet:
case QPainterPath::CurveToElement:
                    d->activeStroker->cubicTo(points[0], points[1],
                                              points[2], points[3],
                                              points[4], points[5]);
evidence.reason: Sink reads 6 qreals (3 points) for a cubic curve, but the only bound on this path, `while (points < lastPoint)` (line 111) with `lastPoint = points + (pointCount<<1)` (line 88), guarantees merely that 2 qreals remain. Instantiated trigger: elementCount()==1, points buffer of exactly 2 doubles, types == {CurveToElement}; the loop is entered (base < base+2) and points[2]..points[5] read 32 bytes past the 16-byte allocation; the values become rendered stroke geometry via fill(). No `points + 6 > lastPoint` check exists anywhere in the function.

Same defect on the cosmetic-pen affine path: the three QPointF loads consume 6 qreals while the loop guard `while (points < lastPoint)` (line 167) only ensures 2 remain; a trailing CurveToElement with 2 or 4 qreals left reads out of bounds.

Origin of the tainted data and the only bound: the types stream and points buffer enter directly from the public parameter `path`; `lastPoint` bounds only the points pointer (2 qreals per iteration) and no types-array length is ever consulted, so the decode loop trusts the type byte `*types` to be consistent with the remaining point count — the consistency check whose absence causes the out-of-bounds reads at lines 124-126 and 184-187.

assumptions: QVectorPath::isEmpty() is assumed to return true exactly when elementCount()==0; under that semantics the `if (path.isEmpty()) return;` check (lines 9-10) validly guards the first-element reads at lines 139/203 and the implicit-close reads of path.points()[0..1].

StrokeHandler is assumed to be a growable buffer (the constructor argument at line 13 being a capacity hint). If StrokeHandler had fixed capacity, a later call with a larger path could overflow it, but that cannot be verified from the given code.
QPen/QTransform/QColor/QList internals invoked here (dashPattern, inverted(), setAlpha) are assumed to maintain their own documented invariants.
The stroker/dasher hooks (qpaintengineex_moveTo/lineTo/cubicTo) are assumed to consume coordinates without further bounds requirements on the input buffer.
limitations: Integer overflow candidates at line 13 (`path.elementCount()+4`) and line 88 (`pointCount<<1`) require elementCount near INT_MAX. A legitimate path of that size needs a ~32GB points buffer, and a fabricated count without a buffer is a direct QVectorPath constructor contract violation; the trigger was not instantiated, so these remain speculative.

The unbounded `types` pointer walk (`++types`, `types += 3` with `*types` read each iteration) is real but is the same missing-consistency root cause as the primary finding; the function receives no types-array length, so it cannot bound it independently.

Realistic reachability caveat: applications that only feed paths through QPainter/QPainterPath get internally consistent types/points data; the out-of-bounds trigger requires a caller passing a hand-built QVectorPath whose type stream is inconsistent with elementCount, e.g., a decoder for an untrusted vector format constructing QVectorPath directly or a custom QPaintEngineEx subclass invoked with external content.

NaN extent/patternLength in the dash-approximation branch (line 42) can produce odd rendering (NaN comparisons are false, so dashing proceeds) but reaches no memory, index, or injection sink; not a vulnerability.

verdict.summary: This USB probe helper performs checked allocations and balanced, single frees on every error path. All goto sites assign status before jumping, allocation sizes are fixed constants (2048, 252, MAX_DEBUGFS_ENTRIES-1), and the function contains no memory-copy, index, format, command, path, or crypto sinks. The attacker-reachable branch (malformed USB descriptors failing rsi_find_bulk_in_and_out_endpoints) executes before usb_set_intfdata registration and produces a clean unwind. The one latent hazard — adapter->rsi_dev (and, on late failures, the drvdata registration) surviving kfree(rsi_dev) on error paths — has no dereference or use inside this code; its harmful use exists only in unshown caller/core code, so it remains a speculative lifetime hazard, not a demonstrated vulnerability in this code.

assumptions: rsi_find_bulk_in_and_out_endpoints(pfunction, adapter) and rsi_usb_init_rx(adapter) honor the contracts implied by their use here (nonzero return means failure; rsi_usb_init_rx cleans up its own partial allocations); both are not shown.

The caller of rsi_init_usb_interface tears down the whole adapter object after a failed init (return < 0), so fields written into adapter before failure (adapter->rsi_dev, adapter->device) are not expected to be re-used; this is caller behavior not shown in the given code.
The USB core's handling of interface data after a failed probe (whether drvdata is cleared or disconnect is suppressed) is external to this code and is treated as an assumption, not enforcement.
MAX_DEBUGFS_ENTRIES is a compile-time constant large enough that the debugfs arrays sized by consumers match the (MAX_DEBUGFS_ENTRIES - 1) count; consumers are not shown.
limitations: Speculative CWE-416-pattern hazard: on the error paths, kfree(rsi_dev) at fail_eps/fail_rx runs without clearing the earlier assignment adapter->rsi_dev = rsi_dev, leaving a dangling pointer inside the caller-owned adapter after this function returns. The use site of that dangling pointer is not present in the given code, and a malicious USB device can select the -EINVAL error path via malformed descriptors, so this would become a real UAF/double-free if any unshown teardown path (caller deinit, retry, or disconnect) ever dereferences or re-frees adapter->rsi_dev after a failed init. Trigger precondition not instantiated here.

Speculative: usb_set_intfdata(pfunction, adapter) is not unwound when a later step (tx_buffer kmalloc or rsi_usb_init_rx) fails, leaving stale drvdata after a failed probe; however those failure points are allocation/OS failures rather than attacker-controlled input, and the attacker-descriptor failure path occurs before registration. No use of the stale registration exists in this code.

status is unconditionally assigned before each goto (-EINVAL, -ENOMEM, -ENOMEM), so no uninitialized-return defect exists; if a future edit adds an unchecked-failure goto, that invariant would need re-verification.

verdict.summary: bgp_capability_msg_parse parses attacker-supplied BGP Capability message content. The two `continue` statements inside the MP-capability branch (lines 59 and 66) jump back to the `while (pnt < end)` loop head without executing the loop's only cursor advance `pnt += hdr->length + 3;` (line 102) and without any other state change, so a remote peer sending one small Capability message containing an MP capability with invalid afi/safi (or when override-capability is configured) causes a deterministic infinite loop that wedges the bgpd process at 100% CPU (CWE-835, remote DoS). Additionally, the unconditional `memcpy (&mpc, pnt + 3, sizeof (struct capability_mp_data));` (line 49) is guarded only by the fits-in-message check at line 41, never by a check that hdr->length >= sizeof(struct capability_mp_data); with hdr->length = 0 and pnt + 3 == end it reads 4 bytes past the end of the received message (CWE-125), and those bytes flow into afi/safi values that are emitted to debug logs.

evidence.reason: Root cause of the infinite loop (CWE-835): this `continue` (and the one at lines 58-59 under PEER_FLAG_OVERRIDE_CAPABILITY) returns to `while (pnt < end)` (line 14) while skipping the loop's only cursor advance `pnt += hdr->length + 3;` (line 102); no statement on the path mutates pnt, end, or peer state. Trigger fully instantiated: a remote BGP peer sends a Capability message whose body is {CAPABILITY_ACTION_SET, CAPABILITY_CODE_MP, 3, afi=0x00, 0x00, safi=0xFF}; line 61 rejects the indices and line 66 loops forever, converting a ~6-byte network input into unbounded CPU work and a permanent hang of the routing daemon.

evidence.snippet:
/* Fetch structure to the byte stream. */
      memcpy (&mpc, pnt + 3, sizeof (struct capability_mp_data));
evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds read sink (CWE-125): a fixed 4-byte copy from pnt+3 executed before any check that the capability payload is at least sizeof(struct capability_mp_data). Trigger fully instantiated: with message body {CAPABILITY_ACTION_SET, CAPABILITY_CODE_MP, 0} of length 3, line 17 passes (pnt+3 == end) and line 41 passes at its equality edge (pnt + 0 + 3 == end), then this memcpy reads bytes end[0..3] — 4 bytes past the end of the received message; the values land in mpc.afi/mpc.safi and are printed by the zlog_debug calls (lines 64, 71-75), giving disclosure potential across the network trust boundary.

evidence.snippet:
/* Capability length check. */
      if ((pnt + hdr->length + 3) > end)
evidence.reason: Origin of the unvalidated length at the memcpy sink: this is the only capability-length guard on the path to line 49, and it merely checks that the capability fits within the message (pnt + hdr->length + 3 <= end). It never compares hdr->length against sizeof(struct capability_mp_data), so hdr->length values 0-3 reach the 4-byte copy at line 49 with the read extending past end at the boundary case pnt + hdr->length + 3 == end.

assumptions: sizeof(struct capability_mp_data) is assumed to be 4 bytes (16-bit afi, reserved byte, safi byte); the struct definition is not shown in the given code.

bgp_afi_safi_valid_indices(afi, &safi) is assumed to reject out-of-range afi/safi such as afi=0 or safi=0xFF and to canonicalize safi; the helper body is not shown, so the array-index guard at line 61 for the peer->afc_recv[afi][safi] indexing relies on that documented behavior.

The allocation backing the received message is not shown; whether the 4-byte over-read at line 49 crosses the heap allocation boundary (as opposed to only the logical message boundary) depends on how exactly the message fills the receive stream buffer. No statement in this code bounds the allocation, so no such bound was credited.
limitations: The override-capability `continue` at lines 58-59 shares the same infinite-loop root cause as line 66 but additionally requires the operator to have configured PEER_FLAG_OVERRIDE_CAPABILITY on the peer; the line 66 trigger is unconditionally attacker-reachable and alone drives the verdict.

The out-of-bounds read leaks at most the afi/safi fields of mpc into debug logs and only when BGP_DEBUG(normal, NORMAL) is enabled; its worst-case heap-allocation crossing depends on stream slack not visible in this code, but the read past the validated message region `end` is fully instantiated.

verdict.summary: eval7 is Vim's expression parser dispatch layer. All attacker-controlled expression text enters through *arg and is routed to type-specific helper parsers whose bodies are not shown. The checks that exist inside this function are correctly placed and edge-safe: 'int ret = OK;' initialization, 'rettv->v_type = VAR_UNKNOWN;' sentinel, the NULL-safe 'int evaluate = evalarg != NULL && (evalarg->eval_flags & EVAL_EVALUATE);', the leader guard 'if (ret == OK && evaluate && end_leader > start_leader && rettv->v_type != VAR_BLOB)', the vim9 lambda guard 'if (ret == OK && evaluate)' before the pt_func dereference, the name-length guard 'if (len <= 0) ret = FAIL;' covering every later use of len, the fail-closed 'else if (flags & EVAL_CONSTANT) ret = FAIL;', and the parenthesized-expression error path that does 'clear_tv(rettv); ret = FAIL;'. The candidate defects identified (potential NULL deref of rettv->vval.v_partial->pt_func, a possible s/len mismatch after 's = alias' in the curly-braces name path, potentially uninitialized 'alias', missing legacy-mode register validation before get_reg_contents, NULL name_start reaching handle_subscript) all require a helper function not shown in this excerpt to misbehave or violate its contract. None could be instantiated by statements present in the given code, and the worst-case consequences exhibited are confined to the same editor process that is evaluating the expression. No format-string, command, path, or injection sink exists in this code: all message calls use constant format strings.

assumptions: The expression string pointed to by *arg is NUL-terminated; this is required for the safety of '*(*arg + 1)' in the '.' check and for '**arg != NUL' checks, but is enforced by the eval framework, not by any statement in this code.

get_name_len (not shown) always writes *alias (typically to NULL on entry) and returns a length consistent with the alias when one is produced; the 's = alias' / len pairing in this code is safe only under that contract.

get_lambda_tv (not shown) returns OK, when combined with EVAL_EVALUATE in the shared evalarg, only with a valid VAR_PARTIAL whose pt_func is non-NULL; the dereference 'rettv->vval.v_partial->pt_func' is guarded only by 'if (ret == OK && evaluate)' in this code.

get_reg_contents (not shown) rejects or safely handles register characters that are invalid in legacy script; this code only guards the vim9 path with 'else if (in_vim9script() && !valid_yank_reg(**arg, FALSE))'.

handle_subscript (not shown) tolerates name_start == NULL, which this code passes on all constant, lambda, register, and parenthesized paths since 'char_u *name_start = NULL;' is only overwritten in the variable-name branch.

eval_leader, eval_number, eval_string, eval_lit_string, eval_list, eval_dict, eval_option, eval_env_var, compile_def_function, and eval_func all enforce their documented contracts and do not read past the NUL terminator of the expression text.

VAR_UNKNOWN, which this code sets at entry and can leave in rettv on error branches of case '@' (where ret remains OK), is treated safely by downstream consumers per the code's own comment that clear_tv() can handle it.
limitations: Candidate (CWE-476, speculative): 'ufunc_T *ufunc = rettv->vval.v_partial->pt_func;' dereferences v_partial without a NULL check. Trigger requires get_lambda_tv to return OK with v_partial or pt_func NULL while EVAL_EVALUATE is set in the shared evalarg; no statement in this code produces that value and get_lambda_tv's body is not shown. Worst case is a crash of the same editor process evaluating the expression, with no disclosure or amplification exhibited.

Candidate (CWE-125, speculative): 'if (alias != NULL) s = alias;' replaces the name pointer while 'len' was returned for the pre-alias text; if get_name_len returned an alias shorter than len, 'eval_variable(s, len, ...)' or 'check_vars(s, len)' could read past the alias allocation. The mismatch cannot be produced by any statement in this code; STRNCMP uses ('len == 4 && STRNCMP(s, "true", 4) == 0' etc.) are safe even under mismatch because strncmp stops at NUL.
Candidate (CWE-457, speculative): 'char_u *alias;' is declared uninitialized and read at 'if (alias != NULL)'; only safe if get_name_len always writes *alias, which is not shown.

Candidate (missing validation, speculative here): in legacy script the register character reaches 'get_reg_contents(**arg, GREG_EXPR_SRC)' with no guard in this code (the 'valid_yank_reg' check is vim9-only, and '@' as the final character passes the register value NUL); any memory-unsafe handling of that byte would be a defect inside get_reg_contents, whose body is not shown, so no defective statement in this code could be exhibited.

Candidate (CWE-476, contract): 'ret = handle_subscript(arg, name_start, rettv, evalarg, TRUE);' runs with name_start == NULL on all non-variable paths; whether handle_subscript dereferences it cannot be determined from this excerpt.

Robustness observation, not a vulnerability: the vim9 error branches in case '@' ('semsg(_(e_syntax_error_at_str), *arg);' and 'emsg_invreg(**arg);') leave ret == OK with rettv still VAR_UNKNOWN, so evaluation continues with an unset value after an error has been reported; downstream type handling is not shown and no security impact was instantiated.

Crash-only consequences (e.g., a hypothetical NULL deref in the vim9 lambda path) triggered by an expression sourced from the same unprivileged user running the editor, with no memory disclosure, control-flow hijack, or attacker-scalable amplification exhibited, are classified as robustness issues under the impact model rather than vulnerabilities.

verdict.summary: This is Vim's get_visual_text(). Every memory sink in the function (**pp at line 31, (*pp)[*lenp-1] at line 39, and the mb_ptr2len operand at line 38) is protected on all paths by quotable guards: the same-line check 'if (VIsual.lnum != curwin->w_cursor.lnum) return FAIL', the empty-selection reset 'if (**pp == NUL) *lenp = 0', and the index guard 'if (*lenp > 0)'. Since both branch orderings make *lenp = larger_col - smaller_col + 1 with lenp >= 1, the address *pp + *lenp - 1 lands exactly on the larger column, which is at most the line's NUL terminator, so all reads stay inside the allocated line. The only concrete in-code defect is that the multibyte branch omits the trailing-NUL exclusion that the single-byte branch performs ('else if ((*pp)[*lenp - 1] == NUL) *lenp -= 1'), so a selection ending at the line end (v$) yields a length counting the in-bounds NUL byte; the consequence is confined to the caller's own editor process as odd pattern text, with no out-of-bounds access, disclosure, bypass, or amplification, hence a correctness bug rather than a vulnerability.

assumptions: The invariant that VIsual.col and curwin->w_cursor.col are at most the line length (pointing at most at the terminating NUL) is maintained by Vim's movement and selection code outside this snippet; no statement in the given code enforces or violates it. It is treated as an external invariant, not a guard.
unadjust_for_sel() (line 7) is not shown; its documented role of decrementing a column for 'selection' exclusive, guarded against going below 0, is assumed and cannot be quoted.

mb_ptr2len (line 38) is a callee contract: for UTF-8 it returns the validated character length (1 at a NUL or truncated sequence) and reads at most through the terminator, so it cannot advance the computed length past the line's NUL.
ml_get_curline()/ml_get_pos() are assumed to return valid pointers into the line buffer for existing lines (memline contract).
Callers are assumed to invoke this function only in an active Visual/Select context; the lnum check at lines 8-13 also rejects stale cross-line state.
limitations: Speculative (not instantiable from the given code): if external code ever left VIsual.col or w_cursor.col past the end of the line, lines 23/28 would return an out-of-bounds pointer and line 31/38/39 would read it (CWE-125). No statement in this code produces such a column, so the trigger precondition could not be instantiated.

Speculative: signed overflow of *lenp (lines 24/29) requires columns near INT_MAX (the dollar-selection curswant MAXCOL value is clamped to the line length by movement code not shown), so it is not reachable as written.

Correctness bug, no security effect in this code: on multibyte builds the trailing-NUL exclusion present in the single-byte branch (lines 39-41) is absent, so a selection ending at end-of-line yields a length that counts the terminating NUL byte. All touched bytes remain in-bounds and the effect is confined to pattern semantics in the operator's own process.
The (int)STRLEN cast at line 17 could truncate only for lines larger than INT_MAX bytes, which Vim's MAXCOL line-length cap and practical allocation limits prevent.
Passing NULL for pp or lenp (lines 3-4) would crash the dereferences, but that is an interface-contract violation by an equal-privilege caller, not attack data.

verdict.summary: parallels_open is the intake parser for an untrusted Parallels disk image and validates the magic, version, and catalog size, but stores ph.tracks into persistent driver state (s->tracks) without any validation. A malicious image with tracks = 0 is accepted (open returns success), and the read path of this driver divides guest sector numbers by s->tracks, causing an integer division by zero (SIGFPE) that crashes the QEMU process hosting the image when the guest performs I/O. This is an attacker-reachable denial of service from untrusted image content at a trust boundary.

evidence.reason: Root cause: the attacker-controlled header field ph.tracks is stored into driver state with no validation. The code checks other header fields (magic/version at lines 16-17 and catalog size at line 28: 'if (s->catalog_size > INT_MAX / 4)') but no check on tracks exists anywhere in the function. Trigger fully instantiated: an image with tracks = 0 passes magic/version checks, catalog allocation succeeds, and parallels_open returns 0 with s->tracks == 0; the driver's read path then divides by s->tracks, producing a division-by-zero crash of the process hosting the image (DoS crossing the trust boundary of untrusted image content / guest I/O).

Origin of the tainted data: the raw bytes of the untrusted disk image file, including ph.tracks, ph.catalog_entries, and ph.nb_sectors, are read into the stack header here. These values are attacker-controlled file content, making the subsequent unvalidated store of ph.tracks at line 25 an intake-point validation failure.

assumptions: The declaration of BDRVParallelsState is not in the given code; the analysis assumes catalog_size is unsigned (as in the actual driver), under which the quoted guard 'if (s->catalog_size > INT_MAX / 4)' correctly caps catalog_size * 4 below overflow for every value including the boundary 0x1FFFFFFF and one-past 0x20000000.

The division sink (sector_num / s->tracks) resides in the read path of this same driver, which is not included in the given snippet; the defect attributed here is the missing validation at this intake point, which performs exactly this class of validation for magic, version, and catalog size.
bdrv_pread is assumed to return a negative value on any failure including short reads ('if (ret < 0) { goto fail; }'), so the catalog buffer is not used uninitialized on error paths.
limitations: catalog_size = 0 is accepted by the INT_MAX/4 guard, causing g_malloc(0) to return NULL and passing that NULL to bdrv_pread with length 0; within this code the loop 'for (i = 0; i < s->catalog_size; i++)' executes zero iterations, so no NULL dereference occurs here. Whether the zero-length bdrv_pread dereferences the buffer is outside the given code.

If s->catalog_size were a signed int, a header value of 0x80000000 would bypass the '>' guard (negative after conversion), but the in-code consequences (wrapped g_malloc size, skipped loop, zero-length pread) produce no out-of-bounds access within this function; the struct declaration is not shown.
catalog_size = INT_MAX/4 permits a single ~2GB allocation from a tiny image file; this is bounded by the quoted guard and is not attacker-scalable amplification beyond that fixed cap.
bs->total_sectors (ph.nb_sectors) is unvalidated, but within this code it is only stored as reported geometry; any downstream effect depends on the read path not shown.

verdict.summary: stl_remove_degenerate uses file-derived neighbor indices (neighbor1/neighbor2/neighbor3) and which_vertex_not values (vnot1/vnot2/vnot3) read from the parsed mesh structure without any range validation. The only guards are inequality checks against -1, which do not bound the index. An out-of-range neighbor value indexes stl->neighbors_start out of bounds, and a vnot value less than -1 makes (vnot + 1) % 3 evaluate to -1 or -2 under C truncation semantics, producing an out-of-bounds write into the 3-element neighbor[]/which_vertex_not[] arrays. An attacker supplying a crafted STL file reaches these writes with concrete out-of-range values, corrupting memory in the process that loads the file.

evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds write sink. neighbor1 is only checked with `if(neighbor1 != -1){` (line 61), which does not bound it to [0, number_of_facets), and vnot1 is never validated. Trigger simulated in STEP 4: vnot1 = -2 (file-derived, read at line 57) gives (-2+1)%3 = -1, so neighbors_start[5].neighbor[-1] = neighbor2 writes below the 3-element array; neighbor1 = 100000 against a small mesh writes far past the array. Same defect at lines 66-67 and 74.

Origin of the tainted vnot1: an unvalidated, file-derived value from the mesh neighbor table. No statement in this code constrains it to {0,1,2}; it flows unmodified into the modulo expression at line 62 where a value of -2 (or INT_MAX, causing signed overflow in vnot1 + 1) yields an out-of-bounds index.

Origin of the tainted neighbor1: an unvalidated, file-derived index read from the neighbor table. It is used at line 62 as the outer array index into stl->neighbors_start with only a != -1 check, so any out-of-range value produces an out-of-bounds write.

assumptions: The stl_neighbors struct's neighbor[] and which_vertex_not[] members are 3-element arrays (implied by the % 3 indexing idiom); their exact layout is not shown, but any negative or over-large index computed at lines 62-63, 66-67, 74 writes outside those arrays.
Any range enforcement of neighbor or which_vertex_not values at the parse/build site is code not shown and, per guard anchoring, is treated as nonexistent for this analysis.
stl and its arrays are assumed allocated and consistent as produced by code not shown; only values inside the struct are treated as attacker-influenced.
limitations: The facet parameter is used to index facet_start and neighbors_start with no bounds check; per STEP 1 it is classified as an interface-contract argument (documented domain: valid facet index), and no attacker path within this code's own data flow was shown to produce an out-of-range facet.

If both neighbor1 and neighbor2 equal -1, lines 48-53 call stl_update_connects_remove_1(stl, -1) with -1 as a facet index; this code's own branches produce the -1 argument, but the callee is not shown, so the sink could not be exhibited here and the candidate remains speculative.
vnot1 + 1 overflows for vnot1 = INT_MAX (undefined behavior before the modulo); this is a boundary variant of the same unvalidated-operand sink rather than an independent finding.

verdict.summary: ex_copy() is safe for all inputs within its documented domain (valid source line numbers and destination address). Loop invariants (line1 never outpaces the growing buffer, cursor.lnum always a valid appended-after line, strict per-iteration progress) keep every ml_get/ml_append index in range, the vim_strsave result is NULL-checked, and count/n arithmetic cannot wrap at line-addressable scales. Out-of-range line1/line2/n would require the caller to violate the :copy command's range contract, and the only party able to supply such values runs this process at equal privilege, so no cross-boundary security impact is instantiable from this code.

assumptions: line1, line2, n arrive within the :copy command's documented domain (1 <= line1 <= line2 <= buffer line count; 0 <= n <= line count); range and address validation is performed by the ex command executor (do_one_cmd/get_address), which is not part of the given code and was not used to dismiss any instantiated defect.
ml_get(), ml_append(), u_save(), and appended_lines_mark() operate correctly for valid line numbers; their implementations (including any internal handling of invalid line numbers) are not shown.
linenr_T is a signed long (64-bit on current platforms).
limitations: Speculative (contract-dependent): if the caller passed line1/line2 greater than the buffer line count or line1 < 1, the sink 'p = vim_strsave(ml_get(line1));' would receive an out-of-range index; no bound check exists inside this function. The trigger value is produced by no statement in this code and can only originate from a contract-violating caller at equal privilege, so it is a robustness/contract issue, not a vulnerability in this code.
Speculative: 'count = line2 - line1 + 1;' and 'u_save(n, n + 1)' can overflow only at values near LONG_MAX that cannot address existing buffer lines and are never produced by this code's data flow.
Speculative: an entry value line1 = 0 (e.g. ':0copy') would call ml_get(0), which is not a valid source line; the consequence depends on ml_get's internal validation, which is outside the given code.

verdict.summary: No attacker-instantiable vulnerability found. The sole attacker-controlled input, u64 size, is bounded by the quotable guard `if (unlikely(size > RINGBUF_MAX_RECORD_SZ)) return NULL;` and the capacity guard `if (len > rb->mask + 1) return NULL;`; the space check `new_prod_pos - cons_pos > rb->mask` fails closed under every edge case (empty, exactly-at-limit, one-past-limit, unsigned wrap), the stale cons_pos read is conservative, every locked path unlocks exactly once, and the 8-byte header write at `rb->data + (prod_pos & rb->mask)` cannot go out of bounds because `len = round_up(size + BPF_RINGBUF_HDR_SZ, 8)` keeps producer_pos 8-aligned, which with a power-of-two ringbuf size keeps the masked offset a multiple of 8 no matter what size the attacker passes.

assumptions: RINGBUF_MAX_RECORD_SZ, BPF_RINGBUF_HDR_SZ, and BPF_RINGBUF_BUSY_BIT are not defined in the given code; the analysis assumes the upstream kernel values (HDR_SZ = 8, BUSY_BIT = bit 31, RINGBUF_MAX_RECORD_SZ = UINT_MAX >> 2), which make the u64-to-u32 store `hdr->len = size | BPF_RINGBUF_BUSY_BIT;` and the `round_up(size + BPF_RINGBUF_HDR_SZ, 8)` arithmetic truncation-free for all size values the guard admits.

struct bpf_ringbuf (fields mask, producer_pos, consumer_pos, data) is taken as kernel-internal trusted state: rb->mask = ringbuf_size - 1 with a power-of-two ringbuf_size >= PAGE_SIZE, and producer_pos/consumer_pos initialized to 0 by the map-creation path, which is not shown in the given code.
limitations: Speculative OOB header write (CWE-787): if `prod_pos & rb->mask` could exceed ringbuf_size - 8, the writes `hdr->len = ...; hdr->pg_off = ...;` at `hdr = (void *)rb->data + (prod_pos & rb->mask);` would land out of bounds. Not triggerable from this function's attacker input: `len = round_up(size + BPF_RINGBUF_HDR_SZ, 8)` forces every producer_pos increment to be a multiple of 8, so the masked offset is always a multiple of 8 and at most size - 8; breaking this requires the not-shown creation code to initialize producer_pos unaligned or use a non-power-of-two size, which the attacker supplying `size` cannot cause.

Speculative truncation: `hdr->len = size | BPF_RINGBUF_BUSY_BIT;` narrows u64 size into a u32 field; it would corrupt the length/flag encoding only if RINGBUF_MAX_RECORD_SZ exceeded ~2^30, a compile-time constant the attacker cannot choose, so no trigger was instantiated.

A record may legitimately wrap past the end of the data area by design; correctness of wrapped accesses depends on the consumer/mapping code outside this function (double-mapped data pages), which was not part of the given code and therefore not evaluated.

verdict.summary: ex_copy consumes the Ex-command range (line1, line2) and destination (n) without any validation. The copy loop is bounded only by the attacker-supplied line2 (which the loop body itself increments at line 46) and performs a vim_strsave plus ml_append allocation on every iteration, so a single short command with an oversized range drives unbounded iterations and unbounded buffer growth (CWE-400); line1 simultaneously outruns the real buffer line count and is passed unvalidated to ml_get (line 33), an out-of-range index at the memory-access call site (CWE-125). Additionally, count = line2 - line1 + 1 is never checked for count <= 0, so a reversed range yields a negative count that is written into b_op_end.lnum = n + count and passed to appended_lines_mark(n, count), corrupting mark/operator line-number bookkeeping even though no lines were copied. No bound, sign, or extent check exists anywhere in the function.

evidence.reason: The copy loop's trip count is set solely by the attacker-supplied line2, which the body even increases via `if (curwin->w_cursor.lnum < line2) ++line2;` (line 46), and each iteration allocates (vim_strsave, ml_append). Simulated trigger: line1=1, line2=1000000000, n=1 with a 3-line buffer → u_save(1,2) succeeds, ~10^9 iterations each appending a line; line1 (advancing 1-2 per iteration) exceeds the real line count, after which ml_get(line1) at line 33 receives an out-of-range index on every remaining iteration. No statement in the function compares line1/line2/n against the buffer extent, so the amplification and unvalidated indexing are unguarded.

Origin of the count taint: count is computed directly from the attacker-supplied range with no validation. Edge values: line2 = line1 - 1 → count = 0; line2 = 1, line1 = 5 → count = -3. No `count <= 0` check exists anywhere between this line and its sinks (lines 10 and 50), so the unvalidated, possibly negative count propagates to mark bookkeeping.

Sink for the unvalidated count and destination: with the instantiated reversed-range trigger (line1=5, line2=1, n=1 → count=-3), the loop at line 29 is skipped (5 <= 1 is false), zero lines are copied, yet this statement runs appended_lines_mark(1, -3) telling the mark subsystem that a negative number of lines was appended, and line 10 already stored b_op_end.lnum = n + count = -2. Both n and count arrive here with no bounds or sign check on any path.

assumptions: linenr_T is a signed long; vim_strsave, ml_get, ml_append, u_save, appended_lines_mark, and msgmore are external Vim helpers whose internals are not shown and are not relied on for any guard.

The Ex address parser that produces line1, line2, n (the caller) is not shown; per the analysis rules its validation cannot be quoted and is not treated as existing. This function is judged as the last line of defense at the command-handler entry point.
curbuf, curwin, and cmdmod are editor-internal state and treated as trusted; the attacker-controlled content is the command range and destination values.
limitations: The signed-overflow candidates n + 1 (line 25) and n + count (line 10) require n at the extreme width boundary (LONG_MAX); the shown code contains neither a producer nor a demonstrable input surface for such a value, so that trigger is speculative.

Whether ml_get/ml_append internally bounds-check invalid line numbers is not visible in the given code; the CWE-125 entry rests on the unvalidated index reaching the memory-access call sites at lines 33 and 36 in this function. The CWE-400 finding is independent of callee behavior: the loop, its allocations, and its attacker-set bound are fully visible here.

ml_append's return value is ignored (line 36) and appended_lines_mark runs with the full count even if zero lines were actually copied; the downstream consequences of that inconsistency live in unseen memline/mark code.

If one insisted the Ex range can only ever be typed interactively by the equal-privilege user, the worst case would shrink to a hang/OOM of that user's own editor; this analysis instead treats the command handler as the intake point for command/script-originated Ex input, consistent with the rule that entry-point parameters carrying external content are attacker data.

verdict.summary: dynamicGetbuf computes remain = dp->logicalSize - dp->pos without checking for a negative result; the only guard, 'if (remain == 0) return EOF;', lets negative remain fall through so rlen = remain assigns a negative length that is implicitly converted to a huge size_t in memcpy, causing an out-of-bounds read from dp->data + dp->pos and an out-of-bounds write past the caller's buf whenever the ctx cursor state (dp->pos) exceeds the logical size, with no quotable guard enforcing pos <= logicalSize.

evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted length: this subtraction can produce a negative remain whenever dp->pos exceeds dp->logicalSize; the code contains no statement validating that invariant, so the negative value flows onward unguarded.

Incomplete guard: the only rejection test on remain checks equality with zero; edge case remain = -1 (and every other negative value) falls through to rlen = remain, so the out-of-range condition the memcpy requires to be excluded is not rejected.

Unguarded sink: with logicalSize = 256, dp->pos = 512, len = 1 the simulated run yields remain = -256, rlen = -256, and memcpy receives (size_t)-256 = 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFF00, reading far out of bounds from the heap block and writing past the 1-byte destination buffer.

assumptions: The precondition dp->pos > dp->logicalSize is produced by sibling functions of the same gd IO module (dynamicSeek sets the cursor from caller-supplied offsets; dynamicPutbuf appends) that are not shown; per guard anchoring no enforcement outside this code can be assumed, and this code itself performs no revalidation of pos before using it as a length operand and index.
dp->realSize (allocated size of dp->data) is assumed to cover dp->logicalSize; that relationship is maintained by the module's allocation/append code, not shown.
The caller-provided buf is assumed to have capacity len and the framework is assumed to pass len > 0, per the documented interface contract.
limitations: A negative or zero-length len passed by the framework caller would also produce a huge memcpy size (remain >= len is trivially true for negative len), but all values of len are interface-contract arguments, not attacker data, and no statement in this code can make len negative; this trigger is speculative.

Within this function alone, rlen = min(remain, len) with remain >= 0 keeps dp->pos <= dp->logicalSize, so the negative-remain trigger additionally depends on cursor state established by the module's seek/write paths outside the shown snippet; this dependency is recorded as an assumption rather than an in-code instantiation.

verdict.summary: update_topline() computes scroll state for the operator's own Vim window from window/buffer state and the operator-set 'scrolloff' option. No memory-index, copy, format, command, or authz sink exists in the function; all loop bounds are enforced by quotable in-body counters and breaks (n >= halfheight, lnum <= 0 || line_count > w_height + 1, lnum >= ml_line_count, n >= *so_ptr), so no unshown helper contract is needed for termination. The only arithmetic defects found (long-to-int truncation of n and save_so, and signed overflow of topline/botline +/- so_ptr) require the operator to set scrolloff near 2^31 or 2^62, are not file-attacker reachable ('scrolloff' cannot be set from a modeline), and their worst in-code effect is choosing between scroll_cursor_halfway() and scroll_cursor_top()/scroll_cursor_bot() — a cosmetic scroll-position difference in the operator's own process at equal privilege. Buffer-derived ml_line_count is used only inside comparisons. No primary candidate survives; the code is not vulnerable.

assumptions: hasFolding(), hasAnyFolding(), botline_forw(), diff_check_fill(), scroll_cursor_*(), validate_botline(), and check_top_offset() honor their documented contracts (advance lnum forward/backward to fold boundaries within the buffer, return valid line numbers). These are not relied on for loop termination: the quoted in-body counters and breaks bound every loop independently.

Window state invariants (1 <= w_cursor.lnum, w_topline <= ml_line_count etc.) are maintained by Vim's core code outside this function; within this function these values reach only comparisons and scroll-helper arguments, never a raw memory index.

'scrolloff' (p_so / w_p_so) is a global/window-local option set only by the operator; it is not among options a file modeline may set, so the file originator cannot inject the large values needed for the arithmetic edge cases.
FEAT_DIFF / FEAT_FOLDING conditional blocks are compiled per build; both branches were analyzed.
limitations: Speculative: signed overflow of 'curwin->w_topline + *so_ptr' or 'curwin->w_botline - *so_ptr' would need scrolloff on the order of 2^62, which no statement in this code or realistic input surface produces (operator contract case).

Robustness, not vulnerability: long-to-int truncation of 'n = curwin->w_topline + *so_ptr - curwin->w_cursor.lnum;' when scrolloff >= 2^31 flips the scroll-method choice (scroll_cursor_top vs scroll_cursor_halfway); worst effect is a cosmetic scroll position in the operator's own editor.

Robustness, not vulnerability: with a very large operator-set scrolloff on a very large file, the botline-counting while loop performs O(buffer size) work bounded by the operator's own buffer, at the operator's own privilege, with no amplification beyond the input's own size.

Robustness: 'int save_so = *so_ptr;' truncates a long option on platforms where int is narrower than long; the restore '*so_ptr = save_so;' could corrupt an absurdly large operator option value, with no cross-boundary effect.

verdict.summary: All memory accesses in get_one_sourceline are guarded on every path: ga_grow(120) and ga_grow(1) precede every buffer write; buf[len-1] and buf[len-2] accesses are guarded by '(len == 1 || (len >= 2 && buf[len - 2] == '\n'))', 'len >= 1', 'len >= 2', and the short-circuit conjunct 'ga.ga_maxlen - ga.ga_len == 1' (which implies len = ga_maxlen-1 >= 119 in the file path and len >= 1 in the buffer path, since ga_grow(120) guarantees slack >= 120 before each read); the buflines index is guarded by 'if (sp->buf_lnum >= sp->buflines.ga_len) break;'. No injection, authz, or crypto sinks exist. Residual defects (buffer-source lines of certain lengths spuriously merging via the file-path continue check, embedded-NUL line truncation, OOM data loss, 2^31-scale len overflow) are speculative or confined to misparsing same-author sourced content at equal privilege, so none is a security vulnerability in this code.

assumptions: ga_init2, ga_grow, and ga_concat implementations are not shown; the standard growarray contract is assumed (ga_len <= ga_maxlen maintained, growth on demand, ga_concat copying exactly STRLEN(s) bytes per its internal grow).
The strings stored in sp->buflines.ga_data are assumed NUL-terminated by the (unshown) code that populates them.
sp is assumed non-NULL per the sourcing machinery's documented contract; sp->fp is assumed a valid FILE*.
The caller of get_one_sourceline is assumed to free the returned ga.ga_data (ownership contract).
USE_CRNL is a compile-time flag; the CRNL blocks were analyzed only for builds where it is defined; the non-CRNL paths are unaffected.
limitations: Buffer-source path: 'if (ga.ga_maxlen - ga.ga_len == 1 && buf[len - 1] != '\n') continue;' is a file-read heuristic; for source_from_buf a buffer line leaving exactly one byte of slack can spuriously continue the loop and concatenate the next buffer line into the same logical line. The exact triggering length depends on the unshown ga_grow sizing policy (cannot be quoted per guard anchoring), and the impact is mis-joining two lines from the same buffer the operator chose to source, which crosses no privilege or trust boundary and causes no memory error, so it is a correctness/robustness defect, not a vulnerability.

Embedded NUL bytes in a sourced file truncate the logical line early because 'len = ga.ga_len + (int)STRLEN(buf + ga.ga_len);' stops at the NUL and the buffer-full continue check no longer fires; this misparses same-author script content only.

If ga_grow or ga_concat fails on allocation mid-line, the partial line is discarded and 'sp->buf_lnum++' has already consumed the buffer line, so one line is silently lost; requires OOM that no attacker can induce, so it is a robustness issue only.

Integer overflow of len or ga_len would require a single sourced line of roughly 2 GiB and successful allocation at that scale before any wrap; no wrap is exercised by the code as written, so the trigger is speculative.

verdict.summary: call_qftf_func invokes the user-supplied 'quickfixtextfunc' callback and, on success, checks only `rettv.v_type == VAR_LIST` before dereferencing the returned list pointer (`qftf_list = rettv.vval.v_list; qftf_list->lv_refcount++;`). A callback returning a VAR_LIST typval with a NULL list pointer (e.g., Vim's null_list) passes the type-tag guard, so the refcount increment performs a read-modify-write at a small fixed offset from NULL, crashing the editor process. The missing `rettv.vval.v_list != NULL` check is absent from every path to the sink, and the trigger is fully instantiated by the callback return value, which is this code's input across the script/C trust boundary.

evidence.reason: Root cause: the guard `if (rettv.v_type == VAR_LIST)` verifies only the typval's type tag, never the list pointer. When the user-supplied callback returns a VAR_LIST typval with vval.v_list == NULL (null_list), qftf_list becomes NULL and `qftf_list->lv_refcount++` dereferences NULL, writing at a fixed near-NULL offset and crashing the process. No NULL check on rettv.vval.v_list or qftf_list exists anywhere on the path to this sink.

Origin of the tainted value: the callback selected from 'quickfixtextfunc' (settable by script, including buffer-locally) fills rettv with attacker-influenced content; its v_type and vval.v_list flow unvalidated into the dereference at line 35.

assumptions: call_callback sets rettv to a valid typval when it does not return FAIL (callee contract); rettv is never read on the FAIL path.

The Vim script evaluator can produce a VAR_LIST typval whose vval.v_list is NULL (e.g., Vim9 null_list returned from the callback), and such a typval is delivered verbatim through call_callback into rettv.
Callers of call_qftf_func handle a NULL return value (callback unset, failure, or non-list return), which is the documented behavior of this helper.
list_T.lv_refcount resides at a small fixed offset, so the faulting write is at a near-NULL unmapped address and results in a crash rather than controlled corruption.
limitations: args[0].v_lock (the lock field of the typval_T passed as the callback argument) is never initialized at lines 26-27 (only v_type and vval.v_dict are set); no code in this function reads v_lock, so no impact is instantiated here (potential CWE-457 hardening issue only).

Impact is bounded to denial of service (process crash, potential loss of unsaved editor work); the write address is a fixed offset from NULL and is not attacker-controlled, so no exploitable memory corruption was identified.

The trigger requires the 'quickfixtextfunc' callback to return a null list; callbacks authored solely by the operator running the same process would make this a self-inflicted crash, but 'quickfixtextfunc' is buffer-local and settable by scripts/options the operator did not necessarily author, which is the trust boundary relied on for the verdict.

verdict.summary: issuerAndThisUpdateCheck fails to verify that the issuer string scan loop terminated on a closing double quote. When an attacker-supplied GSER value such as {issuer "rdnSequence:AAAA...} contains no terminating quote, the loop exits with is->bv_len == x.bv_len, and the subsequent advance 'x.bv_val += is->bv_len + 1; x.bv_len -= is->bv_len + 1;' moves the cursor one byte past the end of the input buffer and underflows the unsigned ber_len_t to SIZE_MAX. Subsequent reads (x.bv_val[0] at the space-eating loop and the ',' check, and strncasecmp on later iterations) become heap out-of-bounds reads with a near-unbounded length, enabling a remotely triggerable crash and out-of-bounds read in the parsing process. The thisUpdate branch (lines 107-115) shares the same missing-termination defect.

evidence.reason: Sink: the cursor advance assumes the issuer scan loop broke on a terminating quote. When the loop instead exhausts with is->bv_len == x.bv_len (no closing quote in the attacker's value), x.bv_val is moved to in->bv_val + in->bv_len (one past the buffer end) and the unsigned x.bv_len underflows to SIZE_MAX; no check of is->bv_len < x.bv_len or is->bv_val[is->bv_len] == '"' exists between the loop and this advance.

Origin of the tainted value: this scan loop can exit by loop-condition exhaustion with is->bv_len == x.bv_len when the attacker supplies an issuer string with no closing double quote (or ending in a "" pair), producing the value that lines 78-79 turn into an out-of-bounds pointer and an underflowed length.

Instantiated out-of-bounds use: after the underflow, x.bv_val points one byte past the input buffer and x.bv_len is SIZE_MAX, so this read (and the space-eating loop at line 124, and strncasecmp on any subsequent iteration) reads heap memory outside the attacker-supplied buffer; if the OOB byte is ',' parsing continues over adjacent heap with a near-unbounded length.

assumptions: in->bv_val points to a buffer of exactly in->bv_len bytes (typical for LDAP bervals); under this assumption the post-underflow reads at lines 124/132 are genuinely out of bounds.
This function is the syntax validator invoked on attribute values received from LDAP clients, so 'in' carries attacker-controlled content across a network trust boundary.
ber_len_t is unsigned (typedef of unsigned long/size_t in the OpenLDAP stack), so the 0-1 subtraction at line 79 wraps to SIZE_MAX.
limitations: The thisUpdate branch (lines 107-115) has the same missing terminating-quote check, but its underflow is caught post-hoc by 'if ( x.bv_len ) return LDAP_INVALID_SYNTAX;' at line 141 after only a 1-byte OOB read at line 124; same root cause, folded into the primary finding.

Return values of ber_dupbv_x (line 144) and slap_sl_malloc (line 150) are unchecked; on allocation failure *is is set to a NULL bv_val with non-zero length or a NULL dereference occurs at line 155. Trigger requires allocator failure the attacker cannot directly induce, so recorded as robustness, not vulnerability.
The read is->bv_val[is->bv_len+1] at line 70 when is->bv_len == x.bv_len-1 lands on the in-buffer closing '}' and is not out of bounds.
Continuation past line 133 requires the out-of-bounds heap byte to equal ','; the guaranteed OOB reads (lines 124, 132) occur on every trigger regardless.

verdict.summary: __bpf_ringbuf_reserve truncates the u64 expression round_up(size + BPF_RINGBUF_HDR_SZ, 8) into u32 len. For size near RINGBUF_MAX_RECORD_SZ (e.g. 0xFFFFFFF8, which passes the only guard at line 7), len wraps to 0 or 8, so the space check at line 26 validates a 0/8-byte reservation while the BPF verifier grants the caller a size-byte (~4GB) write window into the returned pointer, producing out-of-bounds kernel writes; hdr->len additionally records the full untruncated size, corrupting producer/consumer accounting and causing out-of-bounds reads for record walkers.

evidence.reason: Origin of the attacker-controlled value: u64 size is the reservation size carried from the bpf_ringbuf_reserve BPF helper, chosen by the loaded (untrusted) BPF program across the verifier trust boundary.

Root cause: the u64 expression round_up(size + 8, 8) is assigned to u32 len (declared line 4). For size >= 0xFFFFFFF1 (which the line 7 guard admits, e.g. 0xFFFFFFF8 -> round_up = 0x100000000), len truncates to 0 or 8, so the record is under-reserved by ~4GB.

The only space guard consumes new_prod_pos = prod_pos + len (line 21) computed from the truncated len; with len = 0/8 it passes trivially, so the reservation is never validated against the true record extent the caller may write.

The header stores the full untruncated size while producer_pos advanced by only the truncated len: instantiated trigger (size=0xFFFFFFF8, len=0, producer_pos unchanged, returned pointer rb->data+8) lets the BPF program write its verifier-granted ~4GB window far past the ringbuf area, and walkers using hdr->len read out of bounds.

assumptions: RINGBUF_MAX_RECORD_SZ, BPF_RINGBUF_HDR_SZ, BPF_RINGBUF_BUSY_BIT and struct bpf_ringbuf_hdr are not defined in the given code; their Linux kernel values are assumed ((u64)UINT_MAX, 8, 1U<<31, {u32 len; u32 pg_off;}). The trigger requires RINGBUF_MAX_RECORD_SZ >= 0xFFFFFFF1, which holds for the real constant (u64)UINT_MAX and even for UINT_MAX - 8.

The caller is assumed to be the bpf_ringbuf_reserve()/bpf_ringbuf_reserve_dynptr() helpers, which pass the BPF-program-supplied u32 size and after a non-NULL return give the program a verifier-tracked PTR_TO_ALLOC_MEM window of exactly `size` bytes (ARG_CONST_ALLOC_SIZE).

Ringbuf data pages are assumed double-mapped in kernel memory (standard kernel implementation) so records up to ringbuf_size stay in bounds; writes beyond 2*ringbuf_size (as in the simulated 100008-byte offset into a 4KB ringbuf) go out of bounds.
limitations: Speculative: rb->consumer_pos is loaded at line 11 before the spinlock while user-space may concurrently rewrite its page; this is not exploitable here because any cons_pos > new_prod_pos makes the unsigned difference at line 26 huge (fails closed) and the page writer is the map owner at equal privilege.
The in_nmi() trylock-failure return and allocation/lock failures are environment conditions an attacker cannot induce; not vulnerabilities.

The BPF_RINGBUF_BUSY_BIT (bit 31) and DISCARD-bit collision for sizes >= 2^30 is folded into the primary truncation finding since it shares the same record-accounting root cause and the same space-check bypass.

verdict.summary: stl_remove_degenerate writes to stl->neighbors_start[neighborN].neighbor[(vnotN + 1) % 3] using neighbor indices and vnot values read directly from the parsed STL state. The only guards are sentinel checks (`!= -1`) that pass any other out-of-range value (e.g., -2, or an index >= number_of_facets), and (vnotN + 1) % 3 evaluates negative for vnotN < -1. A crafted file whose parsed neighbor/which_vertex_not fields hold such values drives an out-of-bounds write with attacker-influenced index and stored value (memory corruption), reachable on every path through the degenerate-facet branch.

evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds write sink: neighbor1 is used as an array index after only a sentinel check `neighbor1 != -1`, which passes any value other than exactly -1 (e.g., -2 or an index past the facet count); the subindex (vnot1 + 1) % 3 is negative for vnot1 < -1; and the stored value neighbor2 is likewise unvalidated. Trigger: a parsed mesh where neighbors_start[facet].neighbor[0] = -2 and which_vertex_not[0] = 1 reaches line 61 and writes neighbors_start[-2].neighbor[2] = 1.
Symmetric out-of-bounds write sink indexed by the unvalidated neighbor2, storing the unvalidated neighbor1; the guard `neighbor2 != -1` performs no range check and no vnot2 range check exists.
Third out-of-bounds write sink: neighbor3 is checked only against the sentinel -1 before being used as an array index, and (vnot3 + 1) % 3 can be negative for vnot3 < -1.

Origin of the tainted index values: neighbor1/neighbor2 (and neighbor3, vnot1-3 at lines 55-58) are loaded from the parsed STL state, which originates from untrusted file content, with no validation anywhere between this load and the write sinks at lines 61-66 and 73.

assumptions: stl->neighbors_start and stl->facet_start are populated by parsing/processing code not shown; per the trust model their contents (derived from an untrusted STL file) are treated as attacker-influenced, and any bound the unseen parser might enforce is an assumption that cannot dismiss the unvalidated writes in this function.
The `facet` parameter is treated as an interface-contract index (callers not shown); no validation of `facet` exists in this code.
stl_remove_facet and stl_update_connects_remove_1 implementations are not shown; their internal behavior was not used to validate or dismiss the writes at lines 61-66 and 73.
limitations: Candidate C3 (out-of-bounds read via unvalidated `facet` at lines 14-17/45) is speculative: triggering it requires a caller violating the index contract, which cannot be instantiated from this code.

Candidate C4 (stale-index write to neighbors_start[neighbor3] at line 73 after stl_remove_facet relocates the last facet) depends on the relocation behavior of the unseen callee and could not be instantiated from this code alone.

The negative-modulo subindex ((vnotN + 1) % 3 = -1 for vnotN = -2) requires a which_vertex_not value below -1; this code itself never produces such a value locally, though it performs no check preventing one from the parsed state.

verdict.summary: drill_parse_T_code fails open on out-of-range tool numbers: the check at lines 63-68 only logs 'Out of bounds drill number' and does not return, so an attacker-supplied drill file with e.g. 'T1500' drives image->aperture[tool_num] (line 72) as an out-of-bounds pointer read and, when the slot reads NULL, image->aperture[tool_num] = g_new0(...) (lines 126-127 / 184) as an out-of-bounds pointer write at an attacker-controlled index (including the exactly-one-past boundary tool_num == TOOL_MAX and negative values admitted by the '+'/'-' gate). Additionally, the Orcad stop-switch path uses get_line(fd++), passing a pointer one struct past the heap-allocated gerbv_file_t and then reading fd->filename through that invalid pointer.

evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted value: tool_num is parsed directly from the untrusted drill file, with sign characters admitted by the earlier character gate, and flows unchecked into array indexing.

Fail-open guard: the body contains only the error report and no return/clamp, so an out-of-range tool_num (e.g. 1500 from 'T1500', or exactly TOOL_MAX, or negative) continues to be used as an index; the minimal fix (return -1 here) is absent from the block and from every later path.

Out-of-bounds read sink: attacker-controlled tool_num indexes the fixed-size aperture pointer array with no enforced bound; the read may fault, yield a garbage pointer later dereferenced at line 114, or read NULL leading to the OOB write.

Out-of-bounds write sink: a freshly allocated heap pointer is stored at image->aperture[tool_num] with the unvalidated tool_num (trigger 'T1500' with no size definition), corrupting memory past the aperture array.

Invalid pointer use: fd++ advances the gerb_file_t pointer itself past the heap object, so get_line (and the later fd->filename read on line 30 within the Orcad 'TCST' path) accesses out-of-bounds memory; trigger is a drill file containing the sequence TCST plus one trailing byte.

assumptions: TOOL_MIN/TOOL_MAX and the declared size of image->aperture (APERTURE_MAX) are not visible in this snippet; per gerbv's definitions TOOL_MAX equals the aperture array size (1000), so values satisfying tool_num >= TOOL_MAX index past the array. The code's own message 'Out of bounds drill number' confirms such values are considered invalid for indexing.

Implementations of gerb_fgetc, gerb_fgetint, gerb_ungetc, get_line, and read_double are not shown; their behavior (including possible internal overflow in gerb_fgetint) is assumed conventional and was not relied on to dismiss any candidate.
The caller is assumed to have consumed the leading 'T' before invoking this function, as implied by the comments and the fd->ptr -= 4 rewind.
limitations: The '\n'/'\r' restoration check inside the 'if (EOF == temp)' branch is dead code (temp equals EOF there); a parsing quirk with no demonstrated security effect.

The signed overflow in '16 + 8 * tool_num' (undefined behavior for large tool_num) only feeds a diameter double and is reachable only after the out-of-bounds access has already occurred, so it adds no independent finding.
drill_stats_add_to_drill_list receives the out-of-range tool_num, but its implementation is not shown and no defect is claimed there.

verdict.summary: This function is a packet batch iteration wrapper for IP fragment extraction. It delegates all packet content validation and fragment handling to external functions (ipf_is_valid_v4_frag, ipf_is_valid_v6_frag, ipf_handle_frag) whose implementations are not shown. No direct memory access, copy, allocation sizing, or injection sink operates on attacker-controlled data within this function's own statements. Mutex lock/unlock pairing is correct. The int pb_idx vs size_t pb_cnt type mismatch is theoretical only (requires >2^31 batch size, not producible from visible code). No fully instantiated vulnerability trigger exists in the given code.

assumptions: The DP_PACKET_BATCH_REFILL_FOR_EACH macro correctly iterates and handles the refill mechanism; its implementation is not shown in the given code.
The dp_packet_batch_refill function correctly handles the pb_idx parameter and packet placement; its implementation is not shown.
The ipf_is_valid_v4_frag and ipf_is_valid_v6_frag functions independently validate packet content and length regardless of dl_type; their implementations are not shown.
The ipf_handle_frag function properly takes ownership of the packet when returning true; its implementation is not shown.
The ipf parameter is a valid non-NULL pointer to initialized IPF state, as per the function's documented contract with its OVS datapath callers.
Packet batch sizes are bounded well below INT_MAX by OVS infrastructure (NETDEV_MAX_BURST), though this bound is not visible in the given code.
limitations: Candidate: signed/unsigned mismatch between pb_idx (int) and pb_cnt (size_t) — speculative; would require a packet batch exceeding INT_MAX entries, which no visible data flow can produce. Recorded as robustness concern only.

Candidate: validation functions called outside ipf->ipf_lock mutex — speculative; cannot demonstrate from given code that ipf_is_valid_v4_frag or ipf_is_valid_v6_frag access shared mutable state in ipf. Race window not exhibitable as two ordered operations with attacker interleaving.

Candidate: dl_type from flow metadata potentially not matching actual packet ethertype (type confusion) — speculative; depends on whether ipf_is_valid_v4_frag/ipf_is_valid_v6_frag independently validate packet content, which cannot be verified from given code.
Candidate: packet lifetime/ownership after ipf_handle_frag returns true — speculative; depends on ipf_handle_frag's internal ownership semantics, not shown.

Known OVS CVEs (e.g., CVE-2022-4337 integer underflow) affect ipf_is_valid_v4_frag/ipf_is_valid_v6_frag implementations, not this wrapper function. Analysis of those defects requires the callee source code.

verdict.summary: The function is a thin batch-iteration wrapper from Open vSwitch's IP-fragmentation module. Every packet is either refilled into the batch or deleted exactly once on each path, the ipf mutex is locked and unlocked symmetrically around the only shared-state call (ipf_handle_frag), and no attacker-influenced value reaches a memory, size, injection, or authorization sink within the shown statements. All defect candidates (stale batch slots after dp_packet_delete, an unlocked ipf_is_valid_* check, a possible double lock in the callee, an int/size_t width mismatch on pb_idx) depend entirely on the semantics of the DP_PACKET_BATCH_REFILL_FOR_EACH macro and of the callees, none of which are present in the given code, so no trigger could be instantiated from the shown statements alone.

assumptions: The macro DP_PACKET_BATCH_REFILL_FOR_EACH, dp_packet_batch_refill, dp_packet_batch_size, and dp_packet_delete are not defined in the given code; their iteration, compaction, index-bounding, and count-update behavior cannot be quoted and is treated as an unverifiable contract rather than a fact.

ipf_is_valid_v4_frag, ipf_is_valid_v6_frag, and ipf_handle_frag are not shown; it is assumed they parse the packet and manage ipf state, and that ipf_handle_frag does not itself acquire ipf->ipf_lock (otherwise the caller-side lock would deadlock).
Callers supply non-NULL ipf and pb, packets owned by pb, and a dl_type consistent with the batch's flow classification (interface contract).

Packet batch sizes are bounded by the datapath framework far below INT_MAX, so the int pb_idx versus size_t pb_cnt width difference cannot produce a negative index; no statement in the shown code itself performs any arithmetic on these values.
limitations: SPECULATIVE use-after-free: if DP_PACKET_BATCH_REFILL_FOR_EACH/dp_packet_batch_refill do not compact slots and reduce the batch count when dp_packet_delete frees a packet, pb->packets could retain dangling pointers; this could not be proven or disproven because the macro and refill helper are not part of the given code.

SPECULATIVE race: ipf_is_valid_v4_frag/ipf_is_valid_v6_frag are called before ovs_mutex_lock(&ipf->ipf_lock); if they read or write mutable shared ipf state, a cross-thread race would exist, but their implementations are not shown and no interleaving pair of operations is exhibited in this code.

SPECULATIVE deadlock/hang: if ipf_handle_frag internally locks the same non-recursive mutex, the shown caller-side lock would hang the datapath thread; callee internals unknown, and the worst case would be termination/hang of the operator's own process, not a cross-boundary impact.

SPECULATIVE width issue: pb_idx is int while pb_cnt is size_t; an out-of-range or negative pb_idx could only arise from the macro (not shown) and requires a batch larger than INT_MAX, which cannot be instantiated here.
