verdict.summary: In parse_command_modifiers(), when an ex-mode command line begins with the Visual range "'<,'>" followed by command modifier(s) and then end-of-line (use_plus_cmd set at line 47), the rewrite path computes len = STRLEN(cmd_start) (line 336), moves the modifiers to orig_cmd, and executes STRCPY(orig_cmd + len, "'<,'>") (line 341). The allocation still contains the skipped 5-byte "'<,'>" prefix, so it holds exactly 5+len+1 bytes (valid indices 0..5+len); the STRCPY writes 7 bytes at indices len..len+6, writing its terminating NUL exactly one byte past the end of the heap allocation. Concrete trigger (simulated): ex mode with a 2-line buffer and cursor on line 1, input line "'<,'>silent": 12-byte allocation, len=6, STRCPY writes indices 6..12, index 12 out of bounds. This is an attacker-instantiable out-of-bounds heap write (memory corruption) triggered solely by command-line content processed across Vim's input trust boundary; the code contains no bounds check on any path to this sink.

evidence.reason: Unguarded out-of-bounds write (CWE-787, root cause CWE-131 buffer size miscalculation). len = STRLEN(cmd_start) measures only the text after the skipped "'<,'>" prefix, but the allocation retains the prefix: it holds 5+len+1 bytes. STRCPY(orig_cmd + len, "'<,'>") writes 7 bytes (6 chars + NUL) at indices len..len+6, so the NUL lands at index len+6, exactly one past the last valid index len+5. Trigger fully instantiated: ex-mode line "'<,'>silent" (use_plus_cmd set at line 47), 12-byte heap allocation, len=6, write at indices 6..12 with index 12 out of bounds. No check anywhere in the function bounds this write; the only branch guards (eap->cmd > cmd_start, use_plus_cmd) do not limit the destination extent.

Taint origin and size-mismatch source: the attacker-controlled "'<,'>" prefix (matched at line 17 by STRNCMP(eap->cmd, "'<,'>", 5)) is skipped by advancing the pointer 5 bytes, creating cmd_start = orig_cmd + 5 while the allocation still includes the 5 prefix bytes plus the NUL (5+len+1 bytes total). The later rewrite at line 341 writes 7 bytes at orig_cmd+len without accounting for the retained prefix, producing the one-past-the-end write.

assumptions: The ex-mode command line that eap->cmd points into is exactly sized by the caller (e.g., a saved copy of the line); if the caller's buffer had extra slack, the single NUL byte written at orig_cmd+len+6 could land within that slack. No statement in this code guarantees either case; the defect exists for exactly-sized lines, the standard ex-mode case.

checkforcmd_noparen/checkforcmd_opt are assumed to advance the passed pointer past the matched command text and require a non-alphanumeric terminator (their behavior is external to this code but is not relied on to dismiss any candidate).
skip_vimgrep_pat_ext is assumed to return NULL or a pointer within the line and to set reg_pat when returning non-NULL; its internals are not shown.
exmode_active together with getline equal to getexmodeline/getexline is provided by the ex-mode caller (do_exmode); this was used only to instantiate the trigger state, not to dismiss a candidate.
limitations: Line 316: cmod->cmod_verbose = atoi((char *)eap->cmd) + 1 has no overflow check; an extremely long digit run could overflow the signed int (UB). No memory-safety consequence is demonstrated in this code, and command-line length bounds practical impact; recorded as a robustness issue, not a vulnerability.

Lines 188-196 (filter case): when vim_regcomp returns NULL the break at line 193 skips the restore *nulp = c, leaving a NUL punched into the command line. This corrupts only the attacker's own in-buffer command text (no out-of-bounds access); robustness issue.

The non-ex-mode memmove path (lines 345-347) was edge-tested and writes strictly within the original allocation; the p[-1] and eap->cmd[-1] reads (lines 177, 255) are preceded by matched-command pointer advances and are in bounds; the tab number is guarded by the quoted check at line 274.
The overflow writes a single NUL byte one past the allocation; practical exploitability beyond heap corruption/crash is limited, hence medium severity.

verdict.summary: In the FTPWHO block, when strlen(name) equals sizeof shm_data_cur->filename exactly, the else branch computes the memcpy source index as 'sl - sizeof shm_data_cur->filename - 1U' in size_t, which underflows to SIZE_MAX; &name[SIZE_MAX] wraps to name-1 and the memcpy reads one byte out of bounds before the name buffer (and fills the shared filename field without a NUL terminator). A remote authenticated FTP user triggers it with a single STOR command carrying a filename of exactly that length; the out-of-bounds byte is copied into the shared-memory ftpwho entry readable across a process/privilege boundary.

evidence.reason: Sink of the primary defect. The guard 'if (sl < sizeof shm_data_cur->filename)' (line 149) routes sl == N (N = sizeof shm_data_cur->filename) into this branch; then 'sl - sizeof shm_data_cur->filename - 1U' evaluates to (size_t)0 - 1U = SIZE_MAX, so &name[SIZE_MAX] wraps to name-1 and memcpy reads name[-1], one byte out of bounds before the attacker-supplied name buffer, copying it into the shared ftpwho structure. Additionally the copy of exactly N bytes leaves shm_data_cur->filename unterminated. Trigger fully instantiated in STEP 4 by a STOR command whose filename length equals sizeof shm_data_cur->filename.

Taint origin: sl is the length of the attacker-controlled FTP filename parameter 'name'. No statement in this code bounds sl, and the only comparison against the buffer size (line 149, 'if (sl < sizeof shm_data_cur->filename)') sends the exact-boundary value sl == sizeof shm_data_cur->filename into the defective else branch.

assumptions: FTPWHO is compiled in and shm_data_cur is non-NULL at the time of an upload; both are preprocessor/global conditions outside this code.

The length of 'name' is not bounded by any statement visible in this code; it is assumed the FTP command layer permits a filename of length equal to sizeof shm_data_cur->filename (no such limit is quotable here, so it cannot be used to reject the candidate).
QUOTAS, WITH_TLS, and SHOW_REAL_DISK_SPACE availability depends on build flags not shown; the primary finding does not depend on them.
The underflowing pointer arithmetic &name[SIZE_MAX] is assumed to wrap to name-1 on the target (LP64) as it does in practice; formally it is undefined behavior.
limitations: If ul_init() fails (line 165), ulhandler.total_uploaded is read uninitialized at lines 192, 237 and 250 (CWE-457); no statement in this code can make ul_init fail on attacker input, so the trigger is speculative. The QUOTAS quota-exceeded path sets overflow=1 before goto afterquota, so it takes the addreply branch at line 242 and never reaches the displayrate read.

FSTATFS(f, &statfsbuf) at line 179 uses fd f after '(void) close(f);' at line 173; no fd-allocating statement occurs between them in this code, so the call fails with EBADF and the block is inert (robustness/dead code, no security effect).
In the else branch the shm filename field is never NUL-terminated for any sl >= sizeof filename; over-reading by downstream shm consumers (e.g., pure-who) is outside this code.

TOCTOU/hardlink races around rename(name, atomic_file) and unlink(atomic_file) require an attacker with local filesystem access at equal privilege, which the FTP write path itself does not grant; not instantiated.
The global no_truncate is set by autorename and never restored in this function; no cross-boundary security effect was instantiated from this state carryover.

verdict.summary: load_image computes the brush buffer size as bh.width * bh.height * bh.bytes in 32-bit unsigned arithmetic (guint32 header fields), which wraps modulo 2^32 for permitted header values (e.g. width=65536, height=32769, bytes=2 yields size=65536 instead of ~4 GB). The only guard, 'G_MAXSIZE / bh.width / bh.height / bh.bytes < 1', is evaluated in 64-bit gsize width and can never fire for allowed values on 64-bit builds, so the wrap is unguarded. The undersized heap buffer then receives writes indexed by the unwrapped loop bound ('i < bh.width * bh.height') in the bytes==2 conversion loop, causing a massive heap out-of-bounds write; the bytes==4 path similarly causes a large out-of-bounds read in gimp_pixel_rgn_set_rect. A small attacker-authored brush file (~64 KB) corrupts the heap of the process opening it.

evidence.reason: This is the only size-overflow check, but the division is performed in gsize width (G_MAXSIZE = 2^64-1 on 64-bit builds), so for permitted values (width,height <= 262144, bytes <= 18, product <= ~2^40.6) it can never be < 1; it does not bound the 32-bit product computed at line 121 below the 2^32 wrap point.

evidence.snippet:
size = bh.width * bh.height * bh.bytes;
  brush_buf = g_malloc (size);
evidence.reason: Origin of the defect: bh.width/bh.height/bh.bytes are 32-bit guint32 fields (targets of g_ntohl), so the product wraps modulo 2^32 before being stored in gsize size. Trigger values width=65536, height=32769, bytes=2 pass the line 47-51 guard yet produce size=65536 instead of 4295032832, yielding a drastically undersized heap allocation.

evidence.snippet: for (i = 0; i < bh.width * bh.height; i++, buf++)
evidence.reason: The loop bound is the un-wrapped 32-bit product w*h (2147516416 for the trigger header), with no comparison against the wrapped allocation size; iteration therefore runs ~2.1 billion times over a 65536-byte buffer.

Heap out-of-bounds WRITE sink: with i ranging to bh.width*bh.height-1 = 2147516415 but brush_buf allocated only 65536 bytes (line 122), the first write at i=65536 is one byte past the buffer and writes continue far beyond it; *buf (line 199/201) likewise reads out of bounds from i=32768. Concrete trigger: 64 KB brush file with header version=1, width=65536, height=32769, bytes=2.

Out-of-bounds READ sink (same root cause): with width=65536, height=65537, bytes=4 the wrapped size is 262144, but the rectangle set copies the true w*h*4 (> 4 GB) bytes from the undersized buffer, reading adjacent heap memory into the created image (disclosure potential).

assumptions: BrushHeader fields are 32-bit guint32: they are the direct assignment targets of g_ntohl (lines 38-44), and the error printf casts them to unsigned long for %lu; the wrap analysis depends on this 32-bit width, which is standard for the GIMP brush header.

G_MAXSIZE equals the maximum of gsize (2^64-1) on the dominant 64-bit deployment, making the line 51 guard vacuous there; GIMP_MAX_IMAGE_SIZE is at least 65536 (it is 262144 in gimplimits.h), so the trigger dimensions pass the line 47-48 range checks.

gimp_pixel_rgn_set_rect copies bh.width*bh.height*bh.bytes bytes from the supplied buffer (standard tile-region behavior); this only supports the secondary OOB-read finding, not the primary OOB write at line 205, which is fully instantiated inside this code.
limitations: On 32-bit builds (gsize 32-bit, G_MAXSIZE = 2^32-1), the line 51 guard does reject the demonstrated trigger values, so the wrap is primarily exploitable on 64-bit builds.

Secondary, non-primary issues: (1) line 97 g_new(gchar, bn_size) allows a transient allocation of up to ~2 GB driven by the attacker-controlled header_size before the short-read error path frees it (bounded amplification, CWE-400 flavor); (2) line 109 passes temp (exactly bn_size attacker bytes, no guaranteed NUL terminator) to gimp_any_to_utf8 with length -1, which may read past the buffer inside the callee, but the defective read is in code not shown and cannot be quoted; (3) if the wrapped size is exactly 0, g_malloc(0) yields NULL and later uses crash with a NULL dereference, a variant of the primary wrap defect rather than a separate root cause.
Version-1 files skip the magic-number and header_size checks (case 1 has none), which slightly eases trigger construction but is not itself a memory-safety defect.

verdict.summary: _inplace_src_spans writes span-derived coverage bytes into the pixman mask buffer through the cursor m (*m++ = coverage; memset(m, coverage, --len); m += len) with no bound of m against the mask allocation anywhere in the function. m is only reset to base when a run is exactly coverage 0xff with len >= run_length or exactly coverage 0x0; any run with intermediate coverage accumulates attacker-geometry-derived bytes without limit, so a long partially-covered run (e.g., spans {x=0,coverage=0x40},{x=8192,coverage=0x40}) drives memset past the end of the heap-allocated mask, an out-of-bounds heap write with attacker-influenced length and content reachable when rendering untrusted vector content.

evidence.reason: Unguarded memory-write sink: the coverage byte and memset length derive from the attacker-influenced span run length, and the cursor m is advanced without any comparison against the mask buffer bounds; the only resets are 'm = base' in the solid/empty branches (lines 51 and 80), so any intermediate-coverage run whose accumulated length exceeds the externally allocated mask width writes out of bounds. Simulated trigger: spans {x=0,cov=0x40},{x=8192,cov=0x40}, num_spans=2 → line 16 false (coverage != 0xff), line 53 false (coverage != 0x0) → memset(base+1, 0x40, 8191) overflows the mask allocation.

Origin of the tainted length: len is computed directly from the attacker-influenced span x coordinates and flows unchecked into the memset length at line 85 (after --len) and the pointer advance m += len at line 86; no statement in this function bounds len or the accumulated m - base distance.

assumptions: The pixman mask buffer obtained at line 6 via pixman_image_get_data(r->mask) has a finite size not visible in this code; the function never queries the mask width or stride, so no quotable bound on m exists here.

r->u.composite.run_length, r->src, r->mask, r->u.composite.dst and the src_x/src_y offsets are internal renderer state initialized by renderer setup code not shown; treated as contract (valid non-NULL internals).

Span x values are assumed non-decreasing per the pair-walking design; this is not enforced in this code, but a descending pair yields a negative len which fails the 'len > 1' check at line 84 and adds no new sink.
limitations: Boundary defect at exactly num_spans == 1: the do-while body executes once and reads spans[1] at line 15 one past the end, and the post-loop check at line 92 reads the same out-of-bounds element, with the garbage value potentially reaching the memset length. This trigger requires the not-shown scan converter to emit exactly one span for a row; no statement in this code produces that count, so the trigger precondition could not be instantiated and the candidate is speculative (potential CWE-125).

The overflow magnitude depends on the external mask allocation size, which is not determinable from this code; the defect proven here is the absence of any bound check on the write cursor and length at the sink.

pixman_image_composite32 calls receive raw widths and coordinates (e.g., spans[0].x - x0, spans[1].x - spans[0].x, h); pixman performs its own clipping, so these are not treated as memory-unsafe sinks in this analysis.

verdict.summary: issuerAndThisUpdateCheck fails to verify that a closing double quote was found before advancing the parse cursor: when the thisUpdate (or issuer) string runs to the end of the input without a terminating quote, or when a "" escape ends exactly at the window end, 'x.bv_val += len + 1; x.bv_len -= len + 1;' moves x.bv_val one byte past the end of the attacker-supplied buffer and wraps the unsigned ber_len_t x.bv_len to a huge value. The subsequent 'x.bv_val[0]' reads in the space-eating and comma checks then read out of bounds, and on matching bytes the parser continues reading adjacent heap memory, giving a network-reachable out-of-bounds read.

evidence.reason: The scan loop (lines 107-111) exits with tu->bv_len == x.bv_len when no closing '"' exists; there is no check that a quote was found before this advance. With input "{thisUpdate "AAAA...A}" (length >= 39, braces per lines 19-21), tu->bv_len + 1 exceeds x.bv_len by one, so x.bv_val becomes in->bv_val + in->bv_len (one past the buffer) and the unsigned x.bv_len wraps to a huge value; the following reads of x.bv_val[0] (lines 122, 130) are out of bounds.

Same missing closing-quote guard on the issuer side: either an unterminated issuer string (is->bv_len == x.bv_len after the loop at 65-77) or a "" escape pair at the last two window bytes (line 73, 'is->bv_len += 2;', reaching exactly x.bv_len) makes is->bv_len + 1 exceed x.bv_len, pushing x.bv_val one byte past the input buffer and wrapping the unsigned x.bv_len, leading to the out-of-bounds reads at lines 122/130.

Out-of-bounds read sink: after the underflow at lines 112-113 (or 78-79), x.bv_val equals in->bv_val + in->bv_len and x.bv_len is the wrapped huge value, so 'x.bv_val[0]' reads one byte past the attacker-supplied buffer; if that byte is a space the loop walks the pointer further through out-of-bounds heap, and line 130 'x.bv_val[0] != ','' can resume parsing out-of-bounds memory.

assumptions: ber_len_t is an unsigned type (as in the ber/berval API this code is written against), so 'x.bv_len -= is->bv_len + 1' / 'tu->bv_len + 1' wraps instead of going negative.

'in' carries an externally supplied value (this routine is a syntax-validation/normalization helper invoked on protocol-supplied attribute values); even judged standalone, its data-carrying parameter is attacker-data per the STEP 1 model.
The exact allocation backing in->bv_val is not shown; the analysis treats in->bv_val + in->bv_len as the end of the object, so reads at or beyond it are out of bounds.
limitations: ber_dupbv_x (line 142) and slap_sl_malloc (line 148) results are unchecked; on allocation failure the copy loop would write through a NULL ni.bv_val and '*is = ni' would store a NULL berval. This requires an environment/allocation failure not inducible by the attacker (size is bounded by input length), so it is a robustness issue, not a vulnerability in this code.

The eat-spaces loops evaluate x.bv_val[0] before the x.bv_len condition; while the cursor is still inside the buffer this only reads the final '}' byte and is in bounds — it becomes the out-of-bounds sink only via the confirmed underflow.
The one-past read at line 70 (is->bv_val[is->bv_len+1]) lands on the final '}' at most, which is the last byte of the buffer, so it is in bounds and not a separate finding.

verdict.summary: getInfoForId detects a missing id but does not terminate the not-found path: after the STFATAL log the function falls through to 'return it->second;' with it == idInfoMap.end(). An attacker-supplied id absent from the map therefore dereferences the map's end iterator, copy-constructing the returned TerminalUserInfo from out-of-bounds/uninitialized memory past the sentinel node (potential disclosure of adjacent memory or crash); if STFATAL does abort, the same input yields an externally triggered denial of service. The required early exit (return/throw) after the not-found check is absent from every path in the given code.

evidence.reason: The not-found branch only logs (STFATAL) and contains no return, throw, or abort, so control falls through and line 7 dereferences the end iterator when the attacker-supplied id is absent from idInfoMap — an out-of-bounds/uninitialized read copied by value into the returned TerminalUserInfo. The instantiated trigger is any call with a nonexistent id; the early-exit guard that would prevent this use is absent on every path.

Origin of the tainted value: the attacker-controlled 'id' parameter is looked up here, and find() returns idInfoMap.end() for any id not present in the map, producing the iterator that is later dereferenced without a guard.

assumptions: The STFATAL macro is not defined in the given code; whether it terminates the process cannot be quoted and is not relied upon. If it is [[noreturn]], the defect becomes an attacker-triggered abort (denial of service across the service boundary); if it only logs, the end-iterator dereference executes as analyzed. Either way the missing early exit after the not-found check is the defect.

The id parameter is treated as attacker-data per the trust-boundary model: a UserTerminalRouter keyed by ids that can 'no longer exist' indicates ids originate from external sessions/requests; if in the actual deployment all callers were same-privilege with self-supplied ids and STFATAL aborts, impact would reduce to a robustness issue.
limitations: No race condition exists inside this function: the lock_guard<recursive_mutex> is held across both idInfoMap.find and the copy in the return statement, so no interleavable pair of operations on the map is exhibit within this code.

Exact disclosure content depends on the standard library's map layout and the definition of TerminalUserInfo (not shown); the concrete impact ranges from garbage/uninitialized bytes (including map-internal pointers) returned to the caller to a segmentation fault.

verdict.summary: getInfoForId tests for a failed map lookup but the error branch only logs (STFATAL) and contains no return, throw, or abort, so control falls through to `return it->second;`, which dereferences the past-the-end iterator returned by find(). For any id absent from idInfoMap — a case the code itself anticipates ("an id that no longer exists") and which an untrusted caller supplying the id key can trivially produce — this is undefined behavior: an out-of-bounds read of the map sentinel whose garbage value is returned to the caller (disclosure potential) or a process crash (denial of service across a service boundary). No guard exists on any path between the check and the dereference.

evidence.reason: Root cause: the failed-lookup branch body contains only the STFATAL log statement with no return/throw/abort, so on the miss path (it == idInfoMap.end(), triggered by any attacker-supplied or stale id not present in the map) control reaches `return it->second;` and dereferences the past-the-end iterator — an out-of-bounds read / undefined behavior whose value is returned to the caller.

Origin of the tainted value: find() on the externally supplied id string returns idInfoMap.end() for any id not in the map, producing the invalid iterator that line 6 dereferences; the code's own equality check on the next line proves this miss case is reachable.

assumptions: The semantics of STFATAL are not defined in the given code; per guard anchoring the analysis does not credit it with terminating execution. If STFATAL does abort, the line-6 dereference is unreachable and the impact reduces to a denial-of-service (process abort) triggered by an unknown id supplied across a service boundary.

No caller is shown; per STEP 1 the data-carrying id parameter (a lookup key/token) is treated as attacker-influenced, consistent with the code's own message "an id that no longer exists" indicating erased ids and stale references occur in practice.

verdict.summary: rrlen is declared uint16_t while its value is computed as strlen(provider_name) + 15 + 4*sizeof(struct SignedCert) + 2 in size_t; the only guard rejects strlen(provider_name) >= 0xffff0000, which is far above the 16-bit truncation point at 65536. A provider_name of length 65536 - 17 - 4*sizeof(struct SignedCert) (about 65000-65400 bytes) passes the guard, makes rrlen truncate to 0, malloc(0) returns a non-NULL minimal chunk, and snprintf(rr, (size_t)-1, "%s 86400 IN TXT \"", provider_name) writes the full ~65 KB attacker-controlled string into it: a heap buffer overflow with attacker-chosen content and length.

evidence.reason: The only length guard on the attacker-data provider_name rejects strlen >= 0xffff0000, but the value it feeds (rrlen) is a uint16_t that truncates at a sum of 65536; a ~65023-byte provider_name passes this check (65023 < 0xffff0000) yet makes the computed length wrap to 0, so the missing-check site for the truncation is this guard.

The size_t sum (e.g., 65023 + 15 + 496 + 2 = 65536) is truncated on assignment to the uint16_t rrlen (declared line 19), yielding rrlen = 0, and malloc(rrlen) allocates a zero-sized chunk; this is the buffer size miscalculation (CWE-131) that produces the undersized allocation.

With rrlen == 0, rrlen - 1 evaluates to (int)-1 and converts to size_t SIZE_MAX, so snprintf writes the entire attacker-controlled provider_name plus the 15-char literal plus NUL (~65039 bytes) into the malloc(0) chunk returned non-NULL by glibc (the if(!rr) check at line 51 passes), a heap out-of-bounds write (CWE-787).

assumptions: sizeof(struct SignedCert) is not shown in this code; for any fixed value S in [0, 129], a provider_name length of 65536 - 17 - 4*S (in [65018, 65519]) makes rrlen truncate to 0, so the trigger is instantiable regardless of the exact struct size.

malloc(0) is assumed to return a non-NULL minimal chunk (glibc/POSIX common behavior); if it returned NULL, the error path at lines 51-54 would return -2 and the overflow would not occur on that path.

provider_name, signed_certs and rotated_certs arrive through the dnscenv parameter as config/file-origin content this code does not validate elsewhere; per the intake-point rule they are treated as attacker-data, and the code's own attempted length guard shows defensive intent toward provider_name.

limitations: The rrlen == 1 variant (provider_name length making the sum congruent to 1 mod 65536) leaves the malloc(1) buffer uninitialized because snprintf with size 0 writes nothing; the subsequent strlen(rr) at lines 59/61/70 reads uninitialized heap, so its value cannot be concretely instantiated by any statement in this code — speculative, though it shares C1's root cause.

When every certificate byte expands to the 4-char form \%03d, the snprintf sizes using rrlen - 1 leave room for only rrlen - 2 content chars, so the trailing double quote at line 70 is silently dropped and a malformed local-data string is inserted at line 71; this truncation is in-bounds and is a robustness defect, not memory unsafety.

First, the dependents loop starts at the file-supplied extras[j].dependentsStartArrayIndex and iterates depArray[k] with no bound against depListCount (the only loop condition is the terminator test depArray[k] != 0xffff), and each entry's dep_index (only masked to 0..0x7fff by '& 0x7fff') is used for deps[dep_index]++ and img[dep_index] with no check against imagesCount, yielding heap out-of-bounds write and reads. verdict.summary: gdImageFillToBorder recurses once per image row/pixel region with no depth limit; recursion depth and total frame count are governed by attacker-controlled image dimensions and pixel contents (im->sy, pixel colors). A tiny crafted image (e.g., 1 x 100000 uniform non-border pixels) drives ~10^5 nested stack frames when a privileged service fills it, exhausting the process stack (denial of service / attacker-scalable amplification). The only guards (if (y > 0), if (y < ((im->sy) - 1)), and the (c != border) && (c != color) pixel gate) bound single steps, not cumulative depth.

evidence.reason: Uncontrolled recursive call in the above-loop. The gate at line 48 (if ((c != border) && (c != color))) only excludes border-colored and already-filled pixels, and the vertical guard if (y > 0) bounds one step; nothing bounds cumulative recursion depth. With an attacker-supplied image of sy = 100000, sx = 1, uniform pixels = 5, called as (im, 0, 99999, 1, 2), each nested frame recurses to y-1, producing a nest of depth ~10^5 and stack exhaustion.

Symmetric uncontrolled recursive call in the below-loop, gated only by if (y < ((im->sy) - 1)) and the pixel test at line 71; the same crafted tall image with a small starting y drives an equally deep downward nesting chain. No depth counter or worklist exists anywhere in the function.

assumptions: gdImageGetPixel/gdImageSetPixel are external helpers not shown; their internal bounds handling (libgd's gdImageBoundsSafeMacro returning -1 / ignoring out-of-range writes) is assumed but cannot be quoted from the given code.

It is assumed the image object im originates from decoding untrusted data in the attacker's deployment (e.g., uploaded image processed by a service), which is the model under which the recursion depth (im->sy, pixel values) is attacker-controlled.
limitations: Speculative: x and y are never validated against im->sx/im->sy at entry (no statement checks x < im->sx); if x >= im->sx, line 27 leaves rightLimit = x out of range and lines 42/65 scan out-of-range indices into gdImageGetPixel/gdImageSetPixel. Triggering requires a caller passing out-of-range coordinates (contract violation) and OOB effects inside helpers not shown, so it is not confirmed in this code.

Benign quirk: when color == border the fill escapes the intended border region because the recursion gate collapses to c != border; this is a functional correctness issue with no demonstrated security impact.

Worst outcome of the confirmed recursion defect is process crash/stack exhaustion (availability), not demonstrated memory corruption; it is still a vulnerability because a remote untrusted image originator crashes a higher-privileged processing process with a trivially small input (attacker-scalable amplification).

verdict.summary: do_mouse() indexes TabPageIdxs[mouse_col] on mouse-drag paths without any bound on mouse_col. The only check, 'mouse_col < Columns', guards the click path alone. mouse_col/mouse_row come from decoded terminal mouse escape sequences (attacker-controllable, e.g. via a malicious file written to the terminal) and are not clamped to Vim's screen width here. After one valid tabline click sets the static in_tab_line = TRUE, a drag event carrying an out-of-range column (SGR mouse encoding allows coordinates up to 2015, far beyond typical Columns) reaches TabPageIdxs[mouse_col] and reads out of bounds on the heap (the CVE-2021-3778 class of bug). The unvalidated value c1 then feeds tabpage_move().

evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds read sink: TabPageIdxs is indexed by attacker-controlled mouse_col with no bound check on this drag path (the only 'mouse_col < Columns' check in the function, line 275, is on the click path only). Trigger instantiated: a valid tabline click sets in_tab_line = TRUE (line 277), then a drag event with mouse_row == 0 and mouse_col = 500 (SGR-encoded) executes TabPageIdxs[500] on an array sized for Columns entries.

Second unguarded out-of-bounds read sink: reached when the line-257 row check fails, so mouse_col has no bound of any kind; a drag with in_tab_line TRUE (set by a prior click at line 277) and any mouse_col value >= Columns indexes TabPageIdxs out of bounds.

Origin of the trigger state and of the violated invariant: this click path is the only place mouse_col is bounded ('&& mouse_col < Columns)') for TabPageIdxs indexing, demonstrating the array's domain; it also executes 'in_tab_line = TRUE;', the static state that later admits the unguarded drag paths, on which no equivalent bound exists.

assumptions: TabPageIdxs is allocated with Columns entries elsewhere in the codebase (allocation not shown); the domain [0, Columns) is inferred from this code's own click guard 'mouse_col < Columns)'.

The terminal mouse decoder (term.c, not shown) sets mouse_row/mouse_col from escape-sequence coordinates and does not clamp them to Vim's screen dimensions; SGR mouse encoding permits coordinates up to 2015.

The trigger requires the user to have 'mouse' enabled and the tabline displayed (firstwin->w_winrow > 0); these are configuration states, consistent with the historical CVE-2021-3778 threat model where a malicious file injects mouse escape sequences into the terminal.
limitations: The click guard 'mouse_col < Columns)' has no lower bound, so a negative mouse_col would also index out of bounds; however, no statement in the given code can produce a negative column (the decoder is not shown), so this variant remains speculative.

Unchecked inc() return in the double-click whitespace loop ('while (gc = gchar_pos(&end_visual), VIM_ISWHITE(gc)) inc(&end_visual);') relies on inc() clamping at end-of-buffer (upstream behavior); no trigger instantiated from the given code.

verdict.summary: This PCI probe function fails closed on every checked error path and guards every memory/index sink reachable in its own body: the ioremap pointer is NULL-checked before any MMIO access, per-cpu and trans allocations are checked, the hardware revision is validated against the all-ones failure value before use, DMA mask fallback terminates in a hard error, and hw_id_str is written with a sizeof-bounded snprintf and a constant format string. The two residual hazards are non-instantiable from the given code: cfg_trans->base_params is dereferenced without a NULL check, but cfg_trans is a driver-authored contract argument whose content no statement here produces or parses, so a NULL base_params cannot be exhibited; and the alloc_workqueue return is unchecked, but failure there requires kernel memory exhaustion no attacker can induce.

assumptions: iwl_trans_alloc zeroes or fully initializes the returned struct so that trans_pcie fields (msix_enabled, rba, inta_mask) are not attacker-influenced uninitialized reads; not shown in the given code.
iwl_pcie_set_interrupt_capa (not shown) is the sole setter of trans_pcie->msix_enabled; its correctness cannot be verified here.

The macros CSR_HW_REV_STEP, IWL_PCIE_MAX_FRAGS, IWL_TFH_NUM_TBS, IWL_NUM_OF_TBS and the type/width of trans->hw_id and trans->hw_id_str are not shown; they are assumed to be well-formed kernel definitions.

cfg_trans comes from the caller's PCI ID table and is assumed non-NULL with valid base_params; the given code never checks cfg_trans or cfg_trans->base_params, and no statement in this function can produce a NULL value for them.
Cleanup helpers called on error paths (iwl_pcie_free_ict, iwl_trans_free, free_percpu) and iwl_pcie_init_msix_handler error cleanup are external and assumed sound.
limitations: Speculative: `if (!cfg_trans->base_params->pcie_l1_allowed)` dereferences cfg_trans->base_params with no NULL guard anywhere in the given code. The trigger precondition (a driver config entry with base_params == NULL selected by an attacker-chosen PCI device ID) cannot be instantiated from this code; if such a table entry exists in the caller, the result would be a kernel NULL dereference (DoS) during probe. The fix would be a one-line `cfg_trans->base_params &&` check; I searched the given code and it is absent, but the trigger remains contract-speculative.

Robustness: `trans_pcie->rba.alloc_wq = alloc_workqueue("rb_allocator", WQ_HIGHPRI | WQ_UNBOUND, 1);` does not check the return value; a NULL workqueue would crash a later queue_work caller, but NULL only occurs under kernel memory exhaustion during probe, which no attacker input in this function can induce, and the allocation size is a fixed constant (no amplification).

The MSI-X branch error path (`if (ret) goto out_no_pci;` after iwl_pcie_init_msix_handler) relies on cleanup inside that helper for partially initialized MSI-X state; the helper is not shown, so its adequacy is unverifiable.

verdict.summary: gdImageFillToBorder clamps x and y only against the upper bounds (`if (x >= im->sx)`, `if (y >= im->sy)`) and never rejects or clamps negative values. A caller-supplied negative y survives to every sink: it is passed as the row index to gdImageGetPixel/gdImageSetPixel, and, because the Below-branch guard `if (y < ((im->sy) - 1))` is true for every negative y, the recursive call `gdImageFillToBorder(im, i, y + 1, border, color)` passes still-negative y+1, producing a recursion chain whose depth equals the attacker-chosen |y|. A single argument such as y = -1000000 (with any border >= 0, admitted by the `border < 0` return, and any color != -1) drives ~10^6 nested stack frames and Theta(|y|*sx) work, exhausting the stack and crashing the process that services the attacker's request — attacker-scalable denial of service — while also handing out-of-domain row indices to the pixel accessors.

evidence.reason: This is the only bound applied to the attacker-supplied coordinate y, and it clamps only the upper bound. No statement in the function rejects or clamps y < 0, so any negative y (e.g., y = -1000000 passed to this exported fill API) proceeds unvalidated into the pixel-access calls and the recursion below; the missing-check site for the primary defect.

Recursive sink reached with attacker-controlled negative y: the enclosing guard `if (y < ((im->sy) - 1))` (line 56) is satisfied by every negative y, and the recursive argument y + 1 is still negative for y < -1. Instantiated trigger: with y = -1000000, border = 1, color = 0 on any image, each frame recurses once with y incremented by 1, building |y| nested stack frames (about 10^6) and Theta(|y|*sx) work — stack exhaustion / unbounded resource consumption from one small input.

The unvalidated negative y is used directly as the row index handed to the pixel accessors gdImageGetPixel/gdImageSetPixel (same uses at lines 33/36 and 59). Because the loop's break condition compares against a border known to be >= 0 (enforced by `if (border < 0) { return; }`), an out-of-range row read returning -1 never matches border, so the loop always traverses the full width and sets leftLimit, keeping the negative-y flow alive into the recursive branches.

assumptions: gdImageGetPixel/gdImageSetPixel are not part of the given code; analysis assumes the documented libgd contract that they clip out-of-range coordinates (gdImageGetPixel returning -1). The STEP 4 stack-exhaustion trigger was instantiated under that documented behavior; if the accessors instead index without clipping, the same unvalidated negative y additionally yields direct out-of-bounds read/write of rows above the image, making the defect strictly worse.
im->sx and im->sy are assumed >= 1; image creation code is not shown.

The function is an exported public API whose x, y, border, color are plain ints; in real deployments (e.g., PHP's imagefilltoborder) these originate from untrusted callers across a service boundary, which is the attacker model used.
A default process stack on the order of a few MB is assumed, so |y| around 10^5-10^6 exceeds it; any larger negative int is accepted since y is a plain int.
limitations: Negative x is accidentally safe: with x < 0 the loop `for (i = x; i >= 0; i--)` never executes and `if (leftLimit == -1) { return; }` exits before any sink.

The `x + 1` signed overflow at line 32 (i starting negative) would require im->sx near INT_MAX; no statement in this code makes allocation of such an image attainable, so this candidate is speculative.

color == border does not cause infinite recursion here: each recursion seed is verified `c != border && c != color` by the parent and is painted to color by the child's seek-left first iteration before any other caller can re-seed it, so in-domain recursion terminates.

Memory-corruption impact cannot be proven inside this code because the pixel-array indexing sinks live in the helpers; the confirmed, helper-independent impact is attacker-scalable stack exhaustion (denial of service) plus out-of-domain row indices being passed to the accessors.

verdict.summary: sug_filltree walks the case-folded trie loaded from a spell file with stack arrays sized MAXWLEN (arridx, curi, tword, wordcount) but never bounds the descent depth. depth is incremented once per nonzero byte (tword[depth++] = c) and the word length is attacker-controlled by the spell file content, so a trie encoding a word longer than MAXWLEN-1 produces out-of-bounds stack writes at tword[depth], arridx[depth], curi[depth] and wordcount[depth], with attacker-influenced values (idxs[n], the byte c). No check of depth against MAXWLEN exists anywhere in the function, enabling memory corruption from a malicious .spl file.

evidence.reason: Root cause and sink: depth is incremented per nonzero trie byte with no upper bound check, and these statements write tword[depth], arridx[depth], curi[depth], wordcount[depth] into fixed MAXWLEN stack arrays. A spell file whose folded trie contains a word of MAXWLEN+1 bytes (attacker-controlled byts/idxs content) drives depth to MAXWLEN and past it, writing one-past-the-end and beyond on the stack with attacker-influenced values (idxs[n] and c). No 'depth < MAXWLEN' guard exists on any path (only 'depth >= 0' and 'depth > 0' appear).

Origin of the tainted data: the byte trie and index array parsed from the (untrusted) spell file; their content controls the branch at 'c = byts[n]' and the depth growth at the sink, instantiating the trigger.

assumptions: It is assumed (not quotable from this code) that the tree-loading code that fills sl_fbyts/sl_fidxs may validate child indices; that enforcement is outside this function, so candidates C2 (idxs[arridx[depth]] = wordcount[depth] with an out-of-range file-derived index, line 40) and C3 (unbounded read byts[n] with n = arridx[depth] + curi[depth], lines 51-54) could not have their harmful values instantiated from statements in this code and do not drive the verdict, though no bound check on arridx[depth] or n exists here either.

MAXWLEN's numeric value is defined outside this snippet; the overflow triggers at depth == MAXWLEN regardless of its concrete value, since the only writes are at index depth and depth grows without bound.
limitations: words_done is unsigned and wraps after 2^32 words (lines 68, 63-65); no security effect, dismissed.
The NUL-skip loop at lines 77-81 is correctly guarded by 'n + 1 < slang->sl_fbyts_len', verified at the boundary.

verdict.summary: No exploitable vulnerability found in the given code. The attacker-influenced value sampleSize (from the user's $sample stage) is used only in floating-point plan-choice heuristics and constructor arguments whose definitions are not part of this code; no memory, index, allocation, injection, or crypto sink inside this function consumes it unsafely. The two division sites are guarded on every path: the sharded-path division is protected by the early return 'numRecords <= 100' (which forces numRecords >= 101 on the only path), and the time-series division is protected by 'if (!(bucketUnpacker && numRecords))', which the code explicitly added to prevent the NaN case described in its own comment. Pointer casts match the dynamic types established by the immediately preceding make_unique statements, and the TrialStage raw pointer remains valid across the unique_ptr move.

assumptions: sampleSize is assumed to be validated as a non-negative integer upstream in the $sample aggregation parser (DocumentSourceSample), which is not shown in the given code; this code contains no such check. Even without that assumption, no sink inside the given code uses sampleSize in a memory-unsafe or injectable way.
numRecords is assumed to be a non-negative record-store count supplied by trusted catalog code (contract input); the code additionally guards the boundary cases 0 and negative itself.
gTimeseriesBucketMaxCount is assumed to be a validated, admin-set server parameter with a positive lower bound enforced by MongoDB's parameter framework, which is not shown.
limitations: Speculative: if an operator set gTimeseriesBucketMaxCount to 0 (outside its documented valid range and not attacker-writable), then with sampleSize = 0 the expression 'sampleSize / (kCoefficient * numRecords * gTimeseriesBucketMaxCount)' would evaluate to 0/0 = NaN, and NaN propagation through std::min/std::max would pass an unspecified minAdvancedToWorkRatio to TrialStage. The trigger requires admin misconfiguration, not attacker input, so it is not treated as a vulnerability in this code.

Robustness only: an out-of-domain sampleSize (e.g., negative) that bypassed upstream parsing would alter only floating-point plan-selection heuristics within this code; any harmful use would have to occur inside SampleFromTimeseriesBucket / TrialStage, whose implementations are not part of the given code and were not analyzed.
The function's return type is omitted from the snippet, making the mixed returns (std::pair{nullptr,false} vs execStatus.getStatus()) unverifiable; treated as an excerpt artifact, not a defect.

verdict.summary: This is the Linux kernel esp_output_head (net/ipv4/esp4.c) outbound ESP path. Every memory sink is guarded on-path and edge-tested: the trailer write is bounded by 'tailen <= skb_tailroom(skb)' or by a successful skb_page_frag_refill/skb_cow_data; the frag index is bounded by 'nr_frags < MAX_SKB_FRAGS' under '!skb_cloned(skb)'; all return paths initialize nfrags. The only unvalidated use, esp->esph in the esph_offset computation, is a pointer read whose staleness could only arise if the unshown callee esp_output_encap reallocated the skb head; that precondition cannot be instantiated from this code, and the potential write through esp->esph occurs in the caller. No attacker-instantiable vulnerability exists in the given code.

assumptions: esp->tailen == esp->tfclen + esp->plen and is non-negative, and esp->esph points into the current skb data at entry: these invariants are established by the in-kernel caller (esp_output_tail) and are not shown in this code; the guards here protect tailen bytes, so a violated invariant would overflow esp_output_fill_trailer, but no statement in this code can produce such values.
esp_output_encap, skb_cow_data, skb_page_frag_refill and pskb_put behave per their kernel contracts (success implies the requested tailroom/frag capacity); these callees are not shown.
ESP_SKB_FRAG_MAXSIZE bounds data_len + tailen into a range far below the 32-bit wrap point of allocsz.
limitations: Speculative: if esp_output_encap (unshown) can reallocate the skb head (e.g. an espintcp path calling pskb_expand_head/clone), the 'esph_offset = (unsigned char *)esp->esph - skb_transport_header(skb)' computation would use a stale pointer, producing an arbitrary offset written back into esp->esph after skb_cow_data, an out-of-bounds write in the caller. The reallocating precondition could not be instantiated from the given code, so this is not counted as a vulnerability here.

Speculative/contract: a negative esp->tailen would pass 'tailen <= skb_tailroom(skb)' and reach pskb_put(skb, skb, negative) causing skb_put underflow/BUG, but tailen is a kernel-internal derived value no attacker can make negative.
Speculative: unsigned wrap of 'skb->data_len + tailen' in allocsz requires a ~4GB skb, unreachable from any shown statement or realistic packet construction.
Verified non-defects: all return paths initialize nfrags (walked all five control-flow paths); the nr_frags < MAX_SKB_FRAGS guard is correctly strict and edge-tested at MAX-1 and MAX.

verdict.summary: The only attacker-influenced input is the guest-controlled register index s->reg, and its sole sink, the array read s->edid_blob[s->reg % sizeof(s->edid_blob)], is bounded by the in-code modulo at the sink itself; for every possible value (0, max of any width, negative-signed promoted to size_t, at-limit, one-past-limit) the resulting index lies in [0, sizeof(edid_blob)-1]. No out-of-bounds, injection, allocation, crypto, or amplification sink exists in this code.

assumptions: The struct definition (I2CDDCState) is not shown; s->edid_blob is assumed to be a fixed-size array member with size >= 1 (a zero-size or flexible member would make sizeof degenerate), as in the upstream QEMU i2c-ddc device where the EDID blob is 128 bytes and reg is uint8_t.
Initialization of s->edid_blob is assumed to occur at device realize/reset in code not shown; this analysis cannot quote it.
The i2c parameter is assumed non-NULL per the I2C bus core's contract for slave callbacks.
limitations: Speculative candidate: NULL or mistyped i2c pointer passed by the bus core would crash inside I2CDDC(i2c)/field access; trigger requires the framework caller to violate its documented non-NULL contract, so it is a contract issue, not a vulnerability in this code.

Speculative candidate: if the device state were never initialized, the guest could read uninitialized EDID bytes; the initialization site is outside the given code, QEMOM device instances are zero-allocated, and the bytes returned are the guest's own device descriptor, so no cross-boundary disclosure was instantiated.
Register wraparound of s->reg++ was analyzed and is benign: every wrapped value is re-bounded by the modulo on the next read.

verdict.summary: The retab implementation's memory operations are exact-fit and consistently guarded: the allocation size equals the sum of the three writes performed (prefix, replacement whitespace, suffix with NUL); col never passes the NUL terminator on any path; vcol is capped below MAXCOL by a check executed every iteration before vcol is consumed; the u_save failure and alloc failure paths both terminate the loops via the new_line NULL flag; and the tabstop argument is range-checked (negative, zero, > TABSTOP_MAX) in the non-vartabs build. No trigger for memory corruption, an out-of-bounds access, injection, or attacker-scalable amplification could be instantiated from the code as written. Residual risks are contract-bound: division uses curbuf->b_p_ts whose >=1 domain is enforced by option code not shown, and the vartabs end block assumes set_string_option_direct does not itself free curbuf->b_p_vts_array (the code reassigns the array immediately after, which would double-free otherwise; this exact pattern is long-shipped upstream).

assumptions: curbuf->b_p_ts is assumed >= 1 (and curbuf->b_p_vts_array consistent with b_p_vts); their domains are enforced by Vim's option machinery, not by any statement in this code, so ':retab 0' resolving to new_ts = curbuf->b_p_ts cannot cause division by zero from this code's own flow.

set_string_option_direct("vts", ...) is assumed to assign the option string without freeing/replacing curbuf->b_p_vts_array; if it did, the subsequent 'curbuf->b_p_vts_array = new_vts_array; vim_free(old_vts_ary);' would double-free. This behavior is not visible in the given code.

tabstop_set/tabstop_fromto are assumed to honor their contracts (reject invalid values, never return negative counts); ml_get is assumed to return a valid line for the command range, and eap->line1/line2 to be within buffer bounds as adjusted by the ex-command machinery.
mb_ptr2len is assumed not to consume a NUL byte as part of a multibyte sequence (UTF-8 continuation-byte masking rejects 0x00), which is what keeps col <= STRLEN(ptr) on the advancement path.
limitations: Speculative division-by-zero via ':retab 0' in the non-vartabs build requires curbuf->b_p_ts == 0, which no statement here can produce; the trigger precondition could not be instantiated.

Speculative double free of old_vts_ary in the FEAT_VARTABS end block requires set_string_option_direct to already free curbuf->b_p_vts_array; not instantiable from this code and historically contradicted by this pattern shipping in Vim for years.

On a 32-bit target (long = 32 bits), (long)STRLEN(ptr) of a >2GB line could wrap and miscalculate the alloc size; requires a platform/size combination not exercised by the code as written (declared long arithmetic stays below ~3*MAXCOL on 64-bit).
If ml_replace returns FAIL (out of memory), the freshly allocated new_line is neither stored nor freed (minor leak on an OOM-only path); no security impact.
The 'vcol >= MAXCOL' break can skip retabulating the pending whitespace run of extremely long lines; this is a functional limitation, not a memory-safety defect.

verdict.summary: No reachable vulnerability in the given code. The attacker-controlled 32-bit verdict code is validated by an on-path masked switch restricting it to NF_ACCEPT/NF_DROP/NF_QUEUE or the explicit NFT_* constants, with every other value rejected by `return -EINVAL;`. Chain references from attacker-supplied names/ids are checked with `if (IS_ERR(chain)) return PTR_ERR(chain);` on both lookup paths, jump-to-base-chain is rejected by `if (nft_is_base_chain(chain)) return -EOPNOTSUPP;`, and the historical set-element/binding-chain UAF vector is blocked by `if (desc->flags & NFT_DATA_DESC_SETELEM && chain->flags & NFT_CHAIN_BINDING) return -EINVAL;` before `chain->use++`. Remaining concerns (helper NULL-vs-ERR_PTR contract, commit-mutex serialization of the use counter, netlink attribute policy enforcement) reside in code not shown and are recorded as assumptions.

assumptions: nft_chain_lookup and nft_chain_lookup_byid return ERR_PTR (not NULL) on failure per kernel helper contract; this code only checks IS_ERR(chain), so a NULL return would be missed — but no statement in this code produces NULL.
nft_verdict_policy and nla_parse_nested_deprecated validate the types/lengths of NFTA_VERDICT_CODE, NFTA_VERDICT_CHAIN, and NFTA_VERDICT_CHAIN_ID; the policy table is not shown.
nf_tables batch operations hold the netfilter commit mutex, serializing the non-atomic `chain->use++` against concurrent transaction commits.
limitations: Speculative: if a chain lookup helper could return NULL instead of ERR_PTR, `nft_is_base_chain(chain)` would NULL-deref; not instantiable from the given code.

High bits of a verdict whose masked low byte is NF_ACCEPT/NF_DROP/NF_QUEUE (e.g. 0xFFFFFF00) pass validation; they only influence nf_hook verdict semantics (queue number selection / ignored bits), with no memory-safety, authz, or amplification effect inside this code.

Older kernel versions of this function lacked the inner masked-verdict switch and the SETELEM/binding check; both are present verbatim here, so those historical CVEs do not apply to this code as given.

verdict.summary: No demonstrable vulnerability in this code. All memory-access sinks are guarded by quotable checks on every path (e.g. 'if (ccline.cmdpos >= ccline.cmdlen) break;' before the K_RIGHT reads; 'ccline.cmdpos > 0' before the cmdbuff[cmdpos-1] read; 'if (ccline.cmdbuff != NULL)' before history writes; the 'depth == 50' recursion limit is safe because '++depth'/'--depth' move in unit steps on all paths). assumptions: ccline.cmdbuff is allocated with capacity for at least ccline.cmdlen+1 bytes and terminated with NUL at index cmdlen; the allocation/resize logic (alloc_cmdbuff/realloc_cmdbuff) is not shown, so this invariant is an assumption, though the code itself writes 'ccline.cmdbuff[ccline.cmdlen] = NUL;' treating index cmdlen as valid.

put_on_cmdline, cmdline_paste, bracketed_paste and cmdline_insert_reg (not shown) are assumed to insert only complete multi-byte characters, so cmdbuff never ends with a truncated lead byte; the K_RIGHT loop's '(*mb_ptr2len)' increment and the unguarded while-condition read 'ccline.cmdbuff[ccline.cmdpos]' could otherwise index past the terminator.

cmdline_wildchar_complete (not shown) is assumed to keep wim_index within the bounds of wim_flags[] (MAXWIM entries); this function resets 'wim_index = 0;' but never bounds-checks it before 'wim_flags[wim_index] & WIM_LIST'.
safe_vgetc, trigger_cmd_autocmd, init_ccline, hist_char2type, mb_head_off and mb_ptr2len are assumed to honor their documented contracts; no violations could be instantiated from the given code.
The editor is single-threaded and there are no async re-entrant frees of ccline.cmdbuff between the 'vim_free(new_last_cmdline);' and 'new_last_cmdline = vim_strsave(...)' statements.
limitations: Speculative (not a vulnerability in this code): heap out-of-bounds read via 'ccline.cmdbuff[ccline.cmdpos]' in the K_RIGHT while-condition if cmdpos overshoots cmdlen on a truncated multi-byte character; the truncated character cannot be produced by any statement shown here.
Speculative: 'ccline.cmdbuff[ccline.cmdlen] = NUL;' in the Ctrl_U case would write out of bounds if cmdpos > cmdlen (making cmdlen negative); no shown statement can push cmdpos beyond cmdlen.
Speculative: 'wim_flags[wim_index]' OOB read requires wim_index beyond the array, which is only modified inside the unshown helper cmdline_wildchar_complete.

Robustness-only (equal-privilege process of the typing user): hypothetical crash scenarios driven purely by a user's own keystrokes in their own editor process would fall under discipline 3's robustness carve-out; none were instantiated anyway.

The 'depth == 50' exact-equality recursion limit was edge-tested and found safe: depth changes only by ++depth at entry and --depth at theend on every exit path, so it always hits 50 exactly and never exceeds it.

verdict.summary: No exploitable defect found in xfrm_expand_policies as given. The function consumes lookup results (pols[0], and pols[1] from xfrm_policy_lookup_bytype) that can be NULL or ERR_PTR, but every dereference is guarded: pols[0] is validated by 'if (*num_pols == 0 || !pols[0])' followed by 'if (IS_ERR(pols[0]))', and pols[1] is validated by 'if (IS_ERR(pols[1])) { xfrm_pols_put(pols, *num_pols); *num_pols = 0; return PTR_ERR(pols[1]); }' before '(*num_pols)++', so the final loop 'for (i = 0; i < *num_pols; i++)' can never reach index 1 with a NULL or error pointer. This guard is exactly the fix for the historical CVE-2023-3776 crash pattern; the remaining failure scenarios require a caller violating the num_pols<=1 entry contract, which this code's own flow cannot produce.

assumptions: The bound keeping xfrm_nr at or below XFRM_MAX_DEPTH is enforced in policy-creation code (copy_templates) outside this snippet and could not be quoted; however, xfrm_nr is a u8 field, so even the unbounded worst case yields *num_xfrms <= 510 in an int accumulator with no overflow or truncation at any sink in this code.
xfrm_pols_put and xfrm_policy_lookup_bytype implementations are not shown; analysis of their reference-counting and return-value semantics relies on their documented kernel contracts.
Kernel callers (xfrm_lookup/xfrm_bundle_lookup) are assumed to pass num_pols of 0 or 1 and a pols array with room for at least 2 entries; this is an interface contract, not a guard in this code.
limitations: Speculative (contract-only): if a caller passed *num_pols >= 2 at entry with pols[1] NULL or stale, the loop 'if (pols[i]->action != XFRM_POLICY_ALLOW)' would dereference it. No kernel caller does this and this function's own flow never raises *num_pols above 1 without first validating pols[1], so the trigger could not be instantiated; precondition not instantiated: entry *num_pols > 1.

Speculative: a stale pols[1] from a previous invocation reusing the caller's array is never read, because index 1 is only accessed when *num_pols == 2, which is set only after pols[1] is freshly assigned and validated in the same invocation.

Robustness only: on the IS_ERR(pols[0]) error path *num_xfrms is left at its entry value; callers that ignore the negative return could read a stale count, but no such caller behavior is evidenced and no security consequence arises inside this code.

The historical crash this function's IS_ERR(pols[1]) guard fixes (ERR_PTR dereferenced at pols[1]->action, CVE-2023-3776 pattern) is fully remediated in the given code; the check precedes (*num_pols)++ on the only path and resets *num_pols to 0 before returning.

assumptions: init_ccline() and put_on_cmdline() (not shown) allocate ccline.cmdbuff with capacity >= cmdlen+1 and maintain cmdbuff[cmdlen] == NUL and 0 <= cmdpos <= cmdlen; these invariants are relied on by the Ctrl-U shift and the K_RIGHT while-condition read at index cmdlen.
