verdict.summary: All memory-write sinks into the single buffer (alloc(STRLEN(path) + BASENAMELEN + 5)) were traced and fit within the allocation under the stated design invariant that readdir never returns a d_name longer than BASENAMELEN: the pattern copy loop writes at most STRLEN(path)+1 bytes; 'STRCPY(s, dp->d_name)' plus the worst-case starstar append ('/**' + path_end + NUL) consumes at most STRLEN(path)+d_name_len+4 bytes, exactly absorbed by the +5 slack. No length check on dp->d_name exists in this code, so an overflow would occur if any filesystem returned a name exceeding BASENAMELEN, but that precondition is uninstantiable on conforming systems (creation of names over NAME_MAX fails with ENAMETOOLONG) and cannot be produced by any statement here. The EW_NOTWILD fnamencmp window shift after backslash removal is an in-bounds correctness bug only. ReDoS, NULL-deref on vim_regfree, and glob-complexity candidates stay below the security bar: they require the equal-privilege pattern author to trigger degradation of their own process, and '**' recursion is bounded by the quotable 'stardepth < 100' with an interrupt check.

assumptions: BASENAMELEN is not defined in the given code; in Vim's vim.h it is 1000, chosen to dominate NAME_MAX (255). The safety of 'STRCPY(s, dp->d_name);' and the '/**' append depends on this unquoted constant.
The kernel/filesystem enforces NAME_MAX (255) on d_name returned by readdir(); this bound is enforced outside the given code and cannot be quoted from it.

mac_precompose_path (not shown) is assumed to honor its documented contract: it returns a precomposed path no longer than the decomposed input and sets *precomp_len accordingly; NFC precomposition is length-non-increasing for UTF-8.
vim_regfree (not shown) is assumed to tolerate a NULL regprog (reachable when regcomp fails with EW_NOTWILD set).
alloc() is assumed to allocate exactly the requested byte count with no extra slack (Vim's alloc/lalloc semantics).
limitations: C1/C2 (CWE-120/787 class heap overflow at 'STRCPY(s, dp->d_name);' and 'STRCPY(buf + len, "/**"); STRCPY(buf + len + 3, path_end);'): SPECULATIVE. The trigger requires a directory entry name longer than BASENAMELEN, which cannot be planted on mainstream filesystems (ENAMETOOLONG) and is not producible by this code's own data flow; on a hypothetical non-conforming or synthesized (FUSE) filesystem returning over-long d_name, the missing length check would be exploitable.

C3 (MACOS_CONVERT 'mch_memmove(buf, precomp_buf, precomp_len);'): SPECULATIVE, requires mac_precompose_path to violate its contract by returning a precomposed string longer than the input or misreporting precomp_len.

C4: after the backslash-removal loop ('STRMOVE(p, p + 1); --e; --s;'), the EW_NOTWILD comparison 'fnamencmp(path + (s - buf), dp->d_name, e - s)' uses a shifted, shortened window of path, causing wrong match decisions; all reads remain in bounds (end index e-buf <= STRLEN(path)), so this is a correctness bug, not memory unsafety.

C5: regcomp/vim_regexec on an attacker-influenced pattern; worst case is CPU burn inside the pattern author's own process at equal privilege, and compile failure is handled ('if (regmatch.regprog == NULL && (flags & EW_NOTWILD) == 0) ... return 0;').
C6: vim_regfree(NULL) reachable when regcomp fails with EW_NOTWILD; worst case is a crash of the same unprivileged process the input author already controls.

C7: multiplicative directory scanning for patterns like '*/*/*/...' is inherent globbing semantics (same as shell glob); '**' depth is capped by the quotable 'stardepth < 100' with 'ui_breakcheck(); if (got_int) return 0;'.

verdict.summary: squashfs_opendir parses attacker-controlled squashfs image data with a heap out-of-bounds read. The read index `bytes` and the loop extent `size` are computed solely from unvalidated inode fields (`bytes += (*i)->offset; size = (*i)->data + bytes;`) and are never checked against the actual allocated size of `directory_table`; inside the loop, `bytes` advances by attacker-controlled amounts (dirh header, dire->size + 1) with the `bytes < size` test applied only at group boundaries, so every `memcpy` from `directory_table + bytes` (dir header, dir entry, and name of attacker length dire->size + 1) can read past the end of the table. The only guards present (`dir_count > SQUASHFS_DIR_COUNT`, `dire->size >= SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN`) bound the destination structures, not the source reads. Out-of-bounds heap bytes flow into dire->name and are copied into extraction directory entries, giving disclosure potential in addition to crash; the trigger is fully instantiated by a crafted image processed by the operator.

evidence.reason: Origin of the unbounded index: the parse extent `size` and the start index `bytes` are computed exclusively from attacker-supplied inode fields read from the filesystem image, with no check anywhere in this code that they lie within (or do not overrun) the allocated extent of `directory_table`. A crafted inode (data/offset larger than the remaining table) instantiates an out-of-bounds read on every path into the loop.

Sink: the directory header is read from `directory_table + bytes` with no bound on `bytes + sizeof(dirh)` against the table end, and no recheck of `bytes` before this read inside the loop (the only test, `while(bytes < size)`, runs at group boundaries against the attacker-derived `size`). The minimal fix (reject if the read would exceed the table extent) is absent from every path, confirmed by exhaustive search of the function.

Sink: attacker-controlled length `dire->size + 1` bytes are copied from `directory_table + bytes` with no check that the source range lies within the table. The existing guard `if(dire->size >= SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN)` (lines 81-84) bounds only the destination stack buffer, not this source read; out-of-bounds heap bytes copied here become the entry name and are retained via strcpy into dir->dirs[].name, giving disclosure potential beyond the crash.

assumptions: `directory_table` is a finite in-memory buffer whose contents and allocated size are established outside this function; its size is never referenced in this code, which is precisely why the extent check is missing.

`lookup_entry` returns an offset within `directory_table` for a genuine metadata block start, or -1; this contract is honored in the trigger (the attacker references a real block), so the OOB arises from the unvalidated inode offset/data extent, not from lookup_entry.
`read_inode` decodes inode fields straight from the image; no validation of start/offset/data is visible in this code, and none can be credited to it.
`check_name` (not shown) is assumed to reject '/', '.', and '..' in names; if it does not, extraction-time path traversal would be an additional issue unverifiable from this code.

`struct dir_ent`'s name array (not shown) is assumed to be at least SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN + 1 bytes, matching the `dire->size >= SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN` guard; strcpy at line 107 cannot be edge-tested against an unseen definition.
limitations: Signed-int overflow of `bytes` to a negative value (making `directory_table + bytes` point before the buffer) is a plausible secondary path, but the inode field widths (`(*i)->offset`, `(*i)->data`) are not shown, so this trigger could not be fully instantiated; the primary OOB read does not depend on it.

Destination-side overflow of `strcpy(dir->dirs[dir->dir_count].name, dire->name)` depends on the unseen `struct dir_ent` definition; treated as contract, and the dire->size guard makes it consistent with upstream definitions.
Correctness of `check_name` and of `SQUASHFS_DIR_COUNT` against the on-disk format's true maximum cannot be verified from the given code.

verdict.summary: PipeSocketHandler::listen copies the attacker-influenced endpoint path into the fixed-size sockaddr_un.sun_path buffer with strncpy(dst, src, sizeof(dst)) and performs no length check and no explicit NUL termination. When endpoint.name() is at least sizeof(sun_path) bytes (108 on Linux, 104 on macOS), sun_path is left non-terminated; the subsequent unlink(local.sun_path) and ::chmod(local.sun_path, ...) then read past the end of the 108-byte array (stack out-of-bounds read), and the socket is bound to a silently truncated path, with chmod on the mismatched garbage-extended name failing and FATAL_FAIL aborting the process. The trigger is a single over-length path value that nothing in this code rejects.

evidence.reason: strncpy fills all sizeof(local.sun_path) bytes without a NUL terminator when pipePath.size() >= sizeof(local.sun_path); no length guard exists anywhere in the function, so unlink(local.sun_path) treats the non-terminated buffer as a C string and reads past the end of sun_path (out-of-bounds stack read). Trigger: endpoint.name() of length >= sizeof(sun_path) reaches line 15 unvalidated.

Second C-string sink fed by the potentially non-terminated sun_path: ::chmod reads past the 108-byte array, and on the garbage-extended/truncated name failing, FATAL_FAIL aborts the process, giving an attacker-supplied over-length path a deterministic crash of the listening process in addition to the out-of-bounds read.
Origin of the tainted value: the path is taken verbatim from the public API parameter endpoint with no validation of length or content anywhere before it reaches the strncpy sink at line 15.

assumptions: sizeof(sockaddr_un::sun_path) is 108 bytes on Linux and 104 on macOS; the defect boundary is a path of exactly that length or longer.
FATAL_FAIL is assumed to abort or exit the process on a failing return value, consistent with its name; its definition is not shown.
initServerSocket(fd) (line 13) is an external helper whose behavior is not shown and is treated as trusted.
Kernel-side handling of a non-NUL-terminated sun_path passed to bind with sizeof(sockaddr_un) is outside this code and is not relied upon.

The attacker model treats endpoint.name() as capable of carrying content from across a trust boundary (public API parameter carrying a path); if in deployment it is solely operator-controlled local configuration of equal privilege, the abort-only outcome degrades to a robustness issue, though the out-of-bounds read remains.
limitations: TOCTOU between unlink (line 16) and bind (line 18): a local attacker able to write to the socket directory could plant a file in the window, making bind fail and FATAL_FAIL abort the process; speculative because directory writability and a won race could not be instantiated from this code.

Permission window between bind/listen (lines 18-19) and chmod (line 21): the socket file is initially created with mode 0777 & ~umask and only later restricted to 0700, allowing a racing local connection under a permissive umask; speculative because the umask value and race win are not established by this code.

An empty endpoint name makes sun_path[0]==0, binding to the Linux abstract namespace with no file, after which chmod("") fails and FATAL_FAIL aborts; this requires a contract-violating input (empty path) and is abort-only.

unlink (line 16) removes any pre-existing filesystem object at the caller-chosen path; this is inherent to the listen-on-path interface contract rather than an injection in this code, though it becomes dangerous if the endpoint path is ever composed from untrusted components.
::listen(fd, 5) (line 19) has its return value unchecked; robustness only with no security effect.

verdict.summary: SQClass::NewSlot stores script-controlled keys and values, but every memory sink in this function is indexed by member descriptors that this code itself creates as valid vector sizes at insertion time (_make_field_idx(_defaultvalues.size()) / _make_method_idx(_methods.size())), field descriptors are intercepted before method indexing by the quoted guard 'if(_members->Get(key,temp) && _isfield(temp))', and the metamethod index is guarded by the quoted '(mmidx = ss->GetMetaMethodIdxByName(key)) != -1'. The vectors only grow, so all indices remain in bounds; index truncation at 2^24 members aliases in-bounds slots and requires gigabytes of allocation, and storing non-closure values into _methods via bstatic is a type-safe SQObjectPtr store whose call-time handling is outside this code. No trigger with a cross-boundary memory-safety, injection, authz, or crypto consequence could be instantiated.

assumptions: Definitions of _isfield, _member_idx, _make_field_idx, _make_method_idx are not shown; upstream Squirrel masks member indices to 24 bits (MEMBER_MAX 0x00FFFFFF). Reductio: without masking, the first field override would index _defaultvalues[0x02000000] and crash immediately, which never occurs, so an in-bounds mask must exist.
SQVM::IsEqual (callee, not shown) is assumed to always write its 'res' out-parameter before returning; upstream assigns res on every path (same-type raw compare, numeric compare, or false).
SQTable::Get is assumed to leave its out-value untouched on a miss, so 'SQObjectPtr temp;' remains OT_NULL when the key is absent; SQTable::NewSlot is assumed to overwrite an existing key's value.
SQClass copy/inheritance (not shown) is assumed to preserve the descriptor-to-vector correspondence (upstream copies _defaultvalues, _methods and clones _members together).

Non-closure values stored into _methods (reachable when bstatic is true, e.g. 'static' class members or a 'static constructor = <non-closure>' making _constructoridx point at a non-closure) are assumed to be type-checked at the VM call site before being invoked; that call site is outside this code.
SQClosure's destructor is assumed to release the _base reference added by '__ObjAddRef(_base);' when the closure is destroyed; if not, the effect is a reference-count leak, not memory corruption.
limitations: C1 (index truncation, CWE-131/190): a script adding >= 2^24 (16,777,216) members makes _member_idx wrap to a small in-bounds value, causing silent wrong-slot default-value corruption (no out-of-bounds access); reaching it requires multi-gigabyte allocations, so OOM dominates. Not a memory-safety vulnerability.

C2 (CWE-457): 'bool isconstructor;' is uninitialized before SQVM::IsEqual(...); harmful use would require IsEqual to skip writing res, which is a callee contract violation; even a garbage-true only assigns _constructoridx to the exact slot created by the following push_back.

C3: bstatic=true allows non-closure values (and metamethod-name bypass of _base cloning) into _methods; within this code the stores are type-safe SQObjectPtr writes, and the only potential harm is at call sites not shown.

C5: the return value of _members->NewSlot(...) is ignored; on allocation failure a member is appended without a _members entry, desynchronizing the structures. Requires allocation failure the attacker cannot selectively induce.

C6: metamethods can be added or overwritten on a locked class ('if(_locked && !belongs_to_static_table) return false;'), but this is the deliberate design (closures and statics remain mutable after instantiation) and is performed by the script at equal privilege.

verdict.summary: Stack-based buffer overflow in the BMP V4/V5 header path: when the attacker-controlled biSize field equals 108 or 124, ReadOK is called with biSize - 4 (104 or 120) bytes to be written into the 64-byte stack array 'buffer', overwriting up to 56 bytes past its end with attacker-supplied file content. No check anywhere bounds the read length against sizeof(buffer).

evidence.reason: Sink: for biSize == 108 or 124 (admitted by the branch at lines 189-190), this reads 104 or 120 bytes from the attacker-supplied file into 'unsigned char buffer[64]' declared at line 4, a stack out-of-bounds write of up to 56 attacker-controlled bytes. No guard in the function bounds biSize - 4 against sizeof(buffer), and ReadOK receives no destination-capacity argument.

Trigger: a 4-byte attacker-controlled field set to 108 or 124 selects the V4/V5 branch whose only length expression, biSize - 4, exceeds the 64-byte destination; this is the sole condition on the path and it instantiates the oversized read.
Taint origin: biSize is parsed directly from attacker file bytes with no range validation other than the branch dispatch, and flows to the length argument of the overflowing ReadOK at line 194.

assumptions: ReadOK(fd, buffer, n) is assumed to be an fread-style wrapper that writes up to n bytes from the file into the supplied destination; its call signature carries no destination capacity, so it cannot internally cap the write at 64 bytes.
ReadImage, ReadColorMap, ReadChannelMasks, setMasksDefault, ToL/ToS, and at_bitmap_init are not shown; their internal behavior is an assumption and was not used to dismiss any candidate.
int is assumed to be 32 bits, consistent with the literals 0x7fffffff and -2147483648 used in the guards.
limitations: fclose(fd) at the cleanup label runs with fd == NULL when fopen fails (fd = fopen(filename, "rb"); if (!fd) { ... goto cleanup; }); a NULL-dereference crash, but the only consequence is termination of the process of the party supplying the path, so it is a robustness defect here; it would be a denial of service only if a service passed attacker-controlled paths.

ColormapSize = (Bitmap_File_Head.bfOffs - Bitmap_File_Head.biSize - 14) / Maps; can be negative (e.g. bfOffs = 0, biSize = 40, biClrUsed != 0, biBitCnt <= 8) because only the upper clamp 'if (ColormapSize > 256) ColormapSize = 256;' exists; the negative value reaches the unseen ReadColorMap, where no harmful use could be instantiated from the given code.

In the biSize == 108/124 branch, masks[4] is left uninitialized when biCompr is neither BI_BITFIELDS nor BI_RGB (that branch has no memset, unlike the biSize == 12 and 40 branches) and is passed to the unseen ReadImage (CWE-457 pattern); the use of the uninitialized values is outside the given code.
biClrUsed is unbounded when biBitCnt > 8 (the check 'if (Bitmap_Head.biClrUsed > 256 && Bitmap_Head.biBitCnt <= 8)' does not apply) and is passed to the unseen ReadImage.

The final at_bitmap_init truncates biWidth/biHeight with (unsigned short) casts; dimensions up to about 0x7fffffff/biBitCnt pass the quoted guards, so values above 65535 are truncated; the effect depends on at_bitmap_init/ReadImage internals not shown and could not be instantiated as an over-read here.

Verified safe: the biSize 56-64 branch reads at most 60 bytes into buffer[64]; the width/height/plane/bit-count overflow guards were quoted and edge-tested (no division by zero, products bounded below 0x7fffffff, rowbytes fits int); the 'BA' loop is bounded by file exhaustion.

verdict.summary: sug_filltree walks an attacker-supplied spell-file fold tree (sl_fbyts/sl_fidxs) using fixed MAXWLEN stack arrays indexed by an unbounded depth counter and by unvalidated tree index values. Nothing in this function bounds depth before descending (tword[depth++] = c and the following three indexed stores), so a tree path longer than MAXWLEN causes ascending out-of-bounds stack writes of attacker-chosen bytes; likewise idxs[n] is loaded into arridx[depth] with no range check against sl_fbyts_len and is then used to read byts[] and to write idxs[arridx[depth]] = wordcount[depth] at an attacker-chosen offset.

evidence.reason: Primary defect: unbounded depth. Each non-NUL byte read from the attacker-file-derived tree increments depth and writes tword[depth], arridx[depth], curi[depth], wordcount[depth], all declared with MAXWLEN elements (lines 6-13). No statement in the function compares depth with MAXWLEN or any upper bound (only 'depth >= 0' at line 37 and 'depth > 0' at line 43 exist). Trigger: a crafted .spl fold tree containing a path of 101+ non-NUL bytes drives depth to MAXWLEN, and line 88 then writes one attacker byte past each array, with depth growing without limit on further descents — stack memory corruption in the process loading the malicious spell file. Line 89 is also the origin of the tainted index for the second finding.

Second confirmed defect: arridx[depth] is assigned at line 89 from idxs[n], an entry of the spell-file-derived index array loaded at line 28, and is never range-checked against sl_fbyts_len anywhere in this function (sl_fbyts_len is used only at line 79 to bound the NUL-skip scan). An attacker-chosen out-of-range value produces an out-of-bounds read at byts[arridx[depth]] (line 39) and an out-of-bounds write at idxs[arridx[depth]] (line 42) at an attacker-controlled offset.

Supporting sink on the same unvalidated data flow: n is computed as the unvalidated arridx[depth] plus curi[depth], whose only cap is byts[arridx[depth]] (line 39), i.e., a count read from the attacker tree at a possibly out-of-range offset. byts[n] is then read with no comparison of n against sl_fbyts_len, enabling an out-of-bounds read whose value (c) is subsequently written into tword and processed as word data.

assumptions: MAXWLEN is defined in a header not shown; it is assumed to be 100, matching the fixed-size arrays arridx/curi/tword/wordcount. The overflow triggers at depth == MAXWLEN regardless of the exact constant, since no depth bound exists in this code.

sl_fbyts/sl_fidxs are produced by the spell-file tree loader (not shown). If that unshown code rejects trees deeper than MAXWLEN and only ever stores in-bounds values into sl_fidxs, the triggers for both findings would be blocked upstream; per guard-anchoring discipline that enforcement cannot be relied on here because it is not quotable from the given code, so it is recorded as an assumption rather than a dismissal.
idx_T is assumed to be a signed int (Vim's typedef), allowing negative and up-to-INT_MAX index values in idxs entries.
got_int, line_breakcheck(), spell_soundfold(), and tree_add_word() are external; their behavior (including tsalword output sizing) is taken on contract.
limitations: words_done wraps at 2^32 leaf words (lines 65-67 split it into 16-bit halves), producing duplicate word numbers; reaching that scale requires a multi-gigabyte spell file and yields no amplification beyond file size, so it is not treated as a vulnerability.

The OOB read at line 56 additionally depends on the attacker tree's internal consistency (a node claiming more siblings than remain in byts); this is folded into the unvalidated-index finding and shares its upstream-loading caveat.

tword is properly NUL-terminated at line 60 before being passed to spell_soundfold, so no unterminated-string finding arises within this function; tsalword buffer sizing is spell_soundfold's contract.

verdict.summary: parseDragons validates only that at least 1 byte remains (off < r_buf_size) before performing fixed 4-byte magic comparisons at b and b+8, so a crafted file leaving fewer than 12 bytes after the offset causes heap out-of-bounds reads of up to 11 bytes past the malloc'd buffer in a parser of untrusted file content.

evidence.reason: Heap out-of-bounds read (CWE-125): b is malloc(size) where the code guarantees only size >= 1 (lines 4 and 7-8), yet memcmp reads bytes 8-11 unconditionally; a crafted file with off = r_buf_size - 5 (e.g. 5 bytes remaining, bytes 0-3 set to the magic) reaches this statement with a 5-byte allocation, reading 4 bytes starting 3 past the end.

Same defect at the first magic check: with a 1-byte file (off = 0, first byte 0x1a) the line-4 guard passes, size becomes 1, and memcmp reads b[0] (match) then b[1..3] beyond the 1-byte heap allocation.

Origin of the under-validated length: these are the only size guards on the path to the memcmps; they enforce only 1 <= size (upper bound on off, and !size is dead), never the minimum of 12/16 bytes the magic comparisons require.

assumptions: r_buf_read_at honors its interface by writing at most the requested length into b and bounds-clipping reads against the underlying buffer, so the huge address produced by 'off - 8' (line 52) when off < 8 yields a short read caught by 'available != size' rather than an OOB write; this enforcement is in code not shown.
r_coresym_cache_element_new performs its own bounds checking on 'off + 16' against buf; not shown.
The D macro gates debug-only statements, so the r_read_le32(b + 12) read at line 65 executes only in debug mode.
bf, bits and file_name are interface-contract arguments not used as attacker data in this body.
limitations: Memory leak (CWE-401): b is not freed on the early 'return NULL' paths after malloc (lines 16-18 and 53-55); one allocation of up to file-size bytes leaks per parse attempt, but retention is not attacker-scalable beyond the input size, so it is not promoted to a vulnerability.

Width truncation (candidate, speculative): size (ut64) is passed to r_buf_read_at's int-length parameter (lines 15, 52) and the result is stored in int available; triggering harm requires a > 2 GiB remaining region plus unshown callee behavior with a truncated/negative length, a precondition not instantiated in this code.

off - 8 (line 52) can be negative for off < 8 and is widened to a huge ut64 address; the observable outcome here is the error return (plus the leak above), with no memory-unsafe operation in this code.
off + 16 (line 69) could overflow int only for off near INT_MAX, requiring a >= 2 GiB file; consequence depends on the unshown callee, so it is speculative.

The r_read_le32(b + 12) read at line 65 shares the primary missing-minimum-size root cause but is gated behind the debug D macro, so it is folded into the primary finding rather than listed separately.

verdict.summary: squashfs_opendir parses attacker-supplied filesystem image data with no bounds check tying the read cursor `bytes` or the read extent to the allocated directory table. The loop bound `size = (*i)->data + bytes` is derived from attacker-controlled inode metadata, and each iteration reads `directory_table + bytes` for up to sizeof(dirh), sizeof(*dire), or dire->size+1 bytes without verifying the read stays inside the table. A crafted squashfs image therefore drives sustained heap out-of-bounds reads past the directory_table buffer, with overread bytes parsed into directory entries and names that are subsequently used as extracted filenames (disclosure potential) or causing a crash.

evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted loop bounds: bytes is advanced by the attacker-controlled inode offset and size is computed solely from the attacker-controlled inode data field, with no comparison to the actual directory table or block length anywhere in the function.

Out-of-bounds read sink: the only guard, while(bytes < size) at line 50, bounds only the start of the read, never bytes + sizeof(dirh) against the allocated table; with attacker-chosen (*i)->data large, these memcpy calls read heap memory past the directory_table buffer (instantiated trigger in STEP 4).

Secondary OOB read sink on the same data flow: dire->size is bounded only against the destination (line 81), not the source; the copy of dire->size+1 bytes from directory_table + bytes can cross the end of the allocated table, and the overread bytes become directory-entry names surfaced in output.

assumptions: It is assumed lookup_entry returns a non-negative offset into a heap-allocated directory_table buffer and that the surrounding unsquashfs framework supplies read_inode, check_name, and the struct layouts (squashfs_dir_header_2 with a count field, squashfs_dir_entry_2 with name at its end, struct dir_ent with a name array of at least SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN+1); none of these are shown, and per guard anchoring none of them is treated as enforcing a bound inside this code.

The guard if(dire->size >= SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN) is assumed sufficient for the destination write because the buffer is sized sizeof(squashfs_dir_entry_2) + SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN + 1 and the NUL is written at dire->size + 1 <= SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN.
limitations: The strcpy at line 107 and the realloc growth at lines 99-105 were dismissed as vulnerabilities: capacity and source-length guards are present and edge-tested (dir_count = 0, first realloc, size = SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN-1).
size = (*i)->data + bytes can wrap (unsigned data plus int bytes assigned to int size); the confirmed trigger requires no wrap, so the wrap path is not treated as a separate finding.

Attacker-scalable consumption (loop iterations and dir_ent growth bounded by the attacker-chosen data field rather than real table length, CWE-400) is real but secondary here; allocation failure is handled by the quoted realloc NULL check and the dominant impact is the out-of-bounds read.

verdict.summary: squashfs_opendir reads directory headers and entries from directory_table at an offset (bytes) that is never validated against the table's actual allocated size. The walk bound 'size' is computed solely from the attacker-controlled inode fields (*i)->data and (*i)->offset (line 49), and the inner entry loop (line 65) advances bytes with no bounds check at all, so a crafted SquashFS image drives reads (lines 52, 66, 76-77) past the end of the in-memory directory table: out-of-bounds heap read whose contents are copied into directory names used during extraction (information disclosure) or crash the process. The existing guards only cap dir_count and name length; none anchors bytes or size to the table end.

evidence.reason: Origin of the unvalidated walk bound: 'size' is derived from attacker-controlled inode fields (data, offset) with no comparison to the actual length of directory_table, so it can point far past the allocation end.
The only loop guard compares bytes to the attacker-derived 'size', not to the table end; the header read at directory_table + bytes can therefore read out of bounds of the directory_table allocation.

The inner entry loop performs no bounds check on bytes at all: with dirh.count = 255 (dir_count = 256, passing 'if(dir_count > SQUASHFS_DIR_COUNT)' at its boundary), bytes advances past size and past the table allocation, reading entries out of bounds.

The memcpy source read at directory_table + bytes is unbounded with respect to the table allocation; out-of-bounds heap bytes are copied into the name buffer and later strcpy'd into dir entries, disclosing heap memory into extracted filenames (or crashing).

assumptions: lookup_entry (helper not shown) is assumed to return either -1 or a byte offset that is a real position inside directory_table; the vulnerability does not depend on this, since the walk past the table end is driven by (*i)->data/offset and dirh/dire content.

The layout of struct dir_ent (destination of strcpy at line 86) is not shown; its name field is assumed to be at least SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN + 1 bytes, which the line-71 guard makes sufficient. If it were smaller, an additional overflow would exist.
check_name (helper not shown) is assumed to validate '/', '.', '..' as its comment states; its internals cannot be verified from the given code.
Widths of the inode fields (*i)->data/start/offset and the values of SQUASHFS_DIR_COUNT / SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN are not shown; the analysis treats them as attacker-controlled within their natural widths.
limitations: TRACE at lines 55-56 uses %d for the long long 'bytes', a varargs format mismatch producing garbled trace output only; no security effect.

Signed overflow of the int 'size' (line 49) would require (*i)->data near INT_MAX; the field width is not shown and the out-of-bounds read is fully triggerable without any overflow, so no separate integer-overflow finding is made.

The realloc growth (lines 82-83) cannot overflow: dir_count is bounded by the int 'size' divided by the >=4 bytes walked per entry, and the multiplication is performed in size_t; memory exhaustion is subsumed by the unbounded-walk root cause.

verdict.summary: n_start_visual_mode is a short editor state-transition routine. Its only external-facing inputs are the mode character parameter c (used solely in the comparison c == Ctrl_V and the assignment VIsual_mode = c) and editor-maintained cursor/option state. The function contains no loops, no arithmetic on inputs, no memory-copy or indexing sinks, no allocation, no injection surfaces, no crypto, and no authorization logic. Every statement is a comparison or a struct-field assignment, none of which requires a guard that is absent. No trigger with a security consequence crossing a privilege boundary could be instantiated.

assumptions: Behavior of the helpers not shown (conceal_cursor_line, validate_virtcol, coladvance, foldAdjustVisual, conceal_check_cursor_line, trigger_modechanged, setmouse) is outside the given code; no safety or defect claim is made about their internals.
The value of c originates from the editor's own key routing; within this code it is used only in a comparison and a mode-variable assignment, so its provenance does not create a sink.
curwin->w_cursor and curwin->w_virtcol are assumed to be editor-maintained state; this code performs no arithmetic on them that could produce an out-of-range value.
limitations: No candidate defect was generated: the function has no memory, size, index, injection, crypto, or authz sinks, and no loops; the worst conceivable anomaly from a keystroke or file character under the cursor (per discipline 3, same-privilege operator input) would be incorrect visual-mode highlighting, a cosmetic effect with no security impact.
If a defect existed inside coladvance() or the other unseen helpers (e.g., cursor positioning past a line end), it could not be analyzed here because those bodies are not part of the given code.

verdict.summary: The line_size bounds check `if (line_size > DATA_SIZE)` admits the exactly-at-limit value line_size == DATA_SIZE (and anything down to DATA_SIZE-6), leaving no headroom for the unconditional 7-byte padding memset(end_data, 0, 7). With attacker-controlled page resolution/width producing line_size == DATA_SIZE and a rendered scan line whose last byte is non-zero, end_data remains data + DATA_SIZE and the memset writes 7 zero bytes past the end of the stack buffer byte data[DATA_SIZE], corrupting adjacent stack memory while processing an untrusted document.

evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds write sink: end_data = data + line_size (line 29) can equal data + DATA_SIZE when line_size == DATA_SIZE and the scan line's trailing byte is non-zero (attacker-controlled raster content), so memset writes data[DATA_SIZE..DATA_SIZE+6], 7 bytes past the stack buffer byte data[DATA_SIZE] declared at line 10.

Defective bound (origin of the tainted size): the guard uses `>` so the exactly-at-limit value line_size == DATA_SIZE passes, and values down to DATA_SIZE-6 also pass, although the memset at line 45 requires 7 bytes of headroom; no other check between line 29 and line 45 limits end_data.

assumptions: LINE_SIZE is a compile-time macro defined outside the given code; the overflow argument is independent of its numeric value since DATA_SIZE = LINE_SIZE*8 is always a multiple of 8 and exactly representable as a bytes-per-scan-line count.

line_size derives from device resolution and width, which the code's own error message (lines 23-24, 'invalid resolution and/or width gives line_size = %d') treats as configurable inputs; in the Ghostscript threat model a processed PostScript/PDF document can influence these through setpagedevice, making line_size and the raster content attacker-influenced.
limitations: The return value of gdev_prn_copy_scan_lines (lines 30-31) is unchecked, so on a copy failure data[] could be used uninitialized (CWE-457); the trigger is speculative because no statement in this code induces such a failure for lnum < pdev->height with a sufficiently sized buffer.

The transpose loop reads data[] bytes beyond line_size+7 that are never initialized (only 7 pad bytes are zeroed); these reads are in-bounds and, as computed from the output lengths (line_size_color_plane = line_size/9), the uninitialized bytes never reach the printer output or control flow, so this is a robustness issue only.
The byte order of cntc2/cntc1 in the gp_fprintf at the graphics-header emission is a wire-format correctness question, not a security defect.

verdict.summary: add_mtab writes the attacker-controlled strings devname, mountpoint and fstype verbatim into the privileged, world-trusted /etc/mtab file via addmntent without neutralizing newlines or whitespace. An unprivileged invoker of this elevated mount helper can embed a newline (e.g., in a directory name used as the mountpoint) and forge arbitrary additional mtab entries that are parsed as ground truth by other privileged programs, injecting content into a root-owned system file across the privilege boundary.

evidence.reason: Sink: the mntent built from unvalidated external strings is appended to the root-owned /etc/mtab. addmntent emits fields separated by whitespace with a terminating newline, so any embedded newline or space in devname/mountpoint/fstype splits or forges mtab records. No statement in this function screens these fields for special characters before this call, so the sink is unguarded.

Origin of the taint: the function's parameters, which carry content chosen by the unprivileged invoker of this elevated helper (the code at lines 15-20 sets the real uid to the elevated effective uid, confirming the privilege asymmetry), are assigned directly into the mtab record fields with no content validation, and flow unchanged to the addmntent sink at line 104.

assumptions: MOUNTED refers to the system mount table (/etc/mtab), consistent with the lock_mtab/setmntent usage.
addmntent writes the mntent fields verbatim, whitespace-separated, one record per line, as its documented behavior specifies.

The strings devname, mountpoint and fstype originate from the invoker's command line; the code contains no statement validating their content, and any caller-side validation is not shown and therefore treated as non-existent per guard anchoring.

MTAB_OPTIONS_LEN is large enough that the bounded strlcat sequence cannot overflow the calloc'd buffer (all strlcat calls pass the same total-size constant used at allocation, so this is safe regardless).
limitations: If calloc at line 79 fails, mnt_opts is NULL and addmntent at line 104 is still called; worst case is a crash of the elevated helper on an unattacker-inducible allocation failure, not a vulnerability.

atexit(unlock_mtab) at line 43 combined with explicit unlock_mtab() calls (lines 54, 62, 71, 113) may double-release the mtab lock, but the impact depends on the unseen unlock_mtab implementation (whether it removes a lock file or token); cannot exhibit the race as two ordered operations in this code, so speculative.
Early error returns at lines 24, 30, 36 and 41 leave the process-wide blocked signal mask (set at line 33) unrestored; robustness issue in the caller's own process only.
mount_user (line 13) is never freed; a one-shot leak in a process that exits immediately after, not attacker-scalable.

On the addmntent failure path, ftruncate(fd, statbuf.st_size) at line 107 truncates the fd while the stdio stream may still hold a buffered partial record that is flushed by my_endmntent, potentially leaving a truncated mtab line; the trigger requires a mid-write stream failure (disk full/EIO) not instantiable by attacker-controlled state, so speculative.

verdict.summary: squashfs_opendir indexes the heap-allocated directory_table with `bytes`, whose extent is bounded only by the attacker-controlled inode fields `(*i)->offset` and `(*i)->data` (size = (*i)->data + bytes - 3), never by the table's allocated size, causing heap out-of-bounds reads at the dir header swap, dir entry swap, and name memcpy when parsing an untrusted squashfs image; OOB bytes are copied into directory entry names (disclosure potential) and the read volume is attacker-scalable.

evidence.reason: Origin of the unbounded index: the attacker-supplied inode offset is added to `bytes` and the loop extent `size` is computed from the attacker-supplied inode `data` field, with no clamp to the directory table's allocated size (and the long long sum is truncated into int).

Primary sink: `directory_table + bytes` is read with `bytes` bounded only by the attacker-derived `size`, not by the table allocation. A crafted inode with data larger than the real table extent drives reads past the end of directory_table (heap OOB read, e.g. bytes up to ~4GB beyond the table). No check comparing bytes to the table size exists anywhere in the function.

Secondary OOB read sink on the same unbounded `bytes`: the entry header is read from directory_table + bytes, which the loop can advance (via `bytes += sizeof(*dire)` and `bytes += dire->size + 1`) past the table allocation; no bounds check guards this read.

OOB read with disclosure potential: memcpy copies dire->size + 1 bytes from the possibly out-of-bounds directory_table + bytes into dire->name; the guard `if(dire->size >= SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN)` bounds only the copy length and the destination, never the source offset `bytes`. The copied out-of-bounds heap bytes become the directory entry name (strcpy at line 90) and are exposed in extracted output.

assumptions: `lookup_entry` returns either -1 or a byte offset within directory_table (its documented contract); the `bytes == -1` check at line 44 relies on this contract, which cannot be verified from the given code.
`directory_table` is allocated elsewhere with an extent derived from the image superblock; that extent is the bound the loop fails to enforce but its exact size is not visible in this code.
SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN is 256 and struct dir_ent's name field holds at least 257 bytes; the quoted dire->size guard then makes the memcpy/strcpy destination exactly fit at the boundary (size=255).
limitations: Line 49 truncates the long long sum `(*i)->data + bytes - 3` into int size; this width confusion only alters loop termination and is folded into the primary unbounded-index defect rather than reported separately.

`bytes == -1` at line 44 would miss any negative lookup result other than exactly -1; this depends on lookup_entry's contract, which is not violated by any flow inside this code, so it is a contract concern, not an instantiated vulnerability.

The dir_count check (`if(dir_count > SQUASHFS_DIR_COUNT)`) and the name-length check (`if(dire->size >= SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN)`) are present, correctly placed before use, and edge-safe; destination-side overflow of memcpy/strcpy was considered and dismissed.
Attacker-scalable read volume (inode data up to ~4GB driving up to ~4GB of OOB reads) is recorded as an amplification aspect of the primary OOB-read finding, not as a separate CWE-400 finding.

parse_errors: no valid JSON verdict found in output

verdict.summary: n_start_visual_mode() is an internal Vim editor-core routine that sets visual-mode flags, performs a guarded cursor recalculation, copies the cursor position, and updates redraw bookkeeping. STEP 1 found no attacker-data inputs: the sole parameter c is an interface-contract mode character supplied by Vim's own command dispatch, and all other consumed values are internal editor state. No memory allocation, copy length, format string, command/SQL execution, file path, network, or crypto sink exists in the function. The only near-sink memory read, gchar_cursor(), operates on cursor state this code never moves out of range, and the only cursor-affecting call is immediately preceded by validate_virtcol() and followed by clamping coladvance(). No candidate survived trigger instantiation in STEP 4, and the STEP 5 counterfactual search confirmed no missing guard on any path to any sink.

assumptions: The parameter c is supplied by Vim's internal command dispatch tables with values from {v, V, Ctrl_V}; this function performs no parsing or protocol intake of its own, so c is treated as an interface-contract argument rather than attack data.

curwin->w_cursor and related editor state are maintained within valid buffer bounds by the editor core between operations; no statement in this code mutates the cursor except validate_virtcol()/coladvance(), both of which preserve validity.
limitations: Speculative candidate: an out-of-bounds read in gchar_cursor() would be possible if curwin->w_cursor were already invalid on entry (e.g., left invalid by a buffer-manipulation defect elsewhere in the editor). No statement in this code can produce an invalid cursor, so the trigger precondition could not be instantiated here; recorded as an invariant/contract concern external to this function.

Contract robustness note: the function does not validate that c is a recognized visual mode character before storing it in VIsual_mode. Within this code the value only reaches an equality comparison against Ctrl_V and a flag store with no indexing, sizing, or injection sink, so there is no security consequence in this function; downstream misbehavior would require a caller violating its contract.

verdict.summary: parseDragons allocates b with malloc(size) (line 14) but returns NULL without freeing it on the error paths at lines 19-22 and 55-59; the only free (line 71) is on the fall-through path. The leak is attacker-triggerable with an untrusted file: when off < 8 and the magic bytes do not match, the retry read r_buf_read_at (buf, off - 8, b, size) at line 55 uses a negative offset, fails, and line 58 returns NULL leaking `size` bytes per parse; a negative off (accepted because line 4 only checks the upper bound `off >= size`) additionally inflates size at line 7 to bufsize + |off|, so a small crafted file can retain up to ~2GB. Retention accumulates across parses of untrusted binaries, a memory-exhaustion denial of service across the trust boundary.

evidence.reason: Leak sink: for off < 8 the expression `off - 8` is negative, the re-read fails, and `return NULL;` executes while b (malloc'd at line 14) is never freed; the only `free (b);` (line 71) is unreachable on this path. Instantiated trigger: a 32-byte untrusted file without the magic at offsets 0 and 8 with off = 0 reaches line 58 and leaks 32 bytes; the same missing free exists at lines 19-22 for negative off, where line 7 `size -= off;` inflates the allocation to bufsize + |off|.

Origin of the leaked allocation; size here is at least 32 (guaranteed by `if (size < 32) { return NULL; }`) and, for a negative off that passes the upper-bound-only check `if (off >= size)`, equals bufsize + |off|, enabling oversized retained allocations from a small input.

assumptions: r_buf_read_at's implementation is not shown; analysis assumes its interface contract: it never copies more than len bytes into the destination and never reads outside its own RBuffer storage, returning the count actually read (0 or negative for out-of-range addresses). All conclusions about the negative/huge-offset reads at lines 18 and 55 rely on this contract.
The D macro is assumed to be a debug-only construct; even when enabled, the read at b + 12 (line 68) is within the guaranteed 32-byte minimum.
The provenance of `off` in the (unshown) caller is unknown; per the intake rules it is treated as attacker-influenced since every guard on it lives inside this code.
limitations: st64 `size` is truncated to the int len parameter of r_buf_read_at at lines 18 and 55 for buffers > INT_MAX; within this code the `available != size` check (comparing the int return against the full st64) turns this into a failed parse plus the confirmed leak, not memory corruption, assuming the library contract.

Negative `off` is not rejected (`if (off >= size)` checks only the upper bound); given the r_buf_read_at contract the resulting inflated read fails, so the effect is the confirmed leak/over-allocation rather than an out-of-bounds access inside this code.

After a successful retry re-read, if the magic still does not match (lines 60-64), parsing continues anyway into r_coresym_cache_element_new at off + 16 — fail-open parsing, but no sink is visible in this code.
file_name (R_OWN) is also leaked on the early NULL returns; same class, small fixed size.
The `off + 12` addition in the debug eprintf (line 69) can overflow int for extreme offsets; cosmetic only.

verdict.summary: The non-root option whitelist in main() uses `!strchr("hlLUVvpris", c)` to decide which options a restricted (non-root) user may pass to the setuid-root mount(8). On platforms where char is unsigned (CHAR_MAX==255: aarch64, ppc64, riscv64, s390x, arm32 Linux), MOUNT_OPT_SHARED == 256 truncates to '\0' when converted to char inside strchr, and strchr matches the string's terminating null, returning non-NULL. verdict.summary: dnsc_load_local_data computes the TXT record buffer length as a size_t sum (strlen(provider_name) + 15 + 4*sizeof(struct SignedCert) + 2) but stores it in uint16_t rrlen. With a provider name of about 65007 bytes the sum is exactly 65536, so rrlen truncates to 0: malloc(0) passes the NULL check, and 'rrlen - 1' promotes to int -1 and is passed to snprintf as SIZE_MAX, causing a roughly 65KB heap buffer overflow write with fully controlled content. A one-byte-longer name yields rrlen == 1, leaving rr uninitialized so strlen(rr) reads out of bounds and 'rrlen - 1 - strlen(rr)' wraps to a huge size, giving a second out-of-bounds write. No statement in this code bounds the provider name length.

With rrlen = 1, snprintf(rr, 0, ...) writes nothing, leaving rr uninitialized for the strlen(rr) uses at lines 54/56/65 whose size expression 'rrlen - 1 - strlen(rr)' wraps to a huge size_t, producing an additional out-of-bounds write.

assumptions: dnscenv->provider_name and dnscenv->signed_certs are populated by the configuration/certificate loading path not shown in this code; no statement here bounds provider_name's length, and per the analysis rules an external bound that cannot be quoted is treated as nonexistent.

sizeof(struct SignedCert) is taken as approximately 128 bytes (the structure definition is not shown); the trigger threshold is strlen(provider_name) = 65536 - 17 - 4*sizeof(struct SignedCert) regardless of the exact structure size.
malloc(0) is assumed to return a non-NULL minimal allocation, as typical libc implementations do, so the 'if(!rr)' check at line 46 does not block the rrlen = 0 trigger.
cfg_str2list_insert and cfg_strlist_insert semantics are not shown; they are assumed to store the passed strings without introducing additional memory-safety effects in this path.
limitations: The rrlen == 1 variant (provider name one byte longer than the rrlen == 0 trigger) leaves the malloc(1) buffer uninitialized because snprintf with size 0 writes nothing; strlen(rr) at lines 54/56/65 then performs an unbounded out-of-bounds read and the wrapped size expression produces an out-of-bounds write at rr + strlen(rr). verdict.summary: Heap buffer overflow in the gzip EXTRA header field handling (CVE-2022-37434 pattern). When the extra field spans multiple inflate() calls and more bytes have been consumed than fit in the caller's header buffer, len = extra_len - length exceeds extra_max, and the clamp 'extra_max - len' underflows to ~4 billion, so zmemcpy writes far past the end of head->extra with attacker-controlled data (and reads past the input buffer).

evidence.reason: Root cause: the memcpy length clamp computes state->head->extra_max - len in unsigned arithmetic without first bounding len. len equals the number of extra-field bytes already consumed, which can exceed extra_max (e.g. extra_max=5, XLEN=100, field split over two calls: after first call len=0 copies 5 bytes and length=90; on the second call len=10, len+copy=20>5 selects extra_max-len = 5-10 = 0xFFFFFFFB). zmemcpy then performs a ~4 GB out-of-bounds write starting at head->extra+10 and an out-of-bounds read from the input buffer, fully controlled by the attacker-supplied gzip stream.

Origin of the tainted values: the attacker-controlled gzip XLEN field (up to 65535) is loaded into state->length and state->head->extra_len; the partial-consumption state preserved across inflate() calls by 'if (state->length) goto inf_leave;' then produces len = extra_len - length greater than extra_max at the memcpy sink on lines 146-149.

assumptions: NEEDBITS, BITS, DROPBITS, PULLBYTE, LOAD, RESTORE, INITBITS are the standard zlib macros that guarantee bit supply, save/restore have/next/put/hold/bits across calls, and return to the caller when input is exhausted; their definitions are not shown in this code.
inflateStateCheck, inflate_table, inflate_fast, and updatewindow (not shown) are assumed to enforce their documented bounds; no candidate relies on them.

zmemcpy is the platform memcpy; its third argument (uInt result of extra_max - len) is zero-extended to size_t, making the wrapped value ~4294967291 bytes on a 32-bit-or-wider uInt target, which is the behavior exercised by the code as written.
GUNZIP is assumed defined, since the vulnerable path and its code are present under that guard.

verdict.summary: This is the patched form of the Ghostscript jetp3852 driver. Both historical memory-safety defects of this code are closed by quotable, on-path guards: the scan-line size is checked against the stack buffer ('if (line_size > DATA_SIZE) { ... return_error(gs_error_rangecheck); }') before the copy into 'byte data[DATA_SIZE]' and before the 'end_data[-1]' dereference, and the data buffer is zeroed ('memset(data, 0x00, DATA_SIZE);') so no uninitialized byte can reach the 8-entry 'spr40/spr8/spr2' lookup tables. All stack writes (plane_data transpose at i = DATA_SIZE-8, complement/write loop with line_size_color_plane <= 8*LINE_SIZE/9 < LINE_SIZE) fit their buffers exactly at boundary values. The only remaining unguarded sink, spr[dp[k]] indexing, requires a raster byte > 7, which this code cannot itself produce: the memset yields 0 and the scan-line copy yields the device's 8-color palette indices (0-7), a device-contract domain set in code not shown here; producing a larger index would require the not-shown device procs to violate that contract, so the trigger is speculative, not instantiated.

assumptions: LINE_SIZE is a compile-time constant defined outside the shown code; DATA_SIZE = LINE_SIZE*8 and plane_data[LINE_SIZE*3] are consistent fixed sizes.
gdev_mem_bytes_per_scan_line returns a non-negative byte count for one scanline in the same units gdev_prn_copy_scan_lines fills; this is a framework contract not quotable from the given code.

The jetp3852/paintjet device is an 8-color (3-bit) device, so raster bytes written by gdev_prn_copy_scan_lines are color indices 0-7; this domain is enforced by the device definition/encode procs in gdevpjet.c, which are not shown. It is the documented domain of the data consumed here (the code's own comment treats dp[] > 7 as an abnormal, uninitialized condition).
pdev->height is non-negative and the raster for that height is allocated at device-open time, so the per-line loop is bounded by resources the operator's process already committed.
limitations: Speculative (contract-dependent): 'static ulong spr40[8] = spread3(0x40); ... (spr8[dp[3]] << 1)' indexes 8-entry tables with raster bytes and contains no in-function bounds check; if the not-shown device procs ever emitted a byte > 7 into the raster, this would be an out-of-bounds read of static data whose loaded values are written to the output stream. The only trigger this code's own flow historically produced (uninitialized stack bytes) is eliminated by the quoted memset.

Speculative (contract-dependent): the guard 'if (line_size > DATA_SIZE)' does not reject negative line_size; a negative value would require gdev_mem_bytes_per_scan_line to violate its contract (negative device width) and could convert to a huge size_t at gp_fwrite. Not instantiable from this code.

The return value of gdev_prn_copy_scan_lines is ignored; on failure the previous scanline's data is retransmitted. Values remain in the device index domain, so this is a print-output fidelity issue, not memory unsafety.

cnt_2prn is split into 16 bits (cntc1/cntc2); for a pathologically large compile-time LINE_SIZE the count sent to the printer would truncate. Bounded by a compile-time constant; printer protocol issue only.

A very large pdev->height increases loop iterations and output volume, but the height must first pass device-open raster allocation and this behavior is inherent to all printer drivers, at the operator's own privilege, not a defect of this code.

verdict.summary: In the ST21NFCA_EVT_TRANSACTION handler, the length/tag guard uses a faulty conjunction (skb->len < NFC_MIN_AID_LENGTH + 2 && skb->data[0] != AID_TAG) that never bounds the attacker-supplied AID length byte skb->data[1]. An NFC peer can send a short frame (e.g. len=7, data[1]=0xFF) so that transaction->aid_len becomes 255 while the allocation is only skb->len - 2 = 5 bytes; memcpy then writes 255 bytes into the 5-byte devm_kzalloc allocation (heap buffer overflow, kernel memory corruption) and reads 255 bytes past the 7-byte skb (out-of-bounds read). The same unvalidated aid_len drives the OOB index skb->data[aid_len + 2] and the params memcpy (params_len up to 255 copied from skb->data + aid_len + 4 into the same undersized allocation).

evidence.reason: Heap buffer overflow write: aid_len is taken directly from the attacker-controlled byte skb->data[1] (0-255) with no validation against skb->len or the skb->len - 2 sized allocation (line 26). Trigger instantiated with skb->len=7 and data[1]=0xFF: memcpy writes 255 bytes into a 5-byte allocation, overflowing the kernel heap, and reads ~250 bytes past the end of skb.

Defective guard: the && conjunction means a frame with the correct tag byte (0x81) bypasses the minimum-length requirement entirely, and even a frame with skb->len >= NFC_MIN_AID_LENGTH + 2 passes for any content. No statement compares skb->data[1] (aid_len) or the params length against skb->len, so the memcpy lengths at lines 31-32 and 40-41 are unbounded.

Secondary unguarded sinks of the same root cause: skb->data[aid_len + 2] and skb->data[aid_len + 3] index up to 257 bytes into an skb that can be as short as a few bytes (out-of-bounds read), and the params memcpy copies params_len (0-255) bytes from skb->data + aid_len + 4 into the skb->len - 2 sized allocation, overflowing it whenever aid_len + 4 + params_len exceeds skb->len.

assumptions: struct nfc_evt_transaction's exact field layout (fixed-size aid array and flexible params tail) is not shown in the given code; the overflow conclusion does not depend on it, because the total allocation is skb->len - 2 bytes (line 26) while the copy lengths (aid_len up to 255, params_len up to 255) are unbounded.

NFC_MIN_AID_LENGTH and the tag constants are not shown; taken as the spec values (5, 0x81, 0x82). The trigger at skb->len = 7 passes the guard for either value of NFC_MIN_AID_LENGTH <= 5 because 7 < NFC_MIN_AID_LENGTH + 2 is false.
skb is assumed to be a linear buffer with at least skb->len accessible bytes at skb->data (standard kernel skb semantics for short HCI frames); nonlinear frags would not reduce the over-read.
limitations: skb->len - 2 (line 26) can wrap to a huge unsigned value when skb->len < 2 (reachable because the tag byte bypasses the length half of the guard), but devm_kzalloc then fails and the function returns -ENOMEM; worst case is a rejected event, not memory corruption. With skb->len == 2 the zero-size allocation returns ZERO_SIZE_PTR which passes the !transaction check, yielding a near-NULL write — a crash of the kernel process handling the NFC event (denial of service), which is subsumed by the primary unvalidated-length defect.
Early returns at lines 24, 28, and 37 omit kfree_skb(skb), leaking one skb per malformed event; this is a bounded resource leak, not amplified retention.
nfc_se_transaction(hdev->ndev, host, transaction) receives the transaction with aid_len up to 255 and params_len up to 255; downstream consumers are outside the given code and were not analyzed.

verdict.summary: Heap buffer overflow write in the kernel st21nfca NFC driver. The allocation at line 26 uses skb->len - 2 bytes without ensuring it is at least sizeof(struct nfc_evt_transaction) (24 bytes). A remote NFC peer sending an EVT_TRANSACTION event with skb->len = 7 gets a 5-byte allocation, and subsequent writes to transaction->aid (offset 4), transaction->params_len (offset 20), and transaction->params (offset 24, up to 255 bytes) go far out of bounds. The bounds check at line 47 is defeated by an unsigned integer underflow: (skb->len - 2) - sizeof(struct nfc_evt_transaction) wraps to a huge value when skb->len - 2 < 24, so it never rejects. The initial validation at lines 22-24 also uses && where || is required, letting short packets proceed. Result: up to 271 bytes of attacker-controlled kernel heap corruption, exploitable for privilege escalation.

evidence.reason: Root cause: the allocation size skb->len - 2 has no minimum bound check against sizeof(struct nfc_evt_transaction) (24 bytes). With skb->len = 7 from a remote NFC peer, only 5 bytes are allocated while subsequent struct writes reach offsets up to 24 + 255.

Defective guard: when skb->len - 2 < 24, the subtraction (skb->len - 2) - sizeof(struct nfc_evt_transaction) underflows to a huge unsigned value, so params_len (u8, max 255) always passes the check. This is the boundary case the guard was meant to protect.

Sink: writes up to 255 attacker-controlled bytes at struct offset 24 of an allocation that can be as small as 5 bytes (skb->len = 7). With aid_len = 1 and params_len = 255, this writes 255 bytes starting 16 bytes past an 8-byte slab object, causing kernel heap corruption.

assumptions: struct nfc_evt_transaction is assumed packed with layout: u32 aid_len (offset 0), u8 aid[16] (offset 4), u32 params_len (offset 20), u8 params[] (offset 24), giving sizeof = 24 bytes. This is based on the standard kernel definition; if the struct were larger or differently laid out, the overflow magnitude changes but the defect remains.
NFC_MIN_AID_LENGTH is assumed to be 5 (per the ETSI 102 622 comment stating AID length is 5 to 16), making the initial check skb->len < 7.
The skb data and length are assumed to originate from a remote NFC peer across the HCI transport with no prior validation in this file.
limitations: Out-of-bounds reads from skb at lines 40/44/50-51 (reading skb->data[aid_len+2], skb->data[aid_len+3], and memcpy source beyond skb->len) are secondary to the write overflow but also confirmed reachable.

The logic error using && instead of || at lines 22-24 lets both short packets (with correct tag) and wrong-tag packets (with sufficient length) reach the defective code; this is an enabler, not a separate vulnerability.
If skb->len is 0 or 1, skb->len - 2 underflows to ~4 billion, causing devm_kzalloc to fail with -ENOMEM; this path is safe by accident.

verdict.summary: mobi_parse_index_entry walks a raw pointer control_bytes (initialized to buf->data + buf->offset) forward once per tagx->tags[] entry with control_byte == 1, and dereferences it at control_bytes[0] for the first non-control tag. Neither the number of advancing iterations (tagx->tags_count, attacker-controlled TAGX record) nor the pointer itself is ever compared against the buffer allocation or the entry region, so a crafted MOBI file whose TAGX table contains more control tags than bytes remaining after the entry label makes the read land past the end of the heap-allocated record buffer (heap out-of-bounds read).

Instantiated trigger: with a 100-byte record buffer, an IDXT entry at offset 90 of length 5 and a TAGX table of 21 tags where the first 20 have control_byte == 1, control_bytes reaches buf->data + 112 and line 66 reads 12 bytes past the allocation.

Origin of the tainted pointer: control_bytes is captured from the raw record buffer at the post-label position, and the subsequent seek advances only buf->offset, never bounding the separately incremented control_bytes pointer, whose walk length is driven by the attacker-controlled tagx->tags table rather than by tagx->control_byte_count or the entry length.

assumptions: mobi_buffer_setpos, mobi_buffer_get8, mobi_buffer_seek and mobi_buffer_get_varlen enforce buf->offset against buf->maxlen (helpers not shown); all buf reads other than the control_bytes walk are treated as bounded by this.
buf->maxlen (saved as buf_maxlen at line 15) equals the allocated size of buf->data.
indx->entries is allocated with total_entries_count elements and idxt.offsets with entries for curr_number and curr_number + 1 at their parse sites (not shown).
tagx->tags is allocated with tagx->tags_count elements at its parse site (not shown).
INDX_LABEL_SIZEMAX is at least 256 and the label helpers bound their output to the text buffer.
limitations: label_length is reassigned from mobi_getstring_ordt (line 29) or mobi_indx_get_label (line 31) and then used for malloc(label_length + 1) and strncpy reading from the fixed stack buffer text[INDX_LABEL_SIZEMAX] (lines 33, 38); if a helper could return more than sizeof(text)-1 this would be a stack over-read, but that callee behavior cannot be exhibited from this code, so the trigger is speculative (un-instantiated precondition: helper return exceeding the text buffer).

idxt.offsets[curr_number + 1] (line 7) is not validated against the offsets array length in this code; curr_number comes from the internal caller's entry loop, a contract question whose violation cannot be instantiated here.

entry_length = offsets[curr_number+1] - offsets[curr_number] can underflow when offsets decrease, but wrapping the check at line 16 (buf->offset + entry_length) requires SIZE_MAX-scale deltas only reachable on 32-bit size_t targets, which the declared types do not exercise on 64-bit; speculative.

Memory leaks of indx->entries[entry_number].label and .tags on the malloc-failure returns (lines 55, 101, 131) and failure to restore buf->maxlen on error returns (lines 25, 36, 55, 101, 131) are robustness issues confined to the parsing process, not boundary-crossing security impact.

verdict.summary: The GBR brush loader's sanity check only bounds width*height*bytes by 64-bit G_MAXSIZE, but the size is computed in 32-bit unsigned arithmetic ('size = bh.width * bh.height * bh.bytes;'), so attacker header values whose product reaches 2^32 wrap and yield an undersized g_malloc. The undersized buffer is then read out of bounds by gimp_pixel_rgn_set_rect (disclosure into the image) and read/written out of bounds in the bytes==2 conversion loop, giving heap memory corruption from a small malicious brush file.

evidence.snippet:
size = bh.width * bh.height * bh.bytes;
  brush_buf = g_malloc (size);
evidence.reason: Root cause: bh.width/bh.height/bh.bytes are 32-bit fields (byte-swapped with g_ntohl), so the multiplication wraps mod 2^32. Trigger: width=65536, height=32772, bytes=2 gives size=131072 instead of 4295096368; width=262144, height=262144, bytes=1 gives size=0. The wrapped value sizes g_malloc, leaving later accesses out of bounds.

evidence.snippet:
if ((bh.width == 0) || (bh.width > GIMP_MAX_IMAGE_SIZE) ||
      (bh.height == 0) || (bh.height > GIMP_MAX_IMAGE_SIZE) ||
      ((bh.bytes != 1) && (bh.bytes != 2) && (bh.bytes != 4) &&
       (bh.bytes != 18)) ||
      (G_MAXSIZE / bh.width / bh.height / bh.bytes < 1))
evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted, insufficiently validated values: this is the only guard on bh.width/height/bytes, but G_MAXSIZE is 64-bit (the guint32 operands are promoted), so it only rejects products >= 2^64 and lets any product in [2^32, 2^64) through, which then wraps at line 122. Width/height exactly at GIMP_MAX_IMAGE_SIZE also pass the '>' checks.

evidence.snippet: for (i = 0; i < bh.width * bh.height; i++, buf++)
evidence.reason: OOB sink (bytes==2 trigger): the loop bound is the same wrapped 32-bit product (65536*32772 = 2147549184), while brush_buf holds only size = 131072 bytes; from i = 65536 onward '*buf' reads past the allocation.

Heap out-of-bounds WRITE: with brush_buf allocated at the wrapped size 131072, this store at i >= 131072 writes past the buffer for ~2^31 attacker-chosen iterations, corrupting the heap of the GIMP process loading the file.

OOB READ sink (bytes==1 trigger): with width=height=262144 the wrapped size is 0, so g_malloc(0) and read(...,0) both succeed, then this call copies width*height bytes (2^36) out of the 0-byte allocation into the image drawable; the over-read heap contents become visible and saveable image data (disclosure) or crash the process.

assumptions: BrushHeader fields (width, height, bytes, header_size, version, magic_number, spacing) are 32-bit unsigned integers; this is implied by the g_ntohl byte-swaps, the comment 'rearrange the bytes in each unsigned int', and the (unsigned long int) casts in the error message. If they were 64-bit, the wrap at line 122 would not occur.
GIMP_MAX_IMAGE_SIZE is at least 65536 (it is 262144 in GIMP), so header dimensions whose 32-bit product reaches 2^32 pass the limit checks.
The vulnerability manifests on 64-bit (LP64) builds where G_MAXSIZE = 2^64-1; on a 32-bit build G_MAXSIZE = 2^32-1 and the division guard would coincidentally reject wrapping products.
g_malloc/g_new return a valid non-NULL pointer for size 0 and abort the process on allocation failure (standard GLib semantics).
limitations: A version-1 brush with a huge header_size (e.g. 0x7FFFFFFF, so bn_size ~ 2 GB) forces a ~2 GB g_new; on allocation failure GLib aborts the process. Crash DoS from a malicious file, but no memory corruption.
On the 'Unsupported brush depth' error path (reachable with bytes==18 and version 2 with a valid magic), brush_buf and fd are leaked (memory/file-descriptor leak, robustness only).

Line 165 'g_malloc (4 * bh.width * bh.height)' is a second wrap site of the same root cause (e.g. width=height=32768, bytes=1 wraps 4*w*h to 0 and the pattern loop writes OOB immediately), but its trigger additionally requires ~1 GB of brush pixel data in the file; recorded as a manifestation of the primary finding rather than a separate one.

verdict.summary: All pointer dereferences in xfrm_expand_policies are guarded on every path: pols[0] by 'if (*num_pols == 0 || !pols[0])' plus the IS_ERR check, and pols[1] by 'if (pols[1])' plus its IS_ERR check before the xfrm_nr read and before (*num_pols)++. The num_xfrms arithmetic sums two u8 fields into an int, so no overflow is possible regardless of external bounds. The remaining defects (clobbering a live pols[1] if the caller passed *num_pols >= 2, out-of-range loop indices if the caller passed *num_pols beyond the array, negative incoming counts, and num_xfrms exceeding a single policy's template depth for downstream consumers) all require caller-contract states that a network attacker or untrusted-data originator cannot instantiate, since num_pols and the pols array are produced by in-kernel callers and this function's own flow never creates those states. No injection, crypto, authz, or resource-amplification sinks exist in this code.

assumptions: Policy xfrm_nr is bounded by XFRM_MAX_DEPTH at policy insertion in code not shown (net/xfrm/xfrm_user.c copy_templates); within this code xfrm_nr is a u8, so the sum into int num_xfrms cannot overflow regardless.
In-kernel callers invoke this helper with *num_pols set to 0 or 1 and pols sized XFRM_POLICY_ARRAY_SIZE; pols[1] may be uninitialized on entry but is written before any read in this code.
xfrm_policy_lookup_bytype returns NULL, a referenced policy pointer, or ERR_PTR without holding a reference on error, matching the NULL/IS_ERR handling here.
xfrm_pols_put drops exactly npols references, so the error path 'xfrm_pols_put(pols, *num_pols)' with the incoming count of 1 correctly releases only pols[0].
limitations: If a caller ever passed *num_pols >= 2 with a live pols[1], the statement 'pols[1] = xfrm_policy_lookup_bytype(...)' would overwrite a referenced pointer (refcount leak), and on the error path 'xfrm_pols_put(pols, *num_pols)' would then drop the ERR_PTR, causing a crash. This trigger is not instantiable from this code's own flow or by the network attacker model; it is a caller-contract defect only.

If a caller passed *num_pols larger than the pols array, the trailing loop 'for (i = 0; i < *num_pols; i++)' would dereference unvalidated entries; num_pols is kernel-set and never exceeds 2 within this code's own data flow.

A negative incoming *num_pols would skip the loop and return success with a negative count; no statement in this code can produce a negative count (num_xfrms = -1 is a deliberate sentinel for BLOCK policies).

*num_xfrms can reach twice a single policy's template depth when a sub-policy and main policy are combined; consumers of num_xfrms are outside the given code and no sink in this code uses it as an index, size, or copy bound.

verdict.summary: add_mtab writes the attacker-influenced devname and mountpoint strings verbatim into the root-owned /etc/mtab through addmntent without validating or neutralizing record-structuring characters (newline/whitespace). An unprivileged user invoking this privileged helper with a mountpoint containing an embedded newline injects arbitrary forged mtab records, including fake user= entries that can mislead setuid umount authorization and corrupt system mount bookkeeping.

evidence.reason: Attacker-controlled devname and mountpoint (originating from the unprivileged invoker's command line in this setuid-style privileged helper, as evidenced by the in-code signal-protection comment and getusername(uid) for non-root uids) are assigned verbatim into the mntent record with no validation or escaping of newline/whitespace anywhere in the function; this is the origin of the tainted data on the path to the mtab write sink.

Sink: the unvalidated entry is appended to root-owned /etc/mtab (opened at line 50 with setmntent(MOUNTED, "a+")) while the process holds root privileges. glibc's addmntent emits mnt_fsname/mnt_dir verbatim, so a mountpoint such as "/mnt/a\nnone /mnt/secure ext3 rw,user=attacker 0 0" injects a fully attacker-forged record line into the privileged mount table. The minimal fix (reject newline/whitespace in devname/mountpoint before this call) is absent from the code.

assumptions: add_mtab is the mtab-update entry point of a privileged mount helper invoked on behalf of unprivileged users; the code's own statements support this design (setreuid to the effective uid 'prevents unprivileged users from sending signals to this process', getusername(uid) is taken for uid != 0, and toggle_dac_capability elevates DAC rights to write MOUNTED).

glibc's addmntent performs no escaping of mntent fields (it formats "%s %s %s %s %d %d\n" verbatim); neutralization of newlines is the caller's responsibility and is absent here. On libcs that escape fields (e.g., musl) the injection would be blunted.
Newline bytes are legal in filesystem path components, so a mountpoint containing an embedded newline reaches line 59 unchanged after a successful mount.
limitations: If the calloc at line 61 fails, mountent.mnt_opts stays NULL and addmntent at line 86 would dereference it, crashing the privileged process; triggering this requires failure of a small constant-size allocation, which the attacker cannot induce, so it is a robustness bug only.

atexit(unlock_mtab) at line 42 is registered before lock_mtab() at line 43 is known to succeed; if lock_mtab fails, the exit handler remains registered and could remove an mtab lock owned by another process. The implementation of unlock_mtab is not shown, so this race is speculative.
The toggle_dac_capability failure path at lines 38-40 returns without restoring the signal mask (the restore at line 96 is bypassed); no cross-boundary security effect.
A NULL fstype would crash inside addmntent's fprintf; classified as a caller-contract question, not attack data.
The options-string assembly at lines 61-83 is correctly bounded by strlcat with MTAB_OPTIONS_LEN on every path; edge-tested at exactly the limit it truncates cleanly with no overflow.

verdict.summary: In expand_case_fold_string, the character length is computed as len = enclen(reg->enc, p) from the lead byte at p without clamping to the node's end pointer, and len is then used as the copy range in onig_node_str_cat(snode, p, p + len) (and passed to expand_case_fold_string_alt). When the attacker-controlled string node ends with a truncated multibyte lead byte, p + len exceeds sn->end, causing a heap out-of-bounds read of up to mbmax-1 bytes past the string; no statement in the function bounds len by end - p.

evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds read sink: copies len bytes from p with source range [p, p+len) although only end - p bytes are valid. Trigger: string node content ends with a truncated multibyte lead byte (e.g., final byte 0xF0 in UTF-8), so at p = end - 1 the fold lookup returns n = 0 and this copy reads bytes past sn->end. No check anywhere in the function enforces p + len <= end.

Origin of the tainted length: len is derived from the attacker-influenced lead byte at p and is never clamped to the remaining range (end - p) before being used as a memory length; the missing clamp here is the root cause of the out-of-bounds read at line 51.

assumptions: enclen(reg->enc, p) returns the encoding's character length from the lead byte at p without reference to end; this is the standard oniguruma semantics but the helper is not shown in the given code.

ONIGENC_GET_CASE_FOLD_CODES_BY_STR is assumed to be able to return n == 0 (no fold codes) for a truncated multibyte lead byte near end, routing execution into the n == 0 branch containing the onig_node_str_cat sink; the helper is not shown.

Whether the over-read crosses a heap allocation boundary depends on the string node's storage mode (inline node buffer vs heap buffer with capacity tracking), which is internal to code not shown; the logical out-of-bounds access past sn->end is fully instantiated in the given code.

The parser (not shown) is assumed capable of producing string nodes whose end falls mid-character, e.g., via raw byte content in a multibyte encoding; per the analysis rules this cannot be used to dismiss the candidate since the byte range sn->s..sn->end is attacker pattern data at this function's entry.
limitations: alt_num signed overflow is unreachable: n is bounded by the fixed items[ONIGENC_GET_CASE_FOLD_CODES_MAX_NUM] array for built-in encodings and the loop breaks at if (alt_num > THRESHOLD_CASE_FOLD_ALT_FOR_EXPANSION); at most 8 * (MAX_NUM + 1), no wrap.
items array overflow would require a built-in encoding returning n > ONIGENC_GET_CASE_FOLD_CODES_MAX_NUM, which is an internal same-privilege contract violation, not attacker data.
Error paths leak prev_node/snode when goto err is taken (only top_root is freed at err:), but these paths require allocation failure that no attacker can induce; robustness only.

Internals of expand_case_fold_string_alt and expand_case_fold_make_rem_string are not shown; the unclamped len is also passed to the former at line 66, but the n > 0 branch implies the fold lookup parsed the character, so the line 51 sink is the primary confirmed path.
