If a future handshake-layer change allowed 1-RTT read cipher export before client Finished verification, the 'conn.writableBytesLimit = folly::none;' clear would lift anti-amplification protection early; under the current documented contract this path is unreachable.

verdict.summary: send_control_msg copies len bytes of a host-built control message into guest-provided buffers (elem.in_sg/elem.in_num popped from the guest-controlled control virtqueue c_ivq) without verifying that the total guest-declared buffer capacity is at least len. The code itself acknowledges the missing check ('TODO: detect a buffer that's too short, set NEEDS_RESET'). A malicious guest can post a device-writable descriptor shorter than the control message, so the copy at the iov_from_buf call overflows the declared destination in the privileged device-emulation process. Additionally, virtqueue_push reports len bytes written regardless of actual capacity.

evidence.snippet:
/* TODO: detect a buffer that's too short, set NEEDS_RESET */
    iov_from_buf(elem.in_sg, elem.in_num, 0, buf, len);
evidence.reason: Root cause: the copy of len bytes into the guest-supplied scatter/gather list is performed with no check that the sum of elem.in_sg[i].iov_len is >= len; the TODO comment explicitly states this check is unimplemented. Trigger: a malicious guest enables c_ivq and posts a device-writable descriptor of capacity smaller than the control message (e.g., 1 byte vs an 8-byte virtio_console_control event); virtqueue_pop succeeds and iov_from_buf copies len bytes into the undersized guest-declared buffer, an out-of-bounds write in the host-side emulator.

Origin of the attacker-controlled values: vq is vser->c_ivq, populated by the guest driver, so the element's in_sg buffer addresses and lengths returned here are guest-chosen. The guard only tests that the queue is non-empty; it enforces no minimum buffer length, so an undersized or zero-capacity writable descriptor passes through to the unguarded copy at line 15.

assumptions: iov_from_buf's implementation is not shown in the given code; per guard anchoring, any internal clamping it may perform cannot be quoted here and is not treated as an enforcing bound. The only quotable statement about buffer length is the TODO at line 14, which confirms no check exists in this code.

buf and len are host-side values constructed by the device model's control-message send paths (fixed-size events and name announcements); their content is not attacker-controlled, though len determines the overflow magnitude.

virtqueue_pop is assumed to translate guest-physical addresses correctly (memory translation is outside this code) but to enforce no minimum total writable length, which is consistent with the TODO acknowledging short buffers reach this point.
limitations: virtqueue_push(vq, &elem, len) reports len bytes written even when the guest buffer is shorter, confusing only the attacker's own guest driver reading its own memory; this is guest self-harm with no cross-boundary impact and was not counted as a vulnerability.

An element with in_num == 0 results in no bytes being copied under any plausible iovec-copy semantics and only causes the guest-visible byte count mismatch above; not separately exploitable from this code.

If iov_from_buf (helper not shown) internally clamps the copy to the total iovec capacity, the practical impact reduces to a truncated control message affecting only the malicious guest itself; under this framework's guard-anchoring rule that unquotable bound cannot dismiss the unguarded sink, but it lowers confidence in real-world exploitability.

verdict.summary: gf_text_get_utf8_line decodes attacker-controlled file lines into a fixed 1024-byte stack buffer (szLineConv) and scans the caller's lineSize-byte buffer with unbounded indices. In the UTF-16 byte-swap loop, the only exit test is a double-NUL content check with no bound on i against lineSize, so a line that fills the buffer (gf_fgets stores lineSize-1 bytes) drives reads and swap-writes past szLine[lineSize-1], continuing until two adjacent zero stack bytes appear. In the unicode_type<=1 path, the win-CP branch expands one input byte to two output bytes while j is never checked against 1024 or lineSize, overflowing szLineConv (lineSize >= 685) and overflowing the caller's buffer through strcpy for any lineSize. All triggers are instantiated purely from untrusted file content reaching this intake function.

evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds read and write past the caller's szLine buffer: the loop's only termination test is the content check for a double NUL; there is no bound on i against lineSize. With a line filling the buffer (gf_fgets at line 9 stores lineSize-1 bytes plus a terminator at index lineSize-1), for even lineSize the first even index at or past the string end is lineSize itself, so szLine[lineSize] and szLine[lineSize+1] are read and swap-written out of bounds (simulated with lineSize=1024, szLine[0..1022]=0x01, szLine[1023]=0x00, i reaches 1024), and the loop keeps corrupting memory two bytes at a time until a zero pair happens to exist on the stack.

Origin of the attacker-controlled data: the content of the untrusted text file is read into szLine here (up to lineSize-1 bytes), and every defective use below (unbounded j into szLineConv[1024], unbounded i in the swap loop, strcpy of the converted line) is driven by this content.

Sink write with unbounded index: j is incremented for every input byte (plus extra increments in the multi-byte and win-CP branches) and is never compared against 1024 or sizeof(szLineConv) anywhere in the function, so it writes past the 1024-byte stack buffer whenever the converted length exceeds it.

Producing statement for the expansion that breaks the buffer relation: when a high-bit byte is followed by a non-continuation byte, this branch emits one output byte and the fall-through write at line 53 emits a second, so each such input byte advances j by 2 while i advances by 1. Simulated with lineSize=1024 and the line (0xE0 0x41)x511 + 0xE0: len=1023 (line 13) and j reaches 1535, writing szLineConv[1024..1534], 511 bytes past the stack buffer.

Second overflow sink: the converted length j is never related to lineSize before strcpy copies szLineConv into the caller's lineSize-byte buffer. Even a single win-CP expansion on a full line (len=lineSize-1) yields j=lineSize, so strcpy writes lineSize+1 bytes into szLine, a one-plus-byte overflow instantiable for every lineSize; with the expansion pattern it overflows by hundreds of bytes.

assumptions: gf_fgets is assumed to follow the standard fgets contract (read at most lineSize-1 bytes, NUL-terminate, stop at newline); its implementation is not shown. Both primary triggers rely on it filling the buffer with a long attacker line, which is the documented behavior of fgets-style readers.

unicode_type is assumed to be derived from the input file's encoding/BOM detection at call sites not shown; it is treated as an attacker-influenced selector because it encodes a property of the untrusted file.

The canonical caller buffer size (GPAC's GF_TXT_LINE_MAX = 1024, an even value making the swap-loop overrun unconditional) is external knowledge; the code itself imposes no bound on lineSize, which is why the missing j/i bounds are judged as defects of this function as the intake point.
gf_utf8_wcstombs is not shown; its return-value contract (whether it can return exactly 1024 or (u32)-1) cannot be verified from the given code.
limitations: The write szLineConv[i] = 0 at line 79 is a potential off-by-one (i == 1024) or wild write (i == (u32)-1) depending on gf_utf8_wcstombs return semantics that cannot be quoted from the given code; recorded as speculative and not counted in the verdict.
For odd lineSize values, the swap-loop overrun past szLine additionally requires the stack byte just past the buffer to be nonzero; for even lineSize (e.g., 1024) the overrun is unconditional.

The szLineConv[1024] overflow variant (C1) requires the caller to pass lineSize >= 685; this is not provable from the given code alone, but the strcpy overflow of the caller's buffer (lines 56-57) is instantiable for any lineSize with a full line containing one win-CP expansion, so the verdict does not rest on that assumption.
The read szLine[i+1] at line 17 stays in bounds because gf_fgets NUL-terminates the string (fgets contract assumption); it was examined and is not a defect.

verdict.summary: DecodePngV2 leaks the libpng decode state on its DecodeBmp and DecodeAndCropJpeg early-error paths: after png::CommonInitDecode succeeds on attacker-supplied PNG data, the branches at lines 45 and 50 return via OP_REQUIRES(context, false, ...) without calling png::CommonFreeDecode(&decode), even though the sibling early-exit paths do (line 21 for the dimension check, line 56 for allocation failure). Each request carrying a small valid PNG to such an op permanently retains the png_struct/png_info and libpng/zlib internal buffers, so a remote client can grow process memory without bound (memory-exhaustion denial of service). The dimension guards (lines 18-20) and all stride/allocation arithmetic were edge-tested and found sound.

evidence.reason: Missing release of memory on an error path (CWE-401). When op_type_ is "DecodeBmp" or "DecodeAndCropJpeg" and the input is a valid PNG, CommonInitDecode has already succeeded (line 5) and allocate_output succeeded (status.ok()), so the png read state in `decode` is live; these OP_REQUIRES(context, false, ...) statements return from the kernel without any png::CommonFreeDecode(&decode) call. The frees at lines 21 and 56 prove early exits are this function's responsibility. Instantiated trigger: attacker feeds a small valid PNG to a decode_bmp or DecodeAndCropJpeg op in a serving process; each call permanently leaks the libpng state, unbounded across calls (CWE-400).

Origin of the leaked state: on attacker-controlled input this call populates `decode` with the libpng read context (png_struct, png_info, zlib inflate buffers) that the leak candidate abandons at lines 45-53; no release occurs on that path.

assumptions: The internals of png::CommonInitDecode and png::CommonFinishDecode are not shown: their validation of the passed row stride against libpng rowbytes, their handling of interlaced multi-pass reads, and whether CommonFinishDecode frees the context on completion/failure are assumed, not verified.

decode.channels is assumed to be bounded to small values (PNG color types yield 1-4, and channels_ is an op attribute) by code not shown; no bound on it exists in this function, but all uses within this code are mutually consistent.

op_type_ is fixed at kernel construction; reachability of the DecodeBmp/DecodeAndCropJpeg branches assumes a deployment where such an op processes attacker-supplied input (model serving or an untrusted graph), the scenario the code's own comment referencing b/171060723 describes.
limitations: Speculative: if data_type_ were a dtype other than uint8/uint16/float, the else-if chain (lines 59-93) would return an allocated but uninitialized output tensor (potential disclosure); no fourth dtype could be instantiated from the given code.

Speculative: output->tensor<float, 3>() (line 93) on the 4-D DecodeGif-shaped output (line 33) would be a rank mismatch, but DecodeGif's registered output dtype is uint8, so data_type_ == DT_FLOAT with op_type_ == "DecodeGif" could not be instantiated (contract).

Speculative: new uint16[height * width * decode.channels] (line 78) could overflow int only if decode.channels exceeded 4; with the quoted guard total_size < 2^29 the maximum product is 2^31-4, which fits, and no larger channels value is producible from the shown code.

Not provable from the given code: whether CommonInitDecode frees the decode context on its own failure path (the OP_REQUIRES at lines 4-6) and whether CommonFinishDecode frees on success/failure; the leak finding relies only on paths fully inside this function.

Verified safe: the dimension guard (lines 18-20) was edge-tested at 0, negative, exactly 2^27, width*height exactly 2^29, and int-truncation of wide png_uint_32 values, and correctly rejects all of them; all allocation/stride arithmetic using width, height, and decode.channels is internally consistent.

verdict.summary: Stack buffer overflow in gf_text_get_utf8_line: the UTF-8/win-CP conversion loop writes into the fixed 2048-byte stack buffer szLineConv with an unbounded index j. In the non-UTF8 branch each input byte produces two output bytes (line 18 write plus fall-through write at line 53), so j reaches up to 2*(lineSize-1); with a caller lineSize of 2048 and a crafted non-UTF8 line of 2047 high-bit bytes, szLineConv[2048..4094] are overwritten with attacker-influenced data (~2KB stack smash), followed by strcpy of the overlong string. A second confirmed defect: the UTF-16 byte-swap loop has no bound on i and, when the line fills the buffer, reads (and conditionally writes) past szLine at indices lineSize/lineSize+1.

evidence.reason: Sink of the primary overflow: this branch writes szLineConv[j] and increments j, then falls through to line 53 which writes and increments j again, so j advances 2 per input byte. No check anywhere bounds j against the 2048-byte szLineConv; with lineSize=2048 and a 2047-byte non-UTF8 line (e.g. all 0xFF), szLineConv[2048] is written at i=1024 and writes continue to index 4094.

Origin of the tainted data: the attacker-controlled file line (up to lineSize-1 bytes) enters here; strlen at line 13 then sets len up to lineSize-1, and the expansion branch above doubles j per byte, exceeding the fixed 2048-byte destination declared at line 5.

Termination write and copy are equally unguarded: after the loop j can be up to 2*(lineSize-1) (4094 in the simulated trigger), so szLineConv[j]=0 is an out-of-bounds stack write, and strcpy copies the overlong converted string into the caller's lineSize-byte buffer.

Secondary confirmed defect: the loop bound is only a value test on buffer contents, never a bound of i against lineSize. When the UTF-16 line fills the buffer (2047 bytes read, szLine[2047]=0, szLine[2046] nonzero, all earlier even-aligned pairs nonzero, e.g. all 0x41), the swap at i=2046 moves the last byte and i becomes 2048, so line 70 reads szLine[2048]/szLine[2049] out of bounds past the caller's buffer, and lines 71-73 write out of bounds if those bytes are nonzero.

assumptions: gf_fgets is assumed to behave like fgets: read at most lineSize-1 bytes, stop at newline, NUL-terminate; this is what bounds len <= lineSize-1 in the simulation.

lineSize is supplied by callers not shown; the primary overflow requires lineSize >= 1025 (full ~2KB overflow at the natural lineSize=2048 matching the 2048-byte szLineConv). No statement in this code bounds lineSize, and the fixed 2048-byte conversion buffer implies that scale is the intended usage.
unicode_type is assumed to be derived from the file's BOM by the caller; the attacker controls the file content and thus which conversion path runs.
memset at line 8 assumes the caller's buffer is at least lineSize bytes (interface contract).
limitations: Speculative (callee not shown): if gf_utf8_wcstombs (line 78) can return a negative error, the cast to u32 makes i ~4 billion and szLineConv[i]=0 at line 79 writes far out of bounds; if it can return exactly 2048, line 79 is a 1-byte OOB write. Its return-range contract cannot be quoted from the given code, so this candidate was not counted.

Speculative: the extent of the UTF-16 swap-loop walk past szLine (beyond the guaranteed 2-byte OOB read at indices lineSize/lineSize+1) depends on the contents of adjacent stack memory, which the attacker does not directly control.

verdict.summary: This is the hardened form of the AddManySparseToTensorsMap kernel. The historically exploitable heap out-of-bounds write at sparse_handles_t(b) is guarded on every path by 'OP_REQUIRES(context, b > -1 && b < N, ...)' plus 'OP_REQUIRES_OK(context, input_st.IndicesValid());', both edge-correct for b = -1, 0, N-1, N and extreme int64 values. Shape/size consistency (values vs indices rows, shape dims vs indices columns, rank > 1, overflow-checked dim product) is enforced by quoted checks, the gap-fill loop writes only b in [0, N), and all N output entries are written before set_output. Residual issues (int loop counters vs int64 sizes requiring >= 2^31 attacker-supplied entries, int truncation of new_num_elements only affecting framework-side CHECK/abort paths, and O(N) work proportional to the op's own N-element output) are speculative or output-proportional robustness concerns, not instantiated vulnerabilities.

assumptions: The int64 dtypes of sparse_indices and sparse_shape are enforced by the op registration signature outside this code; vec<int64_t>() would otherwise CHECK-fail on mismatch.
MultiplyWithoutOverflow returns the true product when no int64 overflow occurs and a negative sentinel (-1) on overflow; only its sign is consumed here.
sparse::GroupIterable's Group::indices()/values<T>() return the group's row slice, so num_entries equals the group's row count within the validated indices matrix.
SparseTensorsMap::AddSparseTensor stores the tensor and returns a handle without memory-unsafe behavior on valid inputs.
TensorShape/Tensor constructors reject or CHECK-fail on negative or unallocatable dims rather than producing memory-unsafe objects; this absorption happens outside the given code.
limitations: C2 (speculative): 'for (int i = 0; i < num_entries; ++i)' uses an int counter against int64 num_entries; at num_entries >= 2^31 the counter wraps (UB) and would index output_indices_t/output_values_t negatively. Triggering requires the attacker to first supply roughly 8-40 GiB of indices/values tensors (nnz is input-proportional, not amplified), and the practical result is a far-out-of-bounds write that segfaults the same process at 1:1 input scale. No quotable check bounds num_entries below 2^31, but the precondition is a massive attacker-supplied input, so this is recorded as robustness, not an instantiated vulnerability.

C3 (speculative): 'int new_num_elements = 1;' truncates the int64 product, so a dim of exactly -2^32 (or nearby negatives) truncates to 0 and escapes the 'if (new_num_elements < 0)' overflow flag; likewise 'int rank = input_shape->NumElements();' truncates for >= 2^31 dims. The resulting negative dim is consumed only by TensorShape/Tensor constructors whose behavior is outside this code and yields at worst a process abort (crash-only); could not instantiate a memory-unsafe use inside this code.

C4 (resource usage): the gap-fill loop 'for (int64_t b = 0; b < N; ++b)' is bounded only by attacker-declared N and performs one map insertion per missing batch entry; however the op's output tensor itself is N elements ('Tensor sparse_handles(DT_INT64, TensorShape({N}));' must allocate 8*N bytes first), so the work is linear in the requested output and gated by that allocation succeeding - inherent op semantics (one handle per batch entry), not attacker-scalable super-linear amplification.
C5 (contract): dtype and rank/type constraints for the op inputs are enforced by the op registration signature and framework, not by statements in this code.

verdict.summary: adts_decode_extradata is the ADTS muxer's intake point for attacker-controlled AAC extradata, but it uses the return value of ff_copy_pce_data() with no error check: `adts->pce_size = (ff_copy_pce_data(&pb, &gb) + 3) / 8;`. When the attacker-supplied PCE (reached when channel_config == 0) cannot be copied, the int-returning parse helper yields a negative AVERROR value, producing a negative adts->pce_size while the function still sets adts->write_adts = 1 and returns 0 (fail-open). The negative size later reaches length-controlled copies of pce_data during ADTS packet writing, causing a huge-size memcpy / out-of-bounds write and process crash when muxing attacker-supplied media. The only negative checks in the function (`if (ret < 0)` for init_get_bits8 and `if (off < 0)` for avpriv_mpeg4audio_get_config2) gate different calls and never protect line 43; the upstream fix added `if (ret < 0) return ret;` after the ff_copy_pce_data call, which is absent here on every path.

evidence.reason: Unchecked use of a parse helper's return value as a size: ff_copy_pce_data parses the attacker-controlled PCE bits from gb (fed by init_get_bits8 on attacker buf at line 8, positioned at lines 14/27/31/35, gated by `if (!adts->channel_conf)` at line 39) and returns a negative AVERROR code when the copy fails; line 43 consumes it inline with no negative check on any path, storing a negative adts->pce_size (e.g., AVERROR_INVALIDDATA yields (−1094995529+3)/8 = −136874441). The only guards, `if (ret < 0)` (line 9) and `if (off < 0)` (line 12), gate different calls earlier.

Fail-open completion of the failed parse: after storing the negative pce_size, the function enables ADTS writing and returns success (0), so the muxer proceeds with an invalid negative size that later reaches length-controlled copies of pce_data in packet output (negative size converted to a huge size_t), causing an out-of-bounds write / crash when processing attacker-supplied extradata.

assumptions: buf/size carry codec extradata originating from an untrusted media file; this static function's caller passes codecpar extradata, so the content is attacker-data at this intake point.

ff_copy_pce_data (not shown) is an int-returning FFmpeg parse helper that returns a negative AVERROR code when the attacker-controlled PCE cannot be copied into the MAX_PCE_SIZE-bounded PutBitContext; inferred from the int return type and from the negative checks this same function applies to its sibling parse calls (init_get_bits8, avpriv_mpeg4audio_get_config2). This matches the upstream fix that added `if (ret < 0) return ret;` after this call.

Downstream (not shown) adts_write_packet/adts_write_frame_header use adts->pce_size as a copy length (memcpy/avio_write) and test it with a truthiness check, under which a negative value is truthy and converts to a huge size_t.
FFmpeg GetBitContext/PutBitContext framework invariants (input padding, checked reader clipping, put_bits semantics) are not quotable from the given snippet.
MAX_PCE_SIZE and the ADTSContext layout are not shown; pce_data is assumed to be a fixed-size array of MAX_PCE_SIZE bytes as passed to init_put_bits at line 40.
limitations: The rounding in `(ret + 3) / 8` floors instead of ceilings the byte count (upstream later used put_bits_count), which can under-count pce_size by one byte and truncate the copied PCE; it can never over-count, so it is a correctness defect, not a memory-safety issue in this code.
The `adts->objecttype > 3U` check correctly rejects the boundary case m4ac.object_type == 0 (which yields -1 and converts to a large unsigned value); edge-tested and safe.

A direct overflow of pce_data inside ff_copy_pce_data cannot be confirmed from the given snippet because the helper is not shown; PCE field widths bound the copy at roughly 313 bytes and the MAX_PCE_SIZE value is not quotable here.

skip_bits_long(&gb, off) has no in-code bound tying `off` to size*8; safety past the end relies on unquotable framework bitreader behavior, and reads past the end only affect flag/PCE parsing decisions, not memory safety within this code.
pce_size is left untouched when channel_conf != 0; whether it is zero-initialized depends on the caller's allocation (framework), which cannot be quoted from this snippet.

verdict.summary: The allocation size passed to pvPortMalloc, sizeof( Queue_t ) + xQueueSizeInBytes, is computed in size_t with no overflow check. An attacker-controlled queue geometry (e.g., uxQueueLength = 0xFFFFFFFF, uxItemSize = 1) passes both configASSERT checks, including the multiplication-overflow round-trip assert, yet makes the addition wrap to sizeof( Queue_t ) - 1. pvPortMalloc returns a drastically undersized block, pucQueueStorage is computed past the end of that block, and prvInitialiseNewQueue configures the queue to believe gigabytes of storage exist, causing out-of-bounds writes on queue use (heap buffer overflow).

evidence.snippet: pxNewQueue = ( Queue_t * ) pvPortMalloc( sizeof( Queue_t ) + xQueueSizeInBytes ); /*lint !e9087 !e9079 see comment above. */
evidence.reason: Unguarded size_t addition at the allocation-sizing sink: sizeof( Queue_t ) + xQueueSizeInBytes wraps whenever xQueueSizeInBytes > SIZE_MAX - sizeof( Queue_t ). No statement in the function bounds xQueueSizeInBytes against SIZE_MAX - sizeof( Queue_t ); the line-17 assert only validates the multiplication round-trip. Trigger: uxQueueLength = 0xFFFFFFFF, uxItemSize = 1 gives xQueueSizeInBytes = 0xFFFFFFFF, the line-17 assert passes (0xFFFFFFFF / 1 == 0xFFFFFFFF), and the allocation size wraps to sizeof( Queue_t ) - 1 bytes, which pvPortMalloc satisfies, yielding a queue whose storage pointer (pucQueueStorage += sizeof( Queue_t )) lies past the real allocation and whose subsequent item writes overflow the heap.

evidence.snippet: xQueueSizeInBytes = ( size_t ) ( uxQueueLength * uxItemSize ); /*lint !e961 MISRA exception as the casts are only redundant for some ports. */
evidence.reason: Origin of the attacker-controlled size: uxQueueLength and uxItemSize are data-carrying parameters of this public kernel API; their product can legitimately equal values in (SIZE_MAX - sizeof( Queue_t ), SIZE_MAX] without the multiplication itself wrapping, so the round-trip assert at line 17 passes while the value still overflows the addition at the pvPortMalloc sink.

assumptions: configASSERT's definition is not shown; it is assumed to be an active check as written. If it is compiled out (a common production FreeRTOS configuration where the macro expands to nothing), the multiplication-overflow check at line 17 is also a no-op, and the same sink becomes reachable with much smaller values (e.g., uxQueueLength = 0x10000, uxItemSize = 0x10000 wraps the product to 0), reinforcing the finding.
A 32-bit port is assumed (UBaseType_t and size_t both 32-bit), the dominant FreeRTOS target; on a 64-bit port the identical defect exists at the 2^64 scale.

prvInitialiseNewQueue is not shown; it is assumed to store uxQueueLength/uxItemSize and the passed storage pointer into the queue so that item copies on send occur at pucQueueStorage offsets, which is its documented role and the only way the function's outputs are usable.
limitations: uxQueueLength = 0 with asserts disabled is only a semantic error: xQueueSizeInBytes becomes 0, the allocation is exactly sizeof( Queue_t ), and no out-of-bounds access occurs in this code.

The actual out-of-bounds write executes in queue send/receive copy routines outside this snippet; this function's defect is the undersized allocation and the out-of-bounds storage pointer it produces and passes to prvInitialiseNewQueue.

verdict.summary: The dimension-validation block (width/height roundtrip casts, positivity, < 2^27 per dimension, width*height < 2^29) is present, lies on every path before all allocation and stride uses, and is correct at all boundary values: with at most 4 PNG channels, height*width*channels <= (2^29-1)*4 = 2^31-4 fits int, so no allocation-size or stride overflow is reachable. The only unvalidated value, decode.channels, is produced by the not-shown png::CommonInitDecode and is used consistently across the tensor shape, row stride, and buffer count; a harmful value (>= 5 or mismatching the emitted row width) cannot be instantiated from any statement in this code, so that candidate is speculative. OOM from deliberately permitted large dimensions and dtype-contract issues are robustness/contract concerns, not vulnerabilities.

assumptions: png::CommonInitDecode and png::CommonFinishDecode are not shown; it is assumed the former sets decode.width/height/channels from the attacker's PNG (channels 1-4 per PNG color types) and the latter writes decode.height rows of exactly the passed row size into the supplied buffer. These contracts could not be quoted from the given code.

channels_, data_type_, and op_type_ are op attributes fixed at graph-construction time by the operator, not by the party supplying the PNG bytes at inference time; they are treated as internal-trusted configuration.

Op registration outside this code is assumed to constrain DecodePng's dtype to {uint8, uint16, float} and DecodeGif's output to uint8; the DT_FLOAT+DecodeGif combination (output->tensor<float, 3>() on a 4-D tensor) is therefore treated as a contract question.
limitations: decode.channels is consumed with no range check in this code (no quotable guard). If the not-shown CommonInitDecode could be tricked into producing channels >= 5 (int overflow in `new uint16[height * width * decode.channels]` or in the stride `decode.channels * width * sizeof(uint16)`) or a count that underestimates the actual libpng row width, the result would be a heap buffer overflow inside CommonFinishDecode. No statement in the given code produces such a value, so the trigger could not be instantiated (speculative per STEP 4).

Dimensions up to 2^29 pixels are deliberately permitted; a small PNG header can request multi-GB allocations (float output up to ~8 GB plus a ~4 GB uint16 buffer). allocate_output reports OOM via status, but the raw `new uint16[]` in the DT_FLOAT path would abort on allocation failure; since it follows an equal-or-larger successful tensor allocation, this is treated as resource robustness rather than an attacker-instantiated denial of service.

If data_type_ were neither DT_UINT8/DT_UINT16/DT_FLOAT, the allocated output tensor would be returned uninitialized; this is prevented by op-registration constraints outside the given code (contract).

verdict.summary: gopherToHTML writes the line terminator at line[llen + 1] after copying at most TEMP_BUF_SIZE-1 bytes into the fixed-size static buffer declared as LOCAL_ARRAY(char, line, TEMP_BUF_SIZE). llen reaches TEMP_BUF_SIZE-1 both when a gopher response line is exactly at the boundary (the guard 'gopherState->len + llen >= TEMP_BUF_SIZE' passes TEMP_BUF_SIZE-1 through unclamped) and whenever the overflow clamp 'llen = TEMP_BUF_SIZE - gopherState->len - 1' fires (after 'llen += gopherState->len' the value is exactly TEMP_BUF_SIZE-1), so the NUL is written at line[TEMP_BUF_SIZE], one byte past the buffer. A malicious gopher server (network peer of the proxy) triggers this with a single over-long directory line, corrupting memory in the privileged proxy process. Additionally, the host field from the server response is embedded unescaped into client-facing HTML hrefs ('gopher://%s/...' and 'http://%s/...'), enabling HTML/script injection into the page rendered by the requesting client's browser.

verdict.summary: GetDeviceForInput assumes the backing tensor of a LOCAL DT_RESOURCE TensorHandle is a non-empty resource tensor: it retrieves the tensor with only a status check (TF_RETURN_IF_ERROR) and then unconditionally reads element 0 via tensor->flat<ResourceHandle>()(0). An attacker originating tensor data (e.g., an untrusted model/session executed in a shared TensorFlow process) can supply a DT_RESOURCE handle whose tensor has zero elements; the fixed index 0 is then out of bounds, producing a heap out-of-bounds read whose contents (handle.device()) are copied into a string and used in device lookup, causing a crash or potential heap disclosure. No element-count or shape validation exists anywhere on the path.

evidence.reason: Line 14 only checks the retrieval status, not the tensor's shape or element count; line 15 then indexes element 0 of tensor->flat<ResourceHandle>() with no bounds guard. With an attacker-supplied LOCAL handle of dtype DT_RESOURCE whose backing tensor is empty (NumElements() == 0), index 0 is one-past-the-end, yielding a heap out-of-bounds read (CWE-125) caused by unvalidated array index (CWE-129); the OOB ResourceHandle's device string is then copied at line 16 and used at line 20, enabling crash or heap-content exposure.

assumptions: TF_RETURN_IF_ERROR returns the error status and exits the function on failure; otherwise execution continues.

In release builds (NDEBUG), Eigen's operator() bounds assertion inside flat<T>()(0) is compiled out, so the index-0 access on a zero-element tensor is performed without a trap; this matches the upstream TensorFlow fix for this code, which added an explicit NumElements()==0 rejection.
ctx.FindDeviceFromName sets *result to a valid device on OK status and returns an error otherwise (interface contract); no injection sink is reachable from device_name.
tensor_handle is non-NULL per the calling interface (contract, not attack data).
limitations: Line 36, device = absl::get<Device*>(op.Device()), aborts if the op-device variant holds CustomDevice*, but no statement in this code produces that variant and custom-device registration is operator-side, so this trigger is speculative and was not counted.

A dtype mismatch between tensor_handle->dtype and the backing tensor would hit internal CHECKs in flat<T>() (crash only) and requires violating TensorHandle construction invariants (contract), so it was not counted.

A user running this code solely on their own inputs at equal privilege with worst case a crash of that same process would be a robustness issue only; the finding stands because TensorFlow model-serving/session execution makes tensor data cross a trust boundary into the hosting process.

verdict.summary: In the JPEG-LS run-mode decoder, the run length decoded from the untrusted entropy-coded scan (DecodeRun) is used to fill the current line without any check that it does not exceed the remaining line length. The fill loop 'while(run)' only tests run, never length, so a crafted scan with a run longer than m_ulWidth[0] drives lp[cx] past the end of the line buffer and performs repeated out-of-bounds heap writes ('*lp[cx]++ = a[cx] << preshift;'). Length is then driven negative, so the interruption branch and the outer 'while(--length);' continue decoding and writing far beyond the buffer, giving attacker-controlled memory corruption and attacker-scalable amplification.

evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds write sink and missing bound check. The loop condition tests only 'run'; nothing on any path compares run to length or checks length > 0 before the write '*lp[cx]++ = a[cx] << preshift;' (the 'if (length)' check occurs only after this loop, and the comment 'As long as there are pixels on the line.' is not code). When the attacker-encoded run exceeds m_ulWidth[0], lp[cx] advances past the line buffer and each extra iteration writes one element out of bounds; length goes negative, so 'while(--length);' then continues the decode loop ~2^31 more iterations, amplifying the corruption.

Origin of the tainted bound: run is decoded from the attacker-controlled entropy-coded scan bitstream. No statement in this code clamps run to length before it reaches the fill loop, so a crafted scan can supply run > length and trigger the out-of-bounds writes at line 72.

assumptions: DecodeRun is not shown; it is assumed to decode the JPEG-LS run symbol from the bitstream without a clamp visible in this code. Per guard anchoring, any bound it might enforce cannot be quoted and is not relied upon; the missing check at the write sink in this code is the defect.
The line buffers that lp[cx] walk are assumed to hold m_ulWidth[0] samples per component, as implied by 'LONG length = m_ulWidth[0];' (line 33) defining the per-line sample count.
assert() calls (lines 12, 22, 23) are assumed inactive in release builds (NDEBUG), so they are not treated as guards.
limitations: Speculative (trigger not instantiated): if m_ulRemaining[0] is 0 or exceeds INT_MAX when HeightOf() > 0, 'lines' could be 0 or negative and 'while(--lines);' would iterate ~2^31 times; producing that caller state requires scan-setup code not shown, and 'if (lines > 8)' does not catch negative values.

Speculative (trigger not instantiated): arrays line[4], lp[4], a[4]... are indexed by m_ucCount with only 'assert(m_ucCount < 4);' as a guard; a scan header admitting m_ucCount >= 4 would overflow these arrays, but no statement in this code produces such a count.

Speculative (trigger not instantiated): when the DNL path forces lines = 8 (lines 11-14), 'line[cx] = line[cx]->m_pNext;' could walk past a shorter line list and dereference NULL; the line-list length is not visible in this code.

The inner do-while and interruption-branch writes are bounded by 'while(--length);' only when length is non-negative; their corruption role is solely a downstream effect of the primary run-overflow defect.

verdict.summary: FractionalMaxPool's Compute bounds the batch loop by the INPUT batch count (b < input_size[0], line 92) while the output buffer and its Eigen::Map are sized by the OUTPUT batch count (output_size[2]*output_size[1]*output_size[0], lines 67-68), where output_size[0] = floor(input_size[0]/pooling_ratio_[0]) (lines 29-30). The only guard, input_size[i] >= pooling_ratio_[i] (line 19), permits pooling_ratio_[0] > 1, so output_size[0] < input_size[0]) and Eigen::Map::col() performs no bounds checking. out_offset = (b * output_size[1] + hs) * output_size[2] + ws reaches and passes the mapped column count for b >= output_size[0], producing a heap out-of-bounds read-modify-write (lines 114-115) with attacker-scalable extent in a process executing an attacker-supplied model.

evidence.reason: Sink of the out-of-bounds access: out_mat is an Eigen::Map with exactly output_size[2]*output_size[1]*output_size[0] columns (lines 67-68) and Eigen::Map::col() has no bounds check. With the simulated trigger (pooling_ratio=[2,1,1,1], input shape [4,1,1,1]), out_mat has 2 columns but the loop reaches b=2, giving out_offset=(2*1+0)*1+0=2, so this statement reads and writes one or more elements past the heap-allocated output tensor.

Faulty loop bound: the batch loop iterates over the INPUT batch count input_size[0], while the output buffer it indexes through out_offset was allocated and mapped with output_size[0] batches. Whenever output_size[0] < input_size[0] (pooling_ratio_[0] > 1), b exceeds the valid batch range and out_offset passes the mapped column count. No check of b against output_size[0] or of pooling_ratio_[0] == 1 exists anywhere on the path.

Origin of the size divergence: the output batch dimension is computed as floor(input_size[0]/pooling_ratio_[0]). The sole preceding guard (line 19, 'input_size[i] >= pooling_ratio_[i]') passes for pooling_ratio_[0]=2.0 with input_size[0]=4, yielding output_size[0]=2 < input_size[0]=4 and creating the mismatch between the loop bound at line 92 and the allocation at lines 46-50/67-68.

assumptions: GeneratePoolingSequence is not shown; its return value was assumed to be a non-empty sequence of about output_size+1 elements with values within [0, input_size]. This assumption is not needed for the confirmed finding (the out-of-bounds occurs at hs=ws=0 for any non-empty sequence) but bounds candidates 2 and 3 below.

pooling_ratio_, seed_, seed2_, pseudo_random_, overlapping_ are op members populated from GraphDef op attributes; in the untrusted-model threat model the attacker controls them. Their declarations are not part of the given code.

The shape function referenced by the comment at lines 27-28 (core/ops/nn_ops.cc) is not available and, per guard anchoring, was treated as non-existent; notably it would compute the same floor-based output shape and would not prevent the loop-bound overflow.
limitations: Speculative: 'height_cum_seq.size() - 1' / 'width_cum_seq.size() - 1' (lines 94, 102) wrap to SIZE_MAX if GeneratePoolingSequence returned an empty sequence, causing a runaway loop and OOB read at line 96; no statement in this code can produce an empty sequence, so the trigger could not be instantiated.

Speculative: height_start/width_start (lines 96, 106) are not clamped to [0, height_max]/[0, width_max] while the ends are (lines 99, 109); if the unshown helper emitted negative or oversized sequence values, in_offset could go negative or out of range for in_mat. Depends entirely on the helper's behavior.

Not a vulnerability: static_cast<int> of floor(input/ratio) can truncate when pooling_ratio < 1 and dims approach 2^31, but the wrapped value is negative and TensorShape/allocate_output then fails cleanly via OP_REQUIRES_OK.

Not a vulnerability: pooling_ratio_[i] <= 0 with a zero-sized input dimension passes the line-19 guard and can lead to degenerate output_size (0) whose consequences (e.g., division inside GeneratePoolingSequence) occur in the unshown helper; DCHECK_GT at line 31 is a debug-only no-op.

verdict.summary: In the JPEG-LS run-mode path, the pixel fill loop 'while(run) { ... *lp++ = a << preshift; ... run--,length--; }' is bounded only by the attacker-decoded run length and never by the remaining line length 'length'. A crafted entropy-coded stream whose run exceeds the frame width causes a scalable heap out-of-bounds write past 'line->m_pData'; the subsequent 'if (length)' test (nonzero, not positive) then lets the already-negative length continue the outer 'while(++lp,--length)' loop, compounding the overflow.

evidence.reason: Unguarded out-of-bounds write sink: the loop condition tests only 'run', never the remaining pixel count 'length' (which is merely decremented at line 61 and first tested after the loop at line 67, too late, and with a nonzero test that passes for negative values). With run > m_ulWidth[0], *lp++ writes attacker-influenced LONG values past the line buffer allocated for the frame width.

Origin of the tainted count: 'run' is decoded from the attacker-controlled entropy-coded stream (DecodeRun's body is not shown, so no clamping of run to length can be quoted from this code). This unvalidated value directly bounds the fill loop at lines 53-63 with no comparison against 'length' anywhere on the path.

assumptions: DecodeRun's implementation is not shown; any internal clamping of 'run' to the passed 'length' cannot be quoted from the given code and is therefore not treated as a guard (per GUARD ANCHORING).
The line buffer 'line->m_pData' is allocated elsewhere (not shown) with capacity for m_ulWidth[0] samples; the overflow is relative to that width, which the attacker sets in the frame header.
m_ulRemaining[] bookkeeping and the decision to call ParseMCU are maintained by the scan-driver caller (not shown).
limitations: If ParseMCU is invoked with m_ulRemaining[0] == 0 while HeightOf() > 0, 'while(--lines)' wraps negative and 'line = line->m_pNext' walks past the line list (assert(lines > 0) is compiled out under NDEBUG). Trigger requires a caller contract violation, so it is speculative.
The DNL path forces lines = 8 when HeightOf() == 0; whether at least 8 line buffers exist is decided by allocation code not shown.
'a << preshift' can overflow the shift width for large preshift values; this is UB without a demonstrated security consequence.
The 'No error handling here' path when BeginReadMCU fails only skips decoding a truncated MCU; no memory-safety effect is exhibited inside this code.

verdict.summary: No confirmed security vulnerability. All array accesses are properly bounds-checked, the snprintf buffer is correctly sized, NULL checks are present for all pointer dereferences, and the format string is a compile-time constant. The unconditional +1 on argv[arg_start+1] in the else branch is a theoretical concern if the string could be empty, but standard IRC message tokenization does not produce empty arguments.

assumptions: The IRC message parser (not shown) tokenizes message parameters by splitting on spaces and does not produce empty-string arguments from consecutive separators
argv and argv_eol arrays have the same element count (argc), and argv_eol[i] for valid i is non-NULL
IRC messages are bounded in length (512 bytes per RFC 2812), preventing integer overflow in the length calculation
IRC_PROTOCOL_MIN_ARGS(5) macro correctly validates argc >= 5 before proceeding
limitations: The unconditional pointer increment 'argv[arg_start + 1] + 1' (line 24) skips the first character without verifying the string is non-empty. If the IRC parser could produce an empty-string argument (e.g., from consecutive spaces in a malicious server message), this would cause a 1-byte out-of-bounds read past the null terminator. This could not be confirmed as exploitable because the parser's handling of empty tokens is not visible in the given code.
The return value of strdup(pos_realname) is not checked for NULL (allocation failure), but this only results in a NULL realname field, which is handled gracefully by subsequent code.

verdict.summary: No exploitable defect found. All tagstack indexed writes/reads are guarded: the push path first collapses tagstacklen to tagstackidx ('while (tagstackidx < tagstacklen) tagstack_clear_entry(&tagstack[--tagstacklen]);'), keeping tagstackidx within [0, TAGSTACKSIZE-1] at every access; pop/next/prev paths clamp with explicit '< 0' and '>= tagstacklen' checks; matches[cur_match] accesses occur only when num_matches > 0 and after 'if (cur_match >= num_matches) ... cur_match = num_matches - 1'; the prompt selection validates 'i <= 0 || i > num_matches'; the IObuff sprintf/vim_snprintf uses are constant/bounded and fit IOSIZE.

assumptions: TAGSTACKSIZE is a small fixed constant (10 in Vim) and taggy_T entries occupy the w_tagstack array of exactly that size; not shown in the given code.
find_tags() returns num_matches and matches consistent with max_num_matches, and parse_match() fills tagp fields including user_data/user_data_end consistently; both are external helpers not shown.
vim_strsave/vim_strnsave allocate and NUL-terminate correctly; FreeWild frees the matches array; external helpers not shown.
buflist_getfile/buflist_findnr behave per their contracts (may return FAIL/NULL, both handled).
prompt_for_number returns an int within standard range; its interaction with got_int is handled as shown.
limitations: C1 candidate (tagstackidx == -1 via '--tagstackidx' in the full-stack clamp branch) was disproved by simulation: the preceding while-loop collapse makes len==SIZE at the clamp possible only with tagstackidx==SIZE, so the decrement lands on SIZE-1; the pre-collapse loop always runs on the push path.
C3 candidate (cur_match = num_matches - 1 == -1 when num_matches == 0) is unreachable because the enclosing else branch requires num_matches > 0 via the 'if (num_matches <= 0)' check.

C5 (stale curwin after autocommand window switch during jumpto_tag) is at most a robustness/state-consistency concern: the repair 'if (use_tagstack && tagstackidx > curwin->w_tagstacklen)' runs after all indexed writes, and no indexed access occurs afterward in this code.
C4 sprintf into IObuff uses only fixed-width integers and short literals; worst-case length fits IOSIZE. No attacker-controlled length reaches it.

Static mutable state (num_matches, matches) persists across calls; if a caller reentered do_tag concurrently the FreeWild/assign sequence could race, but Vim is single-threaded in this code's execution model; not a trigger here.

verdict.summary: All attacker-data sinks in this LZW decode function are guarded by quotable, edge-correct checks: codes are rejected above the occupied table range, dictionary insertion is skipped when the table is full, and the code width is capped at LZW_CODE_MAX so an out-of-range KwKwK code cannot be read; the output-stack walk strictly decreases and terminates with a write count bounded below the table-scale maximum by the function's own chain invariant. The known defect patterns for this decoder (out-of-bounds dictionary write on a full table; 13-bit code causing an out-of-bounds table read at the full-table boundary) are both closed by the guards at lines 44 and 54. Remaining overflow scenarios depend on state established by lzw__clear_codes and lzw_init, which are not part of the given code, so no trigger could be instantiated here.

assumptions: ctx->table is declared with (1 << LZW_CODE_MAX) entries; the guard 'if (current_entry < (1 << LZW_CODE_MAX))' implies but does not prove this sizing.

ctx->stack_base has capacity of at least (1 << LZW_CODE_MAX) - clear_code bytes, the maximum per-call output length derivable from this code's chain invariant; its actual size is not visible in the given code.
lzw__clear_codes resets current_entry, current_code_size and current_code_size_max, and re-establishes a valid ctx->previous_code; its body is not shown.
lzw_init initializes the root table entries (indices 0..clear_code, plus the clear and EOI slots) and validates initial_code_size so clear_code < (1 << LZW_CODE_MAX).
LZW_CODE_MAX is small enough that (1 << LZW_CODE_MAX) does not overflow uint32_t (upstream value is 12).
lzw__next_code returns LZW_OK only with code_new < (1 << ctx->current_code_size).
limitations: Speculative (stale previous_code after Clear): if lzw__clear_codes resets ctx->current_entry but leaves ctx->previous_code holding a pre-clear code, the first post-clear entry created at lines 44-49 with 'entry->previous_entry = ctx->previous_code' could chain into high pre-clear entries; successive post-clear entries could then compound string lengths to roughly double the stack capacity, or the walk at lines 68-72 could cycle, writing past stack_base without bound. The trigger could not be instantiated because the Clear handling that would or would not reset previous_code is in lzw__clear_codes, which is not part of the given code.

Speculative (out-of-bounds read at line 62): 'ctx->previous_code_first = table[code_new].first_value;' with code_new == (1 << LZW_CODE_MAX) requires ctx->current_code_size > LZW_CODE_MAX so a code equal to the frozen full-table current_entry can be read; this code caps the width ('if (ctx->current_code_size < LZW_CODE_MAX)'), so that state would have to come from lzw_init or lzw__clear_codes, not shown.

Speculative (uninitialized reads): if lzw_init left table entries uninitialized, first-use reads of entry->last_value / entry->previous_entry in the walk at lines 68-73 would be uses of uninitialized memory; root initialization is not shown.
Contract only: a NULL ctx or NULL stack_pos_out would crash the process at the privilege of the party supplying it; classified as interface-contract, not attack data.

The code-width increase check 'if (current_entry == ctx->current_code_size_max)' uses == rather than >=; because current_entry advances in unit steps through every value, == fires correctly each time, and the analysis found no memory-safety consequence — at most a decoding-correctness concern.

verdict.summary: parse_query validates only the QNAME portion of a DNS question record against the packet end (via get_name_len/get_name) and then performs two fixed 2-byte reads (type and class) at p = start + name_part_len without any check that p+4 <= max. An attacker-supplied DNS packet whose question name ends exactly at the packet boundary makes p == max, so pj_memcpy reads up to 4 bytes past the end of the packet buffer; the out-of-bounds bytes are stored in q->type and q->dnsclass and exposed in the parse result, repeatable per query record (qdcount up to 65535).

evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds read sinks: pj_memcpy of 2 bytes into q->type and 2 bytes into q->dnsclass are performed with no comparison of p against max anywhere between the name parse and these reads. When the attacker ends the packet exactly at the end of the QNAME (e.g., root label 0x00 as the final byte), get_name_len succeeds with name_part_len = 1 and p = start + 1 == max, so the first memcpy reads max[0..1] and the second reads max[2..3] — up to 4 bytes past the packet buffer, with the leaked values written into the parsed query structure.

Origin of the tainted pointer: p is advanced past the validated name region using name_part_len from get_name_len, which only certifies the name itself fits within [start, max). At the boundary case where the name consumes the rest of the packet, this assignment yields p == max, and the subsequent unchecked memcpys read beyond the buffer.

assumptions: get_name_len returns PJ_SUCCESS only when the name starting at start fits within max and produces a non-negative name_part_len/name_len; its body is not shown, but the confirmed defect (missing check for the 4 type/class bytes) does not depend on this — it holds even for a perfectly well-formed minimal name.

The packet buffer is allocated to exactly the received packet length by the receiving layer (not shown); if extra slack followed max the reads would stay in-bounds, but no such guarantee is quotable from this code, and max is by definition the end of valid data.

This function is reached from the DNS message parser for network-received packets (e.g., pj_dns_parse_packet iterating over the attacker-controlled qdcount); reachability of parse_query itself is assumed from its role as the query-record intake point.
limitations: Candidate B (get_name_len returning a negative or oversized name_part_len making p wildly invalid) was not instantiated: the callee body is not shown and its failure status is checked at lines 11-12.
Candidate C (pj_pool_alloc failure or name_len+4 overflow) requires environment failure or SIZE_MAX-scale lengths impossible within a packet bounded by max; robustness only.

The crash-only variant (hardened heaps trapping the OOB read) is subsumed by the confirmed read with disclosure potential; impact rating is limited to medium because at most 4 bytes per query record are read past the buffer.

verdict.summary: The Compute method of this op reads the attacker-controlled scalar input num_streams (int64) and passes it completely unvalidated into the QuantileStreamResource constructor and the resource manager. Unlike epsilon, which is explicitly checked ('epsilon > 0'), num_streams has no positivity or upper-bound check anywhere in the function, so negative values (sign-flip to SIZE_MAX-scale when consumed as an unsigned count) or arbitrarily large values (e.g., 2^40, driving unbounded per-stream allocation from a single 8-byte input) are accepted at this public op intake point and persisted into a registered resource, enabling denial of service / resource amplification in any process that exposes this op across a trust boundary.

evidence.snippet:
auto result =
        new QuantileStreamResource(epsilon, max_elements_, num_streams);
evidence.reason: Sink: the attacker-controlled int64 num_streams is passed into the resource constructor with no positivity or upper-bound check anywhere in the function, and the resource is then registered at line 19. Trigger: a client supplies num_streams = -1 or a huge positive value; the epsilon check (epsilon > 0) passes for any normal epsilon, and no statement between line 15 and line 18 inspects num_streams, so the invalid or amplifying count is accepted into the resource.

Taint origin: num_streams is read directly from the op input tensor across the trust boundary; the value is used at line 18 without any validation (contrast the epsilon check at lines 9-11), making this op the unchecked intake point for the stream count.

assumptions: QuantileStreamResource uses num_streams as the number of quantile streams it manages (per its parameter name and signature); the statements that size per-stream storage or loops from this count are in code not shown here.

Input tensor dtype and scalar shape for kEpsilonName/kNumStreamsName are assumed to be enforced by op registration/shape inference in code not shown; scalar<T>() would CHECK-fail on malformed shapes, which cannot be verified from this snippet.
max_elements_ is a kernel member initialized outside this function (constructor/attribute) and its value cannot be inspected here.
CreateResource is assumed to unref/delete result on ALREADY_EXISTS and on failure, as stated in the comment at lines 2-3 and per framework semantics, so no leak is claimed.
limitations: The actual allocation sized by num_streams occurs inside QuantileStreamResource (not shown); the confirmed defect in this code is the missing intake validation, and the downstream amplification could not be simulated statement-by-statement.
epsilon accepts +inf and arbitrarily large values with no upper bound; no security-relevant sink for a large epsilon is reachable in this code, so this is not treated as a finding.
num_streams = 0 is accepted and produces a degenerate resource but no demonstrated crash; the impact cases are negative and huge-positive values.
A memory leak of result on CreateResource failure could not be established because CreateResource's ownership semantics are external to this snippet.

verdict.summary: FreeRTOS xQueueGenericCreate guards both the item-count x item-size multiplication and the sizeof(Queue_t)+storage addition against wrap on the single path before pvPortMalloc ('configASSERT( ( uxItemSize == 0 ) || ( uxQueueLength == ( xQueueSizeInBytes / uxItemSize ) ) );' and 'configASSERT( ( sizeof( Queue_t ) + xQueueSizeInBytes ) > xQueueSizeInBytes );'), rejects uxQueueLength == 0, and NULL-checks the allocation result with a fail-closed return. Edge-value simulation (0, exactly-at-limit, one-past-limit, wrap values such as 0x10000*0x10000 and product 4294967294) shows every out-of-range input is rejected before any sink. No untrusted data is parsed into the parameters within this code, and the only residual concern (checks being configASSERT-based and thus compilable to no-ops, plus a hypothetical cross-privilege caller) cannot be instantiated from the given code.

assumptions: configASSERT is defined by the project configuration (outside this code) and enforces its argument when active; the given code contains the check statements but not the macro definition.
UBaseType_t and size_t widths follow typical FreeRTOS ports (32-bit or 64-bit size_t at least as wide as UBaseType_t); no real port has size_t narrower than UBaseType_t.
pvPortMalloc returns NULL on failure per its documented contract; the quoted 'if( pxNewQueue != NULL )' handles that case.

Callers supply developer-chosen configuration sizes (commonly compile-time constants); no statement in this code ingests external content into uxQueueLength/uxItemSize, so they are classified as contract values rather than attacker-data.
prvInitialiseNewQueue (not shown) initializes the queue consistently with the validated uxQueueLength/uxItemSize.
limitations: Speculative (not a vulnerability in this code): if configASSERT is compiled out (FreeRTOS defines it empty when undefined), 'xQueueSizeInBytes = ( size_t ) ( uxQueueLength * uxItemSize );' can wrap (e.g., 0x10000 x 0x10000 -> 0 on a 32-bit port), producing an undersized pvPortMalloc allocation and a later heap overflow in queue send/receive. Triggering requires both a build configuration not shown and a party at a different privilege invoking this kernel API with those values; neither is instantiated by any statement in the given code. Recommended hardening: replace the configASSERT-based checks with a runtime check that returns NULL.
With assertions disabled, uxQueueLength == 0 creates a zero-capacity queue; downstream handling in prvInitialiseNewQueue is not shown and no memory-safety consequence is demonstrable in this code.
An active configASSERT firing on extreme sizes halts the system; treating that as a cross-privilege denial of service would require an attacker-reachable caller, which is not present here.
ucQueueType flows into prvInitialiseNewQueue and traceQUEUE_CREATE_FAILED, neither of which is shown; no sink exists in this code.

verdict.summary: In the IRC 352 (WHO reply) handler, when the message has exactly 9 arguments and the 9th (argv[8]) is "*", arg_start is set to 9 and line 21 dereferences argv[9] without any check that argc > 9. The only guard on the path, `if (argc > 8)` (line 18), bounds only index 8. argv[9] is one past the last valid argument (the NULL terminator of the split array), so the dereference crashes the client. A malicious IRC server can trigger this with a single crafted 352 message, a remote denial of service across the network trust boundary. The code's own ternary at line 24, `(argc > arg_start) ? argv[arg_start] + 1 : NULL`, proves the state argc == arg_start == 9 is anticipated, yet line 21 dereferences argv[arg_start] before that guard.

evidence.reason: Off-by-one out-of-bounds read / NULL dereference. arg_start is set to 9 based solely on argv[8] == "*" with no validation that argc > 9; the only preceding bound is `if (argc > 8)` (line 18), which guarantees only argv[8]. Trigger: attacker (IRC server) sends a 352 with argc == 9 and argv[8] == "*"; line 18 passes (9 > 8), line 20 sets arg_start = 9, line 21 evaluates argv[9][0] where valid indices are 0..8 — argv[9] is the NULL terminator, so NULL[0] crashes the process (remote DoS). The minimal fix, requiring argc > 9 before selecting index 9, appears nowhere on any path before the sink; the checks at lines 24/25/30/31 execute after the dereference.

assumptions: argv/argv_eol are the argument arrays of the received IRC message built by the protocol dispatcher (not shown); argc is their element count and the arrays are NULL-terminated per the client's string-split convention, so argv[argc] == NULL and the crash at line 21 is a NULL pointer dereference. If the arrays were exactly argc elements with no terminator, line  would instead be a heap out-of-bounds pointer read followed by a wild dereference; the defect at line 21 is unsafe under either construction.
IRC_PROTOCOL_MIN_ARGS(5) is assumed to reject argc < 5; this is immaterial because lines 11-12 enforce argc >= 8 before any argv access in this function.
limitations: Line 30, `pos_hopcount = (argc > arg_start + 1) ? argv[arg_start + 1] + 1 : NULL;`, adds 1 unconditionally; if argv[arg_start+1] could be an empty string, the result would point past its NUL terminator and later be printed as %s at line 99 (out-of-bounds read with disclosure potential). No statement in the given code can be shown to produce an empty argv element (the splitter collapses consecutive separators), so this trigger could not be instantiated from the given code and is recorded as speculative.

Line 42, `length = strlen (argv[4]) + 1 + strlen (argv[5]) + 1;`, could overflow int only for a multi-gigabyte single IRC message, which the IRC line format cannot carry; additionally snprintf at line 46 is bounded by the same length, so no overflow of str_host is producible as written.
The format string at line 83 is a constant literal; attacker data reaches it only as %s arguments, so no format-string injection (CWE-134) exists.

verdict.summary: No security vulnerability is instantiable from the given code. The only memory-copy sink, memcpy(data, ch->sample->data, ch->sample->dataLength), is guarded by construction: the destination is allocated with the identical expression gf_filter_pck_new_alloc(ch->pid, ch->sample->dataLength, &data) and the result is NULL-checked before the copy, so no attacker-controlled sample length can create a size mismatch. Packet loops are bounded (nb_pck=50 per channel, decremented on every send), the channel list count is taken once with no mutation, dep_flags packing and duration multiplication can at worst truncate metadata values with no memory-safety effect, and the remaining potentially harmful paths (NULL read->pid inside the refresh_fragmented block, purge-memory stale offsets, subsample/SAI buffer handling) require states or helper behaviors that no statement in this code instantiates, so they are recorded as speculative limitations rather than vulnerabilities.

assumptions: gf_filter_pck_new_alloc's out-param 'data' is a valid writable buffer of exactly the requested size when the function returns non-NULL (callee contract; the given code checks the return value).
isor_reader_get_sample / isor_reader_release_sample advance ch->sample_num so the stsd-mismatch 'continue' path cannot spin forever (helper behavior not shown in the given code).

gf_filter_pid_get_property and gf_filter_pck_get_data tolerate NULL pid / block-only packets (helper contracts not shown); a NULL read->pid combined with refresh_fragmented under extern_mov was not reachable from the given statements.

ch->sample->data is non-NULL whenever ch->sample->dataLength > 0, per the sample-loading helpers' contracts; the given code contains no statement producing a NULL sample data pointer with positive length.

isoffin_purge_mem only frees memory strictly below its argument offset and reads no attacker-indexed data; its internals are not shown, so the minimum-offset computation here cannot be shown to cause a use-after-free.
limitations: Potential NULL dereference if gf_filter_pid_get_property is called with read->pid==NULL when extern_mov is combined with refresh_fragmented; the state combination and the callee's NULL handling could not be instantiated from the given code (speculative).

dep_flags u8 shift packing truncates if isLeading/dependsOn/dependedOn exceed 2-bit values, and sample_dur *= nb_pack can overflow u32; both only corrupt packet metadata values with no memory-safety or trust-boundary consequence (robustness).
assert(ch->sai_buffer_size) vanishes under NDEBUG, allowing a zero-length PROP_DATA property; harmless metadata only (robustness).

The stsd-mismatch 'continue' path does not decrement nb_pck; termination relies on the release helper advancing sample_num (helper contract), and the work performed is linear in the file's sample count, which is normal demuxing, not attacker-scalable amplification.

verdict.summary: In SampleInterleavedLSScan::ParseMCU, the run-mode fill loop `while(run)` writes samples through `*lp[cx]++` without ever bounding the decoded run against the remaining line length. `run` is decoded from the attacker-controlled entropy-coded bitstream (DecodeRun) and no statement in this code clamps it to `length`; a run exceeding the remaining pixels drives writes past the end of the line buffer (heap out-of-bounds write of attacker-influenced values), makes `length` negative, causes the post-loop `if (length)` zero-test to pass, and leaves the outer `while(--length)` loop unable to terminate, producing scalable heap corruption from a single crafted JPEG-LS scan.

evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted value: `run` is decoded from the attacker-supplied entropy-coded bitstream. `length` is passed as an argument but nothing in this code constrains the returned run to it; any cap inside DecodeRun is code not shown and cannot be treated as a guard.

Unguarded out-of-bounds write sink: the loop is bounded only by `run` and never checks `length > 0`. With width 1 and an attacker-encoded run of 5, writes proceed at offsets 0..4 through `lp[cx]` (line buffer capacity m_ulWidth[0] = 1) — offsets 1..4 are past the buffer end. `length` becomes negative, the subsequent `if (length)` zero-test passes for negative values, and `while(--length)` cannot terminate, so a small crafted input yields unbounded heap corruption. No comparison of run to length exists anywhere in the function.

assumptions: DecodeRun's implementation is not shown; the parameter `length` at line 66 suggests it may be intended to cap the run at the remaining line length, but per guard anchoring an unquotable bound does not exist, and this function is the intake point for the entropy-coded data.

The line buffers (`line[cx]->m_pData`) are allocated by frame/scan setup code not shown; they are assumed to hold exactly m_ulWidth[0] samples per line, which is the natural pairing with `LONG length = m_ulWidth[0];` at line 36.

GetContext, UpdateContext, isRunMode, GolombDecode, InverseErrorMapping, Reconstruct, and Reconstruct's value clamping are not shown; their behavior is assumed per JPEG-LS conventions and none is used to dismiss the primary finding.
limitations: Speculative: `assert(m_ucCount < 4);` (line 26) is the only bound on the component count and is compiled out under NDEBUG; arrays line[4], lp[4], a[4], b[4], c[4], d[4], d1[4], d2[4], d3[4] would be indexed out of bounds if m_ucCount >= 4. The value of m_ucCount is set by scan-header parsing not shown and cannot be instantiated from any statement in this code, so this candidate was not counted.

Potential negative `length` reaching DecodeRun on later outer iterations and the resulting non-termination of `while(--length)` are consequences of the confirmed run-overflow defect, not separate findings.

`UBYTE preshift = m_ucLowBit + FractionalColorBitsOf();` (line 5) can wrap modulo 256 and shift counts >= 32 would be undefined, but the triggering configuration is not producible from statements in this code; robustness concern only.

verdict.summary: In btrfs_rm_device, when the device lookup fails with -ENOENT, the error branch evaluates strcmp(device_path, "missing") without any NULL check on device_path. In the devid-based removal mode (BTRFS_IOC_RM_DEV_V2 with BTRFS_DEVICE_SPEC_BY_ID, where device_path is passed as NULL and devid selects the device), an attacker-supplied nonexistent devid makes btrfs_find_device_by_devspec return ERR_PTR(-ENOENT), and the strcmp dereferences NULL, causing a kernel oops (local denial of service of the entire system). The minimal guard (device_path != NULL before strcmp) is absent from every path in the given code.

evidence.reason: NULL pointer dereference: device_path is dereferenced by strcmp whenever the device lookup returns -ENOENT, with no NULL check anywhere in the function. Trigger: devid-based invocation with device_path == NULL and an attacker-chosen nonexistent devid (line 18 lookup misses), so PTR_ERR(device) == -ENOENT holds and strcmp(NULL, "missing") executes, crashing the kernel.

evidence.snippet:
int btrfs_rm_device(struct btrfs_fs_info *fs_info, const char *device_path,
		    u64 devid)
evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted values: device_path (NULL in the devid-based removal mode) and devid (attacker-controlled u64 selector from the ioctl argument) enter the function here; the devid value determines whether line 18's lookup misses with -ENOENT and reaches the unguarded strcmp on line 22.

assumptions: The ioctl dispatch layer (not shown) passes device_path = NULL when BTRFS_IOC_RM_DEV_V2 uses BTRFS_DEVICE_SPEC_BY_ID, and gates the ioctl on CAP_SYS_ADMIN; this code contains no non-NULL requirement on device_path, so the NULL is a legitimate in-domain value for the devid mode.

btrfs_find_device_by_devspec (helper not shown) returns ERR_PTR(-ENOENT) for a nonzero devid that is not present, per its contract; this code only checks IS_ERR/PTR_ERR and imposes no validation of its own.
btrfs_num_devices and btrfs_check_raid_min_devices internals are not shown; only their signatures are used.
limitations: Candidate: unsigned underflow at line 14 (num_devices - 1 wrapping to U64_MAX if btrfs_num_devices returns 0) is speculative: num_devices is freshly computed from a mounted filesystem and no statement in this code can drive it to 0.

Candidate: underflow of btrfs_super_num_devices(fs_info->super_copy) - 1 in the final update is speculative: it requires the on-disk superblock counter to be 0 for a mounted fs, a state not producible by this code's flow and whose prevention at mount time is not shown.

Candidate: error_undo re-adds device->dev_alloc_list to fs_devices->alloc_list while removal operated on device->fs_devices; for seed devices these differ, but seed devices are read-only (WRITEABLE bit clear) so the branch is not taken and the trigger could not be instantiated.

Candidate: device->name->str dereference in btrfs_scratch_superblocks is guarded by the WRITEABLE device-state bit; missing devices (potentially NULL name) are not writeable, so the trigger could not be instantiated.

Impact of the confirmed NULL dereference is a kernel oops (system-wide DoS) reachable through a privileged ioctl; parties without CAP_SYS_ADMIN cannot trigger it, which constrains the attacker model but not the boundary-crossing crash consequence.

verdict.summary: The batch loop iterates b < input_size[0] (line 85) while the output Eigen map is sized by output_size[2]*output_size[1]*output_size[0] (line 61), where output_size[0] = floor(input_size[0]/pooling_ratio_[0]) (lines 22-23). With an attacker-supplied op attribute pooling_ratio[0] > 1.0 and input batch >= 2, out_offset = (b*output_size[1]+hs)*output_size[2]+ws exceeds the output tensor's column count, so out_mat.col(out_offset) (lines 107-108) performs a heap out-of-bounds read and write with attacker-influenced offset and attacker-controlled data values. No guard exists in this code: the only checks are the 4-D rank check (line 10) and the debug-only DCHECK_GT(output_size[i], 0) (line 24), which passes even in debug for this trigger.

evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted value: output_size[0] is computed from the attacker-controlled op attribute pooling_ratio_[0] with no runtime validation (the only check, DCHECK_GT on the next line, is debug-only and checks positivity only), so output_size[0] < input_size[0] whenever pooling_ratio_[0] > 1.0.

evidence.snippet:
EigenMatrixMap out_mat(output_tensor->flat<T>().data(), output_size[3],
                           output_size[2] * output_size[1] * output_size[0]);
evidence.reason: The output matrix column count (the sink's bound) is derived from output_size[0], i.e., from the shrunken output batch, defining the limit that the batch loop at line 85 violates.

Root cause: the batch loop is bounded by the INPUT batch size (input_size[0]) instead of the OUTPUT batch size (output_size[0]) used to size out_mat; for b >= output_size[0] every out_offset computed at lines 96-97 is out of bounds. No statement in this code bounds b by output_size[0] or validates pooling_ratio_[0].

Sink: unguarded out-of-bounds column index into out_mat. Simulated trigger: pooling_ratio=[2.0,1.44,1.73,1.0], input shape [2,16,16,3] gives out_mat 99 columns, and at b=1, hs=0, ws=0 the value out_offset = (1*11+0)*9+0 = 99 is exactly one-past-the-end, causing a heap OOB read (cwiseMax operand) and OOB write; larger pooling_ratio_[0] pushes writes far past the buffer with attacker-controlled tensor values.

assumptions: pooling_ratio_, overlapping_, pseudo_random_, seed_, seed2_ are op attributes controlled by the author of the graph being executed; this kernel is the intake point for those values, and no validation of pooling_ratio exists in the given code (the comment at lines 20-21 merely references shape logic in core/ops/nn_ops.cc, which is not shown and cannot be relied upon per guard anchoring).

GeneratePoolingSequence is not shown; its documented purpose (non-decreasing cumulative sequence of output_size+1 entries bounded by input_size) is assumed only to instantiate loop execution (sizes >= 2 for valid output_size >= 1); the primary finding does not depend on any contract violation by this helper.
DCHECK_GT (line 24) is a debug-only assertion compiled out in release TensorFlow builds, and even in debug it only checks output_size[i] > 0, which the primary trigger satisfies.
Eigen Map::col() performs no runtime bounds check in release builds (EIGEN_NO_DEBUG), so the out-of-range column access proceeds as a raw memory access.
limitations: Speculative: unsigned underflow of height_cum_seq.size() - 1 (lines 87, 95) if the pooling sequence is empty, reachable when pooling_ratio_[i] < 1 or = 0 makes output_size[i] <= 0 (float division by zero/NaN then static_cast<int> is UB, typically INT_MIN); the trigger additionally depends on GeneratePoolingSequence's unshown behavior for non-positive output_size, so it could not be fully instantiated.

Speculative: height_start/width_start (lines 89, 99) are not clamped, but an OOB read on in_mat.col(in_offset) would require GeneratePoolingSequence to return negative or > input_size values, which contradicts its contract and cannot be produced by statements in this code; height_end/width_end are properly clamped via std::min at lines 92 and 102.

Resource-bound, not primary: signed int overflow in input_size[2]*input_size[1]*input_size[0] (lines 58, 61) and int truncation of dim_size (line 16) require tensors with >= 2^31 elements (multi-GB allocations).
A negative output_size[i] also reaches TensorShape({...}) (line 41); TensorFlow internals (not shown) likely CHECK-crash on negative dims, which terminates only the process without memory corruption.

The local->local dereference is guarded by the checked return of find_site_by_name; a NULL there requires a callee contract violation not producible by this code. If in the deployment context the config file were writable by a less-privileged party, the unsanitized booth_conf->name in the lockfile path at lines 44-45 would become a path-injection concern (no check for '/' or '..' exists).
find_site_by_name's contract is assumed to be: truthy return implies *site was assigned; this code cannot itself produce a nonzero return with local unset.

check_config(type) is assumed to validate the configuration (including local-site selection) sufficiently; its body is not shown, so the compensating role of the gate at lines 36-38 after the deliberately ignored find_myself error cannot be verified.
read_authkey() is opaque here; whether it invokes libgcrypt functions before the gcry_check_version at line 14 cannot be determined from this code.
